0.title: Revelation: The Unveiling of the Victorious Lamb
0.overview:
The message. Revelation shows the church what is really happening in the world. Its first word, apokalypsis, means “unveiling”: not a code for clever readers in the last generation to crack, but a curtain drawn back on what is always true and hidden from ordinary sight. Behind the empire that seems to rule everything stands a throne, and at its centre “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6). Rome asked whether Caesar was lord. Revelation answers, vision after vision, that the slain Lamb is “Lord of lords and King of kings” (17:14), that he is coming again, and that he will make all things new. So it calls a church under pressure to worship, endure and bear witness: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (2:10).

What kind of book it is. Revelation is three kinds of writing at once: an apocalypse, showing earthly events as heaven sees them through symbols, in the manner of Daniel, Ezekiel and Zechariah; prophecy (1:3), God’s word spoken into a real crisis; and a letter (1:4; 22:21) to real congregations, made to be read aloud (1:3). Its images were meant to be heard, felt and answered with worship, not diagrammed. A dragon “with seven heads and ten horns” (12:3) is not a creature to picture but a power to fear: Satan, working in many forms and reaching everywhere.

Background: the writer and the date. The author calls himself simply John, “your brother and partner in the tribulation”, exiled on Patmos, an island south-west of Ephesus, “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9). Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, the earliest witnesses, say he was the apostle John the son of Zebedee. Dionysius of Alexandria doubted it in the third century, because the Greek is so unlike the Gospel’s; but a very different kind of book, written in exile in the idiom of the Hebrew prophets, explains the difference, and the apostle is the more likely author. Irenaeus, who had heard Polycarp, a disciple of John, dates the vision near the end of Domitian’s reign, about AD 95. Some argue for a date before AD 70 under Nero, citing the temple of 11:1–2 and the kings of 17:10; this commentary takes the later date, which the early testimony favours and the churches’ decline suits (2:4; 3:15–17).

The seven churches and their world. John wrote “to the seven churches that are in Asia” (1:4), the Roman province in what is now western Turkey: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, in the order a messenger would reach them along the roads. These cities were proud of their temples to Rome and the emperors; Pergamum was “where Satan’s throne is” (2:13). Honouring the emperor was woven into trade guilds, festivals and the marketplace, and a Christian who held back could lose work, friends and safety. Antipas had been killed (2:13), and Smyrna was warned of prison (2:10). Other churches had grown rich and lukewarm (3:15–17), or were blurring the line through idol feasts and immorality (2:14, 20). The book speaks to churches under pressure and under temptation alike.

Four ways of reading it. Faithful readers understand the book in four main ways; this commentary notes the others at major passages. Preterists, such as R.C. Sproul and Kenneth Gentry in the partial form, see most of it fulfilled in the first century, in Rome and the Jewish War of AD 66–70; they take seriously “the things that must soon take place” (1:1), but struggle to show how it speaks with full force to every age. Historicists, including many Reformers who saw the papacy in the beast, read it as a map of church history. Futurists place most of chapters 4–22 still ahead: historic premillennialists such as George Eldon Ladd and Wayne Grudem expect the church to pass through a final tribulation before Christ reigns on earth for a thousand years; dispensationalists such as John Walvoord and John MacArthur add a rapture before a seven-year tribulation, the most common view in much of American evangelicalism and the sincere reading of many who love Scripture. Idealists see pictures of the conflict between Christ and Satan through the whole age.

This commentary’s reading. This commentary follows the historic Reformed mainstream, amillennial and broadly idealist but anchored in the first century: the book spoke first to seven churches under Rome, then in repeated cycles pictures the conflict of the whole age, ending in Christ’s return. Augustine read it so, as have Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen and G.K. Beale. The seals, trumpets and bowls are not a timetable but parallel series, each running from the cross to the end with rising intensity. The thousand years of chapter 20 are the present age, in which Christ reigns from heaven and Satan is bound, as Jesus bound the strong man (Matthew 12:29), so that he cannot stop the gospel reaching the nations; then come one return, one resurrection and judgment (John 5:28–29), and the new creation. Postmillennial Christians, also with Reformed roots, expect a long gospel age of peace before he returns. Yet the main views agree that Christ has won, the church will endure, and Jesus will return visibly and bodily to make all things new.

How the book makes its case. Chapter 1 shows the risen Christ, “the first and the last” (1:17), among the lampstands, and chapters 2–3 carry his letters to the seven churches, each with a promise for “the one who conquers” (2:7). Chapters 4–5 open heaven: God enthroned as Creator, and the Lamb alone worthy to open the scroll. Then three series of seven show the same age from different angles, each reaching the end: seals (6:1–8:1), trumpets (8:2–11:19) and bowls (chapters 15–16); interludes (chapter 7; 10:1–11:14) show the church sealed and witnessing amid judgment. Chapters 12–14 go behind the scenes: the dragon, thrown down from heaven, makes war on the church through two beasts, the persecuting state and the false prophet who serves it. Chapters 17–18 tell of the fall of Babylon, the city of luxury and seduction, first Rome and then every such world system. In 19:1–20:15 the rider on the white horse defeats the beasts, Satan’s last revolt fails, and the dead are judged. Chapters 21–22 bring the new heaven and new earth, the holy city as a bride, and the tree of life.

Where it leads: to Christ. This is “the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:1). At its heart John is told of “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” who “has conquered”, and turns to see “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (5:5–6). Christ conquers by being slain, and his people conquer the same way, “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11). In him the whole Bible comes home: the exodus plagues return in the trumpets and bowls, the redeemed sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (15:3), and God’s promise to dwell among his people is kept for people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (5:9): “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (21:3). The Bible that began in a garden ends in a garden-city, with the tree of life within reach again (22:2).

For us. Revelation is to be read for comfort and courage, not curiosity; it invites endurance, not date-setting. It tells suffering believers that their tears will be wiped away (21:4), their faithfulness is not wasted, and the powers that seem to rule are already judged. It warns comfortable churches, as it warned Laodicea, that Christ stands at the door and knocks (3:20). It calls us out of the Babylons of our own day: “Come out of her, my people” (18:4). And it joins us to the great multitude who cry, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (7:10). Its last prayer is ours: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (22:20).

1.title: The Son of Man Among the Lampstands
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the book. Before any seal, trumpet or beast appears, John is shown who stands at the centre of everything, and all that follows unfolds under his authority.

The message. The crucified Jesus is alive, he rules, he is coming, and he is among his churches now. Grace and peace come from the eternal God, not from Caesar; the man Rome executed is “the ruler of kings on earth” (v. 5); and the glorified Christ who holds the keys of Death and Hades lays his hand on a fallen servant and says, “Fear not.”

Why it was said. The seven churches of Asia could see the emperor’s temples but not God’s throne. Pressed by emperor worship, idol-feasting guilds and hostile neighbours, some were compromising, some growing cold, one believer had died, and John himself was an exile (see the introduction). They needed to know who was really in charge, and whether he still cared for them.

How the chapter makes its case. The prologue (vv. 1–3) traces the book from God through Jesus Christ to John and the churches, and blesses all who keep it. The greeting (vv. 4–8) comes from Father, Spirit and Son, gives Jesus titles Caesar claimed, breaks into praise to the one who “loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood” (v. 5), announces his visible return, and lets God sign the introduction himself as “the Almighty” (v. 8). Then the vision (vv. 9–20): exiled on Patmos, John sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, drawn from Daniel 7 and 10 and given features that belong to God himself. He falls as though dead and is raised by a touch and a word.

Where it leads. The book’s first vision is not a timetable but a person: Daniel’s Son of Man with the white hair of the Ancient of Days, the high priest tending the lamps, the King whose only weapon is his word. And he is the same Jesus. The one who says “I am the first and the last” (v. 17) also says “I died” (v. 18), and the hand that holds the stars rests on a frightened friend. The keys of death hang at the belt of the man who was crucified.

For us. The first thing Revelation tells any congregation about itself is that Christ walks among the churches. Whoever feels small, pressured or sidelined is shown where the real power lies and whose hand holds the church. Read the rest of the book from here, as John did: low before him, and safe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Revelation is God’s unveiling of Jesus Christ, given to be heard and kept, not decoded. The revelation passes from God to Jesus Christ, to his angel, to John and on to the churches, so nothing here originates with the writer (vv. 1–2). Verse 3 then pronounces the first of the book’s seven blessings, on the one who reads aloud, on those who hear, and on those who keep what is written: the blessing is attached not to understanding the book but to keeping it, because the time is near.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Book to Be Kept

On the chain from God to the churches, and the unveiling, see vv. 1–2; on the blessing for those who keep it, see v. 3.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: One reader stood before a listening house church.

Now: After any chapter of this book, ask whether it left you with an opinion or a resolve.

verseByVerse.quote: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This book is God’s unveiling of Jesus Christ, handed down a sure chain to his servants so that they can see what must soon take place. It is not a code for the clever but a curtain drawn back for frightened churches, and its first subject is Christ himself.

The revelation of Jesus Christ. An unveiling (apokalypsis), the sheet coming off a statue. Revelation is not God encrypting the future for clever readers in the last generation; it is God taking the cloth off the throne room so that a frightened church can see who has been running the world all along. And “of Jesus Christ” is meant both ways: the revelation comes from Jesus, and it is about him. The book has many beasts and many angels, but above everything it unveils him. The first thing God chose to show a frightened church was not a timetable but his Son.

To show to his servants. The servants (douloi, bond-slaves) are all believers, not a spiritual elite; John, who leaned against Jesus at supper, signs himself a slave too. This book is not a document we stand over with a highlighter and a chart, but a word we sit under.

Must soon take place. “Must” (dei) is not blind fate. These things must happen because the Father has decided them, the same word as in “The Son of Man must suffer” (Luke 9:22). The phrase echoes Daniel 2:28, where Daniel saw these things far off; John says they must happen soon. When the horses ride out and the seas turn to blood, nothing will be happening by accident.

Soon. This is the first hard sentence in the book, and smoothing it over would be dishonest: nearly two thousand years have gone by. Three things answer it. First, en tachei can mean “quickly” as well as “soon”, describing speed, not a date; Luke uses it of God, who will give justice speedily (Luke 18:8), in a parable about waiting a long time. Second, the New Testament measures nearness from the cross, not from our diaries: the last days began at Pentecost, and every generation since has lived inside them (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). Third, much of it did happen soon. Within a few years, Christians in the towns it names were losing their trade, their standing and some their lives, exactly as the book said.

By sending his angel. “Made it known” means showed by signs (esēmanen). God speaks in pictures here not to hide the meaning but to drive it home: a Lamb on a throne stays in a frightened mind long after an argument has faded.

Five links in a chain. God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ; Christ sent his angel; the angel brought it to John; John bore witness; the churches heard it read aloud. Like evidence in court, it comes with its chain of custody. The first name on the chain is God, and the last is a congregation crowded into someone’s house.

Who bore witness. Witness is one of the great words of this book. Christ is the faithful witness (v. 5), and believers are killed for their testimony (6:9; 12:11). The Greek martys became our word martyr because so many witnesses paid for what they said, and John is in exile for exactly this (v. 9).

The setting. John wrote from exile on Patmos, most probably about AD 95, to churches pressed by emperor worship, idol-feasting trade guilds and hostile synagogues, some compromising, some growing cold (see the introduction). The book is an apocalypse of symbolic visions like Daniel and Zechariah, a prophecy calling for response (v. 3) and a letter (v. 4). So its images are symbols, not photographs (Christ is not literally a lamb with seven eyes, 5:6), it calls for faithfulness, not speculation, and whatever it means, it must first have made sense to those seven churches.

Who wrote it, and does it matter? The author calls himself John and nothing more, which suggests a man so well known to these churches that he needed no title. From the second century the church identified him as the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, who also wrote the Gospel and the three letters, and their shared language (Word, Lamb, witness, the one who conquers) supports the link; some scholars think of another John, a prophet of the same circle (see the introduction). It matters less than it might seem. The book’s authority rests not on John’s name but on the chain he describes: it is the revelation that God gave to Jesus Christ. Whoever held the pen, the voice is Christ’s.

How should an ordinary Christian read the symbols? With three simple habits. First, look for the book’s own explanation: it often tells you what a symbol means (1:20; 5:6; 17:9, 18). Second, look back to the Old Testament, because nearly every image comes from Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus or the Psalms, and the first readers heard those echoes. Third, ask what the picture does rather than what it would look like in a photograph: a sword from the mouth is not a deformity but a statement that Christ’s word conquers. If a reading needs a newspaper to make sense, or would have meant nothing to a Christian in Smyrna, it has probably gone wrong.

Is this book too frightening or confusing for me? No. It was written for people mostly of little education, many unable to read, to be understood when heard in church. Nobody grasps every detail, but the main message is plain: Christ is alive, he reigns, he sees his churches, he will come, evil will be judged and his people will be with him for ever. Start with chapters 1, 4, 5, 7 and 21 to 22. The frightening parts are warnings and comforts for the church, not threats against the people who belong to the Lamb.

Where Christians differ: how to read Revelation. Preterists see most of the book fulfilled in the first century, in the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70) or the Roman Empire. Historicists read it as a timeline of church history, often identifying the papacy with the beast. Futurists place most of chapters 4–22 in the last years before Christ’s return; dispensationalists among them set it in a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture (Christ first coming unseen to take believers out of the world before the final troubles). Idealists see timeless symbols of the conflict between good and evil. This commentary’s view: the best reading combines the strengths of several, an approach often called modified idealist or eclectic. The book spoke first to first-century churches about real enemies they would face (1:3, 11). Its visions then show, in repeated cycles each arriving at the final judgment (6:12–17; 11:15–18; 14:14–20; 16:17–21), the conflict between Christ and Satan through the whole age between his comings. And it ends with a real, future, visible return of Christ, a final judgment and a new creation. This fits the amillennial reading this commentary follows, in which the thousand years of chapter 20 picture Christ’s present reign through that age, not a future earthly kingdom. It keeps the book speaking to every generation without losing its historical roots or its real future. Many faithful Christians read the book as futurists, some expecting a rapture before a final tribulation; they share the same great hope of Christ’s visible return, and this commentary honours them as brothers.
verseByVerse.note: John wrote on Patmos, probably in the mid 90s AD under the emperor Domitian, though some date it to the late 60s under Nero. “Revelation” translates apokalypsis, an unveiling. The book is full of Old Testament imagery, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah and Zechariah.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses those who hear this book read and keep what it says, because the time for faithfulness is now. The blessing is promised not to those who solve Revelation but to those who keep it.

Blessed. The first of seven blessings in this book (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). The word is makarios, favoured by God, the word of the Beatitudes.

The one who reads aloud. Most early Christians could not read and did not own books; Scripture was read aloud in the gathered church (Luke 4:16; Colossians 4:16; 1 Timothy 4:13). The reader (anaginōskōn) is singular, one voice; those who hear are plural, the room. Picture it: the first day of the week, a room in somebody’s house, one copy of the scroll just arrived by courier. A man stands up with it, and for perhaps an hour and a half nobody moves. Revelation was written to be heard in company, which is why its images hit like hammer blows. If it has felt lifeless on the page, that may be because you are reading silently and alone what was written to be performed aloud.

The words of this prophecy. Revelation claims the authority of the Old Testament prophets (prophēteia), and like Isaiah and Jeremiah it speaks of the future to call people to repent and be faithful now.

Those who hear, and who keep. The blessing falls not on the one who understands but on the one who keeps (tērountes: obeys, holds fast). A man may own every end-times chart ever drawn and miss the blessing, while a widow who could not tell a seal from a trumpet walks straight into it. Revelation is to be kept, like a command, not solved, like a riddle. And keeping is not the price of the blessing: it is pronounced before a single command has been kept.

The time is near. Time here is not clock time but the appointed hour (kairos). A soldier waiting for the order to move does not need to know the minute; he needs to be standing where he was told to stand when it comes. Because the end is near, the response cannot be postponed.

The blessing in his own voice. At the close of the book this blessing returns from Jesus’ own mouth: “And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book” (22:7). The prophecy is about him: “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” (19:10). To keep these words is to keep hold of him, and to be kept by him.

How do you keep a vision? You cannot obey a dragon. But the book answers this itself, and concretely. Keeping Revelation looks like refusing the words that would restore your trading licence (2:13); missing the guild dinner where the meat was offered to an idol, though it costs you the contract (2:14, 20); holding on with little strength left (3:8, 11); staying awake in a church that has drifted off (3:2); worshipping the Lamb and nobody else, whatever the market demands (13:16–17; 14:12). Every one of those can be done this week without owning a single commentary.

In everyday life. When this book last came up in conversation, was the subject a headline, a date, or your own faithfulness? Ask what keeping it would look like this week: a compromise refused, a cold heart warmed, a hard thing held on to.

Do I need to understand Revelation before I can be blessed by it? No, and the verse is built to say so. Understanding matters, and the more you know the Old Testament the more the book will open. But you can receive what it says about Christ, worship and faithfulness on a first hearing, and act on it.

Should our church read Revelation aloud? At least once would be good. It was written for it and takes about an hour and a half. Heard in one sitting, its repeated cycles and great songs of praise (4:8–11; 5:9–14; 7:10–12; 11:15–18; 19:1–8) carry the hearer along, and many who found the book baffling have found it suddenly clear.
verseByVerse.note: The first of seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Greeting to the Seven Churches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What looks like a routine letter opening is a declaration of allegiance: grace and peace come from the eternal God and his Christ, not from Caesar. The blessing comes from the Father who is and was and is to come, from the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness and from Jesus Christ, faithful witness, firstborn of the dead and ruler of kings (vv. 4–5a). Then the greeting breaks off into praise to the one who loves us and has freed us by his blood (vv. 5b–6). Verse 7 announces his public, universal return, and in verse 8 God speaks in his own voice, naming himself the Almighty.
verseByVerse.theology:
Loved, Freed, Made Priests

On the threefold source of grace, see vv. 4–5a; on what Christ has done for us, see vv. 5b–6.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Churches under pressure heard Caesar’s kind of titles given to a crucified man.

Now: Endurance grows from hearing that he loves us now.

verseByVerse.quote: John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace and peace come to the churches from the eternal God, from his Spirit and from Jesus Christ, who already rules the kings of the earth. John’s ordinary letter greeting quietly takes the titles Caesar claimed and gives them to their true owner.

To the seven churches. After the majestic prologue comes the ordinary opening of a letter. Whatever else Revelation is, it is mail, delivered to seven real towns in Asia, the Roman province in the west of modern Turkey. A courier landing at Ephesus would go north to Smyrna and Pergamum, then swing south-east through Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, and John lists them in exactly that order (v. 11): a messenger’s round, not a numerical code.

Seven. Even so, seven runs through this book (seals, trumpets, bowls, blessings, spirits), and in the Bible’s symbolic use of numbers it means fullness. There were more churches in Asia than these (Troas, Colossae, Hierapolis), so the seven are real congregations that also stand for the whole church in every age; each letter says “hear what the Spirit says to the churches”, plural, every time.

Grace and peace. Grace (charis) is God’s undeserved favour, and peace (eirēnē) the reconciliation it brings. A book about to describe seals, trumpets and bowls of wrath opens by wishing the church grace and peace. For the people of the Lamb the first word and the last are grace (22:21).

Him who is and who was and who is to come. Grace and peace come from three sources. The first is God the Father, whose name takes “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14) and stretches it across present, past and future. In Greek the phrase is deliberately ungrammatical: after “from” the words should change their endings, and John leaves them unchanged, as though God’s name stays as it is whatever the grammar requires. And the third part is a surprise: not “who will be” but “who is to come”. God is coming, to judge and to renew (11:17). The emperor’s power was passing; this name was there before Rome and will be there when Rome is a ruin.

The seven spirits. The second source is the Holy Spirit in his sevenfold fullness. Behind the phrase lie the Spirit resting on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2) and Zechariah’s lampstand of seven lamps, which God explains: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:2–6). Later the seven spirits are the seven eyes of the Lamb, sent out into all the earth (5:6). So the greeting comes from all three persons of the Trinity, and the Spirit is named as the one sent into the world where the churches live: by his strength, not their own, they keep what they hear.

The faithful witness. The third source is Jesus Christ, with three titles that echo Psalm 89, which promises David a son who will be firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27, 37). The faithful witness (ho martys ho pistos) told the truth about God before Pilate, and was killed for it (John 18:37; 1 Timothy 6:13). In 2:13 a believer named Antipas, already dead, is given the same title: Christ shares his own name with those who die for him.

The firstborn of the dead. He was not the first person brought back to life; others were raised, only to die again. He is the first to pass through death into a risen life that never ends, and his rising guarantees ours (Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstborn (prōtotokos) also means rank: the heir of a family that will be enormous. Every believer buried since has been buried as his younger brother or sister.

The ruler of kings on earth. Present tense, written by a prisoner of the empire about the man the empire executed: the emperor is already under his authority. The book will show the kings in rebellion (17:2), defeated (19:19), and finally bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (21:24). Faithful witness, firstborn, ruler: prophet, priest and king, in titles of the kind that belonged to Caesar in the public language of the empire. John gives them to their true owner, and the one who holds them has turned his face to his churches with grace and peace.

In everyday life. Whoever holds power over you, an employer, a government, a culture, is under the rule of Jesus Christ. When you are asked to keep quiet about him to keep a contract or a friendship, remember whose title you share: the faithful witness lost everything in Pilate’s court, and now rules the man who sentenced him.

If Jesus rules the kings of the earth now, why does the world look so out of control? Because his reign is real but not yet visible, and works in a way the world does not recognise. He rules as the Lamb who was slain, carrying out his purposes through the very evils that seem to defeat him, as at the cross, where the worst thing human rulers ever did became the salvation of the world. He restrains evil, sets its limits (2:10 gives a persecution ten days) and will judge it fully. The kings do not know they are subjects, but they are; the book’s visions let a struggling church see the throne behind the headlines.

Where Christians differ: who are the seven spirits? Some take them as seven angels, the highest angels standing before God (compare 8:2). Others take them as the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness. This commentary’s view: the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace come only from God, never from angels, and the seven spirits stand within a divine greeting from Father and Son: no angel has ever had grace to give. Revelation’s symbolic numbers make sevenfold a natural way of picturing the one Spirit, perfect and active everywhere (5:6).
verseByVerse.note: The seven churches lay on a circular road in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). “Seven spirits” probably stands for the Holy Spirit in his fullness.

verseByVerse.quote: To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus loves his people now, has freed them from their sins by his blood and has made them a kingdom of priests, so all glory belongs to him for ever. The mere mention of his name turns John’s greeting into worship.

The sentence that breaks. In the middle of a greeting, the mention of Jesus derails John into praise, and he never finishes the sentence. Before Revelation shows a single judgment, it tells the church it is loved.

To him who loves us. The tenses are the whole sermon. “Loves” is present (agapōnti), a love still going on; “has freed” and “made” are past, completed acts. John does not write “him who loved us”, looking back to Calvary as a historical kindness. He writes loves, from a prison island, to people who may be dead within a year. That is the tense that has to hold when a diagnosis comes back, when a congregation shrinks to nine, when the trade guild strikes your name off the list. Not, he loved me once and I must make that last; but, he is loving me now, in this, while this is happening.

Has freed us from our sins by his blood. Loosed, released (lysanti): sin is pictured as a chain, and Christ’s death is the price that broke it. The language comes from the exodus. Israel walked out of slavery because a lamb died and its blood went on the doorframe (the Passover); Christ is the greater Passover lamb, and the slavery he breaks is the guilt of sin, which goes with us wherever we go. What purchased it was not his teaching or his example but his blood (en tō haimati autou), a real death in our place. Penal substitution is assumed here: Christ bore the penalty of our sin, so that the sentence God’s law passed on it was carried out in full on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24), and the song of chapter 5 will say that by his blood he ransomed people for God (5:9). That is why the chain is truly broken. A debt that has been paid cannot be charged again.

A kingdom, priests. The words come from Mount Sinai, where God told a nation of former brick-makers they would be a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9). Now they are said of shopkeepers in Thyatira and slaves in Laodicea, Jew and Gentile together. We are a kingdom (basileian), sharing Christ’s reign (5:10; 20:6), and priests (hiereis), with direct access to God, offering sacrifices of praise and service (1 Peter 2:5; Hebrews 13:15). And it is past tense: the church already is both, now, in its weakness.

Glory and dominion. Glory (doxa) is the splendour due to him; dominion (kratos) is raw ruling power, an imperial word, here assigned for ever to a man the empire flogged and nailed up outside a city wall. Jews reserved such a doxology for God alone; John gives it to Jesus without a pause, because he worships Jesus as God. And “Amen” (so it is, so let it be) was for the whole room to say with him: there is no second name on the list.

What does a priest actually do? Suppose he fits doors for a living. He has access: he walks into God’s presence without an appointment or an intermediary, as no ordinary Israelite could. He carries others in with him: that is intercession, standing at the throne holding somebody else’s name. And he offers sacrifice: praise, a life laid down for others, money that could have been spent elsewhere (Hebrews 13:15–16). A man who prays for his neighbour on the way to work has performed a priestly act, whatever his payslip says.

What it does not mean. Being a kingdom and priests does not mean Christians rule now by political force, or that the church should take over the state. Our reign is shared with the slain Lamb, and it now looks like faithful witness and suffering (v. 9). It will be fully seen in the new creation (22:5).

If every believer is a priest, do we still need pastors? Yes. No Christian needs a human go-between to reach God, and every Christian has a ministry of prayer and service, but not every Christian has the same task. Christ gives pastors and teachers to equip his people (Ephesians 4:11–12), and calls the church to honour its elders (Hebrews 13:17). A pastor is not a priest standing between you and God, but a fellow priest whose work is to open the word and care for the flock, so that all the priests can do their work.

How can I say Christ loves me now when my life is falling apart? Because John said it to people whose lives were falling apart, and he based it on the cross, not on their circumstances. The evidence of his present love is the past act: he has already freed you by his blood, and a love that paid that price will not lose interest halfway (Romans 8:32). His love is not measured by whether this week has gone well. It was proved at Golgotha, and it continues at the right hand of the Father, where he intercedes for you now (Romans 8:34). Feelings rise and fall; the tense of this verse does not.

Where Christians differ: the priesthood of all believers. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that, alongside the shared priesthood of the baptised, there is an ordained ministerial priesthood that offers the sacrifice of the Mass. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never calls church leaders priests in a sacrificial sense. Christ is the one high priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27; 10:12–14), and every believer is a priest with direct access to God through him. Elders and deacons are servants who teach and care, not priests who offer sacrifices.

Textual note. Older manuscripts read “loosed” (lysanti); later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “washed” (lousanti), a difference of one letter in Greek. The older reading is stronger, and both are true in Scripture (7:14 speaks of robes washed in the blood of the Lamb). Similarly, older manuscripts read “a kingdom, priests” and later ones “kings and priests”, with close meaning; and they read “loves” (present) where later ones read “loved” (past).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will return in visible glory, seen by the whole world, including those who pierced him. For those who have rejected him it will be a day of mourning; for his people, the day they have longed for.

The announcement the whole book exists to make. The verse joins Daniel 7:13, one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom, and Zechariah 12:10, Jerusalem looking on the one they pierced and mourning as for an only son. Jesus joined the same two texts (Matthew 24:30), once under oath before the high priest: “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64). The court heard it as blasphemy. This verse declares that it will happen.

He is coming with the clouds. “Behold” (idou) means look! “Is coming” (erchetai) is present tense: so certain that it is as good as under way. Clouds in the Old Testament are the sign of God’s presence: the pillar before Israel (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 19:9). He is arriving as God arrives. And he will come as he left, personally and visibly (Acts 1:9–11).

Every eye will see him. No phrase could be more comprehensive (pas ophthalmos). Whenever somebody announces that the Lord has returned quietly and only the initiated noticed, Jesus has already answered: his coming will be like lightning flashing from east to west (Matthew 24:26–27). Nobody will need to check whether it happened.

Even those who pierced him. A soldier at Golgotha put a spear into the side of a man already dead, to make certain of it (John 19:33–37); to him it was very likely one more day’s work. He will see him again. So will the men who held the hammer, the crowd that chose Barabbas, and all who share their rejection of him. And in Zechariah it is the LORD himself who says, “when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced”. John applies the line to Jesus without explanation, apparently because he sees no difficulty: on that day the whole earth will see that the crucified one was God all along.

All tribes of the earth will wail. To wail is to beat the breast (kopsontai), a funeral’s violent grief. In Zechariah the mourning is repentance; here it seems mainly the grief of the unrepentant facing judgment (Matthew 24:30), though the book also hopes for the nations’ conversion (11:13; 15:4). The face one man has longed for all his life is the face another has spent his life avoiding, and neither will be able to look away.

Even so. Amen. John says yes twice: nai (“even so”) is Greek, and amēn is Hebrew. It will certainly happen.

What it does not mean. This is not a spiritual coming in someone’s heart, nor Christ’s coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 alone. Some do read it that way, taking those who pierced him as the Jewish leaders and the tribes of the earth as the tribes of the land. But “every eye” and “all tribes of the earth” point to the final return, seen by the whole world.

Will people who died long ago see him too? Yes. At his coming all the dead are raised, the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and everyone who has ever lived will stand before him (20:12–13). No one escapes the meeting by dying first. That is sobering for the unbeliever, and glad news for the Christian whose loved ones have died in the Lord: he is bringing them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

Should a Christian be afraid of the second coming? Not with the terror of the unrepentant. For those who belong to him it is the day the bride has been waiting for, and the book ends with the church crying, Come, Lord Jesus (22:20). There is a right seriousness: we will give account (1 John 2:28). But it is the fear of a child who wants to please his father, not of a criminal awaiting sentence. You will be looking on the wounds that saved you.

Where Christians differ: one coming or two? Dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, keeping Israel and the church apart) distinguish a secret rapture, when Christ comes for his church before a seven-year tribulation, from his later visible coming with his church to judge and reign on earth for a thousand years. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches one visible return of Christ. Every eye will see him; there is no secret coming. The gathering of believers to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17) happens at that same public, trumpet-sounding return, which brings the resurrection, the final judgment and the new creation together (Matthew 24:29–31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Revelation itself shows the church on earth through the tribulation, protected but not removed (7:3; 11:1–2; 12:6). Many earnest believers hold the rapture view, and they love the same Lord and long for the same appearing; the difference is about the order of events, not the hope itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, "who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself signs the introduction: he is the beginning and the end of all things, present now, coming, and almighty. Before the visions begin, the churches hear from his own mouth that nothing in them lies outside his rule.

Two brackets around everything. This is one of only two places in Revelation where God the Father clearly speaks in the first person; the other is at the end: “Behold, I am making all things new” (21:5–8). The first says who he is, the second what he will do, and the dragon, the beasts, the martyrs and the burning city all come in between.

I am the Alpha and the Omega. Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω) are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and so hold everything in between: the whole alphabet of history. God is not merely present at the start and waiting at the finish; every letter in between belongs to him. Isaiah heard the same claim: “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6).

Says the Lord God. This is the LORD God (Kyrios ho theos): Israel’s covenant God, of the burning bush and Sinai, who made promises to Abraham and kept them.

Who is and who was. The name returns from verse 4, starting with the present, because that is where a frightened church is standing. God is not chiefly a memory or a hope; he is, in the room where the letter is being read.

The Almighty. Ruler of all (pantokratōr): nine times in Revelation and only once elsewhere in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 6:18), and in the Greek Old Testament the translation of “LORD of hosts”. The churches could see the imperial temple at Pergamum, the magistrate, the empty chair where a brother used to sit. They could not see the throne. So God says it himself: the one who holds all power is not the emperor with his seal ring, and God has not been away.

The Almighty and the Lamb. The book never lets the Almighty stand alone for long. At the centre of the throne stands a Lamb looking as though it had been slain (5:6), and the city’s temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22). That is why Almighty is good news for a church and not only a terror to an empire. Let the seals be opened. He is not braced for what is in them; he wrote them.

In everyday life. Begin prayer with who God is. When life feels out of control, confess that the Almighty is the Alpha and the Omega of your story too: he was there before the trouble began, he will be there when it ends, and he holds every letter in between.

Who speaks here, the Father or the Son? Here it is the Lord God, the Father. But at the end of the book Jesus claims the same title: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last” (22:13; compare 1:17). That is one of the clearest testimonies in Scripture that the Son shares the Father’s deity. Isaiah said there was only one first and last. Revelation gives the title to the Father and to the Son, and does not think it has said two different things.

If God is almighty, why does he let his people suffer? Revelation gives no full answer, but enough to stand on. Nothing happens outside his power. Suffering is allowed for a purpose and within a limit (2:10; 6:11), it refines the church’s faith, and it is never wasted: the martyrs under the altar are told to rest a little longer, and their cries are heard (6:9–11; 8:3–5). Above all, the Almighty answered evil not by staying distant but by sending his Son to suffer it, and he will wipe away every tear himself (21:4). We may not know why this sorrow. We do know who holds it.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “the beginning and the ending” after Alpha and Omega, borrowed from 21:6 and 22:13. The older manuscripts do not have it. The meaning is unchanged.
verseByVerse.note: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.

parallels.desc: I am the first and I am the last

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — The Vision of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a seal is opened or a trumpet blown, John is shown a person, and everything in the remaining chapters happens under his authority. Exiled on Patmos and keeping the Lord’s day, John writes as his readers’ brother and partner in suffering (vv. 9–11). He sees seven golden lampstands and among them one like a son of man, every feature drawn from the Old Testament and several belonging to God himself (vv. 12–16). John falls as though dead, and the hand that holds the stars is laid on him (vv. 17–18). The chapter closes with Christ explaining his own symbols: the churches are lampstands, and their angels are stars in his hand (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man Among the Lampstands

On the priest among the lampstands, see vv. 12–13; on the stars in his hand, vv. 14–16; on the keys of Death and Hades, vv. 17–18.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exile kept the Lord’s day alone on Patmos, and heaven opened (see vv. 9–11).

Now: The one too glorious to look at is the one who says, “Fear not.”

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying, "Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John, exiled for the gospel and sharing his readers’ suffering, was worshipping on the Lord’s day when Christ’s voice commanded him to write to the seven churches. He writes not from above them but from beside them, a partner in the tribulation, the kingdom and the endurance that are in Jesus.

Your brother and partner. He could have written apostle, or the disciple whom Jesus loved. Instead: your brother and partner (synkoinōnos, a fellow sharer). Before he tells them anything new, he tells them he is standing where they are standing.

In the tribulation and the kingdom. In the Greek one “the” ties all three words into a single bundle: the message of the whole book in a phrase. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, persecution; kingdom (basileia) is the reign of Christ; and they come together, not one after the other. A Christian under pressure naturally concludes that it proves God’s absence. John, in more trouble than any of his readers, says the opposite: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33); “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). Neither is only future; John’s readers are already in both.

And the patient endurance. Not resignation or vague cheerfulness but remaining under the weight rather than stepping out from under it (hypomonē). It appears seven times in Revelation, always of the saints (1:9; 2:2, 3, 19; 3:10; 13:10; 14:12). The great Christian virtue in this book is not brilliance or influence. It is still being there.

That are in Jesus. Tribulation, kingdom and endurance are in Jesus, because he had them first. The Christ had to suffer and enter his glory (Luke 24:26); the kingdom is his, and he shares it (1:6); and the endurance is his too: he calls it “my word about patient endurance” (3:10). A believer under pressure is walking in the footprints of his King, and those footprints lead out of the grave.

On the island called Patmos on account of the word of God. Patmos is a small, bare island in the Aegean, some 60 miles (100 kilometres) from Ephesus, the kind Rome used for banishment. Early church writers (Irenaeus, Eusebius) say John was exiled there under Domitian and released after Domitian’s death in AD 96. “On account of” (dia) means because of: he was sent there for his preaching. It looked like the end of a ministry, and it was the beginning of the church’s most extraordinary book.

In the Spirit on the Lord’s day. “In the Spirit” (en pneumati) is a state in which the Holy Spirit gave him prophetic vision, as with Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:12–14); the phrase marks the major sections of the book (4:2; 17:3; 21:10). “The Lord’s day” (tē kyriakē hēmera) is Sunday, when Christians met because Christ rose on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2); the Didache, an early Christian manual, uses the same term. The adjective was also used of things belonging to the emperor. Christians claimed the day for their true Lord.

A loud voice like a trumpet. The trumpet (salpingos) recalls Sinai, where God spoke with a trumpet blast so loud that the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). The voice comes from behind him, as it did for Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:12), and it will turn out to be Christ’s own.

Write what you see in a book. The vision is not given to John to keep; at once he is told to pass it on. And it is one scroll (biblion) for all seven: each church would hear all the letters, and the whole book.

Keeping Sunday on a rock. As far as we know there was no congregation on Patmos, nobody to break bread with. And an old man keeps the Lord’s day anyway, alone, because the Lord rose whether anyone else on the island cares or not. That is where heaven finds him. Rome had shrunk John’s world to thirteen square miles, and the risen Christ used the exile to give the whole church the vision of his throne. No island is so bare that the trumpet cannot sound behind it.

What if the church is losing its place? Many Christians in the West feel something of Patmos now: the church that once helped set the tone of public life is often ignored or faintly embarrassing. The easy responses are to fight to win the old place back, as though the kingdom advanced by influence, or to blend in until there is nothing left to object to. John does neither. On the edge of the empire, with no influence at all, he calls himself a partner in the kingdom. The sociologist Rodney Stark, in The Rise of Christianity, estimated that the church grew by something like 40 per cent a decade through its first three centuries, mostly without power, through ordinary believers who cared for their neighbours and would not stop worshipping Jesus. Its King won his throne by losing everything on a cross, and his people share his kingdom not by grasping for the centre but by enduring faithfully at the edges, where he so often meets them.

How do I endure? Not by gritting your teeth, and not alone: endurance is found “in Jesus”. Take one day at a time (Matthew 6:34). Keep the Lord’s day with God’s people, even in weeks you feel nothing. Say it to God: the psalms of lament let endurance be honest, not stoical. Look at the end: the one coming with the clouds (v. 7) has the last word over whatever is pressing on you. And remember who endured first: Christ stayed under the whole weight of the cross for you, and now calls your endurance his own (3:10). As Timothy Keller often pointed out, in Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, God does not promise to keep his people out of the furnace but to be with them in it, as the fourth figure walked in the flames beside the three young men (Daniel 3:25; Isaiah 43:2).

What it does not mean. Being in the Spirit is not a technique for producing visions. John’s experience was a unique prophetic revelation, given to write Scripture, and now we meet the Spirit’s voice in what he wrote (22:18–19). Nor should it make an ordinary Christian feel second-rate. John was not meditating his way upward; he was keeping Sunday, and the trumpet sounded behind him. Flat prayer and a psalm sung badly are not a lower grade of the same thing. It is the same Spirit.

If I suffer for my faith, has something gone wrong? No. John puts suffering inside the Christian life. If you are mocked, passed over or cut off by family because you follow Christ, you have not left the kingdom; you are sharing what Jesus promised (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). Not every hardship is persecution, and some of our pain is our own fault. But pressure that comes because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus is a mark of belonging, not of abandonment, and calls for endurance, not panic.

How should I keep the Lord’s day? As the day of resurrection, centred on gathering with God’s people to worship, hear the word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper. Christians differ over how strictly Sabbath rest applies (see the box below), but the day is a gift to be received, not a gap to be filled: rest from ordinary work where you can, make room for fellowship, mercy and quiet. If, like John, you are cut off from church by illness, work or distance, keep it anyway. The Lord is risen on Patmos too.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s day Sunday or the day of the Lord? Some take it that John was transported in vision to the future Day of the Lord, the day of judgment. Others hold that Christians should keep Saturday, and that the Lord’s day is the Jewish Sabbath. This commentary’s view: the Lord’s day is Sunday. The Old Testament Day of the Lord is always expressed differently (hēmera kyriou), and early Christian usage of John’s phrase clearly means the first day of the week. The Sabbath command is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), and the Lord’s day is not a burden of rules but the privilege of gathering on the day of resurrection to worship, rest and hear God’s word. Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath command carries over to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), and their view deserves real respect. But Christians set the day apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add in v. 11 the words “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last” and “which are in Asia”. They are absent from the older manuscripts.
verseByVerse.note: Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean, about 40 miles off the coast of Asia. “The Lord’s day” is Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John turns and sees the churches as golden lampstands, with Christ standing among them as priest and king. The first thing the vision shows about the church is who is in the middle of it.

Then I turned to see the voice. You do not see a voice, but this one is so evidently somebody’s that John turns to it as you would turn towards a shout in an empty house.

Seven golden lampstands. What he sees first is the furniture. In the tabernacle a seven-branched lampstand of pure gold burned continually in the holy place (Exodus 25:31–40; Zechariah 4:2–6). Here there are seven separate lampstands (lychnias), the seven churches (v. 20): the one lampstand of Israel has become many, set out along the road. The holy place is no longer a room in Jerusalem but a house in a Roman market town, and the lamp is lit there.

Golden. Small, struggling congregations, some compromised and one nearly dead, are in God’s sight precious metal. The world saw a few dozen tradesmen meeting in a house. Christ sees gold.

A lampstand makes no light. The stand holds the lamp up so the room can see, and it is judged solely by whether the light is high enough to be useful (Matthew 5:14–16). The church holds up the light of Christ. A congregation that is impressive at everything except that has forgotten what it is for.

In the midst of the lampstands. Not inspecting from a height or far away in heaven, but in the middle of them (en mesō), close enough to touch the gold. He walks among his churches (2:1), present to strengthen and to correct.

One like a son of man. The phrase (huion anthrōpou) comes from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man receives from the Ancient of Days a dominion that will never pass away. It was Jesus’ favourite title for himself, and it says two things: on the surface simply “a human being”; underneath, Daniel’s figure whom all peoples serve. He is truly human, and more than human.

A long robe and a golden sash. The long robe (podērēs) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the high priest’s garment (Exodus 28:4), and a golden sash was priestly dress (compare Daniel 10:5). Christ appears as the great high priest, and also as a king. The sash is worn high across the chest, as by one who presides, not one who labours: the sacrifice is finished.

The priest at the lamps. What remains is tending the lamps. Morning and evening a priest trimmed the wicks and topped up the oil so that the flame never went out (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:1–4). That is the place the glorified Christ has taken among his churches, and the letters that follow are his tending of them (2:5). The one with a face like the sun is first of all a lamp-tender.

Is Christ really present in my small, ordinary church? Yes; that is exactly what this vision says. Think of the wet evening when eleven people came, the singing was thin and nobody could think of anything to say afterwards. He was standing in the middle of that room, not disappointed at a distance, but keeping alight a wick anybody else would have written off. He promised it where two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). His presence is not measured by the size of the room or the quality of the music.

Is this vision about churches, or about me personally? Both, but in that order. The lampstands are congregations: Revelation does not imagine a Christian alone with a private faith, but believers held together in local churches, where Christ chooses to be found. He is with each believer always (Matthew 28:20), but if you have drifted from church, see where John sees him standing: among the lampstands.

verseByVerse.quote: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every feature of the risen Christ shows that he shares the majesty of God, and each tells a hard-pressed church something it needs to survive the week. Nearly every detail comes from Daniel 7 and 10 and Ezekiel 1 and 43, and features that belong to the Ancient of Days, God himself, are given to the Son of Man.

White, like white wool, like snow. In Daniel 7 the Ancient of Days has clothing white as snow and hair like pure wool (Daniel 7:9), and the son of man is brought before him. John gives the Son of Man the white hair of the Ancient of Days, without argument. It is the white not of decline but of eternity, wisdom and purity: Christ shares the eternal majesty of God, because he is God the Son (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9).

Eyes like a flame of fire. From Daniel 10:6 (phlox pyros): fire illuminates and consumes, and nothing hides from it. In the letters that follow, this Christ will tell churches what they had managed not to know about themselves: Sardis thinks it is alive, Laodicea thinks it is rich. To Thyatira he introduces himself as the one who searches mind and heart (2:18, 23). To a believer keeping faith where nobody notices, it means nothing done in obscurity has gone unrecorded. To anyone keeping up a respectable front over something rotten, it means the front has never worked for a moment.

Feet like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace. A glowing metal (Daniel 10:6; Ezekiel 1:7; on the word, see below), bronze that has already been through the fire. Any reader who knows Daniel will remember three young men in a furnace and a fourth figure walking in the flames with them, unbound and unburnt (Daniel 3:25). These feet stand firm, unlike the feet of iron and clay on the statue of earthly empires (Daniel 2). Feet also trample, as Christ will tread the winepress of God’s wrath (14:20; 19:15).

The roar of many waters. Ezekiel heard this sound when the glory of God returned to the temple: the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters (Ezekiel 43:2). Stand at the foot of a waterfall in spate and every other sound is simply taken away. That is the volume at which this Christ speaks over the empire, the accuser, and the voice in a believer’s head at three in the morning.

In his right hand he held seven stars. The right hand is the hand of power and possession, and the stars, the angels of the churches (v. 20), are held in it. The churches are in his power, and no one will snatch them out (John 10:28). Domitian issued a coin showing his dead infant son as a god among seven stars. John has seen whose hand really holds the stars.

From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword. Not in his hand; from his mouth. The weapon of this King is speech (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 11:4): “He made my mouth like a sharp sword” (Isaiah 49:2), and at the end he defeats his enemies with this sword alone (19:15, 21). The Roman governor had the right of the sword, the power to execute; Christ’s word is greater. The church has been given no other weapon, and needs none: the word, spoken by people with no power, has outlived empire after empire that banned it.

His face was like the sun. John had seen his face shine like this once before, briefly, at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:2). Now this is simply what his face is like. It is the last detail because nothing can be added after it. He is the light the lampstands were made to carry, shining at full strength in a province that thought it had put the gospel out.

The friend of sinners, the Lord of glory. The hair of the Ancient of Days is on the head of the man from Nazareth; the eyes that wept at Lazarus’s tomb blaze through every disguise; the feet that were nailed are bronze from the furnace; the voice that told a dead girl to arise is louder than the sea. He holds the churches in his hand, he conquers by his word, and his face is the sun. This is who walks among the lampstands, and he is ours.

Is this the same Jesus who took children in his arms? Yes, entirely. This vision shows what was always true of the Jesus who welcomed children and wept at a grave. His tenderness was never weakness, but the kindness of the Lord of glory stooping; his glory is never cruelty, but the strength of the friend of sinners. Know only the gentle Jesus, and he is too small to trust in a crisis; know only the blazing one, and you will be afraid to come near. The next verses put the two together: the same right hand holds the stars and rests on John’s shoulder.

Why should the eyes of fire comfort me rather than frighten me? Because they see what no one else sees: the faithfulness nobody thanks, the temptation resisted in private, the injustice no court will examine. They also see your sin, to bring you to repentance, not despair, because they belong to the one who died for the sins they see. For a believer, the gaze of Christ is the safest place to be known completely, because it is also where you are loved completely.

Uncertain wording. “Burnished bronze” translates chalkolibanon, found only here and in 2:18 in surviving Greek, so its exact meaning is unknown. It was probably a fine, polished bronze or bronze alloy, perhaps a local product of Thyatira, a city of metal-working trades, to which Christ introduces himself with these feet (2:18). The picture is clear even where the word is not: metal glowing from the furnace.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glorified Christ lifts his fallen servant with a touch and a word: he is God, he died and lives for ever, and he holds authority over death itself. The awe remains; the terror is taken away.

I fell at his feet as though dead. This is the man who leaned back against Jesus at supper (John 13:25). Some sixty years later he sees the same person, and his body simply stops holding him up. Isaiah said, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5); Ezekiel fell on his face (Ezekiel 1:28); Peter said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). Nobody in Scripture who truly sees the glory of God finds it comfortable. Holy fear is not a lack of faith but a true sight of who he is.

He laid his right hand on me. That is the hand of verse 16, holding the seven stars. He does not put them down to reach for John: the hand that governs the churches steadies one frightened man on the floor, as in Daniel 10:10, and as Jesus touched the frightened disciples on the mountain (Matthew 17:7).

Fear not. Stop being afraid (mē phobou), the words he used to frightened disciples on the lake. The voice like many waters says the gentlest thing in the vocabulary, and the comfort does not come by making the glory smaller: John is not told that he over-reacted. Christ comforts him where he lies.

I am the first and the last. In Isaiah this is how God distinguishes himself from every rival: “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6; 48:12). Jesus takes it unchanged, as the Father took Alpha and Omega in verse 8: not a lesser god, but the one God, with the Father. And then he adds something Isaiah could not have said.

And the living one. Ho zōn. God is the living God, in contrast to dead idols, and Christ has life in himself (John 5:26), not on loan as we do. He is its source.

I died, and behold I am alive forevermore. No other being can put those two clauses side by side. He says I am the living one, and then: I died, literally I became dead (egenomēn nekros), a real death outside a city wall, with a spear to prove it. Life itself went into the grave and came out, not restored to a life that could be lost again, as Lazarus was, but alive into the ages of the ages. Death can never touch him again (Romans 6:9).

The keys of Death and Hades. Keys (kleis) are authority: whoever holds them decides who goes in and who comes out. Death is the event and Hades the realm of the dead (the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Sheol): the dying and the being dead, which every human being fears in different ways. Later Jewish teachers, in the Talmud, said that the key to raising the dead is one God never hands to anyone else. Both hang from Christ’s belt, won as the only man who has gone into death and walked out under his own power. He will open the graves at the resurrection (20:13), and in the end Death and Hades themselves will be thrown into the lake of fire (20:14).

A locked room with the key in a loving hand. A grave is not a locked room with the key lost. Somebody has the key, and he loves the person inside. For anyone who has stood at a graveside in the rain, that is not a kind thought laid over a hard fact; it is itself the solid fact. The one holding the keys wept at a tomb before he opened it (John 11:35, 43–44). And the fear of our own dying is not answered by being told that death is small, but by the keys, and by whose hand they are in.

Near this Christ, or near a picture of him? If a congregation always leaves a service pleasantly warmed and never once leaves it undone, has it been near this Christ, or near a picture of him scaled down to a size that would not disturb anybody? The answer is not to manufacture fear. It is to preach and sing the Christ of the Bible at his true size, and let him do the rest.

What it does not mean. The keys of Hades do not mean Christ went to hell to suffer further after his death; his suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). They mean authority over death, won by his death and resurrection. Nor does this support the idea of a second chance after death; the Bible gives none (Hebrews 9:27).

In everyday life. If you are sitting with someone who is dying, read them these two verses. And if you are afraid, do what John did: stay low before him, and let him put his hand on you.

Does “Fear not” mean I should never fear God? It means you need never fear being destroyed by him if you belong to Christ. Scripture still calls believers to fear the Lord (Proverbs 9:10; 1 Peter 1:17), and that is not the opposite of this verse but its other half. The fear of the Lord is reverent awe: taking him seriously, trembling at his word, not daring to treat him lightly. What Christ removes is the terror of condemnation (1 John 4:18). John stays on his face, and he stays unafraid. That is the posture of a Christian before Christ: low, and safe.

What happens to a believer who dies? He goes to be with Christ at once. The soul does not sleep; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), and the martyrs in this book are awake before the throne (6:9–11). There is no purgatory, because Christ’s blood has already freed us from our sins (1:5). The body rests until the resurrection, when he will use the keys and raise it, glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 52). The grave is real, but temporary, and the one who holds the key is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ commissions John to write the whole vision, and explains that the lampstands are his churches and the stars their angels, held in his right hand. The book’s first symbols are explained by Christ himself, and that shows how to read the rest.

Write therefore. Christ repeats the command of verse 11, and “therefore” (oun) ties it to what has just happened: because Christ has conquered death and holds its keys, John is to write without fear. The man who was lying on the floor is put back on his feet and handed a pen.

After this. “After this” (meta tauta) echoes Daniel 2:29 and 45. Many read the verse as a three-part outline: what John has seen (chapter 1), what is (chapters 2–3) and what will be after this (chapters 4–22), and 4:1 does open with almost the same words (see the boxes below).

As for the mystery. Christ explains his own symbols, and his method matters more than the explanation: each picture stands for a real thing, and the reader has just been given a rule for the rest of the book by its author. Mystērion in the New Testament is never an unsolvable riddle but something hidden and now told (Ephesians 3:3–5).

The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. Angels (angeloi) can also mean messengers, and each of the seven letters is addressed to the angel of that church (2:1 and the others; on who they are, see below).

The seven lampstands are the seven churches. Christ calls the church to shine for him in the darkness. The lamp is his to light, and his to take away.

Held and surrounded. The stars are in his right hand; the lampstands are around him. Whatever pressure comes in the next twenty-one chapters will arrive at churches already held and surrounded. That is why the letters can be so searching: he can afford to tell Ephesus the truth, because he is not going to lose it.

A star and a lamp. He takes a star and a lamp, the brightest thing in the night sky and the humblest thing in the house, and says to his churches: this is you. The one who died and holds the keys counts a few struggling congregations as stars worth holding, and the light they carry is his own.

What it does not mean. The seven churches are not seven ages of church history, as some have taught (Ephesus the apostolic age, Laodicea the last days). Nothing in the text suggests it, and every church in every age needs all seven letters.

Does my church have its own angel? Possibly, though we should hold it lightly. Angels are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and this verse most naturally pictures an angel connected with each church. But the Bible never invites us to identify, address or pray to such angels, and it forbids worshipping them (19:10; Colossians 2:18). The point is not the angel but the hand: your church is watched over, but it is Christ who holds it and Christ to whom it answers.

Can Christ still remove a church’s lampstand today? Yes. A congregation that abandons the gospel and refuses to repent can lose its witness and cease to be a true church; history is full of buildings where Christ was once preached and is preached no more, and Ephesus itself is now a city of ruins. No true believer is lost by it; Christ never lets go of his own (John 10:28). But local churches are not guaranteed to last. His remedy is simple: remember, repent and do the first works (2:5). The warning is given so that the lamp will not go out.

Where Christians differ: is this verse an outline of the book? Dispensationalists, who expect the church to be taken from the earth before a final tribulation, often take it as a strict outline, with chapters 4–22 entirely future, after the church is raptured at 4:1; careful teachers in that tradition have worked it out at length. Others hesitate, for two reasons. The phrase “what must take place” describes the whole book in verse 1, chapters 2 and 3 included. And the contents resist the split both ways: the letters to the churches are full of the future (a crown, hidden manna, a pillar in the temple, Christ’s coming), while chapters 4–22 are full of the present (a throne occupied now, martyrs already under the altar, a Lamb who has already conquered). This commentary’s view: the phrase describes the whole book: what John saw mixes things that are and things still to come. Chapter 12, for example, goes back to Christ’s birth and ascension. The book is not a strict timeline but a series of visions, each showing the age between Christ’s comings from a different angle and each ending at or near the final judgment. Nothing essential about Christ rests on the question, and where it changes the meaning of a passage the options are set out again there.

Where Christians differ: who are the angels of the churches? Some say human messengers carrying the letters, or each church’s pastor, since each letter rebukes its angel and calls him to repent, a strange thing to say to an unfallen angel. Others say guardian angels assigned to the churches. Others say they personify each church’s corporate character as heaven sees it. This commentary’s view: most likely heavenly angels connected with each church, since every other use of “angel” in Revelation (over sixty) means a heavenly being, and Scripture speaks of angels watching over God’s people (Daniel 10:20–21; Matthew 18:10). Yet the letters are aimed at the congregations themselves: the angel represents the church before God, so to address it is to address the church, and the messages are for every believer (2:7).

Uncertain wording. “Those that are” (ha eisin) most naturally means the things that exist now, as the three-part outline reads it. But in the next sentence the same verb means “stand for” (“the seven stars are the angels”), and some interpreters take it so here: write what you have seen, what it means, and what is to come. Either is possible; either way John is to write the whole vision.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place.<sup>2</sup>He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.<sup>3</sup>Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.<sup>4</sup>John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,<sup>5</sup>and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood<sup>6</sup>and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>7</sup>Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.<sup>8</sup>“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”<sup>9</sup>I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.<sup>10</sup>I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet<sup>11</sup>saying, “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”<sup>12</sup>Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands,<sup>13</sup>and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.<sup>14</sup>The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire,<sup>15</sup>his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters.<sup>16</sup>In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.<sup>17</sup>When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last,<sup>18</sup>and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.<sup>19</sup>Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this.<sup>20</sup>As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”
