keyVerse.quote: Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
keyVerse.note: Here the chapter comes to its point. The Christ of blazing glory claims the title God alone holds in Isaiah, then adds what no one else could say, “I died”, and holds the keys of the realm every human being fears. His first words to his terrified servant remove the fear, so every terror in the chapters ahead reaches churches whose Lord has already been through death and holds its door.

1.reflection:
Verse 3 blesses not those who understand Revelation but those who hear it and keep it. How has the book been used in your experience: as a puzzle to solve or a word to obey? What would keeping it look like for you this week?

John’s greeting gives Jesus titles the emperor claimed: faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, ruler of kings on earth (v. 5). What powers seem to rule your world, at work, in politics or in your own fears, and how does it help to know they are under him?

John calls himself a “brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus” (v. 9). Why do you think suffering and the kingdom belong together? Where do you need endurance at present?

When John saw the risen Christ he fell as though dead, and Christ laid his right hand on him and said, “Fear not” (v. 17). Is the Jesus you worship big enough to undo you, and near enough to raise you? Which of the two do you most need to see?

2.title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 carries the first four of the risen Christ’s seven letters. Before heaven opens in chapter 4, the one John saw among the lampstands (1:12–20) speaks to real congregations, by name, about their real condition.

The message. Christ knows his church completely, and he loves it too much to leave it as it is. He sees what no one else sees: toil nobody thanked, poverty that is secretly wealth, love that is growing, and also love gone cold and false teaching quietly tolerated. He calls each church to repent or to endure, and to the one who conquers, who holds on to him to the end, he promises what Adam lost and more, and at last himself.

Why it was said. These churches faced the pressures of their cities (see the introduction): persecution in cities devoted to Rome and its gods (Smyrna, Pergamum), and the quieter seduction of the trade guilds, whose feasts tied idol worship and immorality to earning a living (Pergamum, Thyatira). Ephesus faced a danger harder to see: a sound church growing cold in its second generation.

How the chapter makes its case. Every letter follows one pattern: Christ introduces himself with a feature from the vision of chapter 1; he says “I know”; he commends, rebukes or both; he calls for repentance or endurance; he bids whoever has an ear to hear; and he makes a promise to the one who conquers. Ephesus is sound but has abandoned its first love (vv. 1–7). Smyrna is poor and facing prison, and receives no rebuke (vv. 8–11). Pergamum held fast when Antipas was killed, but tolerates the teaching of Balaam (vv. 12–17). Thyatira is growing in love, but tolerates a false prophetess (vv. 18–29).

Where it leads. Each letter is a portrait of Christ before it is a verdict on a church: he grips the stars, he died and came to life, he wields the sword of his word, his eyes like fire search mind and heart. His people conquer “by the blood of the Lamb” (12:11), because he conquered first by being slain. And the chapter’s last promise is not a thing at all but a person, Christ himself, “the bright morning star” (v. 28; 22:16).

For us. Every church, and every Christian, will find a likeness somewhere in these letters. Notice which commendation you long to hear and which rebuke makes you uncomfortable; then hear what the Spirit says, and hold on to the one who has never once let go of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — To the Church in Ephesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sound doctrine and hard work cannot make up for lost love. Christ comes to Ephesus as the one who grips the seven stars and walks among the lampstands (v. 1). He praises its toil, endurance and discernment, for it has tested false apostles and found them out (vv. 2–3). But it has abandoned the love it had at first, and the remedy is to remember, repent and do the first works, or lose its lampstand (v. 5; on what that does and does not mean, see vv. 4–5). He shares its hatred of the Nicolaitans’ works, and promises the one who conquers the tree of life that Adam lost (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Orthodox but Loveless

Ephesus had sound doctrine, hard work and endurance, but had abandoned its first love. The cure is to remember, repent and do the works it did at first.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A second-generation church kept the truth and lost the warmth.

Now: Ask what would remain of your faith if the things others can see were taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: "To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: 'The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ speaks to his church as the one who holds it fast and walks in its midst. Before a word of praise or blame, he tells Ephesus who is speaking and where he stands.

The pattern of the seven letters. Every letter introduces its sender with one feature from the vision of chapter 1, and the feature chosen is always the one that congregation most needs to see.

To the angel of the church in Ephesus write. The angel (angelos) is probably a heavenly angel representing the church (see 1:20), but the message is for the whole congregation and beyond it, for all churches: “hear what the Spirit says to the churches”, plural. Ephesus heard Laodicea’s letter read, and so do we.

Holds the seven stars, walks among the lampstands. “The words of” (tade legei) is the Greek form of the prophets’ “Thus says the LORD”: Christ speaks with God’s authority. In chapter 1 he held the stars; here the verb is stronger (kratōn): he grips them. And where he stood among the lampstands, now he walks (peripatōn), as an inspector does, and as a priest went from lamp to lamp. To a church that may lose its lampstand, he first presents himself as the one who holds it firmly and is moving through the room.

The setting. Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, a great port famous for the temple of Artemis. Paul spent nearly three years there (Acts 19; 20:31) and warned its elders that fierce wolves would come in (Acts 20:29–30); Timothy was left there to oppose false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3); tradition says John later lived there. The church was now about forty years old, in its second generation.

Where he is standing before he speaks. Christ begins not with faults but with where he stands. Correction from a stranger feels like an attack; correction from the one who holds you in his right hand is love. Every hard sentence that follows is spoken from inside the room, by someone who has not left and is not going to. The hand that grips the seven stars has never once opened to let a church fall. He walks among his churches not as a landlord but as the bridegroom who gave himself up for her, to present her in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27), words Paul wrote to this very congregation.

What it does not mean. The seven letters are not a forecast of seven eras of church history, with Ephesus the apostolic church and Laodicea the church of the last days, as some sincere teachers have held. These were real congregations, every letter is addressed to all the churches (2:7), and the scheme works only by reading history in hindsight. All seven speak to every church in every age.

Which of these letters is written to my church? Very possibly more than one: correct and cold, poor and hunted, compromised, tolerant of what it should confront, asleep, weak but faithful, comfortable and self-satisfied. Before asking who the Nicolaitans were, ask which commendation you would most like to hear, and which rebuke makes you most uncomfortable. The discomfort is usually the clue. And each letter ends with a promise to the one who conquers, singular.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the greatest city of Asia and home to the vast temple of Artemis. Paul had spent nearly three years there.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name's sake, and you have not grown weary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ sees and honours every hard thing his people have done for his name. Ephesus has worked, endured and guarded the truth against false apostles, and he names it all before he says anything else.

I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance. Every letter begins with “I know” (oida): comfort for the faithful, warning for the compromising. Toil (kopos) is labour to the point of exhaustion; patient endurance (hypomonē) is staying power, remaining under the weight.

Cannot bear. “Cannot bear” (ou dynē bastasai): they practised church discipline, dealing with open sin in the church, and did not tolerate evil in their midst as Pergamum and Thyatira did.

Tested and found false. “Tested” (epeirasas) means put to the proof; “false” (pseudeis) means liars. Travelling preachers moved from church to church, some claiming apostolic authority they did not have (2 Corinthians 11:13), and churches had to test them (1 John 4:1); an early church manual, the Didache, gives rules for doing so (Didache 11). Rejecting a self-proclaimed apostle meant a public fight. Paul had warned this congregation, in tears, that fierce wolves would come (Acts 20:29–31); a generation later Ephesus was still acting on it.

Bearing up for my name’s sake. Two plays on words: they cannot bear evil people, but have borne (ebastasas) hardship for Christ’s name; they laboured (kopos) without growing weary (ou kekopiakes). Nothing done for his name is lost on him: every exhausting week, every hard conversation with a false teacher, every year of faithfulness nobody thanked. And the motive he names is himself, who first carried a heavier load for them (Hebrews 12:2–3); their tests were tests of loyalty to him, for false apostles preach another Jesus (2 Corinthians 11:4, 13).

What can be counted and what cannot. The praise is genuine, which makes verse 4 more serious. A visitor could count everything in these two verses in a single Sunday: the work, the doctrine, the staying power, the discernment. What is about to be named cannot be counted at all; only the eyes like a flame of fire could see it. And a church like this can come to love its own correctness, the feeling of being the ones who got it right, more than the Lord it is right about: trusting in religion rather than in Christ, in its most respectable form, which from outside looks exactly like faithfulness.

How do I test a teacher without becoming suspicious of everyone? Test what is taught, not the personality. Does it agree with the plain meaning of Scripture in context? Does it confess Jesus Christ as God come in the flesh, crucified and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does it lead to holiness, or make sin easy (Jude 4)? Is the teacher’s life consistent with his words (1 Timothy 3:2–7), and does he point to Christ or to himself? Faithful teachers make small mistakes; testing is for protecting the flock from real error, done humbly, with Scripture open, alongside your church and its elders.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church can keep its doctrine and lose its love, and Christ calls that a fall to be repented of. The remedy is to remember, to turn back and to do again the works of love, or the church’s light will go out.

Abandoned. One sentence undoes the tone of everything before it. Aphēkes does not mean cooled by degrees but left behind, let go; it is the verb used of the disciples leaving their nets. Ephesus has not lost its first love as a man loses his keys. It has put it down and walked on.

What is first love? Love for Christ, the astonishment of someone who has just discovered he is forgiven and cannot get over it; and love for one another, which John will not separate from love for God (1 John 4:20–21). A church that stops marvelling at grace soon stops being gracious: the two leave together. Ephesus kept doing and believing the right things, but its battles with false teachers may have left it suspicious and hard, defending the truth without the love the truth produces.

The setting. Paul had praised these believers for their love toward all the saints (Ephesians 1:15). A generation later that love has cooled, as Jesus warned: the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:12).

Picture the difference. Imagine a young congregation in the AD 50s hiding a runaway slave at real legal risk, because they cannot get over having been bought out of slavery themselves. A generation on, the same congregation correctly unmasks a false apostle, and nobody in the room would take such a risk any more. The doctrine is exactly what it was; the warmth has gone.

Remember, repent, and do the works. Christ’s remedy is three verbs in order. Remember (mnēmoneue, keep remembering): not try harder, but look back and compare honestly; and “fallen” (peptōkes) is strong, for losing first love is a fall. Repent (metanoēson): turn round, because this is a sin and not a phase; coldness towards Christ is not a temperament but something to be confessed. Then do the works you did at first: do not wait for the feeling to return, but act.

The heart reached through the hands. That last instruction is enormously freeing. Affection for God cannot be manufactured by effort, and trying breeds despair. Christ asks not for the feeling but for the deeds: the visit you used to make, the giving that used to cost you, the praying before anyone was awake. Do those, leaning on the Spirit who first kindled that love. The heart is not reached by being lectured; it is reached through the hands.

Remove your lampstand. This coming (erchomai) is probably a judgment on this church in history, not the final return. The lampstand is the congregation as a light-bearer (1:20): to remove it means the church would cease to witness and finally cease to be a church. A church that keeps its doctrine and loses its love can run for years on organisation and memory, but the light goes out. The church at Ephesus continued for centuries, which suggests it heeded the warning; today the city is a field of ruins.

What it does not mean. Losing the lampstand does not mean true believers lose their salvation. Christ is speaking about the church as a community and its witness. True believers persevere because God keeps them (John 10:28–29); and one way he keeps them is by warnings like this one, which they heed.

The love that did not leave. Ephesus has let go of its first love, but its Lord has never let go of his: having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1), and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). So the way back is not to stir up a feeling but to look again at the love that came first, his, which went to the cross and has not cooled for a day since. No church has loved him as it should, not even Ephesus in its first warmth; only he has loved the Father with all his heart, and that perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). A cold heart confessed is a forgiven heart (1 John 1:9).

How do I know if I have left my first love? Ask honest questions. Do I still marvel that I am forgiven? Is prayer something I want or something I manage? Do I love fellow believers, especially the difficult ones, or mostly assess them? Am I quicker to spot error than to show kindness? Is my service still for Christ, or habit and reputation? Look not at your feelings on a bad day but at the direction of drift over months and years. And if these questions trouble you, take heart: a heart that worries about its coldness to Christ is not dead, and the concern itself is the Spirit’s work.

What if I never had a dramatic first love to go back to? Then do not chase a feeling you never had; many came to Christ quietly, as children or slowly over years. First love is the love that answers grace: gratitude, delight in Christ, love for his people. The way into it is the way back to it: look at what Christ has done, read the accounts of the cross slowly, confess your coldness, serve someone in his name. Feelings often follow obedience; they rarely come before it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ shares his church’s hatred of what destroys his people, and promises everyone who holds on to him to the end the life that Adam lost. What he says to one church, the Spirit says to all.

Yet this you have: you hate. The rebuke is not Christ’s last word. Hate is said twice, the second time of Christ himself (miseis). Love that cannot hate anything is indifference in love’s clothes: a father who watched his child fed poison and felt nothing would not be gentle. And the object is chosen with care: not the Nicolaitans, but their works. Ephesus has that right while getting first love wrong; Thyatira will do the reverse. Neither is asked to trade one for the other.

The works of the Nicolaitans. Their teaching is set beside Balaam’s in v. 15: idol food and sexual immorality (v. 14). They seem to have taught that Christians could join in pagan feasts and the guilds’ idolatrous life. Ephesus rejected them; Pergamum tolerated them.

Whoever has an ear. Jesus often said, “He who has ears, let him hear” (Matthew 13:9; 11:15). The words are Christ’s, yet they are what the Spirit says: Christ speaks by his Spirit, who lives in every believer and gives the strength to obey (Ezekiel 36:27). And it is churches, plural.

To the one who conquers. The one who conquers (nikōnti, from nikē, victory) closes every letter, and the book defines it: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death” (12:11). The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5–6). Conquering is not winning by force but holding on to Christ, at cost, to the end. Nor are conquerors an elite: everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith (1 John 5:4–5). This is the perseverance of the saints: those God brings to faith he keeps in faith, so that the believer’s holding on is the fruit of God’s holding him (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

The tree of life. The tree of life (xylou tēs zōēs) stood in the middle of the garden (Genesis 2:9), and after the fall a guard barred the way to it, so that fallen humanity could not take and live for ever in its ruin (Genesis 3:22–24). Nobody eats from it again until the Bible’s last chapter, where it stands in the city with leaves for the healing of the nations and no sword barring the path (22:2, 14). Paradise (paradeisos, a Persian word for a garden or park) is the Greek Old Testament’s word for Eden. The exile is over: Christ promises what Adam lost, eternal life in God’s presence.

The true tree and the true refuge. The one who opens the way back was himself hung on a tree. The shrine of Artemis is said to have begun at a sacred tree, and her temple offered asylum to fugitives. Christ offers the true tree and the true refuge, and the sword that barred the path fell on him.

How do I hear what the Spirit says? To hear, in Scripture, is to take in and obey, and the Spirit speaks through the words Christ has already given: these letters are “what the Spirit says”. Read it as addressed to you: where is my church in this, and where am I? Listen with others: sit under faithful preaching, and let a friend tell you what he sees. Notice what stings: the sentence you would rather skip is often the one meant for you. Answer the same day, with a prayer and one small act of obedience (James 1:22). And take heart: the one who says “let him hear” opens deaf ears (Mark 7:34–35); his sheep hear his voice because he first called them by name (John 10:3, 27).

Am I a conqueror if I still struggle with sin? Yes, if you belong to Christ and keep coming back to him. Conquering is not sinless perfection but persevering faith: trusting the blood of the Lamb and refusing to give up on him (12:11). A believer who falls, grieves, confesses and gets up again is conquering. The victory is first the Lamb’s, shared by faith (1 John 5:4), and the struggle itself is a sign of life: the dead do not fight.

Is it ever right for a Christian to hate? Yes, but only what God hates, and as he hates it: what is evil (Romans 12:9), even the garment stained by the flesh (Jude 23). That hatred is aimed at sin and the lies that destroy people, never at the people, whom we are to love, even our enemies (Matthew 5:44). If your hatred of a false teaching makes you want to rescue its victims, it is godly; if it makes you enjoy its teachers’ downfall, it has gone bad.

Uncertain wording. Who the Nicolaitans were is unknown; the name appears only here and in v. 15. Irenaeus linked them with Nicolaus, one of the seven of Acts 6:5, but this is uncertain. The name means roughly conqueror of the people, and since v. 15 sets their teaching beside Balaam’s, some think it was a label for the same party rather than a founder’s name. What they did is clear: they made room for idol feasts and immorality.
verseByVerse.note: The Nicolaitans are unknown outside Revelation; they seem to have taught that believers could take part in pagan feasts and immorality.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — To the Church in Smyrna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness may cost everything, but Christ makes his suffering people rich and keeps them safe. To a church about to face death, he comes as the one who died and came to life (v. 8). He knows its tribulation, its poverty and the slander it suffers, and in his reckoning it is rich (v. 9). He does not deny the suffering to come, but sets bounds on it, gives it a purpose the devil did not choose, that you may be tested, and promises the crown of life (v. 10). The second death cannot touch those who conquer (v. 11). Smyrna receives no rebuke at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Poor, and Rich

Christ, who died and came to life, knows Smyrna’s tribulation and poverty, and says they are rich. Suffering is coming, bounded and purposeful; the faithful will not be hurt by the second death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Polycarp, bishop of this church some sixty years later, served Christ to the fire.

Now: Grace for a trial is given on the day of the trial, not in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: 'The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. "'I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ sees his poor and slandered church as rich. He knows exactly what its faith has cost it, and who is accusing it.

Who died and came to life. Christ introduces himself from the first vision (1:17–18), because this church is about to face death, and the one giving the orders has been dead. The first and the last is the LORD’s own title in Isaiah (Isaiah 44:6; 48:12). Smyrna called itself the first city of Asia, and said it had itself died and come back to life, destroyed around 600 BC and refounded three centuries later. The one who is truly first, and who truly rose, is speaking.

Tribulation and poverty. Tribulation (thlipsin) is persecution. Poverty (ptōcheia) is destitution, a beggar’s poverty, in a rich city. A Christian who would not join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, and a Jewish believer disowned by the synagogue lost the exemption from emperor worship. Their poverty was very likely the price of their faith.

(But you are rich). Into the middle of the sentence Christ inserts a bracket, the heart of the letter. He does not deny the poverty; he sets God’s reckoning beside the world’s: they are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). Laodicea will be told the opposite: rich in its own eyes, but poor (3:17). The two churches that receive no criticism, Smyrna and Philadelphia, are both poor and under pressure; the one with no commendation is the wealthiest. That does not make money evil or hardship holy. It says that Christ does not measure a church’s health the way we do.

The slander. Slander (blasphēmian) is abusive speech. Local Jews apparently denounced Christians to the authorities; once disowned as not Jews, Christians lost the legal tolerance Jews had. In the account of Polycarp’s martyrdom, written by this church, Smyrna’s Jews were said to have joined eagerly in gathering wood for the fire.

A synagogue of Satan. The name describes what they were doing, not their race: by accusing God’s people, they did the work of Satan, the accuser of the brothers (12:10), as anyone does who accuses God’s people, whatever synagogue or church he attends. The true Jew is one inwardly (Romans 2:28–29), and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29).

The setting. Smyrna (modern Izmir), north of Ephesus, was a wealthy port and a beautiful city whose ring of buildings on Mount Pagos was called the crown of Smyrna. It was fiercely loyal to Rome, with one of the first temples to the goddess Roma and a temple to Tiberius, so refusing emperor worship looked like disloyalty. It also had a large Jewish community.

Poverty known from the inside. The Lord who calls Smyrna rich knows poverty from the inside: though he was rich, for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), with no place to lay his head and stripped of his clothes at the end. Every coin his people lose for his name is entered in his book, and what he has made them heirs to no magistrate can confiscate.

What it does not mean. This is not antisemitism, and must never justify it. Christ, John and the first church were Jews, and salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). The words target a particular community that was persecuting Christians, and the charge is spiritual, not ethnic. Reading the verse as a verdict on Jewish people in general has done terrible damage in the church’s history, and is a sin to repent of. Scripture holds out hope for Israel (Romans 11:25–29), and Christians are to love their Jewish neighbours and pray for them.

Does this mean faithful Christians will always be poor? No. Scripture does not make poverty a badge of holiness; it records faithful believers with property who used it for others (Acts 16:14–15; Romans 16:23). Faithfulness sometimes costs money, as it did in Smyrna, and then Christ counts the believer rich. Prosperity is no proof of his favour, nor hardship of his displeasure. Ask not how much you have, but whether any of it was bought with compromise, and whether you are rich toward God (Luke 12:21).

Is calling the poor rich just a way of keeping them quiet? No. Christ names the poverty plainly, and who caused it; he does not offer a feeling in place of bread. The riches rest on a fact, that he died and came to life (2:8), and a risen Lord can make good on promises as no slogan can. The same book pronounces judgment on the merchants who grew fat on a cruel trade, human souls among their cargo (18:11–19). This is not comfort that excuses the oppressor. It is comfort that outlasts him.

In everyday life. If you are slandered for your faith, do not answer in kind; leave the accuser’s work to the accuser and keep doing your Lord’s.
verseByVerse.note: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port, loyal to Rome, with a large Jewish community, some of whom were slandering the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ does not promise his people escape from suffering, but he limits it, gives it a purpose and promises life beyond it. So they need not fear, even if faithfulness costs them their lives.

Do not fear what you are about to suffer. He does not say, do not fear, because you will not suffer. The suffering is confirmed in the same sentence in which fear is forbidden (mēden phobou, fear nothing).

The devil. Devil (diabolos) means slanderer: behind the slanderers and the courts, persecution has a spiritual source. Some of you, not all, so the congregation would live for months not knowing who. Yet the devil acts only within the limits God allows (Job 1–2).

The setting. In the Roman world, prison was not usually a punishment in itself; it was a place to hold people before trial or execution. To be thrown into prison often meant death was coming.

That you may be tested. Then come the words that change everything: a purpose, and not the devil’s. He throws believers into prison to destroy their faith, but another purpose runs through the same event: proving something valuable (peirasthēte, tried, proved). While the devil strikes, he is unwittingly doing the refiner’s work. Job lived through this first (Job 1:12), and Peter told churches in this province that the tested genuineness of their faith was more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). The same event has two purposes, and only one will prevail.

And for ten days you will have tribulation. Ten is a round figure for a complete but limited stretch; Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Daniel 1:12–14). The suffering is real, but it has a stated limit, and the one who states it is not the devil. The Lord of Smyrna has built a fence around his people’s suffering and written its length himself.

Be faithful unto death. Faithful (pistos) means loyal, trustworthy. Unto death (achri thanatou) can mean faithful right up to the end of your life, and it can mean faithful even to the point of being killed. Both were true in Smyrna.

The crown of life. The crown (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath of leaves at the games, withered within a week (1 Corinthians 9:25); and Smyrna’s skyline was called the crown of the city (see the note on vv. 8–9). Christ offers instead a crown that is life itself (James 1:12).

The faithful one asks for faithfulness. The command comes from the faithful witness (1:5), who became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and who died and came to life (2:8). He does not ask Smyrna to walk anywhere he has not walked. And the crown is his to give because he won it: faithfulness unto death is following him to the place where death was beaten.

Endurance, not stoicism. A believer facing something frightening needs to know not so much that it will end as whether it means anything. This says it does: what is coming at you has been given a purpose it did not choose, and that purpose is not your destruction.

Is the crown of life only for martyrs? No. It is eternal life itself, given to all who remain faithful to the end (James 1:12), including the believer who dies quietly in a hospital bed after a long life of ordinary faithfulness. What the martyr shows openly, every believer shows in his own way: that Christ is worth more than life.

What if I am afraid I would deny Christ under pressure? Many are, and the fear is not unbelief. Nobody feels able to face a prison, and Peter, who was certain he could, could not (Luke 22:33, 57). Grace is not issued in advance for a trial you are not in; it is given on the day, in the cell, as Christ promised (Luke 21:14–15). Smyrna was told not to generate courage but who would be with them. Your part today is faithfulness in the smaller costs; his is the strength for the great ones.

In everyday life. Pray today for believers in prison for Christ; there are many, in many countries, and they are your brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: “Ten days” probably means a short, limited time.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever the world does to Christ’s people, it cannot touch them with the death that matters most. The one who conquers will never be hurt by the second death, God’s final judgment.

The second death. “Will not be hurt” (ou mē adikēthē) is the strongest “not” in Greek: will certainly never be hurt. The phrase second death occurs only in this book, which explains it as the lake of fire after the final judgment (20:6, 14; 21:8): the first death is physical, the second eternal separation from God under his judgment.

What is not promised. Smyrna is not told it will escape the first death; several will not. But the magistrate’s power stops there: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). Christ offers his most faithful church not protection from the death it fears but safety from the far worse death it has not thought about, the only consolation that holds when the cell door shuts.

Polycarp. Polycarp, bishop of this church about sixty years later, may have heard this letter read as a young man. Urged by the proconsul to swear by the fortune of Caesar and revile Christ, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and Christ had never done him wrong: how could he blaspheme his King and Saviour? They burned him in the stadium, and the church of Smyrna’s account says he asked to be left unfastened, because the one who gave him strength to endure the fire would give him strength to stay still in it. The letter had done its work.

How can a loving God allow a second death? Because he is also just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is not small. The second death is his righteous judgment on those who refuse him to the end, and it will be seen to be right (16:5–7; 19:1–2). But this verse turns the doctrine into comfort and invitation: the second death has no power over anyone in Christ, who bore the judgment in their place (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10), and the way out is open to anyone who will come to him now.

In everyday life. If someone you love does not yet know Christ, let the reality of the second death make you pray and speak, gently and soon.

Where Christians differ: is the second death the end of existence? Annihilationists hold that the second death means the wicked cease to exist after judgment; some sincere evangelical believers hold this, pointing to texts that speak of destruction (Matthew 10:28). This commentary’s view: Revelation describes the lake of fire as torment day and night for ever and ever (20:10; 14:11), and Jesus spoke of eternal punishment alongside eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The second death is called death because it is the final loss of all that makes life life: God’s presence and favour. It is conscious, eternal punishment, which is exactly why the promise here is so precious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — To the Church in Pergamum
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church that stands firm under persecution can still be undone by compromise from within. To Pergamum, seat of the governor’s sword and centre of emperor worship, Christ comes with the sharp two-edged sword of his word (v. 12). The church held fast his name even when Antipas, his faithful witness, was killed (v. 13), but it has let some remain, unchallenged, who hold the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans: the guild feasts with their idol meat and immorality (vv. 14–15). The whole congregation is called to repent, or Christ will come and fight the false teachers himself with the sword of his mouth (v. 16). To those who refuse the idol feasts he promises hidden manna, a white stone and a new name (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Strategy

Pergamum held fast under the sword but tolerated the teaching of Balaam, the invitation to compromise at the idol feast. The whole church is called to repent of its silence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Guild banquets tied a man’s livelihood to idol meat.

Now: The argument for compromise is always reasonable. Christ offers hidden manna and a new name instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: 'The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. "'I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ knows how hard the place is where his people live, and honours them for confessing his name there even when it cost a life. He speaks as the one whose word, not the governor’s sword, has the last say over life and death.

The sharp two-edged sword. Pergamum, the old capital of the province, was probably still the seat of the Roman governor, who had the right of the sword: the power to execute. To this city alone Christ introduces himself with the sword of 1:16. The governor’s sword was lent to him by Rome, and he used it on Antipas. Christ’s sword is his word: it comes from his own mouth, was received from no one, and truly decides life and death; and he will use it against the false teachers (v. 16).

I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Dwell (katoikeis) means settled, permanent residence, and the same root is used of Satan at the end of the verse. They live there; he lives there. They did not choose the place, and Christ knows how hard it is (on what Satan’s throne refers to, see the end of this note). Faithfulness is measured on the ground a person is actually standing on, and some believers stand on very hard ground by appointment, not by mistake.

Hold fast my name. In a city where a governor held the sword, both verbs are specific. Hold fast (krateis): go on saying the name in public. Deny (ērnēsō): disown. When the question came, formally, before a magistrate, they did not give the required answer. The demand was rarely a long renunciation; usually it was to say Caesar is Lord and offer a pinch of incense, perhaps curse Christ, and then believe what you liked in private. Pergamum would not. “My faith” (tēn pistin mou) means faith in me, or the faithfulness owed to me.

Antipas my faithful witness, killed among you. The name occurs only here; later tradition says he was roasted in a bronze bull. What is known is his title. In 1:5 Christ himself is the faithful witness (ho martys ho pistos), and he hands his own description to a man who bore witness the same way, to the death. And he was killed among you, not merely in your city: they had watched it happen, and Christ names their friend in front of everyone. Nothing done to them happened out of sight.

The governor’s seat is empty. The Lord of Pergamum once stood before a Roman governor who held the power of the sword, told the truth and was killed, telling him he would have no authority at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:10–11). Now the governor’s seat is empty, and the name of one faithful man from Satan’s hill is read in every church on earth, because Christ chose to keep it.

Martyr or fanatic? To many modern ears martyr has turned sinister: we have watched people die for a cause while taking strangers with them. But a life with nothing worth dying for is not obviously saner, only smaller. The real question is not how strongly you believe but what your belief does with a sword. As far as we know, Antipas took none up; he would not give the answer Pergamum required, and the sword was used on him. The fanatic makes others pay for his cause. The martyr, whose name in Greek simply means witness, pays himself, and dies praying for those who kill him, as his Lord did: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). A faith whose founder died for his enemies cannot be served by killing them, and that is what makes it safe to have something worth dying for.

Should I move away from a place, or a job, that is hostile to my faith? Not necessarily. Christ did not tell Pergamum to leave, and Christians are placed in hard places to be light there (Matthew 5:14; Jeremiah 29:7). A wise believer may move when staying would require sin, when his family is in real danger, or when a door opens that is not an escape from faithfulness (Matthew 10:23). Ask whether you are escaping the cost of faithfulness or following where it leads. Pray, take counsel, and wherever you are, hold fast his name.

In everyday life. When you are asked for your small pinch of incense, the sentence you do not believe, the silence that keeps the peace at your Lord’s expense, remember Antipas, whose name is known in heaven while the governor’s is forgotten.

Uncertain wording. What “Satan’s throne” refers to is uncertain. Pergamum’s hill, a huge cone of rock crowned with temples, held several candidates: the Great Altar of Zeus, shaped like a throne on a mountain; the shrine of Asclepius, the healing god whose emblem was a serpent and who was called Saviour; the governor’s seat of judgment; and the province’s first temple to a living emperor, Augustus, with Roma. The best explanation is the city’s leadership in emperor worship, joined to the governor’s power to condemn Christians. Political power, false salvation and a serpent, all on one hill.
verseByVerse.note: Pergamum was a centre of emperor worship and home to a great altar of Zeus, which may be one reason it is called the place “where Satan’s throne is”.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church that stands firm against persecution can still be undone by seduction from within. Pergamum has let some in its membership teach that the idol feasts and their immorality are harmless.

But I have a few things against you. The problem is not that Pergamum has denied Christ under pressure, because it has not. The problem is what it has permitted inside the room while standing firm at the door: “you have some there”. The charge is against the church for having them, unchallenged, in the membership. Its sin is not that a few people were wrong, but that it let them stay.

The teaching of Balaam. Balaam was hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel, and three times could not: every time he opened his mouth a blessing came out (Numbers 24:10–17). So he gave other advice, as Moses later reveals (Numbers 31:16): draw Israel into sin. Israel joined the Moabite feasts, ate the sacrifices, committed immorality and bowed to Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand died (Numbers 25:1–9). What could not be cursed from outside was seduced from inside. And it is called teaching (didachēn): a doctrine that justified the behaviour, taught within the church. At Pergamum too persecution had failed, so Satan changed strategy, and seduction was working. The New Testament remembers Balaam as the prophet who led God’s people into sin for profit (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

A stumbling block. A stumbling block (skandalon) is the bait stick that springs a trap, and so anything that makes people fall.

The Nicolaitans. “So also” (houtōs): the Nicolaitans’ teaching is Balaam’s, or very like it (see the note on vv. 6–7). Ephesus hated their works; Pergamum has some who hold their teaching. (On whether coldness or tolerance is the safer mistake, see vv. 18–19.)

Idol food and immorality. In a Roman city the two usually arrived on the same evening. Trade guilds were religious associations, each with a patron deity, and membership meant banquets in the temple precincts, where the meat had been offered on the altar and the later evening often involved sexual licence. Refuse the dinner and you are outside the guild; outside the guild there is no work. Eating in the temple at a feast in the god’s honour was taking part in idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:19–22), and the Jerusalem council had asked Gentile believers to abstain from both (Acts 15:29).

Two tables. Behind the guild dinner stands Paul’s question: whose table are you at? The bread is a participation in the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). The compromisers said the idol was nothing, so the meal was nothing; Christ’s answer is that his own table is not nothing, for he gave his body and blood for his people. The Lord who could not be cursed out of loving his people will not let them be seduced out of it either. His jealousy is a husband’s, and it is love.

Balaam’s argument today. The compromisers were not arguing for wickedness: a man has to feed his family, the ritual means nothing, God looks on the heart. Few readers are asked to burn incense. Many are asked to say something in a meeting they do not believe, to stay quiet where speaking would cost a promotion, to laugh along at the table, to sleep with someone they are not married to because everyone does. The stumbling block is laid not before people who want to fall but before people who need the work. So ask: what do I believe I cannot live without? The income, the approval, the place at the table: that is where the stumbling block will be laid, and it is the thing to hand back to Christ before the moment comes.

Does this contradict Paul, who allows eating meat bought in the market? No. Paul allows market meat without questions (1 Corinthians 10:25), but he too forbids idol feasts: you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). Christ condemns what Paul condemns. Ordinary things in an unbelieving world do not defile; taking part in another god’s worship, or in sin dressed up as custom, does.

Where is the line between living in the culture and compromising with it? Ask three questions. Does this require me to do what God forbids, or to hide Christ when faithfulness calls me to own him? Does it mean taking part in false worship or celebration, rather than simply being among unbelievers? And is my real reason fear of loss, dressed up as wisdom? Christians can work in secular jobs, attend a colleague’s wedding and eat at a neighbour’s table; Jesus ate with sinners. But when the price of belonging is sin, the answer is no, even if it costs the job. When the case is unclear, take counsel from mature believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church must repent of the error it tolerates, or Christ will deal with it himself, by his word. Silence in the face of false teaching is itself something to repent of.

Therefore repent. Two words (metanoēson oun), addressed to the whole congregation, including the majority who have done nothing wrong except let it happen. The church must repent of tolerating the faction, and the faction of its teaching. A church is answerable for what it tolerates, and silence is a decision.

I will come to you soon. As at Ephesus, this is a coming in judgment on this church within history, not the final return, and “soon” (tachy) means without delay. God’s patience is real, as the next letter shows, but it is patience with a purpose, not tolerance without a limit.

War against them. He comes to you; he wars (polemēsō) against them. The pronouns separate, deliberately. Christ will conduct a battle inside the congregation, against the false teachers, with the faithful majority in the room. A church that refuses to act against error does not escape the action; Christ takes it himself.

The sword of my mouth. The sword is his word of judgment, which in 19:15 strikes the nations; Christ fights for the purity of his bride with the word that made the worlds. It also shows what the church’s own instrument should have been: not force, but saying the true thing out loud, which nobody in Pergamum was doing. Rome’s sword had not moved these believers; the danger was a weapon they did not see, false teaching aimed at the purity of the church, which nobody was guarding.

Balaam’s end. Balaam himself was once confronted by the angel of the LORD with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:23, 31). He spoke true prophecy, blessed God’s people against his own financial interest, and predicted the star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17). And he died by the sword among the kings of Midian, on the side of the enemies of the people he had blessed (Numbers 31:8). Saying true things about Christ is not the same as being on his side, and a man can do the first for years while drifting into the second.

Does Christ really fight against people inside his own church? Yes, against those who lead his people astray and will not repent. Not everyone on a church roll belongs to Christ (1 John 2:19), and he will not let wolves feed on his flock for ever. He fights by his word: error exposed, consciences troubled, judgment falling, persistent offenders sometimes removed. For the faithful this is protection. For anyone drawn into error, the verse’s first word is still open: repent. The sword is the last resort of a Lord who would much rather heal.

What should I do if my church tolerates false teaching? Begin with prayer and your own heart, and be sure the issue is real error, not preference. Then speak humbly and privately to the elders, with Scripture open (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1), and be patient. If the leaders themselves teach serious error about the gospel, or refuse to deal with open, unrepentant sin, and will not listen, you may need to leave quietly for a faithful church, for your own and your family’s sake. But do not leave in pride, nor stop loving the people you leave.

In everyday life. If you are tolerating a sin because confronting it would be uncomfortable, Christ calls you to repent, as the one whose blood has already paid for what you bring him. The door that stands open in this verse is open now.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who give up the world’s feasts and favour for Christ will be fed, welcomed and named by Christ himself. Each gift answers something they had lost.

Three promises against the guild. Each promise reverses something the compromisers were arguing for. They wanted the guild dinner; Christ offers hidden manna. They wanted the guild’s token of admission; Christ offers a white stone. They wanted to keep their standing in the city; Christ offers a new name.

The hidden manna. Manna, the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), was kept in a jar in the ark, behind the veil, hidden (Exodus 16:33–34; Hebrews 9:4). Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid the ark before the temple fell (2 Maccabees 2:4–8), and some expected manna to fall again in the Messiah’s days. The argument in Pergamum was about meat: eat what the temple provides, or lose your income. Christ answers with a different menu. Israel in the desert was fed by God alone for forty years, with no fields and no guilds, and the speaker here said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35, 48–51). Those who refuse idol food will eat the bread of heaven, Christ himself, at the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9).

The bread behind the curtain. The manna lay behind a curtain no ordinary Israelite could pass, and the true Bread from heaven opened the way through by giving his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51; Hebrews 10:19–20). What was hidden in the holiest place he now gives, himself, to tradesmen shut out of every dinner in the city.

A new name. A new name (onoma kainon) marks a changed identity given by God: Abram became Abraham, Simon became Peter (Isaiah 62:2). It may be the believer’s new name, or Christ’s own, known truly only to those who know him (3:12; 19:12). Either way the name is private: only the one who receives it knows it. Christ’s knowledge of each of his people is particular, not generic. He is not handing out identical certificates to a crowd.

What the city takes and Christ gives. A tradesman who refuses the guild dinner loses his contracts, his standing and his good name in the city, and the cost is real. But a name is kept for him that the city could not give and cannot take.

What it does not mean. Nothing here supports secret knowledge for spiritual elites, as later Gnostic groups taught. The new name is known by the one who receives it, and every conquering believer receives one.

Does God really know me personally, or just love his people in general? Personally, and this verse is deliberately intimate. If God’s love has felt like a general policy, saving crowds but perhaps not noticing one obscure believer in one unglamorous town, here is a private name, on a stone, in his hand, for you. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and he chose you before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4).

Will I lose my own identity in heaven? No. A new name fulfils the person rather than erasing him: Abraham was still the man from Ur, Peter the fisherman, but each became more truly himself. In the new creation you will be you, healed and free from sin. What will be gone is everything false sin attached to your name: the shame, the labels, the reputation the world gave you.

Uncertain wording. What the white stone (psēphon leukēn) means is genuinely uncertain. A juror dropped a white pebble for acquittal and a black one for condemnation; a victor at the games might receive a token admitting him to the banquet; a guest received an inscribed ticket to a feast; inscribed stones were worn as amulets. Given the banquet here, a likely meaning is a ticket to the messianic feast, with a sense of acquittal as well: those shut out of the guilds’ feasts are admitted to Christ’s. If acquittal is in view, the stone pictures justification: the Judge declaring the guilty not guilty, because Christ has borne the sentence (Romans 8:33–34). What all the proposals share matters more: the stone is small, personal, handed to one person, and it is what gets him in.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the white stone is uncertain; white stones were used as tokens of acquittal and as tickets of admission to feasts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — To the Church in Thyatira
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love and service cannot excuse tolerating what destroys Christ’s people. Thyatira, the least distinguished of the seven towns and full of trade guilds, receives the longest letter. Christ comes as the Son of God, with eyes like a flame of fire (v. 18), and commends a church growing in love, faith, service and endurance (v. 19). But it tolerates a self-styled prophetess he calls Jezebel, who teaches Balaam’s programme again and has refused the time given her to repent; he will judge her, and all the churches will know that he searches mind and heart (vv. 20–23). The faithful are given no other burden than to hold fast until he comes (vv. 24–25), and are promised a share in his rule and the morning star, who is Christ himself (vv. 26–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Warm but Undiscerning

Thyatira grew in love, faith, service and endurance, yet tolerated a self-appointed prophetess teaching compromise. Christ gave her time to repent; to the faithful he lays no other burden than to hold fast until he comes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a guild town, her teaching offered relief with a spiritual justification.

Now: The faithful in a compromised church are not asked to fix it, only to hold on, and they are promised the morning star.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: 'The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. "'I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God, whose eyes miss nothing, sees and praises a church that is growing in love. Thyatira is warmer and busier for him than it was at first, and he says so before anything else.

The words of the Son of God. The title (ho huios tou theou) appears only here in Revelation. In a city that honoured Apollo and the emperor as sons of Zeus, Christ declares himself the true Son of God, echoing Psalm 2, quoted in vv. 26–27. The least celebrated town receives the longest letter, from the highest title in the book.

Eyes like a flame of fire. From John’s first vision (1:14): eyes that see through every disguise, chosen for this church because Thyatira’s problem is hidden inside a congregation that looks healthy from outside. He will search minds and hearts (v. 23).

Feet like burnished bronze. In a town of metalworkers: refined bronze out of the furnace, shining and hard. Feet that stand firm and trample evil.

The setting. Thyatira, southeast of Pergamum, was probably the least important of the seven cities: no great temple, no governor, no natural defences. It was a centre of manufacturing, and inscriptions show an unusual number of trade guilds there, among them wool-workers, dyers, potters and bronze-smiths; Lydia, the seller of purple cloth, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). Each guild had a patron god and held feasts in its honour, and membership was almost necessary for anyone who wanted to work. The city’s chief god, Apollo, was worshipped as son of Zeus.

Love and faith and service and patient endurance. Among the warmest commendations given to any church. Love (agapēn) produces service (diakonian); faith (pistin) produces patient endurance (hypomonēn). The very things Ephesus lacked, Thyatira had in abundance.

Your latter works exceed the first. Unlike Ephesus, which had declined from its first love, Thyatira was growing. The Son of God turns his blazing eyes on a small manufacturing town and finds love there, and says so first. He notices growth that no historian recorded.

Which is more dangerous, cold orthodoxy or warm tolerance? Both, and that is the point. A church can be warm, caring and growing, and still be in serious danger: warmth is no substitute for discernment, any more than discernment was for warmth at Ephesus. Most of us are sure which is the real peril, and that the failing we see in others is the serious one. Chapter 2 rebukes both, in neighbouring letters, from the same eyes of fire. Whichever you find easy to condemn is probably not the letter written to you. The goal is not a midpoint between truth and love but the fullness of both, as in Christ, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira was a town of trade guilds, whose feasts honoured pagan gods. Lydia came from there.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ holds his church responsible for letting a self-appointed prophetess lead his people into sin. He has patiently given her time to turn; she has refused, and his patience has a limit.

You tolerate that woman Jezebel. The verb aimed at the church is tolerate (apheis, let alone). Nobody is accused of believing her; they are accused of letting her go on teaching. Jezebel is almost certainly a symbolic name, as we might call someone a Judas, for a real and probably influential woman in the church whose teaching had the old Jezebel’s effect.

The setting. Jezebel was the Phoenician wife of King Ahab (1 Kings 16:31). She promoted Baal worship, killed the LORD’s prophets, arranged a judicial murder for a vineyard, and led Israel into idolatry, which Scripture calls whoredom and sorcery (1 Kings 18:4, 19; 21:1–16; 2 Kings 9:22). She was the Old Testament’s great example of a powerful person leading God’s people into false worship from inside.

Who calls herself a prophetess and is seducing my servants. “Calls herself” (hē legousa heautēn): she appointed herself, and the church had not tested it, as Ephesus did (v. 2). Claiming to speak for God made her hard to challenge. And she was seducing (plana, leading astray, the word used of Satan, who deceives the whole world, 12:9) not outsiders but my servants, Christ’s own people.

Balaam’s programme again. She teaches what Balaam taught in v. 14, idol food and sexual immorality, now with a prophet’s authority: probably that Christians could join the guild feasts, perhaps because the deep things of Satan could not harm a truly spiritual person (v. 24).

Why nobody confronted her. Her doctrine solved a real problem: if the evening at the temple is only a formality, a cloth-dyer can keep his guild membership and his contracts. She was offering not vice but relief, with a spiritual justification attached. It is very hard to confront someone who is telling frightened people what they urgently want to be true.

I gave her time to repent. Time (chronon): Christ had been patient, perhaps through warnings from the church, perhaps simply by his own forbearance (Romans 2:4). The delay was not indifference. But the second verb is in the present tense: she refuses, and goes on refusing (ou thelei, does not want to). Her problem is not ignorance but an unwilling heart. She has been given room, she knows what it is for, and she goes on saying no. Mercy refused long enough does not become permanent tolerance; it runs out, and the next verse shows what that looks like.

The prophet who did not call himself. Jezebel appointed herself. Christ is the true Prophet Moses foretold (Deuteronomy 18:15), whose teaching was not his own but the Father’s (John 7:16–18). She offered a freedom that left people in their sins; he sets people free indeed (John 8:36). And she was seducing people he had freed by his blood (1:5). The anger in this letter is the anger of a Redeemer watching what he bought being stolen.

Delay is not always absence. The years in which the false teaching flourished were years the Lord was holding open: what looked like God ignoring an outrage was God waiting for a woman to turn. He is not slow, as some count slowness, but patient (2 Peter 3:9). Sometimes the silence a believer finds unbearable is mercy extended to somebody he has written off. Sometimes it is extended to him.

Are there prophets like this today, and how should I treat someone who claims a word from God? The apostles and prophets laid the foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon complete, this commentary holds, charitably, that the revelatory gift of prophecy has ceased; many sincere believers disagree, and they are brothers and sisters. Many continuationists (who hold that the gift continues) agree that any prophecy today must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it. Either way, anyone claiming a word from God must be tested by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). A message that makes sin acceptable, contradicts Scripture, or adds a requirement or freedom the Bible does not give is not from God, however impressive the speaker. You need not be unkind; you do need to say no.

In everyday life. If you find yourself drawn to a teacher mainly because he or she tells you what you want to hear about your money, your body or your comfort, take that as a warning sign rather than a confirmation.

Where Christians differ: does this passage forbid women from teaching? Some use it against women preaching; others say it shows women prophesied and taught, and the problem was only false teaching. This commentary’s view: Jezebel is rebuked for false teaching and immorality, not for being a woman who spoke. Scripture recognises women who prophesied (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5), and church office is settled elsewhere. This commentary holds the complementarian view that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), while women serve in many vital ministries; many faithful Christians read those passages differently, and they are brothers and sisters. The lesson here is for every teacher, male or female: no claim to speak for God licenses contradicting his word. The same teaching was condemned at Pergamum with no reference to anyone’s sex, and the parallel there is Balaam, a man.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ will judge those who refuse to turn from false teaching and its sin, so that every church learns that he sees the heart. Yet even in the sentence of judgment the door of repentance stands open.

A sickbed. The bed (klinēn) is also the couch on which the guild banquets were eaten and the sin committed: the bed she chose becomes the bed she cannot leave (compare 1 Corinthians 11:30). And throw is the verb used of the devil throwing believers into prison at Smyrna (v. 10): a different hand, a different purpose.

Unless they repent. Those who commit adultery with her are those who follow her teaching. And there is the door, standing open in the middle of the sentence of judgment. Even now, with the verdict pronounced, anyone who will turn may turn. Christ’s warnings are meant to bring people back.

Strike her children dead. This is the sentence that makes readers flinch, and like the old Jezebel’s terrible end (2 Kings 9:30–37) it should not be waved away. First, “her children” (ta tekna autēs) are not her literal sons and daughters but, in an Old Testament way of speaking, her spiritual offspring: followers who have taken her teaching so deeply into themselves that they pass it on. The verse distinguishes those who commit adultery with her, who may still repent, from her children, who have become her. Second, this severe judgment on those who refuse to turn (on the wording, see the end of this note) is what Scripture consistently says is the end of persistent, chosen rebellion. Christ is not more severe here than the New Testament elsewhere; he simply says it more directly.

He who searches mind and heart. Searches (eraunōn) means examines. Mind and heart is literally kidneys and hearts (nephrous kai kardias): in Hebrew thinking the kidneys, deepest in the body, held the deepest emotions, and the heart thought and will. It echoes the claim God makes for himself alone: “I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways” (Jeremiah 17:10). Christ takes the LORD’s role. He sees what a person cannot reach in himself, beneath any show of spirituality, and he says so to a church that could not tell a prophetess from a fraud. That is terror to the hypocrite and rest to the believer, for the one who sees everything bore our sins and still holds the door of repentance open in the very sentence of judgment.

According to your works. A principle of judgment throughout Scripture (Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Is that not salvation by works? Scripture says both: no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done. They answer different questions. Nobody is accepted by God on the strength of his works; works show whom he belongs to, and God rewards them. Fruit does not make a tree alive, but fruit is how a living tree is known.

Each of you. Verses 20 to 23 have been about her and them; the last clause turns to each of you, putting the whole congregation, one by one, in front of the eyes of fire.

Does God still send sickness as judgment today? He can, and Scripture records it (Acts 5:1–11; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but we are never given the right to read it into another person’s illness. Most sickness is simply part of living in a fallen world, and the godliest believers suffer it (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; 1 Timothy 5:23). If you are ill and your conscience is troubled about a specific, unrepented sin, confess it to God and put it right, and receive his forgiveness (James 5:15–16). If your conscience is clear, do not let anyone burden you with the idea that your illness is punishment. For those in Christ, even discipline is a Father’s love, never condemnation (Hebrews 12:6; Romans 8:1).

In everyday life. Being searched to the heart is frightening only as long as we are hiding something. If a persuasive voice has drawn you into sin, his sentence still contains the words unless they repent. Turning to him today is easier than tomorrow.

Uncertain wording. Strike dead is literally kill with death (apoktenō en thanatō). In the Greek Old Testament the word death often stands for the Hebrew word for pestilence, and Revelation uses it so in 6:8, so the phrase probably means kill with a deadly plague; it may simply be an emphatic way of saying put to death. Either way it is a severe judgment on those who refuse to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ lays no new burden on the faithful in a compromised church: they are simply to hold on to the gospel they have until he comes. He sees through the flattering offer of deeper secrets, and he will deal with the false teaching himself.

The rest of you in Thyatira. The tone changes completely. Christ addresses separately those who had quietly refused, which is itself a kindness. He knows exactly who had said no.

The setting. Second-century Gnostic groups boasted of knowing the deep things, secret knowledge for the initiated, and some taught that the truly spiritual could indulge the body without harm. Jezebel’s teaching seems an early form of this.

No other burden. This sentence is for anyone who is tired. Burden (baros) echoes the Jerusalem council, which laid on Gentile believers no greater burden than to abstain from idol food and immorality (Acts 15:28–29). Christ adds no new requirement, no secret knowledge, no campaign to purge the church; he will deal with Jezebel himself. Believers in difficult churches who feel answerable for every error nobody else confronts are carrying a weight they were never given. The letter puts it where it belongs: on the one with the eyes of fire.

Hold fast until I come. That is the one thing: not advance or reform, but hold (kratēsate), gripping what they already have, the apostolic gospel. And there is a time limit: until I come, the first clear mention in the letters of his final coming. A believer is not asked to grip in the dark for ever; he is asked to grip until a specific person arrives, and that person is already on his way.

How do I hold fast? The grip Christ asks for is less clenched teeth than a child holding a father’s hand, and the father is holding too (John 10:28–29). What you hold is not a feeling but “what you have”, the gospel. Keep hearing it where the gospel is preached and the Lord’s Supper given (Romans 10:17). Say it back to yourself: Christ died for my sins, he rose, he is coming. Keep the small habits of prayer and Scripture even when they feel thin; Thyatira was asked not for heroics, only not to let go. Decline the shiny offer that makes the old gospel seem small. Hold on together, near believers who will notice if you drift (Hebrews 3:13). Your hold will sometimes slacken. His never does, and that is why yours lasts.

Should I stay in a church where error is tolerated, or leave? Christ told the faithful in Thyatira not to leave but to hold fast, and said he would deal with Jezebel himself. So do not leave lightly, nor make yourself responsible for fixing everything: speak the truth when you can, keep your own faith clean, pray and wait. But if the leaders themselves deny the gospel or require you to accept sin, and will not listen, it may become right to go to a faithful church, especially for your children’s sake. Thyatira still had a true congregation; not every building with a cross on it does.

How do I recognise a deep things offer today? Every generation produces some version of it, and it always flatters. It promises insight ordinary Christians lack, through a special teacher, technique, experience or method. It makes the plain commands of Scripture seem childish or optional for the mature. And it tells you that you are freer and more enlightened than people still worried about holiness. Real growth looks different: deeper humility, simpler trust in Christ, greater love, and more obedience to the plain things. If something new makes the old gospel seem small, it is not from God.

Uncertain wording. “What some call the deep things of Satan” can be read two ways. Christ may be repeating the faction’s slogan with one word changed: they were very likely advertising the deep things (ta bathea) of God (1 Corinthians 2:10), an advanced spirituality that could walk through the guild feast untouched, and Christ changes “God” to “Satan”, and the boast collapses. Or they claimed that exploring sin from the inside, the deep things of Satan, was a mark of maturity. Either way, Christ calls the teaching by its real name.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who hold on to Christ to the end will share his rule over the nations, and, best of all, they will have Christ himself. Believers with no power at all are promised the Messiah’s own inheritance.

Keeps my works until the end. My works (ta erga mou) stand over against Jezebel’s works (v. 22): the two ways through life in a guild town. Until the end: conquering means lasting to the end (see the note on vv. 6–7).

Authority over the nations. The longest and strangest promise goes to the least important town. Christians in Thyatira had no power at all; some had lost their guild membership and could not work. To them Christ promises a share in his rule over the nations (3:21; 20:4–6; 22:5; 1 Corinthians 6:2–3).

A rod of iron. Verses 26 and 27 quote Psalm 2, where the nations rage against the LORD and his anointed King, his Son, and God says: “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8); the King will break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel (Psalm 2:9). Rule (poimanei) is literally “shepherd”, though here the rod is used in judgment. Thyatira’s potters knew that a fired pot can only be broken, not reshaped. Opposition to Christ will be utterly broken.

Even as I myself have received authority from my Father. Psalm 2 is about the Messiah, and Christ shares its promise with his people: the authority the Father gave him (Matthew 28:18) he gives to those who conquer, as the Son shares his inheritance with the sons of God (Romans 8:17). The church’s authority is never its own (12:5; 19:15). And the King of Psalm 2 did not take the nations by breaking them first. He let himself be broken, and the Father gave him the nations as the reward of his obedience (Philippians 2:8–9). Now he shares that inheritance with dyers and potters who lost their guild places for his name.

The morning star. Every other promise in the letters is a thing: a tree, a crown, a stone, a name, a pillar, a throne. This one is a person. The morning star (ton astera ton prōinon), the planet Venus, shines before dawn announcing the day, and the last chapter says who it is: “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (22:16). Behind it stands Balaam’s own prophecy, a fine irony in a letter about his teaching: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). Christ is that royal star. Roman generals are said to have honoured Venus as the star of victory, but Christ is the true sign of triumph.

The star that means the sun is coming. The morning star shines brightest in the last hour of the night, and it means the sun is coming. So the last word to Thyatira is not authority after all. To a congregation holding on until he comes, the final promise is that he will give them himself. Every other reward is something from his hand; this one is the hand. Every believer who has held on in a difficult church, in an unremarkable town, doing work nobody recorded, has been looking at the same light.

What it does not mean. Ruling with a rod of iron does not mean Christians now seek political power to impose the faith. Christ breaks his enemies by his word and at his coming. Our part now is faithful witness.

What does reigning with Christ look like now, in an ordinary life? Mostly what it looked like in Thyatira: faithfulness without power. Believers are already seated with Christ (Ephesians 2:6), and share his rule as his word goes out and the nations are discipled (Matthew 28:18–20): praying with authority for the world, refusing to bow to the market’s idols, standing for truth, serving as he served, overcoming evil with good (Romans 12:21). It does not look like dominance. The authority is real, but for now it wears the shape of the cross, and it will be seen openly when he comes.

Will the saints really judge and rule? Yes. Scripture says the saints will judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:2–3), and will reign with Christ for ever (22:5). We do not know all that this involves, but the weak and despised of this age will be honoured with responsibility in the age to come, under Christ and in perfect agreement with his justice. It is not revenge but the restoration of the dominion God gave Adam at the beginning (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6), now held in Christ, the true and better Adam.

In everyday life. If you feel powerless, holding on in a small place, keep doing the plain obedient things his Spirit is working in you. He rose while it was still dark, and the day is coming.

Where Christians differ: when do believers rule the nations? Premillennialists, dispensational Christians among them, see this fulfilled in a future thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns, reading Revelation 20 as following chapter 19 in time; many godly believers hold this view. This commentary’s view: this commentary is amillennial.
