Revelation often retells the same age from different angles, and the New Testament places the resurrection and judgment of all together at Christ’s one return (John 5:28–29), so the thousand years picture the present age. Believers already share Christ’s reign in a hidden way, as a kingdom of priests (1:6), and those who die in Christ reign with him now in heaven (20:4–6). The rule over the nations is completed at his return, when his enemies are judged (19:15) and his people reign with him for ever in the new creation (22:5). There is no separate future millennium on earth, though those who expect one share the hope that matters most: Christ will return in person and reign.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.<sup>2</sup>”‘I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false.<sup>3</sup>I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.<sup>4</sup>But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.<sup>5</sup>Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.<sup>6</sup>Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.<sup>7</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’<sup>8</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life.<sup>9</sup>”‘I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.<sup>10</sup>Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.<sup>11</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.’<sup>12</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword.<sup>13</sup>”‘I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.<sup>14</sup>But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality.<sup>15</sup>So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.<sup>16</sup>Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’<sup>18</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze.<sup>19</sup>”‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.<sup>20</sup>But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.<sup>21</sup>I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works,<sup>23</sup>and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.<sup>24</sup>But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden.<sup>25</sup>Only hold fast what you have until I come.<sup>26</sup>The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations,<sup>27</sup>and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father.<sup>28</sup>And I will give him the morning star.<sup>29</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

keyVerse.quote: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
keyVerse.note: The four letters ask for different things, love rekindled, endurance, repentance, holding fast, but all of them come down to this: stay loyal to Christ whatever it costs. The command comes from the faithful witness who was himself obedient to death and came to life, so the crown he promises is his to give. Every promise to the one who conquers is gathered up in it.

2.reflection:
Christ begins every letter with “I know”. What in his knowledge of these four churches do you find most comforting, and what most searching? How does it help that the one who knows everything is the one who holds the churches in his right hand?

Ephesus was right but cold; Thyatira was warm but tolerated error. Which danger is your church, and you yourself, more likely to fall into, and which do you find easier to condemn in others? What would it look like to be full of both grace and truth?

Smyrna was told that suffering was coming, but that it had a limit and a purpose (v. 10). How does that change the way you face hardship for your faith, and the way you pray for believers in prison today?

Balaam and Jezebel offered believers a way to keep their place at the guild table. Where are you asked for a small pinch of incense, at work, among friends or online, and which of Christ’s promises in this chapter helps you to say no?

3.title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 completes the seven letters of the risen Christ (2:1–3:22) with Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, the last stops on the courier’s road, and leads straight into the open door of heaven in chapter 4.

The message. Christ’s verdict on a church is not its reputation. The church with a name for being alive is dead; the church with little power is the one he has loved and will keep; the church that says “I need nothing” is poor, blind and naked. Yet he speaks to all three in order to save them.

Why it was said. The churches faced pressure and comfort alike (see the introduction). Philadelphia, small and denounced by its local synagogue, needed to know that Christ was for it. Sardis and Laodicea faced no persecution; comfort had done what pressure could not, and they needed the truth about themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. Each letter has the same shape: a title of Christ, a verdict, a call, and a promise to the one who conquers. To Sardis (vv. 1–6) he calls a dead church to wake, remember and repent, and promises the faithful few white garments and a name never blotted out. To Philadelphia (vv. 7–13) the holder of the key of David sets an open door before a weak church, promises to vindicate and keep it, and makes it pillars in God’s temple. To Laodicea (vv. 14–22) the Amen exposes a useless, self-sufficient church, counsels it to buy from him, explains his rebuke as love, and knocks.

Where it leads. In every letter the cure is Christ himself: the one who was dead speaks to a dead church; the key-holder opens what no one can shut; the Amen offers riches bought at his own cost. The chapter ends with the highest promise of all given to the worst church, a seat on his throne, “as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne” (v. 21). The Lord who will come with the clouds (1:7) is the same one who stands knocking at a single door (v. 20).

For us. The seven letters are a mirror in which any church, and any believer, can find itself; seven, the number of completeness, makes them a portrait of the church in every age. Ask which of these churches you most resemble, and listen to the one who says to each, “I know your works”, and who knocks, still, at any door that will open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — To the Church in Sardis
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church can have a name for being alive and be dead, and only the life-giving word of Christ can wake it. He comes as the one who holds the Spirit and the churches, and gives the bluntest verdict in the letters, with no heresy or persecution in sight (v. 1). He calls Sardis to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember the gospel it received and repent, or he will come like a thief, as attackers twice took the city by its unwatched cliff (vv. 2–3). Yet he counts the few who have not soiled their garments, and promises white clothing, a name never blotted out of the book of life, and his own confession of their name before his Father (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Name for Being Alive

Sardis had a reputation for life and was dead. Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember and repent, and he counts the few who have not soiled their garments.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The city had twice fallen to a night climb while the guards slept.

Now: Ask whether the reasons you would give for your church’s health are reasons Sardis could have given.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: 'The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ, who gives the Spirit and holds the churches, tells Sardis that its reputation for life hides a dead church. His eyes see past what everyone says about a congregation to what is actually there.

The seven spirits and the seven stars. The seven spirits are the one Holy Spirit in all his fullness (1:4), who gives life, and a dead church needs nothing so much as him. The seven stars are the churches held in Christ’s hand (1:16, 20): this church is still his. Jesus said the hour was already here when the dead would hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear would live (John 5:25). This letter is that voice, spoken into a congregation with a name and no pulse.

A name for being alive. The bluntest verdict in the seven letters. The reputation (onoma, name) is real: the congregation is well regarded, busy enough to be admired across a province. Yet it is dead (nekros). There is no heresy here, no Jezebel, no persecution; Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned, perhaps because there was nothing worth attacking. It had the appearance of godliness but denied its power (2 Timothy 3:5). Christ describes not an empty building but a full one, with nothing inside. A body laid out with its hands folded can look, from the doorway, very much like a man asleep.

The setting. Sardis, south-east of Thyatira, had been the capital of Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for his wealth. Its acropolis was thought impregnable, yet it fell twice by surprise (see vv. 2–3). Rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 17, by John’s day it was prosperous but living on its past glory, with a large Jewish community and a great temple of Artemis. The church had caught the city’s condition: a famous name, and little life.

He has been dead himself. The one who writes to a dead church walked out of a sealed tomb with the keys of Death and Hades in his hand (1:18). Sardis had a famous name and a quiet grave; he has the name above every name and an empty one. No congregation is so far gone that his voice cannot reach it.

Living inside the reputation. The eyes that wrote this letter are the eyes of flame from 1:14, and they do not read reviews. This is the hardest church to diagnose from inside, because the evidence a member would reach for, our history and what people say about us, is the very thing being contradicted. Reputation is one of the heart’s favourite substitutes for God: it lets a person, or a church, feel alive on other people’s good opinion. The cure is not to despise what others think but to care more about what Christ sees.

How can I tell whether a church, or my own faith, is alive? Not by activity or reputation, which Sardis had, but by the marks of the Spirit. Is Christ himself loved and spoken of, or only the church’s programmes and history? Is God’s word believed, preached and obeyed? Is there real repentance when sin is exposed, rather than management of appearances? Is there prayer that expects God to act, and love that costs something? Are people being brought to faith and growing? If these are absent for years, the name is outliving the life.
verseByVerse.note: Sardis had been a great royal city. Its seemingly impregnable citadel was taken by surprise more than once in its history.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ calls the sleeping church to wake, hold on to the gospel it first received and repent, before he comes upon it without warning. The remedy for a dead reputation is not more activity but the old message taken to heart again.

Wake up. The first of five commands governs the rest. “Wake up” (ginou grēgorōn) means become watchful and stay alert: a lasting watchfulness, not a single act. It is an odd thing to say to a corpse, the first hint that “dead” in verse 1 is a verdict on the congregation as a whole, not on every member; verse 4 confirms that a few are alive.

Strengthen what remains. There is something left. Strengthen (stērison) means brace: put your weight under what is still standing, a handful who still pray, a half-abandoned practice, a doctrine still confessed without conviction.

Not complete in the sight of my God. Not wrong, not false, but unfilled (peplērōmena): outwardly correct, inwardly empty. In the sight of the province their works were finished enough to build a reputation on. Two audiences, two verdicts, and only God sees the inside.

Remember, keep it, and repent. As at Ephesus (2:5), the remedy is memory. Received (eilēphas) and heard (ēkousas) are the words used for the apostles’ gospel being handed on (1 Corinthians 15:1–3). Sardis does not need a new message; it needs the old one to mean something again. Keep on keeping it (tērei), and turn round (metanoēson): this church still possesses the truth and has stopped being changed by it.

If you will not wake up. Christ turns the city’s own history into a warning. Sardis stood on sheer cliffs and was thought impregnable, yet it fell twice the same way. In 546 BC, Herodotus tells, a soldier of Cyrus watched a defender climb down for a dropped helmet, noted the route and led a party up it; in 214 BC a Cretan climber did the same at night. Twice Sardis lost everything because nobody was watching the one place that did not seem to need watching. The city’s old fault has become the church’s.

Like a thief. Unexpectedly, as Jesus warned (Matthew 24:42–44) and Paul repeated (1 Thessalonians 5:2–6). It may mean a judgment on Sardis in history, or Christ’s final return (16:15). Elsewhere his coming is the church’s hope (2:25; 3:11); here it is a threat: “I will come against you.” The event is the same; what differs is which side of the wall you are on. For the watchful it is no threat (1 Thessalonians 5:4), and he sounds the alarm in advance so that those who wake may meet him as the bridegroom they long for.

The one whose works were complete. The one giving this verdict speaks of “my God”, as he did on the cross (Matthew 27:46) and on the morning he rose (John 20:17), and he alone has ever stood before that God with works filled to the brim. He finished the work the Father gave him (John 17:4), and with his last breath said that it was finished (John 19:30). That is why the remedy is memory, not effort. What Sardis received was the news of that finished work: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). A church with half-done works is cured not by doing more of them but by going back to the one whose work needs nothing added. His obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9), so that even their unfinished works are accepted for his sake.

What it does not mean. Coming like a thief means unexpectedly, not secretly. Many earnest Christians expect a secret rapture, and they love his appearing; but the New Testament uses the thief picture of the one visible return (1 Thessalonians 5:2–4; 2 Peter 3:10). Every eye will see him (1:7); those not watching will be caught unprepared, as Sardis was by its enemies.

What does staying awake look like in an ordinary week? Not anxious date-setting or constant intensity, but the steady habits of someone who expects his Lord. Pray, including for his coming (22:20); keep listening to God’s word, alone and with his people; deal with sin while it is small. Ask where your unguarded cliff is: the one area of life you have assumed needs no watching. And stay among believers who will tell you the truth about yourself (Hebrews 3:13). Spiritual sleep rarely starts with a decision to stop believing; it starts with a hundred small neglects that each seemed harmless.

What if I have already drifted asleep? Then this letter is for you, and it begins with hope: something remains, and Christ is speaking because he means to wake you. Do not wait to feel alive; do what he says, in his order. Remember the gospel, hold on to it, and turn back to him in plain repentance, naming what put you to sleep. Then strengthen what is left: go back to church, open the Bible, pray, and tell a mature Christian where you are. Sleepers are woken one call at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in a dead church Christ knows his faithful few by name, and he promises every conqueror white garments, a name that can never be erased, and his own confession of that name before the Father. None of the three is earned; each is his gift.

A few names in Sardis. Names (onomata), the same word as the church’s reputation in verse 1. The shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3) is counting them one at a time.

People who have not soiled their garments. Soiled (emolynan) is stained. Clothing pictures a life (Jude 23; Zechariah 3:3–5): these few had not been stained by compromise. Sardis was famous for its wool and dyeing, and in the ancient world a soiled robe could bar a worshipper from a temple. Whatever kept them clean was probably unremarkable and unrewarded at the time. But Christ was watching, and he answers with three promises.

Walk with me in white. The first is fellowship: they will share the company of Christ. White was worn at festivals and victories, and in this book it is the dress of heaven (6:11; 7:9; 19:14). Worthy (axioi) is not a claim about merit. Four chapters later the robes are washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Blood does not whiten cloth: the impossible picture is deliberate, and it shows that the whiteness comes from Christ’s death, not from them. Their lives fit the gift; they did not earn it, and even the fine linen of 19:8 is granted to the bride, not woven by her. And every conqueror, not only the few in Sardis, will be clothed so, in the robe of righteousness that Christ gives (Isaiah 61:10).

Never blot his name out. The second promise, with the strongest negative in Greek (ou mē). Cities erased a name from the citizen register at death or disgrace. The book of life (biblou tēs zōēs) is God’s register of those who belong to him, an idea that goes back to Exodus 32:32–33, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1, and in this book its names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). The register that matters is not kept in Sardis, and no scribe anywhere has authority to reach it.

I will confess his name. The third promise, and the best. Confess (homologēsō) is acknowledge openly, echoing Jesus’ word that whoever acknowledges him before men, he will acknowledge before his Father (Matthew 10:32). A believer whose faithfulness nobody recorded will one day hear his name said aloud by Jesus Christ before the Father and the angels.

Names that matter, white bought with red. Sardis had a name and no life; these few had life and no name. He will speak their names where a name is worth having, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The Lamb whose book it is was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37) and cut off from the land of the living (Isaiah 53:8), so that the names in his book would never be cut off. The white he gives was bought with red, and not one name in his book will be missing on the day he reads it.

How can I know my name is written in the book of life? You cannot read the book, but you can see its fruit. Names were written by God’s free choice before the world began (Ephesians 1:4), and the evidence that yours is there is that you have come to Christ: you trust him alone for forgiveness, you love him, however weakly, and you want to follow him (John 6:37; 2 Peter 1:10). Look for assurance not in a feeling or a past decision alone but in Christ. Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20), a joy meant for ordinary believers.

What if I have been ashamed of Christ in the past? Then remember Peter. He denied Jesus three times with oaths; Jesus restored him three times by a charcoal fire (John 21:15–19); and he went on to confess Christ before the council and, at the last, in his death. The promise is not for those who have never failed, but for those who come back and keep confessing him. If fear has kept you quiet, confess it to him; he forgives it. Then take the next opportunity to own him, gently and plainly. Your past silence does not cancel his present welcome.

Where Christians differ: can a name be blotted out of the book of life? Arminian Christians (who hold that a true believer can finally fall away), many of them earnest and godly, read this verse as implying that believers who fail to persevere can have their names erased and lose their salvation, pointing to texts that speak of blotting out (Exodus 32:33; Psalm 69:28) and to the warning of Revelation 22:19. This commentary’s view: the verse is a promise, not a threat. Christ never says he blots anyone out; he says he will never do it. Names in the Lamb’s book were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8), so those who belong to Christ cannot be removed. Those who never persevere show that they were never truly written (1 John 2:19). The warnings in these letters are the means God uses to keep his people persevering; the promises assure them that he will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — To the Church in Philadelphia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Weakness is no barrier to Christ’s approval: the church with little power that keeps his word receives no rebuke and some of the richest promises. Christ comes as the holy and true one who holds the key of David (v. 7), and sets before this small church, shut out by its local synagogue, an open door no one can shut (v. 8). Its accusers will learn that he has loved it (v. 9), and he will keep it in the hour of trial coming on the whole world (vv. 10–11). In a city often shaken by earthquakes, the conqueror will be a pillar in God’s temple, never to go out, bearing the names of God, of the new Jerusalem and of Christ himself (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Little Power, No Rebuke

Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before a weak church that has kept his word. Its accusers will learn that he has loved it; the faithful will be pillars in the temple of God and bear his names.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A small congregation in an earthquake town had been told it had no share in the promises.

Now: Christ measures a church by faithfulness, not size.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. "I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy and true Christ, who alone decides who enters God’s house, has opened a door for this weak but faithful church that no one can shut. He names its little power without a word of rebuke, because it has kept his word.

The words of the holy one, the true one. These titles, unusually, are not drawn from chapter 1. The holy one (ho hagios) is God’s own title: “To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One” (Isaiah 40:25). The true one (ho alēthinos) is the genuine, as against the counterfeit. To a congregation told by the synagogue across the street that it was not the real people of God, the sender is the Real One, the Holy One of Israel himself. That is why no one can shut what he has opened.

The key of David. Quoted almost word for word from Isaiah 22:22, where the key of the house of David, the steward’s badge of authority over who is admitted to the king’s house, is laid on Eliakim’s shoulder. Christ, David’s greater son, decides who enters the kingdom. Whoever in Philadelphia claimed the right to say who was in, the decision was made elsewhere.

An open door. Two meanings fit: the door into the kingdom (thyran ēneōgmenēn), held open for a congregation told it had no right of entry, and a door for the word, as Paul used the phrase (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3), fitting a city on the road inland. The church put out of the synagogue has been given a door nobody can close, and a door out into the world besides.

But little power, and yet you have kept my word. Small in numbers, influence and resources (mikran dynamin), and faithful. Christ neither rebukes their size nor tells them to grow; he names the weakness as a fact. Weakness is not failure. Of the two churches in which he finds nothing to criticise, one was poor and hunted and the other small and weak.

The setting. Philadelphia, south-east of Sardis, was the youngest of the seven cities, named after Attalus II, called Philadelphus (lover of his brother). It stood at the gateway to the high plateau of Phrygia and is often said to have been founded to spread Greek culture eastward: a city with an open door. Wrecked by the earthquake of AD 17, whose aftershocks drove many to live outside the walls, it was rebuilt with help from Tiberius. Like Smyrna, the church faced hostility from the local synagogue.

Is a small church a failing church? No. Philadelphia is the letter written to every church of thirty people in a place nobody has heard of, holding on, keeping the word, and quietly convinced that God is at work somewhere else with more resources; and it contains no rebuke at all. Size is not the measure Christ uses. A small church should still pray for growth and walk through the doors God opens, but it should not despise itself. Christ does not.

How do I know which door God has opened for me? Usually by looking at the people and opportunities already in front of you, rather than waiting for a dramatic sign. Paul saw open doors where people were ready to listen, even amid many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9). Who around you is asking questions, going through a hard time, or open to friendship? Pray for opportunities (Colossians 4:3), then take the small ones: an invitation, an honest answer, an offer of help in Christ’s name. If one door closes, it was not the only door. Christ holds the key, and he does not run out of doors.
verseByVerse.note: Philadelphia was a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

parallels.desc: he shall open, and none shall shut

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ promises that the church’s accusers will one day acknowledge that he has loved it, and that because it has endured he will keep it through the coming hour of worldwide trial. Meanwhile it must hold fast, for he is coming soon.

The synagogue of Satan. As at Smyrna (2:9), the phrase needs a guard: this is not a statement about Jewish people. The writer and his Lord were Jews, and Paul longed and prayed for the salvation of his kinsmen (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1). The charge concerns one group in one town denouncing its Christian neighbours: by rejecting the Messiah and persecuting his people, they had forfeited the name, and their claim was a lie (pseudontai).

Bow down before your feet. Isaiah prophesied that the nations who oppressed Israel would bow at Israel’s feet (Isaiah 45:14; 49:23; 60:14). Here the roles are reversed: Christ applies the promise to a small congregation of Gentile and Jewish believers, not abolishing it but showing who the true Israel turns out to be, as Paul argues in Romans 9 to 11, where he also holds out hope for ethnic Israel (Romans 11:25–29). Bow down (proskynēsousin) is not worship of the church but acknowledgement that it is God’s people, whether through their conversion (Romans 11:11–14) or at the judgment, when every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11).

They will learn that I have loved you. The point of the bowing is not humiliation: the sentence ends not with “before your feet” but with this. Loved (ēgapēsa) points to a love already shown in a deed, and this book has named the deed: “To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood” (1:5). It also echoes Isaiah 43:4, where the LORD tells Israel that they are precious in his eyes and that he loves them. The love the synagogue claimed for itself belongs to the despised church. The vindication promised is not that its opponents will be crushed but that they will find out the truth: not that Philadelphia was right, but that Philadelphia was loved.

My word about patient endurance. However the phrase is taken (see “Uncertain wording” below), it points to Christ’s own endurance. Before he asked any church to endure, he endured. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), endured hostility from sinners, and for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2–3). Dared to come down from the cross, he stayed (Matthew 27:40–42). Philadelphia’s endurance is not a strength it has to find in itself but a share in his (2 Thessalonians 3:5), which is why the promise that follows rests on his keeping, not theirs.

I will keep you from the hour of trial. Keep from (tērēsō ek) is guard from, with a play on words: because you have kept my word, I will keep you. The hour of trial (tēs hōras tou peirasmou) is the testing of the whole world that the seals, trumpets and bowls describe (on whether the keeping means being taken out of the world, see “Where Christians differ” below).

Those who dwell on the earth. Throughout Revelation this phrase means unbelievers, the world in rebellion against God (6:10; 13:8; 17:8). The trial is aimed at them, not at the church.

So that no one may seize your crown. First the promise, “I am coming soon” (tachy), repeated three times in the last chapter (22:7, 12, 20). Then, as to Thyatira, the instruction: hold (kratei, grip). Someone may seize (labē) the crown (stephanon), as a rival takes an athlete’s wreath; it is already theirs in promise, and worth guarding.

Not spared his hour. There was an hour from which the Son would not ask to be kept: “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:27–28). Because he was not spared his hour, his people are kept in theirs. The crown he holds out was won under a crown of thorns, and he will not let anyone take theirs.

If Christ keeps his people in the hour of trial, why do Christians still suffer? Because the keeping is protection from what would destroy them, not exemption from all pain. The believers in Revelation are sealed so that God’s judgments do not fall on them (7:3; 9:4), yet they are hated and sometimes killed by the beast (13:7). Christ guarantees that nothing will separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39), that their faith will not finally fail (Luke 22:32), and that they will never face God’s wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). If you are suffering, you have not been left out of the promise; you are being kept inside the storm, as the disciples were kept in the boat. Ask him not to remove you but to keep you; and if you are opposed for your faith, do not strike back, but pray that your opponents will learn that Christ loves you by coming to love him too.

Could someone really take my crown? Not by force against Christ’s will, since no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). Like a parent’s warning, it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people holding on. A crown can be seized only by letting go of the one who gives it, which is what false teachers, persecutors and the lure of an easier life invite us to do. The true believer hears it and grips harder, and that gripping is the evidence of the grace that keeps him. Take the warning seriously, and the promise more seriously still.

Where Christians differ: is this a promise of a pre-tribulation rapture? Dispensationalists (who see distinct purposes of God for Israel and the church) read “keep you from the hour of trial” as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth before a final seven-year tribulation. Teachers such as John Walvoord and Charles Ryrie argued it with care, and the argument has real force: the promise is deliverance from an hour, not merely from harm within it, and the trial is explicitly worldwide. This commentary’s view: the same words appear in John 17:15, where Jesus prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one. To keep from is to protect within, not to remove from. Revelation consistently shows God’s people sealed and protected in the midst of the judgments (7:3; 9:4; 12:6, 14), while they still suffer at the hands of the beast. The promise was made to a church in the first century, which was never raptured; it was preserved. God protects his people from his wrath and from losing their faith, not from all suffering. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

Uncertain wording. “My word about patient endurance” is literally “the word of my endurance” (ton logon tēs hypomonēs mou), a compressed phrase. It may mean Christ’s command to endure, as the ESV takes it, or the message of his own endurance, the gospel of the one who endured the cross. Both fit and both are true; the second deserves full weight, because Christ’s endurance is the source and pattern of theirs (Hebrews 12:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ promises the weak but faithful a permanent, honoured place in God’s presence, marked with the names of God, of his city and of Christ himself. Those shut out on earth will never be shut out there.

A pillar in the temple of my God. A pillar (stylon) speaks of permanence and honour. In an earthquake it was the part of a building that stood firm, and cities sometimes honoured a distinguished citizen with an inscribed pillar in a temple. This is said to people whose city had been shaken flat in AD 17 and who had lived in the fields because no roof could be trusted. Paul called church leaders pillars (Galatians 2:9); here every conqueror is one.

Not architecture but presence. The new Jerusalem has no temple building, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22). To be a pillar there is to belong permanently in God’s presence. The ground under Philadelphia moved again and again; everyone in that little church who held on is a pillar in a temple that has never shifted an inch.

Never shall he go out of it. Certainly never again (ou mē … eti): no more running into the fields at three in the morning. Whoever Christ brings into God’s presence will never be put out: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

The name of my God. Then three names, written on him. A name marks ownership. The high priest wore “Holy to the LORD” on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38), and believers bear God’s name (14:1; 22:4), in contrast to the beast’s mark (13:16–17). This mark is not degradation but belonging.

The new Jerusalem. The city of God, the bride of the Lamb (21:2, 10): citizenship, given to a congregation put out of its synagogue (Philippians 3:20; Hebrews 12:22). Philadelphia had twice been renamed to flatter emperors, as Neocaesarea and as Flavia, and those civic names faded with the dynasties. This one is written on the person.

My own new name. Christ’s own name (19:12, 16), not yet fully disclosed: he has a name written that no one knows but himself. There is more of Christ still to be revealed, and those who will bear his name include a handful of people with little power in a town on a fault line.

My God, four times. The temple, the name, the city, coming down from my God. The risen Christ cannot describe the reward without naming his Father as his own, and that is the reward: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). Everything promised here belongs first to the Son and is shared with those who belong to him. The weak are made pillars because the Son has brought them into his own place.

In everyday life. When the ground moves under you, a diagnosis, a redundancy, a family upheaval, remember the promise made to a city that knew earthquakes: you have a place in God’s presence that no aftershock can reach.

Is the new Jerusalem a place, or the people of God? Both. The city is the bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9–10), the redeemed themselves in their final glory; and it is the home where God dwells with them on a renewed earth (21:1–3), a real place, not a cloud or a mood. To bear its name now means you already belong to that people and are on your way to that home: your citizenship is in heaven even while your passport says something else (Philippians 3:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — To the Church in Laodicea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most dangerous condition of all is to need nothing from Christ, and he loves such a church too much to leave it there. He comes as the Amen, the faithful and true witness, and the source of God’s creation (v. 14). Like the town’s tepid piped water, neither healing like hot springs nor refreshing like cold water, the church is useless, and he is about to spit it out (vv. 15–16). Rich, it does not know that it is poor, blind and naked, and he counsels it to buy from him gold, white garments and eye salve (vv. 17–18). His rebuke is love; he stands at the door and knocks, offering to eat with anyone who opens (vv. 19–20), and promises the conqueror a seat with him on his throne, grounded on his own finished victory (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Useless, Not Merely Lukewarm

Laodicea’s water was neither hot nor cold and good for nothing, and so was its church. Rich and self-sufficient, it did not know it was poor, blind and naked. Christ counsels it to buy from him, disciplines because he loves, and knocks at the door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A city that refused imperial relief produced a church that said, “I need nothing.”

Now: Ask who in your town is helped because your church exists, and open the door to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: 'The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word about Laodicea, Christ shows himself utterly reliable, utterly truthful, and the source and ruler of all creation. To a church in which nothing is solid, the remedy begins by naming the one who does not shift.

The Amen. Three titles, and each is a rebuke before a word of criticism is spoken. Amēn means it is firm, it is so: the word a congregation says to put its weight behind a prayer. Isaiah 65:16 speaks literally of the God of Amen, and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20). To a church that is neither one thing nor the other, the sender is wholly and unchangeably what he is. Your own Amen at the end of a prayer is not a full stop but your weight leaning on God’s Yes.

The faithful and true witness. A faithful witness will not lie; a true one reports what is actually there. He has never told a lie, not even a kind one, and these credentials come just before the most unflattering assessment given to any church.

The beginning of God’s creation. Beginning (archē) here means origin, source, ruler. Colossians, which Laodicea had heard read (Colossians 4:16), says that by Christ all things were created and that he is the beginning (Colossians 1:15–18). He rules everything God made, including Laodicea’s banks, wool and medicine.

The setting. Laodicea, south-east of Philadelphia, stood in the Lycus valley at the junction of three trade roads, near Colossae and Hierapolis. It was the richest town on the circuit, a banking centre famous for glossy black wool and for a medical school linked with a Phrygian eye powder. When an earthquake devastated it in AD 60, it rebuilt itself from its own wealth, without help from Rome, as Tacitus records. Its weakness was water, piped in through an aqueduct. Paul mentions the church in Colossians 2:1 and 4:13–16.

How do I answer someone at my door who says this verse proves Jesus was created? Gently, and from the Bible they are holding. Show that archē means source or ruler as well as first in a series, as we speak of the principal of a school. Then turn to 1:8 and 22:13: if the Father is the beginning without being created, so is the Son, who takes the same title (see the box below). Then, more important than winning, say why it matters: only God can save, and the one who died for us is God the Son.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ was created? The ancient Arians (fourth-century followers of the teacher Arius), and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, read “the beginning of God’s creation” as meaning that Christ was the first being God created. This commentary’s view: the word archē can mean the beginning in the sense of the source or ruler, and that is its meaning here. Revelation gives Christ the titles of God: the first and the last (1:17), the Alpha and the Omega and the beginning and the end (22:13), worshipped with the Father (5:13). John’s Gospel says all things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3); so he cannot himself be a made thing. Christ is the uncreated source of creation, not its first product.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea, about ten miles from Colossae, was a wealthy banking and textile city. Rebuilt without imperial aid after an earthquake in AD 60, it prided itself on needing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ finds Laodicea useless, like its tepid water, neither healing nor refreshing anyone, and warns that he is about to spit it out. His complaint is less about the church’s feelings than about its fruitlessness.

Neither cold nor hot. One of the most often misread verses, and the local water probably explains it. Nearby Hierapolis had famous hot springs, used for healing; Colossae is usually said to have had cold, refreshing water. Laodicea’s water was piped in from a distance, arriving tepid and full of minerals (its pipes show thick calcium deposits): the kind of water people spit out. Cold (psychros) and hot (zestos, boiling) are not points on a scale of spiritual temperature. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes; both are useful. Lukewarm water is useless.

Would that you were either cold or hot! Christ is not saying it would be better to be against him than half-hearted (see “Where Christians differ” below). His complaint is that the church is useless: a city with everything, supplying nothing. Of all the conditions in these letters, the hardest to do anything with is the one doing no harm and no good. A congregation examining its feelings will always find some warmth; this verse asks something more searching: what is your church for? If the building were sold, who outside the membership would notice, and what exactly would they miss?

I will spit you out. Lukewarm (chliaros) is tepid; the verb (emesai) is to vomit, the involuntary reaction of a body to what it cannot keep down, as of a man handed a cup of Laodicean tap water. Yet “I am about to” (mellō) leaves time for repentance (v. 19). His disgust is the disgust of love that will not settle for less than our good.

Water from the spring. What Christ wants from Laodicea is what he himself has always been. He healed the sick, called the weary to come to him for rest (Matthew 11:28), and promised rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit (John 7:37–39). A church joined to him carries that water to others. Laodicea’s works were tepid because they were its own, drawn through a city’s pipes rather than from the spring; the cure is not to work harder but to go back to the source.

What it does not mean. Being spat out does not mean that true believers lose their salvation. Christ is warning a church as a whole, much of which, like Sardis, may never have been truly converted. The response he wants is repentance (v. 19).

Am I lukewarm? This verse frightens sensitive readers and hardly troubles the people it was written for, which is itself the pattern the letter describes. A Christian alarmed by verse 16 is, by that reaction, showing that it is probably not describing him; lukewarmness does not worry about itself, and Laodicea was entirely comfortable. The better questions are these: does anyone find healing or refreshment because of my prayers, my words, my time, my money? Have I come to feel that I need nothing from Christ? If the honest answer troubles you, do what verse 19 says, and you will not stay lukewarm.

Where Christians differ: what do hot and cold mean? The common reading takes hot as spiritually zealous, cold as openly hostile, and lukewarm as half-hearted; on that reading Christ would prefer open hostility to half-heartedness. This commentary’s view: the local water explains the image better. Both hot and cold water are good; lukewarm water is useless and sickening. Christ wants no one cold toward him, but his church useful, either healing or refreshing, by real faith and love. Laodicea’s self-satisfied religion did no good to anyone.
verseByVerse.note: Often explained from local water: hot springs at nearby Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, while Laodicea’s piped-in water arrived tepid. Both hot and cold are useful; lukewarm is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laodicea thinks itself rich and self-sufficient, but Christ sees a beggar, blind and naked, and offers from himself the wealth, clothing and sight it cannot produce. Each part of his counsel aims at one of the town’s sources of pride: its banks, its black wool and its eye medicine.

For you say. Christ quotes the church’s own sentence back at it, the only place in the seven letters where a congregation is allowed to speak. It echoes Hosea 12:8, where Ephraim boasts that it is rich and that no one can find sin in it. Being rich is not a sin. Having prospered is not a sin. Needing nothing is the death of the Christian life, because the whole of that life runs on asking.

The town seeps through the walls. Laodicea had rebuilt itself without an emperor’s relief, and it is very hard to be a self-sufficient city for a generation without becoming a self-sufficient church. Self-sufficiency may be the most respectable idol there is, because it looks like good management. Its quiet creed is that I can look after myself, and grace offends it for the simplest of reasons: grace is only for people who admit that they cannot.

Wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. Wretched (talaipōros) is Paul’s word for himself in Romans 7:24; pitiable (eleeinos) is said of a church that pitied nobody. Then three that answer the three industries: poor (ptōchos, a beggar) to the banking town, blind (typhlos) to the town of the eye clinic, naked (gymnos) to the town that clothed the empire in black wool. And the governing phrase, “not realizing” (ouk oidas, you do not know), is the whole tragedy of the letter. Christ knows their works (v. 15); they do not know their own condition. Smyrna was poor in money and rich before God (2:9); Laodicea is rich in money and poor before God.

I counsel you to buy from me. Counsel (symbouleuō) is advise, not command: to the church he has threatened to spit out, Christ speaks as a friend, inviting the wealthiest town on the circuit to go shopping. It echoes Isaiah 55:1: “Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.” They must come admitting they have nothing to pay with.

Gold refined by fire. The banking town has no real wealth. What is offered is gold that has been through the furnace (pepyrōmenon ek pyros): the true riches of faith tested by trials, the image Peter used (1 Peter 1:7), and the treasure of Christ himself.

White garments. White, in a town whose fortune was built on glossy black: the righteousness Christ gives (3:4–5; 19:8). In Scripture nakedness is a picture of shame and judgment (Ezekiel 16:37), and from the first garden only God could cover it (Genesis 3:7, 21). The one thing Laodicea could not manufacture is the one thing it needed to wear.

Salve to anoint your eyes. Salve (kollourion) is eye ointment. Laodicea’s medical school is thought to have made a compound for weak eyes, sold across the province: the town could sell sight to strangers and could not see itself. It needed the sight only Christ’s Spirit gives, to see its real condition and his glory (Ephesians 1:18), and the first effect would be that the congregation finally read verse 17 as a description of itself.

What the merchant paid. Each thing Christ offers he obtained at his own cost. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). The soldiers stripped him and divided his clothes (John 19:23–24), and he hung exposed so that sinners might be clothed. He opened the eyes of a man born blind (John 9:39). The gold, the cloth and the salve are what Christ is and gives, and the price was paid on his side of the counter. Every one requires the same first move: coming to him with empty hands and asking. That is what “I need nothing” makes impossible, and why this is perhaps the most dangerous condition of the seven.

How should a well-off Christian live in the light of this letter? Gratefully, generously and watchfully. Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on uncertain riches but on God, who richly provides everything to enjoy, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Give regularly and sacrificially; use your home and resources for others; keep praying for what you seem not to need, because you do; and watch for the moment comfort makes church, prayer or Scripture feel optional. Wealth is a trust, not a verdict. The poorest believer and the richest come to Christ the same way: as beggars.

verseByVerse.quote: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s rebuke is love, and he stands outside his own church, knocking, ready to come in and share a meal with anyone who opens. The threat to spit them out was never a farewell.

Those whom I love. After everything that has been said, this. The verb is not the usual agapaō but philō, often used of affection between friends, the word used of the Father’s love for the Son and of Jesus’ love for Lazarus (John 5:20; 11:36). Reprove (elenchō) means expose, convict; discipline (paideuō) means train and correct, as a parent trains a child. Christ’s harsh words are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

The rebuke explained. The sentence comes from Proverbs 3:12, where the LORD reproves the one he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights, the text Hebrews uses to explain why the hard things God sends are not rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11). The threat to spit them out was Christ refusing to leave Laodicea alone, and the churches that received no rebuke were not the better loved. Indifference does not bother to correct.

So be zealous and repent. The first command is continuous: keep on being zealous (zēleue, burn with zeal), a word from the same family as zestos, hot, in verse 15. For the lukewarm church, the cure for tepid is not warm. It is boiling. The second is a single decisive act: repent (metanoēson), now. Neither is a feeling to be worked up from within; both answer the love he has just declared.

I stand at the door and knock. The best-known sentence in the letters, usually quoted apart from its setting. Stand (hestēka) is I have taken my stand; knock (krouō) is keep knocking, like the beloved in the Song of Songs who knocks and says, “Open to me” (Song of Songs 5:2). Christ stands outside a church that thinks it needs nothing, with its Lord on the wrong side of the door; inside it is in session, busy, and has no idea.

If anyone. It is singular (ean tis). The letter has addressed a congregation throughout, and at the decisive moment it narrows to one person. A whole church may be lukewarm; the door is opened by individuals, and nobody in Laodicea had to wait for a majority. What stands on the step is not a summons but Christ himself, with the evening free and the table ready.

Eat with him. What he offers on the other side of the door is not a rebuke but a meal. The word (deipnēsō) is the unhurried evening meal. In the ancient world eating with someone was the public sign of accepting them (see meals and reclining at table); it is what got Jesus into trouble (Luke 15:2), and he shared meals with his disciples after rising (Luke 24:30; John 21:12). To the church he has just called wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked, the offer is dinner, and “he with me” makes it shared both ways: he comes as a guest and stays as the host, and this book will end with a wedding supper (19:9).

The love that bled. He who stands outside the door of his church once suffered outside the gate of his city (Hebrews 13:12), shut out so that sinners could be brought in. The love that rebukes is the love that bled, and the meal he offers is already paid for, the table laid with his own body and blood.

Is the hardship in my life God’s discipline? It may be, and if you belong to Christ, it is never his rejection. Discipline in Scripture is training, the way a father shapes a son, not only punishment; it can come through rebuke, through the consequences of sin, or through hardships with no link to any particular sin (Hebrews 12:7–11). You need not identify the reason for every trial. Ask what God may be teaching you, confess any sin you know of, and trust that he is treating you as a beloved child. The evidence of his love is not the absence of correction but the cross, and the promise that discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

What does opening the door look like for a believer? Hearing his voice in his word and doing what it says. Admit to him in plain words that you have been carrying on without him; repent of the specific things that crowded him out, whether busyness, comfort, a habit or a grudge; and make room for him again, in unhurried prayer, in reading Scripture to meet him rather than to tick a box, and at his table with his people, where he invites himself to eat with them. Listen for the knock in the passage that unsettles you, the sermon that names your comfort, the friend who asks a hard question. He has not been waiting with folded arms. He has been knocking, and he is eager to come in.

Where Christians differ: an invitation to unbelievers? This verse is often used in evangelism, as Christ knocking at the door of an unbeliever’s heart, waiting to be invited in. This commentary’s view: in context it is addressed to a church, calling professing believers to repent and restore fellowship with Christ. It can rightly be applied to unbelievers, since the gospel calls everyone to turn to Christ, and many professing members of Laodicea were probably not truly converted. But the verse does not mean that Christ is helpless until a sinner decides to let him in. Scripture teaches that the dead sinner can respond only because God first gives new life (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:1–5). When Christ knocks, his voice is powerful: it opens deaf ears, and his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). The free invitation and God’s sovereign grace stand together.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The highest promise of all seven letters, a seat with Christ on his throne, is given to the worst church, and it rests on Christ’s own finished victory. It leads straight into chapters 4 and 5, where John sees that throne and the Lamb who conquered.

To sit with me on my throne. Grant (dōsō) is give: a gift, not an earned right. Not near the throne, not in front of it, but on it, sharing Christ’s royal rule (Matthew 19:28; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 20:4; 22:5). God has already raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).

As I also conquered. The second half of the sentence is the reason for the first. Christ conquered (enikēsa, a finished victory) by his death and resurrection (5:5–6), and sat down at the Father’s right hand (Hebrews 1:3; 12:2); his throne and the Father’s are one (22:1, 3). The victory is not pending; the seat is not empty. The dragon, the beast, the harlot city and the ranks of the martyrs all arrive after this verse, on the far side of a finished victory. Every promise to the churches rests on that conquest, and the Victor has made room on his throne for those who answer his knock.

What conquering has meant. These two chapters have defined the word, and the definition decides who this promise is for. It has not once meant achievement. At Ephesus it meant recovering a love that had been put down. At Smyrna it meant not denying him in a cell. At Pergamum it meant refusing a dinner invitation. At Thyatira it meant holding on. At Sardis it meant keeping a garment clean when nobody was looking. At Philadelphia it meant keeping his word with very little strength. And at Laodicea it means getting up and opening a door. The throne of the universe is promised to people whose great victory was answering a knock.

The seven promises together. The tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a new name, authority and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed, a pillar that never shakes, a seat on the throne: every one is given to ordinary believers in seven unremarkable towns, and every one is, in the end, Christ himself and life with him.

Let him hear. The final call, for the seventh time, to every church since. The next words in the book are “After this”, and a door opens in heaven.

What it does not mean. Sharing Christ’s throne does not mean believers become gods or share his divine nature. It means they share in his reign as redeemed human beings, kings and priests under him (1:6; 5:10).

I am so weak; how can I conquer? By trusting the one who already has. The promise is grounded in his victory, not yours: “as I also conquered”. Your conquering is joined to his, as a soldier shares the triumph of a general who has already won the war. It looks like the small things these letters have named: coming back when you have drifted, saying no to compromise, holding on, opening the door. And he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Weakness is not disqualification; it is where his strength is seen (2 Corinthians 12:9).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: ‘The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. “I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.<sup>2</sup>Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God.<sup>3</sup>Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.<sup>4</sup>Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.<sup>5</sup>The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.<sup>6</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’<sup>7</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: ‘The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.<sup>8</sup>“I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.<sup>9</sup>Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you.<sup>10</sup>Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.<sup>12</sup>The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name.<sup>13</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’<sup>14</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: ‘The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation.<sup>15</sup>“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot!<sup>16</sup>So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>For you say, “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,” not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.<sup>18</sup>I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.<sup>19</sup>Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent.<sup>20</sup>Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.<sup>21</sup>The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.<sup>22</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.‘”

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
keyVerse.note: The best-known sentence in the letters is spoken to the worst church. The Lord whose verdict has exposed Laodicea as poor, blind and naked does not walk away; he stands outside, knocking, and offers not a rebuke but a meal. It shows the heart behind every warning in this chapter: Christ rebukes because he loves, and he comes in to anyone who opens.

3.reflection:
Sardis had “the reputation of being alive” but was dead (v. 1). What do churches, and Christians, tend to treat as signs of life? What signs would Christ look for in your church and in you?

Philadelphia had “but little power” and yet received no rebuke at all (v. 8). How does this letter encourage small churches and ordinary believers? What open door has Christ set in front of you?

Laodicea said, “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing” (v. 17). How does comfort make it hard to feel our need of Christ? What would it look like to come to him to “buy” what only he can give (v. 18)?

Christ stands at the door and knocks, offering to eat with anyone who opens (v. 20). Why is it striking that he says this to a church? What might opening the door look like for you this week?

4.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Throne Room of Heaven
4.overview:
Where we are. After the seven letters the view rises from the roads of Asia to heaven itself. Chapters 4 and 5 belong together at the hinge of the book: before any seal is opened, any judgment falls or any beast appears, John is shown the room from which everything that follows comes.

The message. The universe has a centre, and it is an occupied throne. The God who sits there is holy beyond measure, ringed by his covenant faithfulness, and worshipped without ceasing as the Creator by whose will all things exist. History is not in the hands of Caesar or of chaos.

Why it was said. The churches lived under an emperor who liked to be hailed as “our Lord and God”, in cities proud of their temples to Rome (see the introduction). Some faced prison and death; others were tempted to bow. Before the storms ahead, they needed to see who sits on the throne.

How the chapter makes its case. Christ’s voice calls John, not the whole church, through an open door, and in the Spirit he sees an occupied throne (vv. 1–2). The one seated is described only in light and colour, encircled by the rainbow of the covenant (v. 3). Around it sit twenty-four elders, the whole people of God, already wearing what the letters promised; from it comes Sinai’s thunder; before it burns the Spirit (vv. 4–5). The sea lies stilled to glass, and four living creatures, creation at its highest, never cease to sing “Holy, holy, holy” (vv. 6–8). Whenever they give glory, the elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne and praise God as Creator (vv. 9–11).

Where it leads. The chapter is deliberately unfinished: its song is about creation, and the next chapter’s new song is about redemption, sung to the Lamb who was slain. Yet the room already points to him. The voice that calls John up is the risen Christ, who has sat down with his Father on his throne (3:21); the holiness Isaiah saw was his glory (John 12:41); and the cherubim around the throne once guarded the mercy seat where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. The throne John sees is the throne the Lamb shares.

For us. Look first where John was told to look: at the throne before the headlines. Then worship as heaven worships, giving him the honour that belongs to no one else, and lay down before him every crown you were given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Throne Room of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the church is shown a single judgment, it is shown that the universe is ruled from an occupied throne, by a holy Creator whom all heaven worships. Summoned through an open door, John sees one seated on the throne (vv. 1–2), described only as light like precious stones, within the covenant rainbow (v. 3). Around it sit twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns; from it come Sinai’s lightning and thunder; before it burn the seven torches of the Spirit (vv. 4–5). Beside a sea like glass, four living creatures, drawn from Ezekiel’s cherubim and Isaiah’s seraphim, never cease to sing “Holy, holy, holy” (vv. 6–8). Whenever they give glory, the elders cast their crowns before the throne and praise God as Creator (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Throne Comes First

Before any seal is opened, John is shown an occupied throne, ringed by a rainbow and surrounded by unceasing worship: holy, holy, holy. The Creator of all things is worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Domitian liked to be called “our Lord and God”; the elders give those words to the true throne.

Now: Lay down every crown you were given before the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this." At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ calls John up through heaven’s open door to see earth’s history from above, and the first thing he sees is a throne with someone seated on it. Before any trouble is shown, the church is shown who rules.

A door standing open in heaven. “After this” (meta tauta) means after John saw these things, not necessarily after the events of chapters 2 and 3 in history; it marks a new vision (7:1, 9; 15:5; 18:1), not the next instalment of a timetable. The door has been opened and stands open (thyra ēneōgmenē). Philadelphia was promised an open door (3:8); Laodicea had Christ knocking at a closed one (3:20); now heaven’s own door stands open.

The first voice. This is the voice of the risen Christ of the first vision (1:10–13), who has just told Laodicea that he conquered and sat down with his Father on his throne (3:21). He does not invite John into a room he has never entered. He is the forerunner who has gone ahead of his people behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20), and the door stands open because the one who holds the key of David has opened it (3:7).

Come up here. John is summoned, in vision, into heaven, to see earth’s history from heaven’s point of view. “Must” (dei) is God’s sure plan, as in 1:1: nothing John is about to see is improvised.

At once I was in the Spirit. The second of four times the phrase marks a new stage of the book (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10). John did not bring this on by any method of his own; the Spirit did it to him.

A throne stood in heaven. Then the sentence the whole book turns on. Nothing else is described first: a throne (thronos), and somebody on it. The word occurs about forty-seven times in Revelation, more than in all the rest of the New Testament together: the book’s central symbol, God rules. Rome’s throne, and Satan’s (2:13), are rivals that will fall. And its position is deliberate. Before one seal is opened, before a single horseman rides, before the dragon appears or the beast rises out of the sea, John is shown a throne that is occupied. Whatever comes in the next eighteen chapters happens in a universe where that throne stands.

With one seated on the throne. Seated (kathēmenos): God is not anxious or pacing; he sits, at rest, in sovereign control. In reverent restraint John does not describe God in human form, only his radiance (v. 3), and throughout the book he is simply the one seated on the throne. He has never once stood up in alarm.

The setting. The vision draws on the great throne visions of the Old Testament: Isaiah 6, with the seraphim crying “Holy, holy, holy”; Ezekiel 1, with its four living creatures, rainbow and crystal expanse; and Daniel 7, where the Ancient of Days sits in judgment. For readers whose emperor expected to be hailed as lord and god, this chapter declares who truly sits on the throne of the universe.

Is this where believers who have died are now? In a real sense, yes. The throne room is the presence of God, and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Revelation shows the martyrs before the throne (6:9–11) and a great multitude serving God in his temple (7:15). So a believer who dies goes to be with Christ in this presence, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body and the new creation (21:1–4). The symbols are not a map, but the reality behind them is where your believing loved ones are.

How does a throne in heaven help me when my life is falling apart? It does not explain your trouble, and it was not meant to. It tells you who is in charge of it. The first thing God showed churches facing prison and death was not a way out but an occupied throne. Nothing in your life is outside his rule: not the diagnosis, the betrayal, the loss, or the news. When you pray, begin there, as the Lord’s Prayer does: “Our Father in heaven.” A morning can have John’s order: look first to the one who is seated, and only then at the headlines. The ground under you may shake. The throne does not.

Where Christians differ: is John’s ascent the rapture of the church? Dispensationalists often read “Come up here” as a picture of the church raptured before the tribulation, noting that the word “church” does not appear on earth from chapter 4 until 22:16. That observation is a real feature of the text, and the reading is held by many believers who love this book. This commentary’s view: the call is to John alone, to receive a vision; nothing suggests the whole church is taken up. Ezekiel was lifted up by the Spirit in vision in much the same way (Ezekiel 8:3; 11:1). The church appears throughout chapters 4–22 under other names: servants of God (7:3), saints (13:7), those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (12:17), the bride (19:7). The saints are under the altar (6:9), sealed (7:3) and conquering by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). The word church is absent because the visions use symbolic language, not because the church has gone. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John describes God only by light and colour, blazing brilliance and fiery red, and around the throne a rainbow of covenant mercy. The holy Judge is encircled on every side by his promise.

Jasper and carnelian. John describes no face, no form, no figure, no size. Jasper (iaspidi) is later described as clear as crystal (21:11): brilliant, throwing light in every direction. Carnelian (sardiō) is a fiery red stone, probably named after Sardis: deep and burning, perhaps God’s blazing holiness, even his wrath (on the stones, see “Uncertain wording” below). Blazing light and blood-red fire, and no shape between them.

Why no face? Not because there was nothing to see. No one may look on God and live (Exodus 33:20); he dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). Every prophet who came close had the same difficulty. Ezekiel piles up qualifiers until the grammar buckles: “the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (Ezekiel 1:28). Isaiah described the train of a robe and the smoke (Isaiah 6:1–4). Here John twice says only “the appearance of”. That restraint is itself a mercy, and a warning to anyone who wants a picture: every attempt to draw God ends in something smaller than God, which is why the second commandment forbids images of him.

A rainbow like an emerald. Then a third colour, and it changes everything: green, encircling the throne completely, so that no one can approach from any direction without coming through it. The rainbow entered Scripture at the end of the flood, when God set his bow in the cloud as the sign of a covenant, often understood as a warrior hanging up his weapon, turned away from the earth: “When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant” (Genesis 9:16). It was a promise given after judgment had fallen, to a world that had just seen what God can do.

The order is the theology. Set the three colours together in John’s order: blazing holiness, burning judgment, and around the whole throne, without a gap, a covenant promise. A covenant is a binding promise by which God pledges himself to a people, and he will not violate it (Psalm 89:34). The throne of judgment is surrounded by grace. Trumpets, bowls and plagues are about to be poured out from this room, and every one of them will come out from inside a rainbow.

The first and the last of his people’s stones. On the high priest’s breastpiece, where the names of Israel’s tribes were carried before God, the sardius (carnelian) was the first of the twelve stones and jasper the last (Exodus 28:17–20). The first and the last is what Christ called himself (1:17). The God of this throne has always carried his people on the heart of their high priest, and that high priest has now come: Jesus, who holds his priesthood permanently and always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25).

Every way in passes through the green. The covenant he made with Noah after the waters he has crowned with a better one, made in the blood of his Son (Luke 22:20). So the light no eye can bear and the fire no sinner can survive are encircled on every side by faithfulness, and there is no direction from which his people come to him that does not pass through the green.
