Will we ever see God’s face? Yes, in Christ. “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (22:4). The pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Even now God’s glory is seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6): whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). What sinful eyes cannot bear now, glorified eyes will see with joy: the highest happiness of heaven.

Why does the rainbow matter if God is about to judge the world? Because it tells you what kind of judge he is. It does not mean there will be no judgment, but that his judgments come from a throne bound by covenant faithfulness and serve his purpose of rescuing and renewing. For a believer the rainbow says that the storm coming out of the throne will not touch the promise around it. God has bound himself to you, in Christ, at his own initiative, and he cannot go back on it.

Uncertain wording. Ancient names for precious stones do not map neatly onto modern ones. “Jasper” (iaspis) was used of various stones, not only the opaque one that now bears the name, and since 21:11 calls it “clear as crystal”, John may mean something like a diamond or rock crystal. “Carnelian” (sardion) is almost certainly a red stone, and “emerald” (smaragdos) most likely green. The word for “rainbow” (iris) can also mean a halo of light, so John may picture a green radiance circling the throne rather than a many-coloured bow. The point is clear even where the details are not: dazzling brightness and fire, encircled by the sign of God’s covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Around God’s throne the whole people of God are already seated, robed and crowned, while from the throne come the lightning and thunder of Sinai and before it burns the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Majesty, terror and welcome share one room.

Twenty-four elders. Elders (presbyterous) sit on thrones, so they share in God’s rule; they wear white, so they are pure; they wear golden crowns (stephanous, victors’ wreaths), so they have conquered. White garments were promised to the conquerors at Sardis (3:5), the victor’s crown at Smyrna (2:10), a throne at Laodicea (3:21). Every reward held out to the seven churches is already being worn in the throne room. Each rests on what Christ did: the robes are white because they were washed in his blood (7:14), and the thrones are shared because he conquered and sat down on his (3:21). The promises are not hopes that may or may not come true. They are already there in the room.

Lightning and thunder. This is Sinai. When God came down on the mountain there were thunders and lightnings, a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). The same lightning, rumblings and thunder return at the climax of each series of judgments (8:5; 11:19; 16:18), each time intensified, linking them to this throne: God is about to act. The peace of heaven is not the peace of a library. It is the peace of people standing perfectly still in the presence of something that could level a mountain.

Seven torches of fire. John interprets the symbol himself, as at 1:20, and the sevenfold Spirit has already been named (1:4; 3:1). Zechariah’s lampstand stands behind the image (Zechariah 4:2–6): the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Fire speaks of holiness, light and purifying power, and the Spirit is before the throne, ready to be sent out into all the earth (5:6). The Spirit at work in seven struggling congregations is the Spirit blazing in front of the throne of God. Indeed everything in this chapter is located from that one fixed point: around the throne, from it, before it, on each side of it.

Sinai with a mediator. Hebrews sets this same thunder beside the gospel: believers have come not to a mountain burning with fire and storm but to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood (Hebrews 12:18–24). The thunder has not been turned down. What has changed is that Jesus, the go-between, stands between it and his people. And the fire that blazes before the throne is not kept there: the risen Christ has poured out that Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33), so that the weakest believer carries in his heart a flame from the throne room of God.

If lightning comes from the throne, how can I approach it with confidence? Through the High Priest who sits at its right hand. Because we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, we may draw near to the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16). The lightning is real: God is holy, and no sinner can stand before him on his own merits. But the elders sit in white, near the storm, unafraid, because their robes have been washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). You come the same way: not hoping to be tolerated, but welcomed for Christ’s sake.

Where Christians differ: who are the twenty-four elders? Some see them as an order of angels, a heavenly council around God (Psalm 89:7), since they appear alongside the living creatures and are distinguished from the redeemed multitude of 7:9. Others see them as representing the whole people of God, Old Testament and New: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. A third reading notes that David divided the priests into twenty-four courses, so that twenty-four could stand for the whole priesthood. This commentary’s view: the second view is the most likely. The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations (21:12–14), a clear twelve plus twelve. The elders receive what the seven letters promise to conquering believers: white robes, crowns and thrones. They represent the one people of God, redeemed from both covenants, already worshipping in heaven. The church on earth is represented before the throne.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty-four may combine the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles — the whole people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the throne the sea, the ancient picture of chaos, lies still as glass, and around it four living creatures, creation at its highest, watch and worship. Nothing that threatens the church is outside this room or beyond his control.

A sea of glass. Two qualifiers in a few words, “as it were” and “like”, the marks of a man describing something for which no word exists: a floor before the throne, flat, shining and utterly still. Ancient glass was usually cloudy; glass clear as crystal was rare and precious. When the elders of Israel saw the God of Israel on Sinai, there was under his feet “as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness” (Exodus 24:10), with the same two hesitating phrases. In Solomon’s temple a huge bronze basin called the Sea stood in the courtyard for washing before the priests could serve: the way to God always ran past water.

The chaos is a floor. In the ancient imagination the sea was chaos itself, restless and full of what could not be tamed, which is why the beast comes up out of it in chapter 13, and why the new creation is announced with the words “the sea was no more” (21:1). Here the sea is glass: still, transparent, with the light going straight through it. Whatever threatens the church in the chapters ahead is in this room already, lying still at his feet. In 15:2 the conquerors stand beside it, singing, like Israel beside the Red Sea.

Four living creatures. Living creatures (zōa, living beings) are not beasts, which is a different word (thēria), used for the evil beasts of chapter 13. They are high angelic beings with Ezekiel’s faces and Isaiah’s wings and song, a blend of cherubim and seraphim, and they are nearest of all, nearer than the elders. Four is the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, 7:1): they seem to represent the whole of creation worshipping its Creator.

Full of eyes. Eyes speak of ceaseless watchfulness and knowledge. Nothing in creation goes unobserved by those closest to the throne, nor by God.

Lion, ox, man and eagle. Each is the highest of a kind: the lion, the noblest of wild animals; the ox, the strongest of domestic animals; man, the wisest of all; the eagle, the swiftest of birds. Together they show all creation, at its best, worshipping God. In Ezekiel each creature had all four faces; here each has one. The nearest beings to the throne are not administrators but worshippers covered in eyes, whose whole work is to see and to say what they see. They fall before the Lamb (5:8, 14), call “Come!” as the first four horsemen ride out (6:1–7), and hand the seven angels the bowls of wrath (15:7): praise and judgment come out of one room because both come from one holy God.

The same stillness on a real sea. The sea that terrified the ancient world lies before his throne as still as glass, and once, on a night in Galilee, the same stillness came down on a real sea at the word of a man who had been asleep in the boat. “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” his disciples asked (Mark 4:41). This room is the answer: the one who said “Peace! Be still!” shares the throne the living creatures surround.

The cherubim and the Lamb. These are cherubim, and Israel knew where cherubim belonged. Two of them were beaten out of gold on the lid of the ark, wings spread over the mercy seat, facing the place where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year (Exodus 25:18–22; Hebrews 9:5). Paul uses hilastērion, the Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid, when he says that God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25): an offering that satisfies God’s just anger at sin, because the one offered bears that anger in the sinner’s place (1 John 4:10). So in the next chapter the Lamb stands between the throne and these four creatures, and they fall down before him (5:6, 8). The beings whose images guarded the place of atonement for centuries bow before the one whose blood made atonement.

What it does not mean. Church tradition, from Irenaeus on, linked the four creatures with the four Gospels, most familiarly in Jerome’s pairing (Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle); Irenaeus himself gave the lion to John and the eagle to Mark. It is a memorable devotional association, but the creatures represent creation worshipping God.

Does all creation really worship God? Yes, in its own way. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1), and the psalmist calls sea creatures, fire, hail, mountains, trees, beasts and birds to praise the LORD (Psalm 148:7–10). They do it by being what he made them to be, and in the next chapter every creature joins the song (5:13). Creation now groans, waiting for the freedom of God’s children (Romans 8:19–22), but it was made for praise and will be renewed for it. When you look at a hawk or a field of cattle, you are looking at worshippers; humans are the ones made to put that praise into words.

Uncertain wording. “Around the throne, on each side of the throne” renders a compressed Greek phrase, literally “in the midst of the throne and in a circle around the throne”. Exactly how John pictures the creatures is uncertain: perhaps one at the middle of each side, close enough to seem part of the throne itself, or, as in Ezekiel 1, bearing it up beneath. Either way, they are nearer to God than anything else in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The creatures nearest God never stop proclaiming that he is holy beyond all measure, the Almighty who was and is and is to come. Of all that could be said of him, this is what heaven says without ceasing.

Six wings. Like the seraphim Isaiah saw in the year King Uzziah died, each with six wings: two to cover the face, in reverence; two to cover the feet, in humility; two to fly, in service (Isaiah 6:1–2). Isaiah heard them call, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!”, and cried out, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:3, 5). These creatures are full of eyes all around and within (on the eyes, see vv. 6–7).

They never cease. Literally, they have no rest (anapausin ouk echousin). Their worship is ceaseless because God’s holiness is inexhaustible. Those who worship the beast also “have no rest, day or night” (14:11), in torment. The same phrase describes the two destinies of creatures: endless joy in worshipping God, or endless restlessness in refusing him.

Holy, holy, holy. Empires have risen and fallen since Isaiah heard these words, and not one has needed changing. Holy is hagios, in Hebrew qadosh: set apart, utterly other, pure. Hebrew often intensifies a word by repeating it, and three times is the superlative: holy beyond all measure. And there is only one attribute of God that Scripture ever trebles like this. Nobody sings loving, loving, loving or mighty, mighty, mighty. God is love and God is almighty, and both are said plainly, but the word said three times before the throne, day and night, is holy. Christians have long seen in the threefold Holy a hint of the Trinity, though the main point is God’s infinite holiness.

What holiness means. Holy means set apart before it means morally pure. God is not a larger version of us, not the best example of anything on our scale; he is in a category with one member, and because he is wholly other, he is wholly pure. Get this wrong and every other doctrine weakens: sin no longer seems an outrage, and grace no longer seems a miracle.

The Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. Almighty (pantokratōr, ruler of all) is the title of 1:8. The three tenses of 1:4 and 8 here run in the order of time, past, present and future: God’s eternity, and his coming to judge and renew. And at the centre stands the present: he is, now.

Whose glory Isaiah saw. John’s Gospel adds a sentence that changes how this song is heard: “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41), and “him” is Jesus. The Lord high and lifted up, before whom the seraphim cried holy, is the one whose glory John saw “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The holiness the seraphim could not look at is his own (John 17:5).

Is God vain to want endless praise? No, and the question deserves a straight answer. Praise is not something God lacks and needs topping up. Father, Son and Spirit have delighted in one another from eternity, and nothing was made to fill a gap. Praise is what happens when anything true is seen clearly. Nobody watching a sunrise over water has to be commanded to say something; the praise is not a tax levied on the viewer but the completion of the seeing. What happens in this room is not flattery but accuracy, and it is for our good: we were made to find our joy in him.

Won’t heaven be boring if it is endless worship? Not if worship is what this chapter shows. Boredom comes when a thing is exhausted. The creatures nearest the throne are covered in eyes, have been looking without pause, and have not yet come to the end of the first word. It is not that they must keep saying it; they cannot stop. Worship in heaven is not an endless church service as we know it but the whole of life, work, fellowship and joy, lived in the open presence of the God who is infinitely worth knowing (22:3–5). The only way it could bore us would be for God to be smaller than he is.

In everyday life. When you next confess your sin, start where Isaiah started, with God’s holiness, and you will find your sin more serious and his grace more astonishing than you had thought.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every time creation praises God, his people bow and lay their crowns before him, confessing that he alone is worthy, because he made all things and they exist by his will. Whatever honour God gives his people, they give back to him.

Whenever the living creatures give glory. Glory (doxan), honour (timēn), thanks (eucharistian): creation praises God for who he is and thanks him for what he has done. “Whenever” makes it a pattern, not a single event: every time the creatures begin, the elders go down.

Who lives forever and ever. Unlike emperors, who live and die. If John wrote, as most think, about AD 95, Domitian was murdered in his own palace within a year or two. The one on this throne has no successor.

The elders fall down and cast their crowns. Two things happen: they fall, and they throw. Worship (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves) involves the body, as with Ezekiel, Daniel and John himself (1:17). Throwing the crown is different: it is a decision about what to do with a reward. A defeated king might lay his crown before his conqueror; Tacitus describes Tiridates of Armenia taking the royal diadem from his head and laying it at the foot of Nero’s statue. These crowns were given, and nobody in that room manufactured one. They are the victor’s wreaths promised in the letters (see the note on vv. 4–5), handed over by Christ himself, and the elders will not keep them on in front of the throne. Their victory was his.

Worthy are you, our Lord and God. Worthy (axios) means deserving, and only God is. A first-century hearer would have flinched at the next phrase. “Our Lord and God” (ho kyrios kai ho theos hēmōn) was precisely the title Domitian liked to hear, as the Roman historian Suetonius reports (dominus et deus noster). The congregations hearing this letter were under pressure to say those words to a man in Rome. John gives them the same words, to say to a different throne.

For you created all things. The reason is stated: “by your will”. God is worthy of worship because he is the Creator: not merely because he is strong, and not merely because he will win, but because everything that exists does so at his pleasure and would stop existing if he stopped willing it. Nothing in the universe is an accident or an afterthought, including a small congregation in Thyatira and the person reading this sentence.

Why is there something rather than nothing? The philosopher Leibniz thought it the first question we have a right to ask. The universe, we are now told, is simply there: a brute fact, with no reason behind it and no one to thank. Many live with that answer bravely, but it is hard to keep it from spreading. If the whole is an accident, so is each part of it, and you with it; meaning becomes something we must invent and prop up ourselves, and worth something we have to earn. The elders give the other answer: everything is here because Someone wanted it here. That is not a cold fact about causes but the warmest fact there is, because the will behind the world turns out to be love.

Through whom all things were made. The New Testament names the one through whom the creating was done: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3); by the Son all things were created, visible and invisible, “whether thrones or dominions” (Colossians 1:16). So the one who takes the scroll in the next chapter is the one through whom the world was made, and the one who made all things comes forward to redeem them. He came into his world and gave himself for it. You are not an accident he puts up with. You were willed, and then you were bought.

A song deliberately incomplete. That is where chapter 4 stops. Its song is about creation, and creation alone saves nobody; the world he made is the world in rebellion against him. In the next chapter a scroll appears that no one in heaven or on earth is able to open, and John weeps. The answer will be a new song, not about creation but about redemption, sung to the Lamb who was slain.

What crowns do I have to cast down now? Anything you are tempted to wear as though you earned it. A capacity, a competence, an upbringing, a marriage, a body that still works, thirty years of faithful service in a church, a ministry others admire. None of it was self-generated (1 Corinthians 4:7). Cast it down by thanking God for it specifically, by using it for others rather than for your reputation, and by refusing to compare yourself with those who seem to have less. What is worn in this life is thrown down in the next, and the sooner a person starts throwing, the less it will cost him at the end.

If God made everything by his will, where did evil come from? Not from God’s creating: everything he made was very good (Genesis 1:31). Evil entered through the rebellion of creatures, angelic and human, who turned from him (Genesis 3; Jude 6). God is not the author of sin, yet nothing escapes his rule, and he governs even evil for his good purposes, as he did supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture does not explain everything about this, and we should not pretend it does. But it shows what God has done about evil: the Creator entered his creation to bear its curse, and the next chapter shows him on the throne as the Lamb who was slain.

In everyday life. When you are asked, in whatever form, to give to someone or something else the loyalty that belongs to God alone, say the elders’ words under your breath: our Lord and God. Only one throne has a right to that title.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.”<sup>2</sup>At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.<sup>3</sup>And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.<sup>4</sup>Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.<sup>5</sup>From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,<sup>6</sup>and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind:<sup>7</sup>the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.<sup>8</sup>And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”<sup>9</sup>And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,<sup>10</sup>the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying,<sup>11</sup>“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

keyVerse.quote: Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.
keyVerse.note: The chapter rises to this song. The elders give the true throne the very title Domitian claimed, “our Lord and God”, and they give the reason: everything exists because God willed it. Before the church is shown the Lamb’s redemption in chapter 5, it is reminded that the world and all its powers belong to their Maker, and that worship is simply giving him what he is worth.

4.reflection:
John saw the throne before he saw any of the troubles of the coming chapters (vv. 1–2). How would it change the way you face the news, or your own troubles, to look first at the one who is seated?

The throne is surrounded by lightning and thunder, and also by a rainbow (vv. 3, 5). How do God’s holiness and his covenant faithfulness belong together? Which of the two are you more inclined to forget?

The living creatures never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy” (v. 8). Why do you think holiness is the one attribute of God repeated in this way? How should a sense of his holiness shape our worship and our confession of sin?

The elders cast their crowns before the throne (v. 10). What gifts, achievements or honours are you tempted to wear as your own, and what would it look like to lay them down before him?

5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 completes the throne-room vision that began in chapter 4. There God was praised as Creator; here John sees the scroll in God’s hand and the one who alone can open it, and everything from the seals of chapter 6 onwards flows from this moment.

The message. The future of the world belongs to the Lamb who was slain. God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation is complete and in his hand, but no creature anywhere is worthy to carry it out. One is: the Lion of Judah, who conquered by dying as a Lamb and by his blood bought people for God from every nation. The crucified one reigns, and heaven and earth worship him with the Father.

Why it was said. The seven churches were small and under pressure, and Rome looked like the power that held the future (see the introduction). John’s tears voice their fear, and every believer’s: that no one will ever put the world right. The chapter answers it not with a timetable but with a person.

How the chapter makes its case. First the crisis (vv. 1–4): a sealed scroll, a search of the whole universe, no one worthy, and a man weeping in heaven. Then the announcement (v. 5): the Lion of Judah has conquered. Then the surprise (vv. 6–7): John turns to see a Lion and sees a Lamb, standing though slain, with all power and knowledge, and he takes the scroll. Last, the worship widens in three circles (vv. 8–14): the elders and living creatures sing a new song of redemption, angels beyond counting join them, and every creature blesses the one on the throne and the Lamb in a single breath.

Where it leads. This is the heart of Revelation and of the gospel. The Lion is the Lamb: power has been redefined by sacrifice. Heaven gives the reason for his worthiness in four words, “for you were slain” (v. 9), and the marks of his death are still on him at the centre of the universe. The chapter that began with the only tears shed in the throne room ends with all creation singing to the Father and the Son together.

For us. When the world looks like a scroll no one will open, look at who holds it. Your prayers are kept in golden bowls before God; you belong to a kingdom of priests bought from every nation; and the way the Lamb conquered, by faithful self-giving rather than force, is the way he calls his people to live.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The future of the world is in the hands of the Lamb who was slain, and all creation worships him with the Father. A herald asks who is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purposes (vv. 1–2), and when the whole universe is searched in vain, John weeps (vv. 3–4). An elder stops his tears: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (v. 5). John looks and sees a Lamb standing as though slain, full of power, knowledge and the Spirit, and the Lamb takes the scroll (vv. 6–7). Then the praise spreads outwards: the living creatures and elders, holding the saints’ prayers, sing that his blood has ransomed people from every nation (vv. 8–10); myriads of angels join in (vv. 11–12); and every creature blesses the one on the throne and the Lamb together (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced, and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God holds his whole plan for the world, complete and sealed, in his own hand, and heaven asks who is worthy to open it. The question is not who is strong enough, but who is good enough.

A scroll in his right hand. In Scripture the right hand is the hand of power and action: “your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy” (Exodus 15:6). The God who made all things holds the whole story of the world in one hand, every page written, every line his.

Written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Scrolls were normally written on one side only; writing on both sides pictures contents that are complete. God is not drafting history as he goes; it is written to the edges. And it is sealed up tight (katesphragismenon): not uncertain, but closed. Nothing in it moves until someone worthy opens it.

A mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice. A herald’s summons to the whole creation (v. 3), and it asks one question: not who is strong or clever enough, but who is worthy (axios), deserving, qualified. Anyone can break a seal; a seal is wax. The future of the world waits for someone good enough, and when the answer comes it will be a Lamb, worthy because he was slain (v. 9).

The setting. Wills, contracts and title deeds were written on scrolls, rolled up and sealed; under Roman law a will was commonly sealed by seven witnesses and opened formally after the death of the one who made it. A sealed book was also a prophetic picture: Ezekiel was handed a scroll written on the front and the back (Ezekiel 2:9–10), and Daniel was told to seal the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9).

What is the scroll? Suggestions include the Old Testament, the book of life, a title deed to the world, a last will holding the saints’ inheritance. The text shows only what happens when it is opened: the sweep of history from the cross to the new creation. So it is best taken as God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation. Opening it means not only revealing that plan but carrying it out: as the seals are broken in chapter 6, things happen on earth.

Is the scroll the same as the book of life? Probably not, though they are related. The book of life (3:5; 13:8; 20:12) is the register of those who belong to the Lamb, never described as sealed; this scroll is God’s purpose in history, judgment and salvation together. Yet the purpose it carries out is the bringing home of every name written in the other book. The plan of history and the list of the redeemed are in the same hands.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of “written within and on the back, sealed” can also be read as written within, and sealed on the back, so it is uncertain whether John pictures a scroll written on both sides or a document written inside and sealed on the outside. Either way the meaning is the same: the contents are full, and fully closed until the right person opens them.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole universe is searched and no one is worthy to open God’s plan, and John weeps, because an unopened scroll means a world that is never put right.

No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth. The ancient way of saying everywhere: heaven with its angels, earth with the living, and the realm of the dead. Within its reach were myriads of angels; every philosopher, reformer, general and king; every saint who had died in faith, Abraham, Moses, David, not worthy even to look inside. The search fails not because the universe is short of strength, but because it is short of righteousness: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). If they were not worthy, neither are we. That is also the best news there is: the worthiness heaven required was never going to be ours. It was going to be our Saviour’s.

I began to weep loudly. Not quiet emotion: John broke down and sobbed (eklaion), and the tense suggests he kept on until somebody stopped him. These are the only tears shed in the throne room anywhere in this book, and two chapters from its end God himself will wipe away every tear from every eye (21:4).

Why so extreme a reaction? Because John has grasped what the closed scroll means. If nobody opens it, the martyrs under the altar are never answered (6:10), Rome goes on for ever, and the seven churches keep meeting in borrowed rooms until they die out one by one. It is a world where nothing is ever put right, history running down like a clock nobody winds. His tears are the right response to a world without a redeemer.

The one the search could not find. The failed search shows, before he appears, what the redeemer must be: one of the race that fell, or he cannot stand in for it (Hebrews 2:17); without sin, or he needs redeeming himself (Hebrews 4:15); and of a worth no creature has, the Word who was God and became flesh (John 1:1, 14). All three meet in one person, and in no other. Heaven, earth and the grave were searched, and the only one found worthy was the one who did not need to be searched for, because he had come looking for us. The universe could not produce a redeemer.

That grief is not exotic. Any honest believer has felt a version of it, reading the news for the fortieth year, or standing in a cemetery where nobody was ever tried for what was done: the suspicion that the scroll will never be opened. John does not tell himself it will probably work out. He weeps, in heaven, and Scripture records it without rebuke. And the weeping is answered, but not by an argument.

If the plan was always going to be carried out, why make John weep at all? So that we know what the answer is worth: a rescue is only understood by someone who has looked at the drop. Had John seen the Lamb first, he would have admired him; having seen the empty universe first, he worships him. The gospel is meant to land not on people managing quite well, but on people who have seen, for one honest moment, that without Christ no one can put the world right, or put them right.

Is it wrong for me to feel this despair? No. To feel the weight of a world not yet put right is to see it truly, and Scripture is full of believers who cried, “How long?” (Psalm 13:1; Habakkuk 1:2; Revelation 6:10). What would be wrong is to stay there as though the elder had never spoken. Weep, and then listen. The Christian is not the person who never feels the darkness, but the person who has been told who walked into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s tears are stopped by news of a person: Jesus, the promised King from Judah and the line of David, has conquered, and so has won the right to open God’s plan.

Weep no more. Literally stop weeping (mē klaie). The tears are not criticised; they are ended, and by an announcement about a person, not by advice. That is the shape of every real Christian comfort: grief stops when somebody walks into the room.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah. The lion (leōn) is royal, powerful and conquering. Dying Jacob called Judah a lion’s cub from whom the sceptre would not depart (Genesis 49:9–10), and Jesus was born of that tribe of kings (Hebrews 7:14): he is the King promised on Jacob’s deathbed nearly two thousand years before. Some Jewish writings of John’s day used this image, and the next, for a warrior Messiah.

The Root of David. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David’s father, on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest, a root that would stand as a signal for the peoples (Isaiah 11:1–4, 10). Root (rhiza) means not only David’s descendant but his source (22:16). Jesus once asked how, if David calls the Messiah Lord, he can be his son (Matthew 22:41–45). Here is the answer: he is David’s offspring and David’s Lord, the branch that grew from the family tree and the root from which the whole tree drew its life. Every thread of Israel’s hope runs to one person, and he has already won.

Has conquered. The verb (enikēsen) is the one in the promise “to the one who conquers” at the end of each of the seven letters (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21). Whatever the churches are asked to do, he has already done, and the tense is past: not is conquering or will conquer, but conquered. The matter is closed. Christ conquered first, and his people conquer through him, by his blood (3:21; 12:11). So the right to open the scroll was not handed to him for his rank alone. It was won.

Conquered whom, and when? Sin, death and Satan, at the cross and in the resurrection. There he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14); and he rose as the firstborn of the dead (1:5). The battle that decides history is not still to be fought at the end of the age. It was fought outside Jerusalem around AD 30, and everything in Revelation from here on is the outworking of a victory already won.

A root out of dry ground. The King promised to Judah grew up “like a root out of dry ground” (Isaiah 53:2), was “cut off out of the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8), and on the third day rose, and the stump of Jesse had a living King again. John’s tears stopped at his name, and every tear on earth will stop at his face (21:4).

In everyday life. When grief over the world or over your own life comes, do not wait for an argument to make it lift. Turn to Christ and say his titles to him: Lion of Judah, Root of David, the one who has conquered. The one who won the war is the one opening the scroll of your days.

If Christ has already conquered, why is the world still so dark? Because a war can be decided before it is over. The decisive battle is won and the enemy’s doom sealed; the remaining fighting is real, but cannot change the outcome. That is what the rest of this book shows: real suffering under seals, trumpets and bowls, a dragon furious because he knows that his time is short (12:12), and through it all the Lamb holding the scroll. The darkness is the last struggle of an enemy who has already lost.

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lion John was promised turns out to be a Lamb, slain yet standing at the centre of heaven, and he takes the scroll from God’s hand. His power is complete, and it was won by sacrifice.

I saw a Lamb. He was told a Lion; he sees a Lamb. That single substitution is a key to the whole book. Revelation will speak the language of conquest, warfare, thrones and armies for seventeen more chapters, and this verse has just defined every one of those words: the Lion conquers as a Lamb, and power has been redefined by sacrifice. Christ did not win by crushing his enemies but by dying for his people (on what the cross conquered, see v. 5).

The Lamb’s name. John’s word is arnion, not the amnos used of Christ elsewhere (John 1:29; Acts 8:32). In form it is a word for a little lamb, though by John’s day it usually meant simply a lamb, and it becomes his main name for Christ, twenty-eight times. In the most violent, thunderous book in the Bible, the conqueror’s name is the plain word for a young sheep.

At the centre. Between the throne and the four living creatures, among the elders: the very centre of heaven, not the edge where a guest or petitioner would stand. Later John speaks of the Lamb “in the midst of the throne” (7:17) and of “the throne of God and of the Lamb” (22:1). He shares God’s throne. There is no other face at the centre of the universe, and there never will be.

Standing, as though it had been slain. Two impossible things in one clause. Standing (hestēkos) is alive, risen, upright. Slain (esphagmenon) comes from a verb used for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat: butchered, not merely killed, and its Greek form describes a past act whose result is still in force. The Lamb is risen, and at the same time visibly, permanently, a slaughtered animal.

With seven horns and with seven eyes. A horn is strength, the emblem of a king (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 18:2): seven horns is complete power, and the Lamb is not weak. Seven eyes is complete knowledge, from Zechariah, where the seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10). The seven spirits are the Holy Spirit in his fullness (1:4), and they are the Lamb’s eyes: the Spirit is his, sent out by him into all the earth (John 15:26; 16:7; Acts 2:33). All-powerful, all-knowing, present everywhere by his Spirit, the Lamb is fully God.

He went and took the scroll. A plain sentence, after six verses of held breath. “Took” (eilēphen) is in that same Greek form again: a decisive act with lasting result. It echoes Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom. The reaching out of that hand unlocks the future of the world: the Lamb receives authority to carry out God’s whole plan for history.

The setting. Every Jewish reader knew what a slain lamb meant. The Passover lamb’s blood on the doorposts turned away judgment (Exodus 12); Isaiah’s Servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing the sin of many (Isaiah 53:7, 12); and John the Baptist pointed to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

The marks are the credential. The one thing never erased from the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. When Thomas needed proof, the risen Christ showed him not a restored body but a scarred one: “put out your hand, and place it in my side” (John 20:27). His death is not a past he has moved beyond but the permanent ground of his authority and our salvation. The Lion of Judah did not conquer by roaring but by bleeding, and the hand that reaches out to take the scroll of history is the hand that was pierced for us.

So is the Lamb a picture of how Christians should live? Yes, and nothing in the book is more practical. The Lamb’s way of victory, through sacrifice, truth-telling and faithful suffering rather than force, is the way he calls his people to walk: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death” (12:11). This does not make Christians doormats or forbid lawful government its sword (Romans 13:4); it means the church never advances Christ’s kingdom by coercion, manipulation or worldly power, and that faithfulness which looks like losing is often how the Lamb wins.

In everyday life. In the meeting where you could win by bending the truth, the family argument where you could crush by being cleverer, the moment you could get even, ask what the Lamb would look like here. His Spirit goes with you. It will often look like losing; so did the cross. And where you fail, he walked this way perfectly in your place, and his blood answers for the rest.

What it does not mean. The Lamb’s gentleness does not cancel his justice; the same book speaks of “the wrath of the Lamb” (6:16). Revelation’s Christ is the slain Lamb who conquers, and the conquering Lamb who was slain.

Does Jesus still suffer in heaven? No. The Greek form means the effect of his death remains, not that the dying goes on. Christ died once for all (Hebrews 9:26–28; Romans 6:9–10), and his sacrifice is finished (John 19:30). He is standing, not lying on an altar; the marks are like a soldier’s scar after he has come home, no longer pain but proof. So the Lord’s Supper is a remembrance, not a repetition: we do not offer Christ again, but feed on a sacrifice completed.

Why does the Lamb take the scroll from the Father, rather than having it already? Because the picture is of the Son receiving, as the risen Messiah, the authority he won. As God the Son he shares the Father’s rule eternally; as the incarnate Son who obeyed to death, he is given the name above every name (Philippians 2:8–11) and all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). There is no rivalry: the Father gives and the Son takes, in perfect agreement.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven falls down before the Lamb as it fell before God, holding the prayers of his people, and sings that he is worthy because by his death he bought people for God from every nation. Those he bought he has made a kingdom of priests, who will reign on the earth.

They fell down before the Lamb. The worship given to the one on the throne in chapter 4 (4:10) is given here to the Lamb, without a word of explanation and without anyone objecting. Yet in this book angels twice refuse worship outright, telling John to worship God (19:10; 22:8–9). No creature may receive it. The Lamb receives it in the presence of God the Father, and heaven approves: Jesus is God.

A harp, and golden bowls full of incense. The harp is for the song about to be sung. The bowls of incense, John says, are the prayers of the saints: incense burned on the golden altar was Israel’s picture of prayer, “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). “Saints” (hagiōn, holy ones) means all believers, not a special class of the especially devout. The prayers of ordinary Christians are held in golden bowls by the highest beings in creation, at the moment the scroll is opened.

None of them evaporated. Not the desperate prayer of a believer in Smyrna the night before a hearing, nor the badly worded prayer at a kitchen table that felt as though it hit the ceiling. They are in golden bowls, and the bowls are full. And some of it is explosive. At 8:3–5 the same prayers are offered on the golden altar, and fire from the altar is thrown onto the earth: the persecuted church’s cries for justice (6:10) come down again as the opening act of God’s judgment on the world that ignored them.

What about prayers that were never answered? Two things are true together. God does not always give what we ask, because he is wiser than our requests: Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). And no prayer of faith is lost; it is woven into his purposes in ways we often cannot see. A mother who prayed for thirty years for a son converted after her funeral did not pray in vain; her prayers were in the bowl the whole time. Keep asking. Nothing put into the bowls is thrown away.

Does this mean the elders pray for us, or that we should pray to saints in heaven? No. The elders present the saints’ own prayers to God; they neither produce them nor are prayed to. Scripture nowhere invites believers to address prayers to departed saints or angels, for “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Pray to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. What this verse adds is not a new channel for prayer but an assurance about where every prayer arrives.

A new song. New (kainēn) in kind, not merely recent. Psalms and prophets call for a new song for a new act of salvation (Psalm 96:1; Isaiah 42:10), and here is a redemption greater than the exodus. Chapter 4 ended with a song about creation; this one has a different subject.

For you were slain. Here is the answer to the herald’s question in verse 2: who is worthy? You are. The ground of the worthiness is not his power, though he has seven horns, nor his knowledge, though he has seven eyes, but his death. What makes the Lamb worthy, in heaven’s eyes, is his wounds.

By your blood you ransomed people for God. “Ransomed” (ēgorasas) is the ordinary word for buying in the market, used also of buying slaves. He went to the slave market of a race that had sold itself to sin and paid with his own blood, and the people he bought now belong to God. This is substitutionary atonement: the penalty our sins deserved fell on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24). We were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

From every tribe and language and people and nation. Four terms, the number of the whole earth, and John varies their order each time he uses them, as if to stop anyone turning them into a fixed list. This fulfils God’s promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Nobody is outside its reach, and nobody is ransomed as a nation or a category: the purchase is of people, out of every group there is.

A kingdom and priests. The same phrase as 1:6, from God’s words at Sinai (Exodus 19:6), and the tense matters: “you have made”, already done, not pending. A kingdom: they belong to the King and share his rule. Priests: they have direct access to God and serve him in worship, intercession and witness. What Israel was called to be at Sinai, the ransomed of every nation now are in Christ.

They shall reign on the earth. The redeemed share Christ’s rule on the renewed earth of the new creation (21:1; 22:5). Salvation is not escape from creation but its renewal.

A Western religion? Many in Europe and North America still assume that Christianity is the faith of the West, and that its decline there is its decline everywhere. The historian Philip Jenkins, in The Next Christendom, showed how over the twentieth century the church’s centre of gravity moved to the global South: a typical Christian today is far more likely to live in Lagos, São Paulo or Manila than in London or Boston. That would not have surprised John. The faith began in western Asia among people the empire looked down on, and it has never belonged to one culture: put to death by his own nation and an occupying empire together, its Lord belongs to neither, and to everyone he bought. The song in heaven has every accent in it, and no one sings it as the host welcoming guests; every voice is there because of the same blood.

In everyday life. Look around your church on Sunday. If there are people there whose language, background or skin is not yours, you are looking at what the Lamb bought. Learn one of their names, and pray for one place in the world where the gospel has not yet reached a tribe or language.

What it does not mean. In this commentary’s amillennial reading, reigning on the earth does not mean a future thousand-year political reign before the final state, though premillennial brothers and sisters expect one (see the introduction).

Can I then tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is able and willing to save all who come to him, and that whoever believes in him will not perish (John 3:16; 6:37). That is the apostles’ gospel and a sincere offer, for the sacrifice is of infinite worth and the invitation is God’s own. Definite atonement (see below) adds not a limit on the offer but a certainty about the result: the Lamb’s blood did not merely make salvation available and wait to see who would take it. It bought a people, and the Spirit will bring every one of them home. So missionaries can go to the hardest places with confidence.

Is a faith that sings about blood not primitive? The song does not celebrate violence. Blood in Scripture stands for a life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11): to sing of the Lamb’s blood is to sing that he gave his own life to set others free, the very opposite of the strong crushing the weak. Every culture honours the soldier who dies for his comrades; the cross is that raised to its height, the innocent Son of God giving himself for the guilty so that their real debt is really paid. What would be primitive is a god who shrugged at evil, or who made someone else pay against his will. This God pays himself, in his Son, freely.

How do I reign now, when my life feels so small? By belonging to the King and sharing his victory. You reign when sin no longer has dominion over you (Romans 6:14), when you pray and heaven’s purposes move, when fear, money and others’ opinion no longer rule you, and when you suffer faithfully rather than giving in. The reign is hidden now, as Christ’s was on the cross, but it is real, and it will be revealed on a renewed earth. The widow praying in a care home is no less a royal priest than the preacher on a platform.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every person, or for his people? Many Christians hold that Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all and actual when people believe; they hold it from a deep conviction that God loves the whole world (John 3:16; 1 John 2:2), and they are brothers and sisters in the same gospel. This commentary’s view: the song says that Christ’s blood actually ransomed people for God, not that it made a ransom possible, and that it ransomed people from every tribe, language, people and nation, not every person in every nation. This is definite atonement: Christ died intending actually to save those the Father gave him (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25), and his death secures their salvation. Its value is infinite, sufficient for all, and the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone. But its design is to save a people chosen from every nation, and it does not fail.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “redeemed us” and “made us kings and priests, and we shall reign”, making the elders sing about themselves. The best manuscripts read “ransomed people” (or simply ransomed for God from every tribe) and “made them … they shall reign”. Some manuscripts also read they reign (present tense) rather than they shall reign. Both are true: believers reign now with Christ in a hidden way (1:6), and will reign fully in the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Countless angels now join the song: the Lamb who was slain is worthy of everything there is to give.

The voice of many angels. The circle of worship widens from the living creatures and elders to the angels, whose singing has been going on out there the whole time John was weeping. A myriad (myrias) is ten thousand, the largest number Greek had a single word for; myriads of myriads is not a count but the language running out, as in Daniel 7:10.

Worthy is the Lamb who was slain. The angels speak of the Lamb rather than to him. The song of verse 9 is sung by those ransomed by his blood; the angels sing of a redemption they have watched but not received, things “into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). Whatever the honour of an unfallen angel, it does not include being bought. The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary congregation has a line in this song that Gabriel cannot sing.

Two songs, one throne. The difference between the two songs is the gospel. In chapter 4 the elders sang, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God”, and the ground was creation: “for you created all things” (4:11). Here the angels sing that the Lamb is worthy, and the ground is the cross: he was slain. The second song could not have been sung by anyone before Calvary.

Seven gifts. Seven qualities, the complete set, and in Greek a single “the” stands before all seven, joining them as one whole. Everything there is to give is given, and it is given to a slaughtered lamb. They are also everything Rome prized and its emperors claimed, and a congregation shut out of the guilds is told where all seven belong, wealth included.

What earth thought worthless. Every one of the seven was refused him once. He who was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9); he had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20); his power hung helpless on a beam, the only honour men paid him was a robe of mockery, and he was laid in a borrowed tomb. Now ten thousand times ten thousand voices give all seven back at once, precisely because he was slain. Nothing in heaven is worth more than the one earth thought worthless.

In everyday life. In a small church on a wet Sunday, with a thin congregation and an out-of-tune piano, remember that you are not the whole choir. You are joining a song that has been going on around the throne beyond counting, and your voice is wanted in it.

Why do the angels worship, if Christ did not die for them? Because they love God’s glory, and in the cross they have seen it more clearly than anywhere else: through the church “the manifold wisdom of God” is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10). They watched the Son make worlds, then leave heaven, sleep in a manger, pray in anguish in Gethsemane and die. They had never seen holiness and love meet like that. If beings who were never lost cannot stop singing about the cross, how much more should those who were?

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At last every creature everywhere blesses God and the Lamb together, and the beings nearest the throne answer, “Amen!”

Every creature. The circle widens one last time and takes in everything that exists (pan ktisma): the three regions searched in verse 3, with the sea added. There the search found nobody worthy; here the whole of it is singing. Nine verses earlier John was weeping in heaven; nothing changed in between except that a Lamb walked forward and took a scroll. He sees ahead to the end, when all creation acknowledges God and the Lamb.

To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. The climax: one doxology, two recipients, no distinction between them. Chapter 4 praised God as Creator and chapter 5 has praised the Lamb as Redeemer; now both are worshipped in a single sentence, in exactly the same words. Revelation nowhere argues the doctrine of the Trinity; it is simply what worship in heaven looks like. This is the book’s clearest picture of the Son’s full equality with the Father.

Blessing first. Four attributes here rather than seven, and the first is blessing. A creature cannot add anything to God; to bless God is to speak well of him, to say back to him what he is. That is the last thing all creation does in this vision: it has nothing to give him but its praise.

Amen. So be it; it is true. The beings nearest the throne, who sing “holy, holy, holy” without pause (4:8), do not add anything; they agree. Then the elders fall down and worship, and the chapter ends in silence: twenty-four figures on their faces, their crowns already on the floor.

A single chord, held for ever. This is the sound the world was made for. Sea and sky and the dark places under the earth, which have groaned under the curse, find their voice, and their first word is blessing, said to the Father and the Son in one breath, because the Son has done what the Father sent him to do, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The silence that once made a man weep in heaven has become a single chord, and it is held for ever.

What it does not mean. Worshipping the Lamb with the Father does not mean there are two Gods. Revelation is strictly monotheistic: the Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3) and receive one worship.

How can creatures in the sea and under the earth praise God? In the way “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1) and the trees of the field clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12): by being what God made them to be and showing his glory. The creation that now groans (Romans 8:19–22) is set free and gives voice to praise: conscious praise from rational creatures, and from the rest the praise of a world put right. Nothing God made is left out of the song.

What comes next. The seven seals are about to be broken, and conquest, war, famine and death ride out of them. Every one is opened by the Lamb’s own hand, and it goes no further than he permits. That is the comfort a reader must carry into chapter 6.

Where Christians differ: will every creature be saved? Universalists, some of them sincerely longing for God’s mercy to reach everyone, read this verse, with Philippians 2:10–11, as meaning that all creatures, including those now in rebellion, will finally be reconciled and saved. This commentary’s view: universal acknowledgement is not universal salvation. Revelation clearly teaches that some will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (14:9–11; 20:10, 15; 21:8). Every creature will confess that God and the Lamb are worthy: for the redeemed it is joyful worship, and for the lost the forced admission of a truth they rejected. God’s glory will be acknowledged everywhere, in mercy and in justice.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals.<sup>2</sup>And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”<sup>3</sup>And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it,<sup>4</sup>and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.<sup>5</sup>And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”<sup>6</sup>And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.<sup>7</sup>And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.<sup>8</sup>And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,<sup>10</sup>and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”<sup>11</sup>Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,<sup>12</sup>saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”<sup>13</sup>And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!”<sup>14</sup>And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

keyVerse.quote: Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation
keyVerse.note: This is heaven’s answer to the question that made John weep: who is worthy? The ground of the Lamb’s worthiness is not his power or his knowledge but his death, and what his death achieved: it did not merely make a rescue possible but bought real people for God from every corner of the earth. Every other song in the chapter grows from this one.

5.reflection:
John weeps because no one is worthy to open the scroll (vv. 3–4), and Scripture records his tears without rebuke. Where do you feel the grief of a world not yet put right? How does this chapter teach us to bring that grief to Christ rather than bury it or stay in it?

John is told of a Lion and turns to see a slain Lamb (vv. 5–6). What does this tell us about how Christ conquers? Where are you tempted to pursue what is good by force, manipulation or winning, rather than by the way of the Lamb?

The prayers of the saints are kept in golden bowls before the throne (v. 8). How does this change the way you think about prayers that seem unanswered or that felt as though they went nowhere?

The new song praises the Lamb because he ransomed people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (v. 9) and made them a kingdom and priests. How should this shape the way we see our own church, Christians in other nations, and our part in mission?

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
Where we are. The Lamb who took the scroll in chapter 5 now begins to break its seals. Chapter 6 opens six of the seven; the seventh waits until 8:1, after the pause of chapter 7.

The message. The troubles of history do not ride at nobody’s word. Conquest, slaughter, famine and death are real and terrible, but they are released by the Lamb’s own hand, held within God’s limits, and heading for a day of judgment. The blood of his people is not forgotten. And on that day one question will be left: who can stand before the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb?

Why it was said. The churches of Asia lived with the empire’s wars and shortages, and some had buried their own: Antipas had been killed (2:13), and Smyrna was warned of prison (2:10). They needed to know whether God had lost control of the world, or forgotten them in it (see the introduction); the comfortable churches needed the warning.

How the chapter makes its case. First, four horsemen ride out (vv. 1–8): conquest, civil slaughter, famine, and Death with Hades behind him, every one “given” or “permitted” what he does. Then the fifth seal turns to the church’s suffering (vv. 9–11): the martyrs under the altar cry, “How long?”, and are given white robes and rest. Last, the sixth seal unmakes every fixed point of creation, and everyone from kings to slaves hides from the face of God (vv. 12–17). This commentary reads the seals, trumpets and bowls not as one timetable but as parallel passes over the same history, each ending at the last day (see vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. The hand that breaks each seal is the hand that was pierced, and the keys of Death and Hades are on his belt (1:18). The martyrs are slain with the word used of the Lamb, and their robes are white with his blood (7:14). The chapter ends with the most startling phrase in the book, “the wrath of the Lamb”: the one the kings of the earth cannot face is the one who bore God’s wrath for all who come to him. So the closing question has an answer, and chapter 7 gives it.

For us. Read the news remembering whose hand is on the seal. Pray the martyrs’ “How long?” honestly. And settle now where you will stand on the last day: behind a rock, or before the throne in a robe washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything that troubles history, from war and famine to the death of the martyrs and the end of the world itself, is opened by the Lamb and runs towards a day of judgment. Four horsemen ride out at his word, bringing conquest, slaughter, famine and death, each acting only by permission and within limits (vv. 1–8). The fifth seal shows the church’s side: the martyrs, safe under God’s altar, cry for justice and are given white robes and rest until their number is complete (vv. 9–11). The sixth seal removes every fixed point of creation, and all humanity, great and small, hides from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb (vv. 12–17). The chapter ends on a question, who can stand?, which chapter 7 answers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb breaks the first seal, and a conqueror rides out: the wars of conquest that fill history are released by the Lamb’s hand, and only by his permission.

The Lamb opened one of the seven seals. Three things govern how this chapter is read. The first is who is doing it. Every horror here is released by the hand that was pierced. The first thing heaven wants a suffering church to know about the troubles of history is who opens them: not chance, not Caesar, not the devil, but the Lamb who was slain, who holds the scroll by right of the blood he shed (5:9). The disasters are not outside his control; they serve his plan.

Come! The second is the summons, calling the horseman out: heaven speaks first, and earth responds. The living creatures, representing creation, summon the judgments that must come before creation is set free.

A crown was given to him. The third is the grammar. Watch through the next seven verses for verbs that say something was done to the riders, not by them: a crown was given, the rider was permitted, they were given authority. “Was given” (edothē) recurs through Revelation for God’s permission. No rider here takes power for himself; even evil powers act only as God allows.

A white horse, and its rider had a bow. The bow was the weapon of the Parthians, the mounted archers of the empire to the east whom Rome feared on its frontier. The crown (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath, not a king’s diadem, and it was given to him: even the conqueror rides only by permission.

Conquering, and to conquer. Invasion and empire-building: not content with one victory, he rides out to win the next. Every empire in history has had this horseman at its head. But every crown the conquerors wear was given and can be taken back, and every empire that rides out bent on conquest rides under the eye of the one who conquered by dying.

The setting. Zechariah saw horses of different colours sent out to patrol the earth (Zechariah 1:8–11; 6:1–8). Jesus spoke of wars, famines and earthquakes as the beginning of the birth pains, followed by persecution, and then the sun darkened and the stars falling (Matthew 24:6–29). The seals follow the same order.

How the seals fit the rest of the book. The seals are the first of three sevens, followed by trumpets (chapters 8–11) and bowls (chapters 15–16). On the reading this commentary follows, held in various forms since Augustine, the three are parallel passes over the same history, each running from the cross to the last day with rising intensity (6:12–17; 11:15; 16:17). Futurist readers take them as consecutive events in a future tribulation; preterist readers see much of the book fulfilled in the first century (see vv. 12–14). The point of this chapter is the same either way: whatever these riders are, the Lamb sends them.

Should I try to match the horsemen to current events? No. Every generation that named this war or that dictator as the fulfilment has been wrong, because the seals describe not one decade but the whole age. That is a relief: you do not need to decode the news to understand it. When armies invade, you already know three things: this was foretold, it is under the Lamb’s authority, and it is not the end of the story.

What it does not mean. The horsemen describe the whole age between Christ’s comings, not only one-time future events. Nor does God’s permission make him the author of human evil: he limits it, uses it and will judge it.

Why would a loving God release such things at all? Because the world is in rebellion against him, and judgment on sin is part of his goodness; a God who let evil run on for ever unpunished would not be loving. And these first judgments are partial, limited and early: warnings loud enough to be heard while there is still time to turn, though many will not (9:20–21). The God who sends the horsemen is the God who, in the previous chapter, sent his Son to die for people from every nation.

Where Christians differ: who is the rider on the white horse? Some, from the early church onward, identify him with Christ, who rides a white horse in 19:11, and read the first seal as the gospel going out and conquering; white is the colour of holiness elsewhere in the book, and the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (Mark 13:10). Others see the antichrist or false messiahs imitating Christ; others, military conquest in general. This commentary’s view: the rider is conquering war, aggression and empire, like the other three horsemen, who all bring disaster. The four belong together as a set of judgments in the order of Jesus’ teaching (wars, then famines and death). Christ in chapter 19 has many crowns and a sword from his mouth, not a bow; and Christ is the one opening the seals, not one released by them. The white may suggest a deceptive imitation of Christ, since conquerors always promise peace and glory, or the white horses of victorious generals.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Come and see”, as if the living creature were speaking to John. The best manuscripts read simply “Come!”, addressed to the horseman.
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second rider takes peace from the earth, so that people turn their swords on one another; and he, too, rides only by permission.

Bright red. Fiery red, the colour of blood. What follows conquest is not peace.

To take peace from the earth. The rider does not bring war; he takes peace away, which assumes that peace was a gift. Ordinary quiet, a night without sirens, children walking to school, is a mercy, and it can be withdrawn.

Its rider was permitted. The permission comes twice in this verse: he “was permitted”, and he “was given” the sword. God is not doing his best against forces he cannot restrain: even the horse of war rides on a permission, and therefore on a leash. That is harder to look at than a God off-stage hoping for the best, and it is the only view with any hope in it.

So that people should slay one another. The Greek means each side killing the other: civil war, the neighbour with the knife, the country that turns on itself. The twentieth century did much of its killing that way, in Rwanda and Cambodia. The verb for slay is the one used of the Lamb who was slain (5:6). Human sin, released and allowed to run, destroys itself, and does to people what it did to the Son of God.

A great sword. The short blade a Roman soldier carried, the word used for the state’s sword in Romans 13:4: the weapon of ordinary state force, handed here to a horseman whose only business is that men should kill each other.

The setting. In John’s day the empire boasted of the Pax Romana, the peace of Rome, kept by its legions. Yet the first century saw civil war in AD 68–69 and the Jewish war that destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

The peace the rider cannot reach. In the upper room, with soldiers already on their way, Jesus left his disciples his own peace, “not as the world gives” (John 14:27), and within hours went to the cross to make it. “He himself is our peace,” Paul says, having broken down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The red horse can take the peace of streets and nations, but not peace with God, because that peace was made not on earth by treaty but by the Lamb, and it is kept in heaven, where no horse rides.

In everyday life. You already hold the peace the rider cannot reach, so be a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9) in the small wars nearest you, at home, at work and in church, where the sin that fuels the red horse works on a smaller scale, and point people to the Prince of Peace.

If God permits this, is he responsible for it? Scripture holds two things together. God is never the author of evil, and no man who takes up a sword can plead that heaven made him do it.
