And nothing happens outside God’s governance, this included. Joseph said both in one sentence about the worst thing his brothers ever did: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The brothers were guilty; God was not idle. Both clauses stand (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both at 5.4).

Does this mean Christians may never serve as soldiers? No. This sword is wielded for slaughter, but the governing authority “does not bear the sword in vain” and is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). John the Baptist told soldiers to be honest and content, not to leave the army (Luke 3:14), and the first Gentile convert was a centurion (Acts 10). The historic Reformed view is that Christians may lawfully wage war upon just and necessary occasions (Westminster 23.2; 1689 24.2); Christians who in good conscience hold otherwise should be honoured. What this verse condemns is not the defence of the innocent but the lust for blood, and it warns that even just wars are fought in a world where the red horse rides.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third rider brings famine, bread weighed out at prices a day’s wage can barely meet; yet a voice from the throne sets its limit.

A black horse! Famine follows an army, the second half of a war: fields trampled, men conscripted off the land, granaries emptied. Black is the colour of mourning and hunger; Lamentations speaks of faces “blacker than soot” and skin hot as an oven in the famine of Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:8; 5:10).

A pair of scales. The scales are the point. Grain sold by weight rather than by the sackful is grain being rationed, and the prophets used exactly this image: “They shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety” (Ezekiel 4:16).

A quart of wheat for a denarius. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2), and a quart (a choinix, about a litre) of wheat was roughly one person’s daily ration; normally a denarius would buy eight to sixteen times as much. A man works from dawn to dusk and earns enough to feed himself and nothing for his family; cheaper barley buys three rations, still little for a household. This is not mass starvation but something more familiar and grinding: a man in full work who cannot feed his family, and can do nothing more about it.

Do not harm the oil and wine! Olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive drought better than grain. The judgment is severe but not total: a warning, not yet the end. Hearers in Asia may also have caught an echo: around AD 92, during a grain shortage, the emperor Domitian ordered half the vineyards in the provinces cut down to grow grain, and protest made him drop it. The emperor’s decree was withdrawn; the limit set by this voice holds.

The cellar and the street. There is irony in the line too. Oil and wine were the produce of estates rather than smallholdings, the goods of the comfortable. This is the injustice of every food crisis: the rich man’s cellar is untouched while a labourer counts out grain by weight in the street outside. Famines are rarely caused by there being no food at all; usually the food is there, and those who die are those who cannot pay for it.

A voice in the midst of the four living creatures. It comes from where the Lamb was standing a chapter earlier (5:6), and it draws the limit of the famine. The one who measures out this hunger is the one who had compassion on a hungry crowd because they had nothing to eat, and fed them (Mark 8:1–9). Famine in this world does not happen behind his back.

What it does not mean. These are not the scales of justice but of scarcity: food weighed out because there is not enough of it.

What should a Christian do when prices soar and money is tight? Trust first: your Father knows what you need, and he feeds the birds, who neither sow nor reap (Matthew 6:25–33); that is no promise of luxury, but you are not forgotten. Then share: the early church met famine by sending relief to believers in need (Acts 11:28–30), and those with oil and wine in the cellar are called to open it. And be honest about which side of the street you are on: if dearer bread is an inconvenience rather than a crisis for you, what are you doing for the person for whom it is a crisis?
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth rider is Death itself, with Hades following to collect what he takes; he gathers up all the great killers of history, yet his power too is given, and measured.

A pale horse! Pale green, greenish-grey (chlōros, the root of our words chlorine and chlorophyll). Used of a body, it is the colour of a corpse.

Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. The only one of the four who is named: Death (ho Thanatos), pictured as a person, and behind him a second figure, Hades (ho Hadēs), the realm of the dead, which receives what Death takes. One kills, and the other collects.

Authority over a fourth of the earth. For the fourth time a rider acts only by permission, and now the permission is measured: a portion, not the whole. The trumpets will touch a third (8:7–12), and only with the bowls does anything become total (16:1). The judgments escalate because they are measured out, in stages, with a purpose.

With sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts. “Pestilence” is literally death, a common word for plague in the Greek Old Testament. The fourth rider sums up the first three and adds disease and wild animals, the great killers of human history. These are the four “disastrous acts of judgment” God named in Ezekiel, “sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence” (Ezekiel 14:21), the Old Testament’s regular list of his judgments on a people who have broken his covenant.

Whose keys? A reader of this book has heard both names before. In the first chapter the risen Christ said, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18). The two riding out at the fourth seal are the two whose keys hang on the belt of the one who opened it. They ride only at his word, and at 20:14 the same two are thrown into the lake of fire. That the Lamb himself lets these killers out is not a comfortable doctrine, but the only alternative is that they ride at nobody’s word at all. The churches in Asia, about to meet the red horse and the pale one personally, were given not an explanation of why, but the identity of the hand on the seal.

If Christians die in the same plagues, what difference does faith make? All the difference, though not always the one we would choose. The same disease may strike believer and unbeliever, but it does not do the same thing to them. For one not in Christ, death ends every opportunity and opens onto judgment. For the believer, Death and Hades ride under his own Saviour, who has come out of death holding its keys; Death can take his body but cannot keep it, and it delivers him to Christ, “for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). The pale horse is a thief to the world and, for the Christian, only a servant opening a door.

Was a pandemic God’s judgment? In the broad sense, yes: every plague belongs to a world under the curse, and every one is a summons to repent, as Jesus said of a tower that fell on eighteen people (Luke 13:4–5). In the narrow sense, we are not told which sins of which people a particular disaster answers, and anyone who claims to know speaks beyond Scripture. The right response is not to point at others but to examine ourselves, care for the sick at cost as Christians have done since the plagues of the Roman empire, and remember how short life is.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those killed for their faith are not lost: they are with God, laid like offerings beneath his altar, and they cry to him to judge and put right what was done to them.

Under the altar. This seal breaks the pattern: no horse, no rider, but a congregation. The altar (thysiastērion) is the place of sacrifice, and in the temple the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at its base (Leviticus 4:7), for “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Paul spoke of his own coming death as a drink offering poured out (2 Timothy 4:6). So heaven has put the martyrs where an offering belongs. Their deaths were not waste but worship, and not one drop of their blood has been forgotten.

The souls of those who had been slain. “Souls” means persons, lives. And “slain” is the word used of the Lamb at 5:6: what was done to Christ has been done to them, and Scripture says so with a single deliberate word. They share his death.

For the word of God and for the witness they had borne. As John himself was on Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9). They died because they would not stop believing and confessing Christ. Antipas of Pergamum, the faithful witness killed where Satan dwells (2:13), would be among them.

O Sovereign Lord, holy and true. What they say is startling. “Sovereign Lord” (despotēs) is the word for an absolute master of a household, chosen because their complaint is precisely that he has the power to act and has not. And because God is holy and true, he must judge evil: a holy God cannot leave murder unanswered for ever, and a true God cannot forget his promise to vindicate his people.

How long before you will judge and avenge our blood? “How long” (heōs pote) is literally until when, the cry of suffering believers in the Psalms and prophets: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1; compare Psalm 79:5–10; 94:3; Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12). “Judge” (krineis) and “avenge” (ekdikeis, see justice done) are courtroom words, and “those who dwell on the earth” is Revelation’s standing name for unbelievers in rebellion against God (3:10). It is a prayer for justice, not personal revenge, and God promises to answer it: “will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night?” (Luke 18:7; Romans 12:19).

In the flow. The first four seals showed what the whole world suffers; the fifth shows what the church suffers, and that heaven has not forgotten it. The martyrs’ “How long?” is answered in stages (6:17; 8:3–5; 19:2): Revelation is, among other things, God’s long answer to this prayer.

Blood that speaks. The cry is old: the blood of Abel cried to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10). But believers have come “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood asks for justice; Christ’s speaks forgiveness, and obtains it. The martyrs can cry for judgment in God’s presence without fear for themselves only because a better blood has already spoken for them. And they cry to a God who has heard a loud cry before: his own Son “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears”, and was heard (Hebrews 5:7), and on the third day the answer walked out of the tomb. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), and his delay is not deafness.

The second burden lifted. Anyone who has been genuinely wronged, assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by somebody who was never charged, often carries a double burden: the injury itself, and the guilt of still minding about it. This verse takes the second one away. The holiest company in Scripture are asking out loud how long justice is going to take, and nobody tells them to stop.

Where are they now? The verse settles in passing a question asked at every funeral. Between death and resurrection believers are conscious, in God’s presence, able to speak, and not yet finished, because the body is still in the ground. Paul says the same: “My desire is to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Not unconscious. Not yet complete. With him.

Should believers pray for vengeance? Did not Christ tell us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and did not Stephen die asking that the sin not be held against them (Acts 7:60)? Four things settle it. First, the martyrs are not asking to do anything; they are asking God to do it. Vengeance belongs to him alone (Romans 12:19): the command is to hand the matter over, not to pretend it does not exist. Second, they name no individuals and ask for no particular punishment; they ask the judge to judge. Third, they ask not for private satisfaction but for justice, which God has promised: a universe in which murder is finally shrugged at is not a kind one. Fourth, the two prayers are not rivals. Christ prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34) and also promised that every hidden thing would be brought into the open (Luke 12:2–3). The one who repents is forgiven; the one who does not is judged. Praying for both is not confusion; it is the whole gospel with nothing left out.

How do I pray this prayer without becoming bitter? Pray it to God, in the words of the Psalms if you need them, rather than rehearsing it privately against the person. Tell him exactly what was done and that it was wrong. Then leave the verdict with him, and ask for the grace to bless the person if they repent. Bitterness is justice held in your own hands too long. The martyrs’ prayer is justice handed over to the only Judge who will get it exactly right, which is why it can be prayed by someone who also forgives.

Do the dead in Christ know what is happening on earth? They know that justice has not yet been done, and Scripture takes us no further. It does not teach that departed loved ones watch over us, hear us or can be spoken to. What it teaches is better: they are with Christ, at rest, conscious, and joined with us in longing for his coming. The communion of saints is real, but it runs through Christ, not around him. Thank God for them and look forward to seeing them; you need not talk to them.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah’s Witnesses, teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, or that the soul does not exist apart from the body. This commentary’s view: the martyrs are conscious, speaking, praying and comforted while their bodies are in the grave. Scripture teaches an intermediate state in which believers are with Christ at once when they die (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not yet in their final state, which comes at the resurrection, but they are with the Lord, at rest (v. 11). Nor is there any purgatory (the Roman Catholic teaching that the saved are cleansed by suffering after death): they are under the altar, in God’s presence, not being purified.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the martyrs with a robe and a word: they are vindicated now and told to rest, because the end will come when the full number of his witnesses is complete.

A white robe. They asked how long, and the answer comes in two parts, neither of them what the question asked for: a garment and a word. The white robe means purity, victory, vindication, promised to the conquerors in Sardis (3:4–5) and worn by the great multitude (7:9), and 7:14 says where its whiteness comes from: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” The robe is not a reward for dying well but the court’s verdict delivered in advance. Paul’s word for this is justification: God pronouncing a person righteous on the ground of what Christ has done, not of what he has done himself (Romans 5:1, 9). The martyrs’ deaths did not earn the robe; the Lamb’s death did, and their faithfulness to death showed whose they were. Many were executed as criminals by lawful courts; heaven has dressed them in the colour of innocence, a robe apiece.

To rest a little longer. They are told to stop working: what is still to be done about the injustice is no longer their assignment. Their rest contrasts with those who worship the beast, who “have no rest, day or night” (14:11), while blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (14:13). And it is a little longer: there is an end, and God calls the wait short. That is time measured in heaven, where a thousand years are as one day (2 Peter 3:8), not in a prison cell, where one day can feel like a thousand years.

Until the number should be complete. “Complete” means filled up. God has a set number of martyrs, as he has of the elect, those he has chosen to save, “the fullness of the Gentiles” coming in (Romans 11:25), and the end will come when his purposes are complete. The number is not a rough count of losses but a list of names: nobody in it is an accident, and nobody outside it will be taken by mistake. He counts them one by one, patient with his enemies, faithful to his friends, certain of the end. It does not mean he takes pleasure in their deaths: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15).

Who were to be killed as they themselves had been. This is very hard. The church was not promised escape from suffering: God is waiting because more are still to come, and they will die the same way. The answer to how long until you avenge our blood is: until the rest of your brothers have shed theirs.

The patience that produced Paul. But consider what else the delay does. God is patient, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9), and every year the judgment is postponed, an enemy of God can be brought in. The man who wrote most of the New Testament’s letters about grace had held the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). He received mercy so that in him, the foremost of sinners, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The patience the martyrs are asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul.

In everyday life. If you are waiting on God for something that has not come, a healing, a justice, a prodigal’s return, his answer to the martyrs was not an explanation but a robe and rest. Both are offered to you first: his verdict over you in Christ, and leave to put down what he has told you to stop carrying. And pray this week for a persecuted church: it may yet see its persecutors become like Paul.

Should I expect to be martyred? Most Christians in history have not been, and most readers of this page will not be. But every Christian is called to be ready, and in parts of the world the number is still being filled; this verse forbids the assumption that faithfulness will be safe. Jesus said that if they persecuted him they would persecute his followers (John 15:20). In the West the costs are usually smaller, a lost promotion, a broken friendship, mockery; prepare for those now, because courage to die for Christ is ordinarily built from a thousand small refusals to be ashamed of him. And when you have been ashamed of him, as Peter was, remember that Christ made the good confession before Pilate perfectly in your place (1 Timothy 6:13), that his faithfulness is counted as yours, and that his Spirit gives the words when the hour comes (Matthew 10:19–20).

If God has fixed the number, why pray or evangelise? Because God fixes the ends and the means together. The God who knows the full number of his people has appointed that they be gathered through preaching, prayer and the church’s witness, often at the cost of suffering. A fixed number does not make the work pointless; it makes it certain. Paul kept preaching in Corinth because the Lord told him, “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:10). The roll is full of names not yet called, and your witness may be how one of them is.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth seal brings the last day itself: every fixed point of creation, earth, sun, moon, stars and sky, is shaken and removed as God comes in judgment.

A great earthquake. The stage of the world is taken down, from the ground upward. In Scripture earthquakes accompany God’s coming in power: “the whole mountain trembled greatly” at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and God has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens” (Hebrews 12:26). Asia was earthquake country: Sardis and Philadelphia had been flattened in AD 17.

Black as sackcloth. Sackcloth was coarse cloth woven from black goat hair and worn in mourning, so the comparison is exact, not merely poetic: the sun itself puts on mourning.

The full moon became like blood. As in Joel: “The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Joel 2:31), words Peter quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

As the fig tree sheds its winter fruit. Isaiah had compared the falling host of heaven to leaves falling from the fig tree (Isaiah 34:4); John sharpens the picture to the fruit. Late figs that never ripened hang on through the winter until the first storm. The lights that sailors steered by, astrologers consulted and emperors stamped on their coins come down like unripe fruit off a fig tree in a gale, and the tree does not notice.

The sky vanished like a scroll. “Vanished” means split apart, removed; Isaiah says “the skies roll up like a scroll” (Isaiah 34:4). The created order as we know it passes away: “the heavens will pass away with a roar” (2 Peter 3:10), and from the presence of him who sits on the great white throne “earth and sky fled away” (20:11). Even the mountains and islands are moved, and nothing is left to hide behind.

The setting. The prophets described the Day of the LORD as cosmic collapse (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31; Haggai 2:6), and Jesus used the same language for his coming (Matthew 24:29–30). It sometimes described the fall of an empire (Isaiah 13, of Babylon), but here its universal scope points to the end of the age.

The fixed points removed. Everything humanity has used as a fixed point is in this list: the ground that does not move, the sun that always rises, the stars that guide you home, the mountains that define permanence. The throne is not. Chapter 4 established where the one fixed point is, and chapter 6 removes every rival. When the sky is rolled up, the throne will be exactly where John first saw it, and the one seated on it will not have moved. He made the sun and he will put it out; he hung the stars and he will gather them in.

The one who rolls up the sky. Hebrews takes a psalm about the end of the heavens and says it was spoken to the Son: “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain … like a robe you will roll them up” (Hebrews 1:10–12). The hand that rolls up the sky in this seal is the hand that opened the seal. And Jesus said that when the sun is darkened and the stars fall, all the tribes of the earth “will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory” (Matthew 24:30). The fixed points are taken away so that he may be seen.

What it does not mean. The cosmic language is not a scientific description of astronomical events but the prophets’ way of describing the shaking and passing away of the created order at God’s coming. It may be literal in part, and it is certainly real; but its point is that nothing in creation can stand before its Creator.

Will the world really end, or be renewed? Both. The present order, scarred by sin, will pass away, but God does not throw his creation away; he makes all things new (21:5). As the flood purged the old world without abolishing the earth (2 Peter 3:6–7), so the fire of the last day will purify and transform a creation that waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–21). The sky rolling up is not the end of everything God made. It is the end of everything that stood between creation and its glory.

Should I be afraid of the end of the world? If you are in Christ, no. For the believer, the day the sky is rolled up is the day of redemption: “straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:28). Fear over world events, war, climate, economic collapse, is answered not by pretending nothing will be shaken, but by knowing the one who cannot be. Christians should care for the world and take real dangers seriously, but they need not panic, because the end of the world is in the same hands as its beginning.

Where Christians differ: is this the end, or a stage on the way? Many futurist readers, including premillennial and dispensational Christians, place the sixth seal early in a future tribulation, with more judgments to follow in strict sequence; they take seriously that the book has an order, and they are brothers and sisters, not opponents. This commentary’s view: the sixth seal describes the final day of judgment itself, when Christ returns. Its language is the language Jesus used for his coming, and the people cry that the great day of wrath has come (v. 17). So Revelation is not one long timeline but a series of parallel visions: the seals take us to the end, and the trumpets and bowls go over the same ground again from other angles, with growing intensity. This is called recapitulation (the same period told again), and it fits the amillennial reading of the book, which takes the thousand years of chapter 20 as the present age.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day everyone, from kings to slaves, will try to hide from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, and the chapter ends with the question of the last day: who can stand?

The kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals. The vision turns from the sky to people. Seven classes are named, in this book the whole of humanity, and five of them are the powerful. The kings are the kings of the earth over whom Christ is already ruler (1:5); the great ones are nobles and top officials; the generals commanded a thousand men each. Those who seemed untouchable, who persecuted the church, are the first to flee.

And everyone, slave and free. Every category that ordinarily protects a person is named, and named uselessly: a king has an army, a rich man can buy his way out. On this day the emperor and the man he owns end up behind the same rock, and the day shows what all such quiet trusts were worth.

Fall on us. The mountains have just been moved (v. 14), and there is nowhere to hide. Given the choice between being buried alive and being looked at, they choose the burial. They do not ask for mercy; they ask to be hidden. This is not repentance but terror.

From the face of him who is seated on the throne. What they are hiding from is not fire, and not an army, but a face. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told that no one could see his face and live (Exodus 33:18–20). Israel’s great blessing was “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25), and the whole hope of this book is that his servants “will see his face” (22:4). The face the redeemed long to see is the face the lost cannot bear.

The wrath of the Lamb. “Wrath” is settled, righteous anger, and lambs do not have wrath. That is the shock, mirroring 5:5–6: there John was told of a Lion and shown a Lamb; here the Lamb is what men flee from. Not a mild Christ who has finally lost his temper, but the same Lamb with the same wounds, and his wrath belongs to the love that bore them, a love that cannot be at peace with evil. The one who died for sinners will judge those who refuse him (John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:31). Nothing is more terrible than mercy refused to the end, because then the only one left to meet is the one who offered it.

For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? The great day is the Day of the LORD, the final judgment (Joel 2:11, 31; Zephaniah 1:14). “Their wrath” is the wrath of God and the Lamb, one wrath. “Who can stand” (tis dynatai stathēnai): who is able to stand firm, survive and be acquitted? The question is left hanging on purpose. It is not only a cry of despair but a real question, and the next chapter answers it. Before the seventh seal is opened, John will be shown a multitude no one could number, “standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (7:9): the very thing this verse asks who can do.

The setting. The prophets had used these words before. Isaiah describes people fleeing into the caves of the rocks from before the terror of the LORD (Isaiah 2:19–21). Hosea says, “they shall say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall on us’” (Hosea 10:8), words Jesus quoted to the women weeping on his way to the cross (Luke 23:28–30). Malachi asks, “who can stand when he appears?” (Malachi 3:2).

Only those who stand in him. The wrath of the Lamb is real, and the Lamb is the one who drank it. On the cross the Father’s face was turned away from his Son, so that the face the kings of the earth cannot bear could shine on sinners in peace. He bore the darkness so that the redeemed might see his face; he was crushed so that they need never ask the mountains to fall. Who can stand? Only those who stand in him. And everyone who stands in him will stand for ever, robed in white, before the throne and before the Lamb.

Two places to stand. The question is not whether the world will be shaken but where you will be standing when the last fixed point goes, and the text offers only two places: behind a rock, or before the throne in a white robe. What separates them is not courage or achievement but the blood of the Lamb (7:14): the wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them.

In everyday life. People hide now in quieter ways, behind busyness, wealth, cleverness or simply never thinking about it, and some of them sit beside us at work. While it is still called today, the shelter is open, for them and for us.

Is an angry God less loving than a calm one? No, the opposite. If someone you love is being destroyed by a drug or an abuser, love does not shrug; it is angry. God’s anger is nothing childish or sudden but his holy love set firmly against whatever destroys his world and his creatures. A God who felt nothing about cruelty and murder would not be kinder, only indifferent. And the wonder of the gospel is that this God bore his own wrath in the Lamb, so that it need not fall on us (Romans 5:9).

Will people get another chance on that day? No. These people know exactly whom they are hiding from, and still ask to be hidden, not forgiven: seeing God does not by itself change a heart that has refused him. Scripture holds out no second chance after death or after his coming: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). That is why the invitation is so urgent now: “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The time to run to the Lamb is before the day of his wrath.

How can I be sure I will stand? Not by examining your courage or your record, but by looking where the multitude in chapter 7 looked: to the blood of the Lamb. If you have turned from sin and trusted Christ, his death has borne the wrath you deserved, and “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Assurance rests on his finished work, confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16) and by a changed life. If your faith is weak, it is still faith in a strong Saviour. Those he has sealed will stand, not because they are strong, but because he holds them.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!”<sup>2</sup>And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.<sup>3</sup>When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”<sup>4</sup>And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.<sup>5</sup>When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.<sup>6</sup>And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”<sup>7</sup>When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”<sup>8</sup>And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.<sup>9</sup>When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.<sup>10</sup>They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”<sup>11</sup>Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.<sup>12</sup>When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood,<sup>13</sup>and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.<sup>14</sup>The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.<sup>15</sup>Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains,<sup>16</sup>calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,<sup>17</sup>for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

keyVerse.quote: Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter drives towards this cry. The powers that seemed untouchable beg the rocks to hide them, not from fire but from a face, and the one they fear is the Lamb, whose gentleness never cancelled his justice. The question it ends with is the question every reader must answer, and the next chapter shows the only people who can: those washed in the blood of the Lamb.

6.reflection:
Every horseman in vv. 1–8 is “given” or “permitted” what he does, and every seal is opened by the Lamb. How does it change the way you hear news of war, famine or disease to know whose hand is on the seal? What questions does it leave you with?

The martyrs pray, “How long … before you will judge and avenge our blood?” (v. 10), and no one tells them to stop. Is there a wrong in your life or your world that you need to bring honestly to God in this way? How can we pray for justice without becoming bitter, and still pray for our enemies?

God answers the martyrs with a white robe and the command to rest a little longer (v. 11). What do the robe and the rest offer you while you wait for something God has not yet done?

The chapter ends, “who can stand?” (v. 17). Why does seeing God not by itself make people turn to him? How would you explain to a friend where a person must stand to be safe on that day?

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 is a pause between the sixth seal and the seventh (8:1). Chapter 6 ended with the kings of the earth hiding in caves from the face of him who sits on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, asking, “who can stand?” (6:17). Before the last seal is opened, John is shown the answer.

The message. God’s people are safe in the storm, and they will stand at the end. Before the winds of judgment blow, he marks every one of his servants as his own; and the same people, a multitude no one can count from every nation, will stand before his throne, washed in the Lamb’s blood, sheltered by his presence, with every tear wiped from their eyes. Judgment falls on the world, but not one of his is lost.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia lived under pressure that could cost them their work, their freedom and their lives (see the introduction), and the seals have just shown war, famine, death and martyrs crying “how long?” (6:10). The fear was natural: if this is what the world is like, will we come through it? Will our faith hold, and does suffering mean God has forgotten us? Chapter 7 answers both fears. On earth you are sealed; before the throne you will be safe.

How the chapter makes its case. Two scenes show one people. In verses 1–8 four angels hold back the winds until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3), and John hears their number, 144,000, counted tribe by tribe like Israel’s army (vv. 4–8): the church on earth, complete, owned and protected. In verses 9–17 he looks and sees a multitude no one could number from every nation, standing before the throne in white with palm branches and crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb (vv. 9–10). All the angels fall on their faces in praise (vv. 11–12). An elder explains that these are coming out of the great tribulation, washed in the Lamb’s blood (vv. 13–14), and so they serve God in his temple under his tent, never to hunger, thirst or weep again (vv. 15–17). As John heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5–6), he hears a number and sees a crowd: the same church, as God counts it and as it appears.

Where it leads. Every comfort in the chapter rests on the Lamb. His name and his Father’s are the seal on their foreheads (14:1); his blood makes their robes white; his throne is their shelter; and the Lamb who was led to the slaughter now shepherds his flock to springs of living water. “Who can stand?” is answered not by the strength of those standing but by the one who was slain for them, and their only song is that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.

For us. Christians read the 144,000 in different ways; this commentary takes them as the whole church, God’s true Israel (the reasons are at vv. 4–8). Either way, the chapter is written for frightened believers. Whatever comes this week, you were marked as his before the storm began, and the end of your road is a crowd you will stand in, singing a song with no line in it about yourself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before judgment falls, God marks every one of his servants as his own, so that the storm cannot destroy them. Four angels hold back the four winds, and an angel from the east with the seal of the living God orders them to wait until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3). As in Ezekiel 9:4, judgment is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked. Then John hears the number of the sealed, 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes (vv. 4–8): God’s whole people, counted like an army and complete, in a tribe list that matches no register in the Old Testament and is arranged to show a new Israel gathered around the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sealed Before the Storm

The winds of judgment are held back until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9. The 144,000 are the whole people of God, counted to the last person; God knows the number exactly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The seal did not exempt them from the tribulation; it marked them as God’s within it.

Now: The text caps nobody’s hope: the next scene is a multitude no one could number.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the storm of judgment breaks, God marks every one of his servants as his own, so that it cannot destroy them. The judgment is not cancelled; it is held back until his people are sealed.

Holding back the four winds. Four angels, four corners, four winds: four is the number of the created world in this book, its compass points and its extent (Jeremiah 49:36). The winds are forces of judgment, perhaps the four horsemen of chapter 6 under another image, since Zechariah links the horses with the four winds of heaven (Zechariah 6:1–5). It is the stillness before a storm. The winds strain against the angels’ hands, the earth holds its breath, and God will not let them blow until every one of his servants has his name on them.

From the rising of the sun. The east, the direction of dawn and, in Ezekiel, of the glory of God returning to his temple (Ezekiel 43:2). Hope comes before judgment. And this fifth angel outranks the four, for he gives them orders.

With the seal of the living God. A seal was a signet ring or stamp, and this one belongs to the living God, not to a dead idol. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, since tampering with a sealed thing was an offence against its owner, and guaranteed that the thing was genuine; all three are in play. The scene recalls Ezekiel 9:4–6, where, before Jerusalem was judged, a man with a writing case marked the foreheads of those who sighed and groaned over the city’s abominations, and the executioners spared them. In John’s world slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded with their master’s or general’s mark.

Until we have sealed. That is the shape of the whole chapter. The judgment waits for one reason: God’s people are not yet marked. Peter gives the reason in a line: the Lord is “patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

Sealed in him. Believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 4:30), in Christ, when they believe in him (Ephesians 1:13). Jesus bore the seal first: “on him God the Father has set his seal” (John 6:27). When this company appears again, the mark on their foreheads is the Lamb’s name and his Father’s name (14:1). The one who will release the winds owns these people, so the winds cannot destroy them. What patience, to hold back the storm of the ages for people who could never have held it back themselves; and what tenderness, that the mark pressed on their foreheads is the name of the Lamb who was slain for them. No wind, no beast and no grave can rub it out.

Whose name is on you? The whole book turns on this mark later. In chapter 13 another power will demand a mark on the right hand or the forehead, without which nobody can buy or sell (13:16–17). Everyone alive is marked by somebody, and the only question is whose name is on you. God’s sealing comes first, six chapters before the counterfeit is even offered.

What it does not mean. Sealing does not protect believers from all suffering or from death; many will be martyred (6:11; 13:7), and the next scene shows this same company coming out of the great tribulation, which means they went through it. It protects them from the wrath of God that falls on unbelievers (9:4), and above all from losing their faith and their place in his kingdom. What is guaranteed is not an easy passage but a safe arrival.

In everyday life. Whatever comes this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the slander, God has marked you as his own, and he does not lose what he owns. And remember who was marked in Ezekiel: those who grieved over the sin around them. If the evils of your culture and of your own heart grieve you, even feebly, that grief is not a sign that you are unmarked. It is one of the Spirit’s fingerprints.

How do I know whether I am sealed? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to everyone who hears the gospel and believes in Christ (Ephesians 1:13). The question is not whether you have had a special experience but whether you have trusted Christ. The Spirit shows his presence in a faith that keeps looking to Jesus, a growing hatred of sin and love of holiness, love for other believers, and his inward witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:15–16). These may be faint at times. The seal does not depend on your feeling it.

Can the seal be broken? No. God seals his own for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). A believer may grieve the Spirit, fall into serious sin and lose for a time the joy of his salvation, but not the seal: those God has truly called he keeps to the end (Philippians 1:6). This is no licence for carelessness; a person content to live in sin should ask whether he was ever sealed at all. It is a comfort for the weak, who fear their grip will fail. Your grip is not what holds you.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sealed are God’s whole people, his true Israel, counted to the last one and drawn up like an army around the Messiah. The number and the list are symbolic, and they teach that not one of his servants is missing.

The number of the sealed. 144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000: twelve (the tribes of Israel) times twelve (the apostles), times a thousand (a vast, complete number), a symbol for the whole of God’s true Israel. Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (Romans 9:6–8); those who belong to the Messiah, Jew or Gentile, are the Israel the promises were made to. So the numbered army here and the uncountable multitude of verse 9 are one company seen from two sides: as God counts them, with nobody missing, and as they appear, beyond counting. The God who numbers the stars and calls them all by name (Psalm 147:4) has numbered his people too.

From every tribe. They are counted tribe by tribe like the fighting men in the census of Numbers 1. In 14:1–4 the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion, follow him wherever he goes, and are called firstfruits for God and the Lamb. They are God’s army, which conquers not by fighting but by following the Lamb.

From the tribe of Judah. The list is strange in four ways. Judah comes first, though Reuben was the firstborn, because the Messiah, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, has just been introduced (5:5). Dan is missing, the tribe that set up an idol and became a byword for apostasy (Judges 18:30–31; 1 Kings 12:29–30). Levi, which received no land and is often left out of lists of tribes counted for war and territory, is counted, perhaps because all God’s people are now priests (1:6). And Joseph appears alongside Manasseh, his own son, while Ephraim disappears. The names are arranged to teach, not to record family lines.

The twelve tribes gathered. The Old Testament lists the tribes about twenty times, in many orders. Ten had been scattered since 722 BC, and Jews looked for God to gather all twelve in the last days (Isaiah 11:12). Jesus chose twelve apostles to sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), forming a renewed Israel around himself. Here that hope is fulfilled: the tribes are gathered, complete, around the Lion of Judah.

If the 144,000 are the church, what of God’s future for the Jewish people? The two do not conflict. The elect of Israel are included in God’s complete number, not set apart from it, and Paul’s hope for Israel (Romans 11:25–26), however it is read, is part of that people being gathered. Christians differ over whether it means a great end-time conversion or the steady gathering of a Jewish remnant through the age, but all agree that it will be by faith in Jesus the Messiah, into the one olive tree.

What do I say when someone at the door says only 144,000 go to heaven? Point gently to the next verse. In the same vision John sees a multitude that no one could number, standing before the throne and serving God in his temple (vv. 9, 15). The teaching that only 144,000 go to heaven while the rest of the saved live on earth cannot be got out of this chapter, which names a number and then at once shows a crowd too large to count. Then turn to the deeper question, who Jesus is, because that is where the real difference lies.

Do I need to know which tribe I belong to? No. The sealed are the servants of our God (v. 3), and the multitude are those who washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (v. 14); neither is a bloodline. If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29).

Why is Dan left out, and does that mean Danites are lost? No one is excluded from salvation by his ancestry. The omission is a warning, not a verdict on bloodlines: the tribe that led Israel into idolatry pictures what idolatry does, in a book that calls Christians again and again to refuse the idols of their age. Some early writers speculated that the antichrist would come from Dan, but the text says nothing of that. No heritage, however privileged, protects a person who turns to idols, and no heritage, however compromised, keeps out a person who turns to Christ.

Where Christians differ: who are the 144,000? Dispensationalists (who see God as working with Israel and the church along two distinct tracks) usually see them as literal ethnic Jews, converted during a future tribulation after the church has been raptured, that is, caught up to Christ before it begins, who then evangelise the world. The text names the tribes one by one, which seems to them a great deal of trouble to go to for a symbol, and many devout believers hold this view because they take God’s promises to Israel seriously. Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that exactly 144,000 people form a heavenly class, while other believers live on earth. Others take them as Jewish Christians within the church, distinct from Gentile believers. This commentary’s view: the 144,000 are the whole church, the true Israel of God, Jew and Gentile together, seen on earth, sealed and protected. Four reasons. First, John hears a number (v. 4) and then sees a countless multitude from every nation (v. 9), just as in 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb: one reality, described first in Old Testament terms and then in its fulfilment. Second, the sealing is for all God’s servants (v. 3), and in 9:4 everyone without the seal is harmed, so the sealed must be all believers. Third, the New Testament calls the church, on the most likely reading, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16), the twelve tribes in the dispersion (James 1:1), and Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). Fourth, the tribe list has been deliberately altered, which signals a symbolic, not a literal, Israel. Nothing in the text supports a special class of 144,000 with a different destiny.
verseByVerse.note: The tribe list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh appear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people sealed on earth will stand before God’s throne, a multitude beyond counting, saved wholly by the Lamb. John sees them from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb (vv. 9–10), and all the angels fall on their faces and add a sevenfold praise, opened and closed with Amen (vv. 11–12). An elder explains who they are: they are coming out of the great tribulation, and their robes are white with the Lamb’s blood (vv. 13–14). Therefore they serve before the throne, God spreads his tent over them, the promises of Isaiah 49:10 are kept, and the Lamb shepherds them while God wipes away every tear (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and sings that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. They came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, and are sheltered by God’s presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hunger, thirst and scorching heat were the daily lot of many first hearers.

Now: God himself will wipe away every tear, every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people God sealed and counted will stand before his throne as a crowd too great to count, from every nation, saying that their salvation is wholly the work of God and the Lamb.

A great multitude that no one could number. After a precise figure comes a crowd nobody can count, and the phrase recalls a promise made to a childless old man outside his tent at night: “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them,” and then, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). The promise to Abraham has been kept. Heaven will not be thinly populated.

From every nation. Four terms, as in 5:9, together meaning all humanity: the Lamb’s blood ransomed people from every group, and here they are.

Standing. This answers 6:17: who can stand? These can, because the Lamb stands for them. While kings and generals crawled into caves, a crowd with no rank, no army and no leverage stands upright before the throne.

White robes and palm branches. White stands for purity and victory, and these robes are white because they were washed in the Lamb’s blood (v. 14); they were promised in 3:5 and given in 6:11. Palms meant victory and celebration. At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel waved palm branches and lived in booths, remembering God’s shelter in the wilderness and rejoicing over the harvest gathered in (Leviticus 23:40–43). This is a heavenly Feast of Tabernacles: the journey really is over, and God will shelter them (v. 15).

Salvation belongs to our God! When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna”, which means “save us” (John 12:13). There the crowd asked God to save; here the crowd declares that he has, and that salvation belongs to him: the choosing, the ransoming, the calling, the keeping, the bringing home, planned by the Father and accomplished by the Son. As Jonah said from the belly of the fish, “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (Jonah 2:9).

Not one syllable about themselves. Some of the multitude died under torture; every one held on when it would have been easier not to. Yet not one syllable of their song is about what they did. They do not sing, “We endured.” They sing that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and there is no second clause. That is the test of whether a person has understood the gospel: if everything you are were explained out loud before the throne, whose name would the account turn on?

In everyday life. When a Christian tells how he came to faith, the story often drifts into being about himself: what he decided, what he gave up. The multitude tells it the other way round, and so may we. And the believer from another country at the back of your church is someone you will stand beside for ever.

Will we keep our nations and languages in heaven? It seems so. John sees people still recognisable as from every nation, tribe, people and language, and at the end of the book the kings of the earth bring the glory and honour of the nations into the new Jerusalem (21:24–26). The gospel does not flatten cultures into one; it redeems people within them and gathers them around one throne. What will be gone is everything sinful in our cultures: the pride, the hostility, the walls. What remains is a unity so rich that it needs every tongue to sing it.

Does “no one could number” mean that most people will be saved? Scripture does not give the proportion, and Jesus warned that the gate is narrow and those who find it are few (Matthew 7:13–14). Yet heaven is no tiny remnant huddled in a corner: gathered from every age and nation, the redeemed are countless. The narrow gate makes us urgent about our own souls and our neighbours’; the size of the crowd makes us confident that the gospel will not fail. God is not saving a few survivors from a lost world. He is gathering a world.
verseByVerse.note: John hears a number (v. 4) but sees a multitude no one can count — likely the same people seen from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the angels of heaven fall on their faces and confirm the redeemed’s cry with complete praise to God. The song of the saved sets the whole host of heaven worshipping.

All the angels. At the centre is the throne, around it the living creatures and elders, and in the outer ring all the angels (5:11). Yet the multitude stands “before the throne and before the Lamb” (v. 9), which seems to put the redeemed nearer than the angels. We should not build on it, but the picture is striking: ransomed sinners before the throne, and the beings who never fell in the outer ring.

They fell on their faces. They have been standing; now they go down, because a crowd of forgiven human beings has said that salvation belongs to God. There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10); here is joy over a countless multitude.

Amen! The word means it is firm, it is so: they agree with the multitude’s cry, and their hymn begins and ends with it.

Seven words of praise. Seven is the number of completeness: everything there is to give, given. The list almost repeats the sevenfold praise of the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving in place of wealth, probably not by accident. Wealth is what a conqueror receives; thanksgiving is what a redeemed people offer. The worship of chapters 4 and 5 has returned, now for what the Lamb’s death has produced, and the next sound heaven makes after this Amen, when the seventh seal is opened, is silence (8:1).

The redeemed sing, and heaven agrees. The song that puts the angels on their faces was started by people who had been slaves, shopkeepers, soldiers, prostitutes and thieves, out of every language on earth. Angels long to look into the salvation preached to us (1 Peter 1:12); here they see it close up, and this is what seeing it does to them. They can only confirm a song they cannot sing on their own account, because nobody has ever ransomed an angel.

The Amen on the throne. In this book Amen is one of Christ’s own names (3:14), and all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Every promise to rescue, forgive, gather and bring home was made good in Jesus, and the crowd in white is the proof. The angels can only confirm the song; he is the reason it is true. And the God they worship was on that throne when the seals were breaking and the winds straining against the angels’ hands, and he is on it still. The oldest servants of God bow lowest at the newest song, and he is worthy of every word they say.

Do we worship with the angels now? Yes. When the church gathers, it comes to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:22–23). That does not mean we pray to angels or seek their presence; they are fellow servants who point away from themselves (19:10). It means that the smallest Sunday gathering is joined to a worship far larger than itself, and your Amen at the end of a prayer belongs in the same song as theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The countless multitude are those who come through the great tribulation, made clean not by their suffering but by the blood of the Lamb. The elder’s answer tells us both what God’s people must pass through and what alone brings them home.

Who are these, and from where have they come? The elder asks John a question he cannot answer: a teacher’s question, asked to give the answer rather than get one.

Sir, you know. Not evasion but the honest reply of a man who will not guess, as Ezekiel, asked whether the dry bones could live, answered, “O Lord GOD, you know” (Ezekiel 37:3). To admit what we do not know, and wait to be told, is itself a form of faith. And Revelation interprets itself here: the elder supplies the answer.

Coming out of the great tribulation. The Greek verb is present: the ones who keep coming. Not one group arriving at once, but a steady stream, as each believer dies or as the age ends. And it is the great tribulation, one the readers already know. Daniel spoke of a time of trouble such as never has been, when God’s people will be delivered (Daniel 12:1), and Jesus of “great tribulation” (Matthew 24:21). John has already called himself his readers’ partner in the tribulation (1:9), using the same word of his own present situation, and Jesus said plainly, “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33).

Made them white in the blood. The sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward is impossible on purpose: blood does not whiten cloth. But one blood in the universe does what no other can, and its effect is not a stain but a whiteness nothing else produces. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7); “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). Israel washed their garments to meet God at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14); these have washed theirs in something better.

Their action, his detergent. The verb is active: they washed. There is something a person must do, and the whole book is an appeal to repent, hold fast and come. But the sentence carries its own safeguard: they washed in the blood of the Lamb. The action is theirs; the detergent is entirely his. Their sufferings did not whiten them; trusting his blood did. No one in that crowd will ever say, “I made myself clean.” Every one will say, “He did it,” and it will be the truest thing they ever said.

From where have they come? The elder’s second question is the deeper one. They came from every nation, out of the great tribulation, some from under the executioner’s sword, and none of that is the answer. They came from the blood of the Lamb. Every person in that crowd arrived by the same road, there is no second road, and no one can tell a better story about the journey than the person next to him.

So will Christians go through the tribulation? Yes, and we are in it now. Scripture nowhere promises a secret removal of the church before trouble comes. Jesus asked the Father not to take his people out of the world but to keep them from the evil one (John 17:15), and Paul told new converts that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). For most believers in history, and many today, that has meant prison, poverty or death; for others, quieter pressures. Christ will return once, visibly, to gather his people and judge the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Until then, the promise is not escape but keeping.

Is it not narrow to say there is only one road? Every view of salvation has a narrow door somewhere: the moralist lets in only the good, the modern sceptic only the open-minded. The gospel’s door is narrow in a different way: the only qualification is to admit you have none, and come to the Lamb. That is why the crowd that comes through it is the widest in history (v. 9). A salvation won by goodness would be open only to the decent. A salvation given by blood is open to the thief, the persecutor and the respectable sinner alike.

How do I wash my robe in the Lamb’s blood? By coming to Christ as a sinner, admitting that your robe is stained beyond your power to clean, and resting your whole weight on his death for you. And you keep coming back to the same fountain: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). So when you sin this week, do not try to scrub the stain out with good resolutions before you dare approach God. Go straight to the blood. It is the only thing that has ever made anyone white.

Where Christians differ: what is the great tribulation? Dispensationalists understand it as a specific seven-year period at the end of history, after the church has been raptured (caught up to Christ beforehand), and see this multitude as those converted during that time. They read promises such as 3:10 and 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as promises of removal, and they love the Lord’s appearing as much as anyone; this commentary reads those verses as promises of keeping and of meeting the Lord at his one visible coming. This commentary’s view: the great tribulation is the suffering of God’s people throughout the whole age between Christ’s comings, which John and his readers were already in (1:9; 2:9–10; Acts 14:22). In the Olivet discourse (his teaching on the Mount of Olives about the end) Jesus spoke of it first in the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (as preterist readers rightly stress), and that siege also pictures the tribulation of the whole age (Matthew 24:21–22); Scripture expects a final intensification before the end (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), and no secret rapture removes the church from it. The multitude is the whole number of the redeemed, from every nation, coming out of that tribulation through all history, and the present tense, “coming out”, suits a continuing stream. The church is not removed from tribulation; it is brought through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they are washed, the redeemed live in God’s presence for ever, serving him as priests while he spreads his tent over them.

Therefore. The word carries the whole logic of the gospel. Not because they endured, though they did; not because they were faithful under torture, though many were. Because of the washing in verse 14, and nothing else, they stand where they stand.

Serve him in his temple. “Serve” is the service of worship, the word used of priests ministering in the sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5). In the temple only one man went behind the veil, once a year. Here a crowd from every nation is inside permanently, doing priestly work where God dwells: the promise of 1:6 has arrived, a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. In the new Jerusalem, God and the Lamb are the temple (21:22).

Day and night. The phrase is used of the living creatures who never cease (4:8). But there is no night in the city at the end of this book (21:25; 22:5), so it is not measuring hours. It means without interruption: no fatigue, no sin, no Monday.

Shelter them with his presence. Literally, he will spread his tent over them (skēnōsei ep’ autous). It is the word for the tabernacle, the tent God pitched in the middle of Israel’s camp so that he could live among them in the wilderness, where his glory dwelt and cloud and fire sheltered his people (Exodus 25:8; 40:34–38; Isaiah 4:5–6). It is the word of John 1:14, where the Word pitched his tent among us, and of 21:3. The God who once pitched his tent among a wandering people, and then in human flesh in his Son, will at last spread it over a multitude from every nation and never fold it up again. The picture is of nearness: a father pulling a blanket over a child, the cloud standing over the tabernacle. People driven from their homes by persecution are given God himself as their home.

The same throne, two companies. In 6:16 the great ones of the earth begged the mountains to hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne. Here is the same throne and the same one seated on it, and a crowd with no rank at all is sheltered by him. The difference is not in the people. It is in verse 14: the blood of the Lamb.

Will heaven be boring? Only to someone who pictures an endless church service he did not enjoy on earth. This is the joyful work of people made perfect, in the presence of God himself, whose glory is inexhaustible. Revelation speaks elsewhere of reigning (22:5), of the glory of the nations brought in (21:26), and of a city with streets and a river. Service in Scripture includes worship, but also work: Adam was put in the garden to work it (Genesis 2:15). It will not be less than the best of this life. Boredom is a symptom of a fallen heart, and it will not be there.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s presence every bodily misery of this life, hunger, thirst and scorching heat, will be gone for good. The words come almost directly from Isaiah 49:10, God’s promise to exiles coming home, and John gives them to a multitude from every nation: the final new exodus.

Hunger no more. The list is specific and bodily: hunger, thirst, sunstroke. These were not metaphors to the first hearers. The black horse rode out with a pair of scales (6:5–6), and believers in Smyrna were poor as beggars (2:9), very probably in part because of their faith. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger, and whoever believes in him shall never thirst (John 6:35), and believers already taste that satisfaction in him.

Scorching heat. A slave working a field in Asia Minor in August knew exactly what scorching heat does to a man who cannot stop. The psalm promises that the sun shall not strike you by day (Psalm 121:6), and in 16:8–9 the fourth bowl scorches the wicked with fire from the sun; the redeemed are spared.

Why negatives? A negative is the only honest way to describe a condition nobody alive has known. No one can picture a body that never tires, for everyone reading this has been tired every day of his life. What can be pictured is the absence of a particular misery, and that is what John gives: the removal, one by one, of things the reader could name from this week. And the plainness cuts against the instinct to imagine heaven as light, peace and spirits somewhere else. Scripture promises a body that works, food, water, shade, a city with streets in it. Many Greek thinkers wanted deliverance from the body; Scripture promises that the body itself will be delivered.

The one who hungered and thirsted. These promises can be made only because someone bore what they remove. Hunger, thirst and the sun on a labourer’s back belong to the ground God cursed after Adam’s sin: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Genesis 3:17–19). Jesus walked into that curse. He was hungry in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), weary at a well at noon and asking for a drink (John 4:6–7), and on the cross he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), which is why one day nothing accursed will remain (22:3). Behind the words “no more” stands a substitute, who went without so that his people never will.

Your own line in the verse. Take whatever is wearing you down: the illness managed daily, the arithmetic at the end of the month that never quite works, the exhaustion that sleep no longer touches. Each is a hunger of some kind, and each has its line in this verse. The promise is not that you will stop minding about them, but that they will not be there. Meanwhile a meal carried to a neighbour is a foretaste of it: care for the hungry and thirsty now (Matthew 25:35), because the King counts what you do for the least of his brothers as done for him.

Will we eat and drink in heaven? Scripture gives good reason to think so in the resurrection. The risen Jesus ate fish before his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), he spoke of drinking the fruit of the vine new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29), and the end is pictured as a feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9; Isaiah 25:6). But the Christian hope is not to become a ghost. It is to be raised in a body like Christ’s, on a renewed earth, where eating will be joy and not survival.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb who shares God’s throne will shepherd his people to the water of life, and God himself will wipe away every tear. The chapter ends with three promises, and each rests on who the shepherd is.

The Lamb will be their shepherd. A sentence no one but John would have dared to write. “In the midst of the throne” means at the centre, sharing God’s throne. Lambs are shepherded; they do not shepherd. Ezekiel promised that God himself would search for his sheep and set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23), and here the promise is kept. It is the third of the book’s great reversals: the Lion who is a Lamb (5:5–6), the Lamb who has wrath (6:16), and now the Lamb who is a Shepherd. Each time the image that ought to be weak turns out to be the strong one.

Springs of living water. Literally springs of waters of life: not a cistern or a well that must be drawn from, but water rising under its own pressure and never stopping. It is eternal life flowing from God, the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13), the gift Jesus offered a woman at a well (John 4:14) and cried out on the last day of the feast (John 7:37–39), and it is where this book finishes, with the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1).

Every tear. The promise is not that nothing bad happened but that something is done about it afterwards, as Isaiah foresaw: the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8). God knows which tears and whose, and he deals with them himself: not an angel with a cloth, not time healing it, but God personally, close enough to touch a face, as a parent dries a child’s eyes. The promise returns in 21:4: “death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore”.

The shepherd is one of us. Psalm 23, Ezekiel’s promise and the good shepherd who lays down his life (John 10:11) meet here: the shepherd of this flock was himself led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). He knows what they have suffered because he suffered it. He does not direct the flock from a height; he walks in front of it, and he has scars. So here is the full answer to “who can stand?”: a crowd nobody can count, sealed, washed, sheltered under the tent of God and led by a Lamb to water that never runs dry. And there is nothing in the list that any of them did.

Take it as it is written. Anyone who has sat with the dying, stood at a small grave, or kept getting up in the morning after the worst thing, should take this verse exactly as written, not one degree weaker. The tears were real, and they were counted. Read it slowly to someone grieving this week, without explaining it away. And if you are the one weeping, do not be ashamed of the tears. They are not a failure of faith; they are the very thing God has promised personally to deal with. Let the Lamb shepherd you now, through his word, his people and his table, to the springs he has already opened.

Can any future make up for the tears? Dostoevsky put the objection at its strongest. In The Brothers Karamazov Ivan tells his brother Alyosha story after story of children tormented by adults, and says that if eternal harmony must be bought with the tears of even one such child, the price is too high; it is not God he rejects, he says, he simply hands back his ticket. Many feel exactly that, and they are not being shallow; promises of heaven can sound like hush money. (On why God permits suffering at all, see the note on Romans 8:28.) But this verse does not say the tears were worth it, or that they will turn out not to have mattered. It says God will wipe them away himself, and that the one who leads his people there is the Lamb who was slain. Ivan imagined a God who buys harmony with other people’s suffering from a safe distance. The God of this verse paid with his own. The harmony was bought not with the child’s tears but with the Lamb’s blood, and that is the one price that lets a hurt person take the ticket back.
