Will I remember my sorrows in heaven? Scripture does not say our memories will be erased, and the Lamb’s own wounds suggest that the past is not simply deleted. But it will be transformed. The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (Romans 8:18), and what was once only pain will be seen as part of a story that ended in God’s glory and our joy. Joseph could say of his worst years that God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). In heaven every believer will say that of everything, and say it without a tear.

What about loved ones who did not believe? This is the hardest question a grieving Christian asks, and Scripture does not answer every part of it. It does promise that God will wipe away every tear, so nothing, not even this, will spoil the joy of the redeemed; we will see the holiness and justice of God clearly and be wholly at one with him. Until then, do not presume to know the final state of anyone whose last hours you did not see, since God can save to the last breath, and do not let the question keep you from trusting his goodness. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25).

7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea,<sup>3</sup>saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”<sup>4</sup>And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:<sup>5</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad,<sup>6</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh,<sup>7</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar,<sup>8</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.<sup>9</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,<sup>10</sup>and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”<sup>11</sup>And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,<sup>12</sup>saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”<sup>13</sup>Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?”<sup>14</sup>I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

keyVerse.quote: These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s answer to “who can stand?” (6:17). The redeemed do not escape tribulation; they come out of it, and what brings them through is not their endurance but the blood of the Lamb, which makes white what no suffering could clean. It tells every believer both what to expect and what to trust.

7.reflection:
Chapter 7 answers the question of 6:17, “who can stand?” Before you read it, how would you have answered? What does the chapter say makes the difference between those who hide and those who stand?

God seals his servants before the winds are allowed to blow (vv. 1–3), but the sealed still go through the great tribulation (v. 14). What does the seal protect, and what does it not? How does that shape what you pray for in hard times?

The multitude’s song has no line about what they did or endured (v. 10). If you told the story of your own salvation aloud, whose name would it turn on? Where do you find yourself drifting into the centre of it?

Verses 15–17 promise shelter, food, water, shade and the end of tears. Which promise speaks most to you or to someone you know this week, and how could your church give a foretaste of it now?

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
Where we are. The Lamb opens the seventh and last seal (v. 1), and the first series of judgments, which in chapter 6 ran from the cross to the brink of the end, gives way to a second: the seven trumpets (8:2–11:19), which go over the same age again with a louder warning. Chapter 8 holds the seventh seal, the prayers of the saints and the first four trumpets.

The message. God hears the prayers of his people and answers them by judging the world that rejects him and persecutes them; and his judgments in this age are warnings, real but limited, calling a rebellious world to repent before the end. Heaven falls silent, the prayers of all the saints rise before God, and fire from the same altar falls on the earth.

Why it was said. The martyrs had cried, “how long?” (6:10), and believers in Asia prayed with little to show for it, while the empire’s confidence in its harbours, harvests and gods seemed unshakeable (see the introduction). The chapter tells them that no prayer of theirs is lost, that the God who broke Egypt is not retired, and that the things the world leans on can be shaken in an afternoon.

How the chapter makes its case. First, silence (v. 1): heaven holds its breath because God is about to act. Then prayer (vv. 2–4): seven angels receive trumpets, but before any sounds, another angel offers much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and they rise before God. Then the answer (v. 5): fire from that altar is thrown on the earth, with thunder and earthquake. Four trumpets follow (vv. 6–12), striking land, sea, fresh water and sky. Each echoes a plague on Egypt and each is limited to a third: warnings, not yet the end. Last, an eagle cries woe on those who dwell on the earth, for the three trumpets still to come will fall on people themselves (v. 13).

Where it leads. The trumpets are a new exodus, but this time the Lamb comes first. Before a single plague falls, the Passover Lamb has been slain and his people ransomed (5:9). The prayers rise acceptably because he intercedes for us; the fire thrown on the earth had already fallen on him in his people’s place; and the darkness of the fourth trumpet was known in full at noon on the day he died. The trumpets are heading for the seventh, when “the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (11:15).

For us. Keep praying, especially when heaven seems silent: your prayers arrive. Hold loosely what the trumpets strike, the harvests, markets, water and steady days the world relies on, and hear every disaster as a summons to repent and to warn others while it is still daylight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Heaven falls silent, the prayers of God’s people rise before him, and his answer falls on the earth as fire. When the Lamb opens the last seal, heaven holds its breath for about half an hour, the hush before God acts (v. 1; Habakkuk 2:20), and seven angels are given seven trumpets (v. 2). Before any trumpet sounds, another angel offers much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the smoke rises before God (vv. 3–4). Then he fills the censer with fire from the same altar and throws it on the earth (v. 5). The trumpets are God’s answer to his church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opens the last seal, all heaven falls silent in awe, because God is about to act.

The seventh seal. The scroll is fully open, and what happens first is nothing: no rider, no voice. The seventh seal seems to unfold into the seven trumpets, as the seventh trumpet will unfold into the seven bowls. Each series ends at the final judgment, and the next goes over the same ground with greater intensity.

Silence in heaven. The four living creatures have been saying “Holy, holy, holy” day and night without ceasing (4:8). Myriads of angels have cried “Worthy is the Lamb” (5:12). A multitude nobody could number has been shouting that salvation belongs to God (7:10). All of it goes quiet, and John has nothing to write down.

Why the silence? Three explanations fit together. First and most probably, awe: the silence Scripture commands before God acts in judgment. “The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him” (Habakkuk 2:20). “Be silent before the Lord GOD! For the day of the LORD is near” (Zephaniah 1:7). “Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling” (Zechariah 2:13). Each time it is the hush before a verdict, and God rises to act.

Prayer, and the storm. Second, prayer. In the temple, incense was offered while the whole multitude prayed outside at the hour of incense (Luke 1:10), and what comes straight after this silence is an angel offering incense with the prayers of all the saints (vv. 3–4); heaven falls silent so that the church’s prayers can be heard. Third, the stillness before a storm: judgment is about to fall. On any reading the silence is full, and God’s holiness is felt rather than defined: he is so pure and so great that sinless creatures, who have praised him without a pause, stop and say nothing at all.

About half an hour. The vague “about”, in a book of exact numbers, tells us John is describing what it felt like. Half an hour of silence in a room is close to unbearable. Heaven’s praise stops because nothing said would be enough. God does not need our noise to be glorious: the Judge who has heard every prayer is rising to answer, and the quiet is full of him.

The hand on the last seal. In chapter 5 no one in heaven or on earth could open the scroll, and John wept, until the Lamb who had been slain took it (5:9). Every seal since has been broken by that hand, and so is this one. The silence is heaven holding its breath while the crucified Lamb carries God’s purpose into its next stage.

What do I do when God is silent to my prayers? Some have prayed for a year about the same thing, heard nothing, and concluded that no one is listening. This verse does not explain that away, but it shows the nature of heaven’s quiet. It is not absence or indifference. It is the pause of a court before sentence, and it comes immediately before the prayers of the saints are carried up and answered. God being quiet and God being idle are not the same thing. So keep praying through the silence. Tell him honestly that he seems silent, as the Psalms do (Psalm 22:2), and hold on to what he has said in his word while you wait for what he has not yet said.

Should our worship include silence? It is wise and biblical to make room for it: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Much modern worship is afraid of quiet and fills every gap with music or words. A pause after the reading of Scripture, before confession or at the Lord’s Table is not dead time. It says with the whole of heaven that God is about to speak or act, and that we have stopped to listen. Silence needs no special technique; it is simply reverence with the noise turned off.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any trumpet of judgment sounds, the prayers of all God’s people are offered at his throne with incense, and every one of them reaches him.

The seven angels who stand before God. “The” suggests a particular, known group, angels of the highest rank, ready to serve; Gabriel said, “I stand in the presence of God” (Luke 1:19). The trumpets “were given”: they come from God.

What a trumpet meant. Trumpets announced God’s presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), summoned Israel to worship and war (Numbers 10:1–10), brought down Jericho’s walls (Joshua 6:16–20), warned of judgment (Joel 2:1; Ezekiel 33:3–6) and proclaimed the year of Jubilee, when slaves went free (Leviticus 25:9); one will sound when the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52). A trumpet means: attention, something is about to happen, and you cannot sleep through it.

A golden censer. Before a single trumpet is blown, the vision stops. The censer is a firepan for carrying burning coals and incense. In the tabernacle and temple a golden altar of incense stood before the curtain of the Most Holy Place, and morning and evening a priest burned incense on it while the people prayed outside (Exodus 30:1–8; Luke 1:8–10): “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). Here 5:8 is fulfilled, where the elders held golden bowls of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints”. Now the incense is burned.

The prayers of all the saints. Three details matter. The first is “all”: every believer, not only the martyrs, not only the prayers well phrased or persevered in longest, but prayers prayed in the dark, badly, and then forgotten.

Much incense, given. The second detail is that the incense is given to him. The prayers do not go up on their own account; something is added to them at the altar, from the other side, making them fragrant before God. And the altar stands right before the throne, with no curtain: God has set it there for his people’s prayers and supplied the incense himself. He does not merely tolerate our praying; he has built it into the centre of heaven’s worship.

Rose before God. The third detail is the direction: up, before God. The prayers arrive. Not one is lost, and the martyrs’ cry, “how long?” (6:10), is among them. A believer kneels by a bed at eleven at night, says something short and inadequate about a son who will not speak to him, and gets up feeling that nothing has occurred. On the evidence of this verse, something has.

Is this angel Christ? Some have taken him so, since he does a high priest’s work. But John calls him simply another angel, and Revelation never calls Christ an angel; in this book Christ is the Lamb on the throne, receiving worship, not a servant at the altar. More likely he is an angelic servant in the heavenly worship. Yet the reality the picture points to is Christ’s own intercession: because of him alone is any prayer of ours accepted.

In everyday life. Do not wait until you can pray well. Pray the short, tired prayer at the end of the day, especially for persecuted believers, and believe that it arrived. If it helps, keep a simple list of what you have asked and look back at it in six months: many of the prayers you forgot, God has remembered.

Why do my prayers need incense? Because even our best prayers are mixed with sin, distraction and self-interest, and a holy God could not receive them on their own merits. That is no reason to stop praying; it is the reason Christ prays for us. “Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do,” Jesus said (John 14:13). To pray in his name is not to add a formula at the end, but to come trusting that he has made you welcome and that his perfect intercession covers your imperfect words. The Spirit, too, helps us in our weakness, interceding with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Your prayer does not have to be good to be heard. It has to be offered through him.

Where Christians differ: should we pray to angels or saints, or through them? Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have used passages like this to support asking angels and departed saints to present our prayers to God. This commentary’s view: the angel serves in the heavenly worship, offering the prayers before God, but he is not prayed to, and the saints on earth do not address him. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and believers may come boldly to the throne of grace through him (Hebrews 4:14–16). The incense that makes our prayers acceptable is the intercession and merit of Christ, our great High Priest, who always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his people’s prayers with judgment on the world: the fire that falls on the earth comes from the very altar where their prayers rose.

Fire from the altar. The censer that carried the prayers of all the saints up to God is now filled with fire from the same altar. In Ezekiel a man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem in judgment (Ezekiel 10:2). The coal from the altar that touched Isaiah’s lips brought cleansing (Isaiah 6:6–7); here fire from the altar brings judgment.

Threw it on the earth. What went up as incense comes back as fire. The trumpets that follow are the answer to the church’s praying, and it arrives as judgment on the world that made the praying necessary. “The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). The martyrs were told to rest a little longer (6:10–11); this is the “little longer” coming to an end.

Thunder, lightning and earthquake. These are the signs that came from the throne in 4:5 and marked God’s presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), now with an earthquake added. Each series of judgments ends with them, more intensely each time (11:19; 16:18–21), which shows that each series reaches the final judgment.

The kingdom of his Christ. The trumpets are not answering private grudges. The souls under the altar were slain for the word of God (6:9), and the church has prayed “Your kingdom come” since its Lord taught it. The fire thrown on the earth is God taking the side of those who took Christ’s side, and the seventh trumpet will say where it is heading: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (11:15). Every prayer in the censer was in the end a prayer for that. And the fire that falls on the earth does not fall on those who pray, because for them the fire of judgment fell long ago on the Lamb, who bore it in their place.

Moving history from their knees. Prayer, in this book, is one of the means by which God sets his judgments in motion. The most powerless people in the empire, slaves, widows, prisoners awaiting a hearing, were moving history from their knees without seeing a single result. The prayer that seemed to evaporate went into a golden bowl; the bowl went to an altar; and the fire came back down. Ten tired people in a church hall praying for the persecuted church are doing something that echoes in thunder.

What it does not mean. Christians are not to pray for the destruction of their enemies. We pray for God’s kingdom to come, which includes the defeat of evil, and for our enemies’ repentance. God decides how to answer, and his judgments are always just.

If God is sovereign, why does he need our prayers? Not because he cannot act without them, but because he has chosen to work through them, as he works through preaching and all the means he appoints. The God who decreed the end also decreed the prayers that would lead to it, and he gives his people the dignity of taking part. That is why Elijah prayed for rain after God had promised it (1 Kings 18:1, 41–45; James 5:17–18). Sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who actually governs the world, not a God who is hoping things work out.

What should I pray for, then? Begin where Jesus taught us: hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:9–10). Those petitions contain everything in this verse: the defeat of evil, the vindication of God’s people and the coming of his reign. Then pray for persecuted believers by name, for the salvation of the lost, including those who oppose the gospel, and for justice where it has been denied. Bring your own needs too; he cares about them. But let the big prayers have their place, because they are the ones the golden bowls are full of.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s first judgments on a rebellious world are real but limited warnings, calling it to repent before the end. The first four trumpets strike the creation people rely on, each within a third: hail and fire burn the land, a burning mountain turns the sea to blood, a star called Wormwood makes the fresh water bitter, and the lights are partly darkened (vv. 6–12). The pattern is the plagues on Egypt, which struck at false gods and set God’s people free. Then an eagle flying overhead cries woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth (v. 13), one woe for each trumpet still to come; the remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky, each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first trumpet brings a plague like those on Egypt, burning a third of the land: a real judgment, but a limited one, warning the world to repent.

The plagues of Egypt again. After one verse of pure anticipation, ordered and deliberate, the first trumpet sounds, and the plagues of Egypt begin again on a larger stage. That parallel governs the whole trumpet sequence. The first trumpet brings hail and fire, the seventh plague (Exodus 9:23–25). The second turns a third of the sea to blood, the first plague (Exodus 7:20–21). The fourth darkens the lights, the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23). The fifth will bring locusts (Exodus 10:12–15), and the sixth ends with people refusing to repent, as Pharaoh did.

Hail and fire, mixed with blood. Like the plague on Egypt, but worse: blood is added. And they “were thrown”, a divine passive (the Bible’s way of saying God acts without naming him): God throws them.

A third. The seals struck a quarter (6:8); the trumpets strike a third; the bowls will strike everything (chapter 16). The escalation is the argument: these are not the end but warnings that grow louder because they are not heard, and chapter 9 says so outright: the rest of mankind did not repent (9:20). Somebody is holding the line at a third. Judgment that stops short is a warning still waiting for an answer.

Why Egypt? The parallel is not decoration. The plagues had two purposes, both stated in Exodus. They were aimed at the gods of Egypt: “on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments” (Exodus 12:12), and many have seen in them blows at the Nile, the sun and other things Egypt worshipped. And they were aimed at getting a people out: “Let my people go.” So when John dresses the trumpets in the clothes of the exodus, he tells seven small congregations that the empire grinding them is Egypt, that the God who broke Egypt is not retired, and that his purpose is the same: to expose the gods that cannot save, and to bring his people out.

This time the Lamb comes first. In Egypt the plagues fell first, and the lamb came at the end, on the night its blood marked the doors. In Revelation the order is reversed. Before a single trumpet sounds, John has seen the Lamb standing as though slain, and heard heaven sing that by his blood he ransomed a people and made them a kingdom and priests (5:6, 9–10). Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), so the trumpets fall on a world in which the decisive deliverance has already happened. The new exodus does not wait on the plagues. It was won at the cross, and it ends with the redeemed beside a sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb (15:2–3).

If God burns the earth in judgment, should Christians care for the environment? Yes. The earth is the LORD’s (Psalm 24:1), and Adam was set in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), a mandate never withdrawn. That God judges creation because of human sin is no permission to abuse it; if anything, it shows how seriously he takes what happens to his world. We care for creation not because we can save the planet, but because it belongs to God and he means to renew it. Look after it as a steward looks after his master’s estate, knowing the master is coming back.

When a wildfire or a storm destroys a town, is that a trumpet? In the broad sense, yes: every disaster in a fallen world is a trumpet blast, a warning that the world is not as it should be and that life is short. Jesus said so when a tower fell on eighteen people: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:4–5). But we are not told which disaster answers which sin, and Christians suffer them too. The right response is to grieve with the bereaved, help generously and practically, examine our own hearts, and point people to the only shelter no fire can reach.

Where Christians differ: are the trumpets literal events? Some read them as literal future events, perhaps nuclear war or asteroid strikes, and they rightly insist that God’s judgments are real and not mere ideas. Preterists see them in the Jewish war of AD 66 to 70. Historicists match each trumpet to an event in church history, such as the invasions of the Roman Empire by Goths, Vandals and others. This commentary’s view: the trumpets are symbolic pictures, drawn from the plagues of Egypt, of God’s judgments on a rebellious world throughout the age between Christ’s comings. They include natural disasters and ecological catastrophes, real and recurring through history, as warnings to repent; their purpose is stated in 9:20–21: to call people to turn from idols. They are not a timeline to be decoded, but they are real, and they may intensify before the end.
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second trumpet strikes the sea and the trade that sails on it, showing how quickly the systems the world trusts can go down.

Something like a great mountain. John says “something like”: he is describing a picture, not naming an object. The image may suggest a volcanic eruption, and John’s readers would have remembered Vesuvius burying Pompeii in AD 79. It may also suggest a falling empire, since in prophetic language a mountain is often a kingdom, immovable and dominant: Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain which God will make a burnt mountain (Jeremiah 51:25). It is not a prediction of a particular volcano or meteor. And the sea becomes blood, as the Nile did (Exodus 7:20–21), on a greater scale.

A third of the ships. For the churches on the coast of Asia the sea was not scenery but the economy: Ephesus and Smyrna were harbours, and Rome’s grain came by ship. A third of the ships destroyed is a commercial collapse, and the merchants of the earth, who in chapter 18 weep because no one buys their cargo any more (18:11, 17–19), discover that the system they trusted could never bear the weight they put on it.

The sea in this book. The sea is where the beast comes from (13:1), the ancient image of chaos, which is why the throne room has a sea of glass (4:6) and the new creation is announced with “and the sea was no more” (21:1). The second trumpet strikes what the world sails on and the beast rises out of, with a measured third.

Another mountain. Scripture has another mountain. Daniel saw a stone cut out by no human hand strike the great image of the world’s empires and become a great mountain that filled the whole earth, the kingdom the God of heaven sets up that shall never be destroyed (Daniel 2:34–35, 44). Jesus spoke of himself as that stone (Luke 20:17–18), and this book shows where his mountain stands: the Lamb on Mount Zion with his people (14:1). Every empire the world builds is a mountain that can be thrown into the sea. The kingdom of Christ is the one mountain that grows, and the people on it are not going under. He made the sea and set its bounds; in the flesh he walked on its waves and with a rebuke made its storm lie down. The ships of every empire can go down together, and no one he holds will sink.

What has any of this to do with me? Look at what gets hit: not temples and armies but the earth a man farms, the sea he trades on, the water he drinks and the light he works by, the things that let us believe tomorrow will be much like today. Anyone who has watched a business fail, or a pension shrink in a crash he did not cause, has met the second trumpet in miniature. Not that such an event is a punishment aimed at him; Scripture is careful about that (Luke 13:4–5). The point is what it reveals: each of these systems holds up somebody’s confidence, and each can be cut by a third in an afternoon. The only thing this book has shown that cannot be taken down is the throne, and it was shown first, on purpose, before any of this began.

Is it wrong, then, to save, invest or run a business? No. Scripture commends work, diligence and wise provision (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8), and trade is part of the ordinary good life God gives. What this trumpet warns against is trust: “As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Use money; do not lean on it. Be generous with it, because generosity is the surest sign that your heart is not anchored to the ships.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third trumpet makes the world’s fresh water bitter and deadly, a judgment that fits those who forsake God, the fountain of living waters.

A great star. In Revelation stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This may be an angel carrying out God’s judgment, or simply a burning, meteor-like object. It falls on fresh water this time, rivers and springs, the thing no settlement can live without.

Wormwood. Wormwood is a shrub with an intensely bitter taste, and the name gives the meaning: bitterness. In the Old Testament it pictures bitterness and judgment (Jeremiah 9:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19). Those who turn from God’s living water and drink the poisoned waters of idolatry find life bitter: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13; see 9:13–15).

Many people died. This is the first trumpet where the text says plainly that people died. Wormwood is not normally deadly; the image is intensified, and the waters of life become the waters of death.

The judgment matches the crime. Amos accuses those who turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7). In Amos men make justice bitter; here God makes their water bitter. This is the shape of divine judgment throughout Scripture: not an arbitrary penalty attached to an offence, but the offence itself, served back.

Springs of living water. Set this trumpet beside the chapter before it. There the Lamb leads his people to springs of living water (7:17); here a third of the earth’s springs are made bitter. People who forsake the fountain end with wells that poison them, and the fountain is offered again in a person: on the last day of the feast Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The world’s own springs, its pleasures, systems and hopes, can turn bitter overnight. The life Christ gives does not come from them at all, so no star falling on them can touch it. At Marah God showed Moses a log to throw into bitter water and made it sweet (Exodus 15:23–25); here sweet water is made bitter. The God who turns sweet water bitter in judgment is the God who at last hung on a tree to make the bitterest thing in the world sweet for sinners.

What it does not mean. Wormwood is not a code word for a modern disaster such as Chernobyl, whose name relates to the plant; on that logic the verse would have said nothing to the churches John wrote to. Revelation’s symbols draw on the Old Testament, not on modern place names.

What if I am the one who has been made bitter? A person can live for decades on water that has been made bitter, by an injustice never put right, a marriage that went wrong, a betrayal nobody was called to account for, and go on functioning, and never taste anything sweet again. Scripture takes that seriously enough to name a trumpet after it, and warns that a “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15). The way out is not to pretend the wrong did not happen, but to hand it to God the Judge, as the martyrs did (6:10), and to drink from a different spring. The God who made the waters of Marah sweet can do the same in a soul. It is often slow, and usually begins with honest prayer about the very thing that poisoned the well.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth trumpet dims the lights the world steers by, and an eagle warns that worse is coming for those who live for this earth alone. Even the warning of woe is mercy, given in daylight while there is still time.

A third of the sun was struck. “Struck” shares its root with the word for “plague”. God strikes the lights he created, and a world that worships created things instead of the Creator (Romans 1:25) loses part of the light it takes for granted. The word “third” occurs five times in one verse in the Greek (six in the ESV), the drumbeat of the sequence: somebody is counting. The first four trumpets form a set, striking land, sea, fresh water and sky.

The sun god cannot keep his lamp lit. The ninth plague on Egypt was darkness that could be felt, though Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23), and the god it judged was unmistakable: Egypt worshipped the sun, Ra headed its gods, and Pharaoh was his son. The same argument runs in Asia, where the emperor was often associated with the sun; Nero had himself portrayed with rays around his head. And the ancient world steered, planted and read its fortunes by the heavenly bodies. The fourth trumpet strikes the calendar, the compass and the horoscope in a single stroke.

Reliable light. What is taken away is not light in general but reliable light: the confidence that the day will behave as days always have. A partial failure strikes at one of the heart’s favourite idols, control. The steady round of day and night was always God’s promise (Genesis 8:22), never humanity’s achievement, and the fourth trumpet reminds a self-sufficient world whose gift it was.

Darkness at noon. Darkening the day was the prophets’ sign of the day of the LORD: “I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight” (Amos 8:9). Once it happened: “from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour” (Matthew 27:45), while Jesus hung on the cross and cried out that God had forsaken him. The darkness of God’s judgment fell in full on his Son, in the place of everyone who trusts him. The fourth trumpet’s darkness is partial and a warning; the darkness at the cross was the real thing.

The sun may falter; he never does. He made the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day and can dim them with a word, while the gods men worship go dark with them. He alone is the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (James 1:17). In the city to come there is no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (21:23).

An eagle crying. The eagle was the standard of the Roman legions, and a bird of prey circling overhead is a sign of what is about to die. “Directly overhead” is mid-heaven, the highest point of the sky, where everyone on the ground can see and hear. Hosea uses the same picture: “Set the trumpet to your lips! One like a vulture is over the house of the LORD” (Hosea 8:1).

Woe, woe, woe. A cry of grief and doom: three woes, one for each of the trumpets still to come (9:12; 11:14). The remaining three will fall on people directly, with demonic torment and death, and chapter 9 opens the shaft of the bottomless pit. The phrase “those who dwell on the earth” becomes a fixed label in this book. It almost never means simply everyone alive, but unbelievers in rebellion against God, people with no other citizenship who want none (6:10; 13:8). The saints live on the earth too, but they are never called earth-dwellers.

A mercy in the shape of a threat. The eagle’s cry comes in advance, in daylight, to people who still have time. Every warning in Revelation is an act of patience: God does not want anybody caught unawares.

In everyday life. There is usually someone we have meant to talk to about Christ for years. Someone once warned us, and Christ brought us in; now his Spirit gives his church power to do the same, with tears (Acts 1:8).

Can a Christian be an earth-dweller? Not in John’s sense, because the phrase describes where a person’s heart lives, not where his feet stand. But Christians can drift toward it, living as though this world were all there is. The test is simple and searching: if everything in this chapter happened, the land, the sea, the water and the light, what would you have left? If that question frightens you, the fear itself is a sign that your heart is turning homeward, and Christ casts out no one who comes to him (John 6:37). Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour (Philippians 3:20). Live here fully, love your neighbours, work hard; but keep your passport in the right place.

Are we near the last trumpets? On the reading followed here, the trumpets sound throughout the age between Christ’s comings and may grow louder as the end approaches, so in one sense every generation hears them. No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), but the end is always near enough to matter. The right question is not how close the last trumpet is, but whether you are ready if it sounded tonight.

Uncertain wording. The Greek word (aetos) normally means an eagle, but it can also cover the large carrion birds we call vultures, as when Jesus said, “Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather” (Matthew 24:28). John may intend either or both: the eagle of Rome’s standards, or the vulture circling over what is about to die. Either way the bird is a herald of doom, and the meaning of the cry is not in doubt.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “an angel flying” instead of “an eagle flying”. The two Greek words (angelou and aetou) look somewhat alike. The best manuscripts read “eagle”.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.<sup>3</sup>And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,<sup>4</sup>and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.<sup>5</sup>Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.<sup>6</sup>Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them.<sup>7</sup>The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

keyVerse.quote: and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
keyVerse.note: Before a single trumpet sounds, the chapter shows where the trumpets come from: the prayers of God’s people, made acceptable before him and answered. Every prayer, including the short and tired ones, arrives. The judgments that follow are not random disasters but God’s reply to his church’s cry for his kingdom to come.

8.reflection:
Heaven, which has praised God without pause since chapter 4, falls silent for half an hour (v. 1). What does that silence teach about God and about what is coming? How do you respond when God seems silent to your own prayers?

The prayers of “all the saints” rise before God with incense that is given, not supplied by those who pray (vv. 3–4). What encouragement does that give for the prayers you think are too weak or too ordinary to matter? Whose prayers, or which of your own, need that encouragement now?

The first four trumpets strike land, sea, fresh water and sky, the ordinary things people rely on, and only a third of each (vv. 7–12). What does that limit say about God’s purpose in disasters? How should Christians respond when disaster strikes near them?

The trumpets echo the plagues on Egypt, but this time the Passover Lamb was slain before any of them sounded. How does knowing that the decisive rescue has already happened change the way you face the troubles of this age?

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Where we are. The trumpets, God’s second series of warning judgments (8:2–11:19), now reach the first two of the three woes the eagle announced (8:13). The first four trumpets struck the creation people rely on; the fifth and sixth strike people themselves, and the forces let loose are no longer natural but demonic.

The message. God gives a world that has chosen the dark over to the powers it has chosen, and even then he keeps every one of them on a leash, keeps his own people safe under his seal, and holds the door of repentance open. Yet judgment by itself changes no one: the chapter ends with the survivors refusing to repent.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia lived under an empire that looked unshakeable, among neighbours devoted to idols, magic and the gods of trade, and like every Roman province they feared the frontier beyond the Euphrates (see the introduction). They needed to know that the evil around them was neither in charge nor able to reach past God’s seal, and why so few were turning to God for all that the world suffered.

How the chapter makes its case. The fifth trumpet (vv. 1–12): a fallen star is given the key to the abyss, and out of its smoke come locusts with the sting of scorpions. They may hurt only those without God’s seal, may not kill, and may torment for just five months; their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the Destroyer. The sixth trumpet (vv. 13–19): a voice from the altar where the saints’ prayers rose orders the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for the very hour, and a countless cavalry breathing fire, smoke and sulphur kills a third of mankind. Then the verdict (vv. 20–21): the rest did not repent of their idols, nor of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts.

Where it leads. Every key in this chapter is borrowed, because the risen Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). The Destroyer can only unmake, but the Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil, and did it by dying (1 John 3:8; Hebrews 2:14). The darkness, torment and forsakenness the abyss pours out fell in full on him at the cross, so that no one sealed as his will ever bear them. And where disaster only hardens, he gives new hearts: the interlude that follows (10:1–11:14) shows the gospel witness through which he does it.

For us. Do not be fascinated by evil or frightened of it: it is real, but it is on a chain, and the name on your forehead is your safety. Do not expect catastrophe to convert anyone, yourself included. Name the warning you have been explaining away and turn from it today, and pray and speak for those whose hearts only God can soften.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Evil is real and terrible, but it moves only by permission, inside limits God has set, and it cannot touch his sealed people. A fallen star is given the key to the abyss, and its smoke darkens the sun (vv. 1–2). Out of the smoke come locusts with the power of scorpions, told to spare the grass and to harm only those without God’s seal (vv. 3–4), and allowed to torment but not to kill, for five months, so that people long for death and cannot find it (vv. 5–6). John describes them in likenesses drawn from Joel (vv. 7–10) and names their king, Abaddon, Apollyon, the Destroyer; then the first woe is reported finished (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer: a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation. Tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fifth trumpet a fallen being is handed the key to the abyss, and the darkness of the pit rises into the world. Judgment moves from nature to people, and from natural forces to demonic ones; but even the pit opens only with a key that was given.

A star fallen from heaven. John sees a star already fallen, and at once it is a person: he is given a key and opens the shaft, which no burning rock could do. In Revelation a star can stand for an angel (1:20).

Who is the fallen star? Many take him to be Satan, and the case is strong: Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18); Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon, “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!” (Isaiah 14:12), has been read that way since the early church; and in 12:9 the dragon is thrown down to the earth. Others see one of God’s angels on commission, like the angel of 20:1 who comes down with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain. This is probably a fallen angel, possibly Satan himself. The text does not settle it, and need not: either way, the key was given to him.

He was given the key. In this book the keys belong to Christ: “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18). Any other key is borrowed, and every detail that follows says the same: the locusts were given power, told what to harm, and allowed only five months.

The abyss. In the New Testament it is where demons are kept and where they do not want to go: the legion in the Gerasene man begged Jesus not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31), and Peter and Jude describe rebel angels kept in chains of gloomy darkness until the judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). The beast rises from it (11:7; 17:8) and Satan will be bound in it (20:1–3).

Smoke like the smoke of a great furnace. The reader is meant to hear Sodom, where Abraham saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28), and Sinai, wrapped in smoke like the smoke of a kiln (Exodus 19:18). Hell’s darkness is rising into the world.

The sun and the air were darkened. Before anything comes out, the light goes, and that is exactly what evil does. It rarely arrives arguing; it arrives as a haze, and things that were clear stop being clear: “The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel” (2 Corinthians 4:4).

No smoke reaches the throne. The smoke from the pit can darken the air for a season. It cannot reach the throne, nor the hearts of his people, where the light of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ shines on (2 Corinthians 4:6).

In everyday life. A Christian need be neither fascinated by the demonic nor afraid of it, because the one who holds all the keys is his. When your thinking about right and wrong goes hazy, and things that were plain start to look complicated, suspect smoke, and go back to the light of God’s word.

Is the devil real, or only a symbol of evil? Real. Revelation pictures him as a star, a dragon, a serpent, but the symbols point to a personal being, a fallen angel who deceives the whole world (12:9), whom Jesus answered in the wilderness and named a murderer and a liar (John 8:44). C. S. Lewis warned that people go wrong about devils in two opposite directions: some laugh them off, and others cannot stop staring at them. Scripture takes Satan seriously and never makes him the centre. He is real, he is hostile, and he is on a chain held by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lets demonic powers loose on a rebellious world, but around his own people he draws a line they cannot cross. The locusts may harm only those who do not have God’s seal.

Locusts. The ancient world’s picture of total devastation: a swarm could strip a region bare in hours. The eighth plague on Egypt was locusts, which covered and darkened the land (Exodus 10:12–15), and Joel pictured a locust plague as an invading army on the Day of the LORD, darkening sun and moon and leaving a garden of Eden a desert behind it (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11).

Wrong in every particular. And that is the point. They come out of the abyss, not off the fields; they sting like scorpions, which locusts cannot; and they may not touch a blade of grass, the one thing locusts exist to do. They are demonic powers wearing the shape of the most feared plague in the ancient world.

The power of scorpions. A scorpion’s sting is rarely fatal to a healthy adult, and it is agonising. Rehoboam threatened Israel with scorpions as an image of intensified cruelty (1 Kings 12:11), and Jesus linked them with the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19). This judgment does not kill, but that does not make it a lesser one.

Not to harm the grass. “They were told”: the divine passive again (God acts without being named). All green grass was burned up at the first trumpet (8:7), yet here it grows again, a clear sign that these visions picture God’s judgments, not one physical sequence in strict order (on reading them as parallel passes over the same age, see the note on 6:12–14).

Those who do not have the seal. There is a fence around people, drawn along one line: the seal of God. Here we first see what the sealing of 7:3 does. God’s people are protected from this demonic torment, as Israel in Goshen was protected from the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:22; 9:4, 26; 10:23); the seal on the forehead is the blood-marked doorpost of the Passover, moved from the house to the person. And since the protection covers all who have God’s seal, it confirms that the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 are all believers.

Nothing shall hurt you. Jesus had already drawn this scene in miniature. When the seventy-two came back rejoicing that even the demons were subject to them, he said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you” (Luke 10:18–19). The fifth trumpet is that promise worked out across history. And he added: rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The safety of the sealed rests on Christ’s authority over the enemy and on their names in the Lamb’s book of life (21:27).

In everyday life. When you feel spiritually attacked, by an accusing thought that will not leave, a temptation that feels unusually strong, a darkness in your mind, do not panic, and do not fight it in your own strength. Remind yourself whose name is on your forehead. Then do the ordinary things the devil hates most: pray, read the word, tell a Christian friend, and get some sleep.

What does the seal actually protect, when Christians still suffer? The seal does not exempt anybody from the great tribulation (7:14) or promise that nothing will happen to you: Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about, go to prison, and die. It sets a limit: the evil one does not touch him who is born of God (1 John 5:18), and nothing can reach past the seal to what you actually are, your union with Christ, your adoption, your inheritance. The torment of a soul handed over to the darkness it chose is not for a sealed person, and the reason is not his courage. It is the name on his forehead.

Can a Christian be troubled by demons? Troubled, yes; owned, no. Believers are told to resist the devil (James 4:7) and to stand against his schemes (Ephesians 6:11), so he does attack them: he tempts, accuses, deceives and stirs up persecution. But a Christian is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), and that house cannot be possessed by another master. A believer in spiritual distress needs no special ritual, only what every Christian has: the word of God, prayer in Jesus’ name, the fellowship and oversight of your church, and confidence that he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The torment God allows is real and dreadful, yet strictly limited, and it is meant to call people to repent. It may hurt but not kill, and only for a season, though those under it will long for a death that does not come.

Five months, but not to kill. Permission again, with two boundaries: they may torment, not kill, and for five months, not a day more. Why five months? Most likely because a locust’s life, from hatching to death, is often said to be about five months, roughly May to September. The number is not a code but one locust season, a bounded stretch of time any farmer could measure. It will feel endless while it lasts; it is not. Its purpose is to bring people to repentance (v. 20).

Like the torment of a scorpion. Agonising but not fatal: perhaps the misery of life under demonic deception, the despair, emptiness, fear and addiction of a life without God given over to the powers of darkness.

Death will flee from them. Existence itself has become the punishment, and the one exit a person would take has been closed. Job speaks of those who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures (Job 3:21), and Jeremiah said the survivors of a judged nation would prefer death to life (Jeremiah 8:3). And still they do not turn to God.

A state worse than dying. The horror of the verse is not that God is cruel, but that there is a state worse than dying, and human beings can reach it by their own steady choosing. The mercy in the passage is the five-month fence God put around it. And the Lord who fences the torment of the abyss went into the deepest torment himself and came out the other side. He was forsaken so that no one who trusts him ever will be.

Is this verse about me, if I have wished I would not wake up? Some will read it as a future horror; others will recognise the country. If you are a Christian who has lain awake and wished not to wake up, this verse is not describing your condemnation, and it should not be allowed to sound as though it is. Wanting to die is not the same as being abandoned by God, and Scripture proves it by the company: Job wanted it, Moses asked God to kill him (Numbers 11:15), Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die soon after the greatest victory of his life (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah asked twice. God rejected none of them for it; he fed Elijah and let him sleep. And the torment here falls expressly on those who do not have the seal of God (v. 4).

What should I do if I am in that dark place? Tell someone this week, out loud: your pastor or a Christian friend. Ask your pastor to help you find a biblical counsellor to walk with you, and see your doctor too, since the body can weigh heavily on the mind; if medicine is prescribed, taking it is no failure of faith. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line today. None of this is weakness; it is what the body of Christ, and the ordinary means God gives, are for. Despair says there is no door. This whole book announces that there is one, opened from the other side at enormous cost by the one who holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Your life is in his hands, and he has not finished with it.
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts picture spiritual evil as it really is: it looks glorious and human, cannot be harmed by ordinary weapons, and stings from behind. Every detail is a likeness, drawn largely from Joel’s locust army.

Like horses prepared for battle. John piles up comparisons, nearly every one introduced by “like”: not a report on a species but what it felt like to look at. Joel had already given locusts the look of war horses, the teeth of a lion and a noise like chariots (Joel 1:6; 2:4–5). The crowns only looked like crowns, a counterfeit authority; everything in this book that is truly crowned is crowned by God. The human faces are the worst detail: whatever this is, it has intelligence and intention, and it looks back at you. And the iron breastplates mean there is no attacking them.

Stings in their tails. The sting is in the back end, and the sixth trumpet will repeat it (v. 19): the injury comes from behind, after the thing has apparently passed.

The true crown and the true face. The locusts have faces like human faces and what only looked like crowns of gold, and nothing about them is human. Later John sees one like a son of man with a golden crown on his head (14:14), whose face shines like the sun in full strength (1:16). His is the real face of a real man, and the real crown, and he did not seize it: he was crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). What the abyss counterfeits, Christ actually is: a man who is also Lord, and who wears his crown because he died.

What does this look like in ordinary life? Weapons change with every generation; the make-up of spiritual evil does not. It rarely looks like a monster. It seems glorious and wears a crown it did not earn: an ideology that promises liberation, a pleasure that promises freedom, a habit that looks harmless in its first year. It has a human face, so it seems reasonable. It is armoured, so argument bounces off it. And it stings from behind, long after it seemed to have passed (see the note on vv. 17–19). Yet it comes up only by God’s permission and goes down at the time he has set. The way to resist is not to study the creature but to stay near Christ, who has already disarmed the powers (Colossians 2:15).

Where Christians differ: what are the locusts? Some popular writers have identified them with modern weapons such as attack helicopters, with rotor blades, tail guns and armoured cockpits. Historicists have identified them with the Muslim Arab armies of the seventh century. Others take them as literal demonic creatures to be unleashed in a future tribulation. This commentary’s view: the locusts are demonic powers, released by God’s permission to torment those who have rejected him, pictured with images drawn from Joel’s locust army. John’s repeated “like” signals symbols, not technical descriptions, and reading modern technology into them ignores how the first readers would have understood the book. They describe demonic torment, real and terrible, wherever people give themselves over to evil, throughout the age and especially toward its end.

Uncertain wording. “Their hair like women’s hair” is not explained, and its point is uncertain. It may describe a locust’s long, streaming antennae; it may recall the Parthians, Rome’s feared eastern enemy, mounted archers who wore their hair long; it may simply add a wild look to the terror. The likely sense is the unsettling mixture of the whole description: part insect, part warhorse, part human, and wholly wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demonic host has a king whose name is Destruction, but he rules only a pit, and his woe passes when God says it has passed. One woe is over; two are still to come.

A king over them. “The locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank” (Proverbs 30:27). These do, and that is what makes the line unnerving: the chaos has a commander. The angel of the abyss is either Satan himself or a high-ranking demonic spirit under him.

Abaddon and Apollyon. Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction) is an Old Testament name for the place of the dead, linked with Sheol and death: “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11). Apollyon means the destroyer. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; Christ came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10).

A barb in the name. Apollo, whose emblems seem to have included the locust, was a god emperors liked to be linked with. A Christian in Ephesus hearing Apollyon read aloud would have caught it: the empire’s god has a name very like destroyer, and what he actually rules is a pit.

His only competence. He cannot create anything at all; his name is his job description. Set him beside the one on the throne: “you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created” (4:11). One makes things out of nothing; the other unmakes what somebody else made, and can be shut in a shaft.

The destroyer destroyed. And the Destroyer has met the one person he could not unmake. The Son of God appeared in order to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he did it by dying: through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Satan’s hold on people was their guilt and their fear of death, and at the cross and the empty grave that weapon was taken from his hand. Apollyon rules a hole in the ground; Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). And he does not only outlast the ruin; he reverses it, beginning with ruined sinners, whom he builds again into sons. Abaddon’s name means destruction. Jesus means the LORD saves.

The first woe has passed. A line of bookkeeping. It confirms that the eagle’s three woes (8:13) are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets: worse is coming. But it says “has passed”. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and then reported finished, and the one who keeps the register has never once lost count.

Are God and Satan two equal powers fighting it out? No, though the fear of two matched forces wrestling for the world, with the outcome uncertain, troubles more Christians than admit it. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer never acts on his own authority; everything he has is given (see the note on vv. 1–2). He is not God’s opposite number but a creature with a leash and a name; his true counterpart, if he has one, is an archangel like Michael (12:7), not the Creator. God has no rival.

Is this the Apollyon of The Pilgrim’s Progress? Yes. John Bunyan took the name for the monster that meets Christian in the Valley of Humiliation, claiming him as his subject. Christian is wounded, thrown down and loses his sword; then he recovers it and, with a word of Scripture on his lips, sends Apollyon flying. So here: the destroyer is real and fierce, and claims what is not his, but the believer resists him with the word of God and the promise of victory, and he flees (James 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment answers the prayers of God’s people and keeps God’s timetable, yet judgment alone does not turn a single heart. A voice from the golden altar, where the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5), releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for the very hour (vv. 13–15). A countless cavalry, breathing the fire, smoke and sulphur of Sodom and wounding with serpent tails, kills a third of mankind (vv. 16–19). And the rest did not repent of their idols, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgment alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth trumpet is God’s answer to his people’s prayers, and it lets loose evil powers he has kept bound until now. The order comes from the very altar where the saints’ prayers were offered.

A voice from the golden altar. Here an angel offered much incense with the prayers of all the saints, and from here fire was thrown on the earth (8:3–5). Now a voice from its four horns releases the sixth trumpet: again God’s judgments answer his people’s praying, issued from the place where it is received.

The horns of the altar. The altar of incense had a horn at each corner (Exodus 30:2–3), and the horns were what a man grasped when he fled to the sanctuary claiming protection (1 Kings 1:50–51). Blood was put on them at the great atoning sacrifices (Leviticus 4:7, 18). Both pointed to Christ. The blood on those horns could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); his blood, shed once for all, secured an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). Whoever takes hold of him by faith is safe from the judgment this voice releases, because the sacrifice for his sins has been made; whoever rejects it faces judgment from the same altar.

Release the four angels. They are bound, and have been for a long time, since somebody had to bind them: evil angels, held in check by God until now (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4).

The great river Euphrates. It was the north-eastern boundary of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Assyria and Babylon had come from beyond it, and in John’s day it was Rome’s eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthians, the one power Rome had never subdued, whose cavalry had destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC. In Revelation place names often carry symbolic meaning (Babylon, Sodom, Egypt), and the river stands for the frontier from which invasion comes. Every horde that crossed a border was on a rope, the rope was in God’s hand, and the hand let go at a moment of its own choosing.

What holds evil back now? God does, through means he has appointed. Paul speaks of something that restrains lawlessness until the appointed time (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7), and Christians have usually understood that to include the restraints of God’s common grace, his kindness to all people, which sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45) and holds back the worst of human evil: lawful government, which bears the sword (Romans 13:4), conscience, the family, and the prayers of the church, salt in a decaying world (Matthew 5:13). We rarely see how much is being held back. Every peaceful year, every war that did not happen, every evil plan that failed, is the four angels still bound. That is why we pray for those in authority, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

Textual note. Some important manuscripts read “a voice from the horns of the golden altar”, without the word “four”. The meaning is unchanged.
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has fixed the very moment of judgment, and the host he releases is beyond counting, yet even it kills only a third.

Prepared for the hour. In the Greek a single “the” covers all four units of time, making them one appointed moment, not a span: the hour, on the day, in the month, of the year. The catastrophe that seems to prove nobody is steering has a time stamp on it, applied in advance. That does not make it good, for God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11); it means history is not a series of accidents interrupted now and then by providence.

A third of mankind. The fraction moves again. The horsemen had a fourth (6:8); the first four trumpets took a third of the earth, the sea, the water and the light; now a third of mankind. Still two thirds are untouched.

Twice ten thousand times ten thousand. Two hundred million, if it is arithmetic, and it almost certainly is not. Ten thousand times ten thousand is the largest number the language could easily say (5:11), and doubling it says: beyond even that. The whole Roman army had perhaps three hundred thousand soldiers.

I heard their number. John did not count them; he was told, exactly as with the 144,000: “I heard the number of the sealed” (7:4). Both are figures of completeness: God’s army, sealed and counted, and the demonic army, vast and destructive.

A matter of proportion. The church in Asia was a few thousand people meeting in houses, against forces beyond counting. And the whole of that host was on the wrong side of a river, tied up, waiting for a word from an altar.

His hour, and ours. The God who fixed the hour of judgment fixed another: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son” (John 17:1). Men tried to arrest Jesus, and no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30); when it came he did not run, for it was for this purpose he had come (John 12:27). Because that hour came, no hour of judgment need ever be ours. And the Father who fixed the hour of the cross fixes every hour in your story too: nothing comes early or late by accident, and you are kept by the timetable that kept him.

Should I be afraid of dying in some catastrophe? If you belong to Christ, your hour is fixed by your Father: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). No bomb, virus, accident or army can take you a moment before he calls you home, or keep you a moment after. That does not make Christians careless, since God works through means and we take sensible precautions; but it frees us from the dread of those who think their lives are at the mercy of chance. Whether death comes in old age or in a catastrophe, for the believer it comes on an appointment kept by a Saviour.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal army of two hundred million? Some popular writers have identified it with a future Chinese army, after a report in the 1960s that China could field a militia of two hundred million. This commentary’s view: the number pictures an overwhelming, uncountable host, demonic more than human, as the horses that follow make clear. Its point is the terror of destruction let loose, not a prediction about any nation, and readings tied to modern nations have repeatedly had to be revised as world politics changed.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The horsemen bring hell’s own fire, smoke and sulphur into the world, and their serpent tails show whose army this is.

Fire, sapphire and sulphur. Red, dark blue like smoke, and the sickly yellow of brimstone: the riders wear what the horses breathe. Fire and sulphur rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and in Revelation they are the elements of the lake of fire (14:10; 19:20; 20:10; 21:8). What comes out of these mouths is the substance of hell breaking out into the world.

By these three plagues. “Plagues” is the word of the exodus again. And the killing is done by what comes out of a mouth. Christ’s weapon also comes from a mouth: the sharp sword of his word (1:16; 19:15). What comes out of a mouth can kill or save.

Tails like serpents. The tails have heads of their own: these horses kill from the front and wound from behind. The Parthian cavalry were famous for shooting arrows backwards over the horse’s rump as they rode away, so that their power seemed to be in their tails.

John has signed the picture. In this book “serpent” belongs to one figure: the great dragon is “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (12:9; 20:2). Whatever the historical shape, the tail that stings from behind belongs to the serpent.

The bruise was the cross. From the first pages of the Bible the serpent’s end was promised: the offspring of the woman would bruise his head, though his own heel would be bruised in doing it (Genesis 3:15). The bruise was the cross. The serpent still bites, but he bites as a beaten enemy, and the one who took his deadliest strike in his own body will have the last word over every lie the serpent has ever told.

Evil does its worst work with its back turned. The moment of the encounter is rarely the moment of the damage. The affair ended years ago; the consequences are only now walking through the door.
