The drinking stopped; the damage to the liver did not. The words were said in one bad evening; the son has not called since.

Is there hope when I am living with the sting of my own past sin? Yes. God does not always remove the consequences of sin: David was forgiven, and still his household suffered (2 Samuel 12:13–14). But the guilt is gone the moment you confess it, and the serpent’s sting has been drawn at the cross: the sting of death is sin, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:56–57). Do the repairing you can: apologise, make restitution, keep faith with those you hurt. Then refuse to let the accuser keep stinging you with what God has forgiven. God is able to bring good even out of the wreckage (Romans 8:28), and he often does it slowly.

How do I pray against spiritual powers without becoming obsessed with them? By keeping your eyes on Christ, not the enemy. We wrestle against the spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), yet the armour Paul describes is almost entirely ordinary: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer at all times in the Spirit. You do not need to name or map demons, or address them in prayer. Pray to the Father, in the name of the Son who has already triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), for his kingdom to come and for deliverance from evil, as Jesus taught us to pray (Matthew 6:13).

Uncertain wording. The middle colour is not certain. “Sapphire” translates a word meaning hyacinth-coloured, which could describe a deep blue or a dark purple, the colour of the hyacinth stone or flower. Most take it as the dark blue of smoke, so that the three colours match the fire, smoke and sulphur the horses breathe, and that is the likely meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after all this, the survivors would not turn from their idols or their sins: judgment by itself does not change the human heart. The trumpets were merciful warnings, and they were refused.

Did not repent. This is the sentence the trumpets have been building toward. Each judgment was limited for the sake of those left, and this verse says what they did with the mercy of being alive. The same words return in 16:9, 11.

Suffering does not automatically produce repentance. Surely if God sent something undeniable, the world would turn? Revelation says it has been tried: the sky has darkened, the water turned bitter, a third of the human race died, and the survivors went back to what they were doing. Suffering hardens as often as it softens, and Pharaoh, whose plagues these are, is the standing proof: plague after plague he hardened his heart (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34), and the last thing he did was drive into a sea that had opened.

Which cannot see or hear or walk. What they will not give up comes in two lists. First the idols, described with the contempt of the Psalms: they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see; those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:4–8; 135:15–17; Daniel 5:23). That last clause is the sting: you become like what you worship. Worship something blind and deaf, and in the end you cannot see or hear either, which is exactly what this chapter has just described. Gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood: idols for the rich and the poor alike.

Behind the idols, demons. Idolatry is not harmless: “what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20). The very powers that tormented them in this chapter are the ones they keep worshipping. And idols include anything people trust and serve in place of God, money, power, pleasure, status: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5).

Murders, sorceries, immorality, thefts. The second list is startlingly ordinary, from the commandments of the second table (the commandments about our neighbour): murder, adultery, theft. Sorceries (pharmakeia, from which our word pharmacy comes) means drugs and potions used in magic and the occult: the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique rather than by trusting God.

Root and fruit. Set the two lists together and the diagnosis is complete. Breaking the first table of the law (the commandments about God himself) always leads to breaking the second (Romans 1:21–32): idolatry is the root; murder, manipulation, immorality and theft are the fruit. A person who has replaced God will end up destroying his neighbour’s life, body, marriage or property. And none of these four is exotic. Every one of them is available on an ordinary Tuesday.

Did not, not could not. The chapter is finally about a door that stayed open and was not used: the judgments were fractional and announced in advance, so that God might be heard. The bondage of the will is real, but it is a bondage they love; the refusal is theirs, and so is the guilt. How can anyone be blamed for what he cannot do without grace? Because this inability is not that of a paralysed man who longs to walk. It is that of a man who will not leave the woman who is ruining him, because he loves her. What holds them is what they want (John 3:19), and no one is excused for wanting evil.

In the flow. As between the sixth and seventh seals, an interlude follows (10:1–11:14), and it answers the problem this verse leaves: if judgment alone does not bring repentance, what will? The witness of a suffering church (10:11; 11:3, 13). The trumpets warn; the gospel is what God uses to turn hearts.

Eyes like a flame of fire. Idols cannot see; the risen Christ has eyes like a flame of fire and says to each church, “I know your works” (2:18–19). They cannot walk; he walks among the seven golden lampstands (2:1). And the psalm’s rule runs in his direction too: those who behold the glory of the Lord are being transformed into the same image (2 Corinthians 3:18). A person who keeps looking at Christ, in his word, slowly comes to see as he sees and love what he loves. Idols make their worshippers blind and deaf. Christ makes his worshippers like himself.

Even our repentance was his gift. The God of this chapter measures his judgments, sends warnings in daylight and holds back the hosts of the abyss to leave room for repentance. And when the human heart still refuses, he does what no trumpet can do: he gives a new heart, puts his Spirit within, and turns the rebel into a son. Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, for even our repentance was his gift.

The sorcery of the self-improved. Few people keep potions now, but the hope behind them remains: that the right technique will put life, luck, love and even death under our control. We track our sleep, optimise our diets, let algorithms choose our partners and fund research to stop ageing. Much of this is good gift (and medicine is not magic: see below). But the French thinker Jacques Ellul warned that modern society had come to treat technique itself, the most efficient method in every area of life, as sacred and beyond question. What matters is what we ask our methods to give us. Sorcery was always a way of getting the goods of life without trusting the giver. The gospel offers the opposite exchange: we give up control and receive a Father. The one who held all authority knelt in a garden and prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), and because he surrendered, we can stop trying to manage our own salvation.

Verse 20 in a life. An idol is whatever you would be unable to give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about, and see how expertly the warning has been explained away. Then do one concrete thing about it this week: remove what feeds it, make the phone call, confess the sin. Repentance is a turning, not a feeling, and the Spirit who gives new hearts gives the strength for it. You will never turn perfectly, but Christ obeyed perfectly in your place (Romans 5:19), so even a halting repentance is welcomed for his sake. And if seeing your idol grieves you, that grief is not hardness. It is the Spirit’s work.

Is my unbelieving friend beyond hope, if even disasters do not move people? No. What disasters cannot do, God can: Paul, dead in sin, was turned around in a moment on the Damascus road. Hardness of heart is a reason to rely not on arguments and circumstances but on the Spirit, who gives new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26). So keep praying for them by name, keep loving them, and tell them the gospel plainly when the door opens. God often uses suffering as the occasion of conversion, but it is always grace, not the suffering, that saves.

Are horoscopes, tarot and crystals harmless fun? Scripture treats them as anything but. They belong to the family of sorceries named here, attempts to know or control the future apart from God. Israel was forbidden every form of divination (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the new believers in Ephesus burned their magic books publicly at great cost (Acts 19:19). Even meant lightly, they train the heart to look for guidance and security somewhere other than the Lord. Your future is not in the stars; it is in the hands of the one who made them.

Does pharmakeia mean Christians should avoid medicine? No. The word here means magic and the occult, not medicine. Scripture treats medical care as a good gift: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Jesus said that those who are sick need a doctor (Luke 5:31). Taking prescribed medication, including for mental illness, is not a lack of faith. What is condemned is using substances to manipulate spiritual powers, or to escape into darkness, instead of receiving God’s gifts with thanksgiving.

Where Christians differ: can people repent whenever they choose? Many Christians, especially in the Arminian tradition, hold that God gives all people a grace that restores the ability to repent and believe if they choose; they hold it out of deep concern for human responsibility and God’s love for the world, and they are our brothers and sisters. This commentary’s view: this verse shows the terrible bondage of the human will apart from grace. Even under overwhelming judgment people do not repent, because their hearts are enslaved to sin and they love darkness (John 3:19). Scripture teaches that sinners are dead in sin (Ephesians 2:1) and unable to come to Christ unless the Father draws them (John 6:44), and that repentance is God’s gift (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). This does not excuse unbelievers; they are responsible for refusing. But it shows why we pray for God to give new hearts, and why we preach the gospel, which is God’s power to save (Romans 1:16).

9.text: <sup>1</sup>And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit.<sup>2</sup>He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.<sup>3</sup>Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth.<sup>4</sup>They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone.<sup>6</sup>And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.<sup>7</sup>In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces,<sup>8</sup>their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth;<sup>9</sup>they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle.<sup>10</sup>They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.<sup>11</sup>They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.<sup>12</sup>The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.<sup>13</sup>Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God,<sup>14</sup>saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”<sup>15</sup>So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.<sup>16</sup>The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.<sup>17</sup>And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.<sup>18</sup>By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths.<sup>19</sup>For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.<sup>20</sup>The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,<sup>21</sup>nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

keyVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter has been building to this verse. The judgments were limited and announced in advance so that people might turn, and they would not: suffering alone does not change a heart. It drives us to the only remedy, the grace that gives new hearts, and it sends the church to pray and bear witness, which is where the next chapter goes.

9.reflection:
Every power in this chapter acts only by permission: the star is given a key, the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months, the four angels are released at an hour already fixed (vv. 1–5, 15). How does that change the way you think about evil you see in the world, or face in your own life?

The locusts may harm only those without God’s seal (v. 4), yet Christians still suffer. What does the seal protect, and what does it not? How would you put that to a believer who is frightened or struggling?

The picture of evil in vv. 7–10 and 17–19 is crowned, human-faced, armoured, and stings from behind. Where have you seen sin look glorious and reasonable at first, and do its damage later? What helps you stay near Christ instead of studying the creature?

After all these judgments, the survivors did not repent (vv. 20–21). Why does suffering so often harden rather than soften? What does that mean for how we pray for, and speak to, people we love who do not yet believe?

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 opens a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets (10:1–11:14), as chapter 7 did between the sixth and seventh seals. The sixth trumpet ended with a world that would not repent (9:20–21); before the last trumpet sounds, the vision turns from the world to the church and its commission.

The message. God will finish what he has begun, and he has sworn it: there will be no more delay, and at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God, his whole saving purpose in Christ, will be completed. Until then his people are to take his word in and speak it to the nations, finding it sweet to receive and bitter to carry.

Why it was said. The martyrs had cried, “how long?” (6:10), and the churches of Asia, small and pressed, could see little sign that God’s plan was moving, while John himself was old and exiled on Patmos, his work apparently over (see the introduction). They needed to know that the end is fixed under oath, that God has told them all they need though not all they might like to know, and that their task in the meantime is witness, at a cost.

How the chapter makes its case. A mighty angel, clothed in borrowed glory and with the rainbow of God’s promise over his head, plants his feet on sea and land, claiming the whole world, with a little open scroll in his hand (vv. 1–2). He roars like a lion, the seven thunders speak, and John, pen in hand, is told to seal up what they said: God keeps back what he chooses (vv. 3–4). The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay (vv. 5–7). Then John is told to take the scroll and eat it, sweet as honey in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, as Ezekiel’s was (vv. 8–10), and is sent to prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings (v. 11).

Where it leads. The scroll John eats is bound up with the purpose the Lamb alone was worthy to open (5:5–9), now handed to his servant to proclaim. The mystery it completes is the plan of salvation in Christ, and the word for its fulfilment echoes the cry from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Its sweetness is the Lamb’s victory; its bitterness is the road he walked first and his witnesses walk after him. And he alone drank the full bitterness of judgment, so that his people never need to.

For us. Trust God with what he has not told you, and do what he has told you. Take his word in slowly until it is part of you, expect it to cost you, and speak it to the people around you: no one who belongs to Christ is discharged from that service while he has breath.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the end comes, God renews his church’s commission: his plan will be finished on time, and meanwhile his people must take in his word and speak it, sweet and bitter as it is. A mighty angel in borrowed glory stands on sea and land with a little open scroll (vv. 1–2). Seven thunders speak, and John is told to seal up what they said, for God keeps back what he chooses (vv. 3–4). The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay: at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God will be fulfilled (vv. 5–7). John eats the scroll, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach (vv. 8–10), and is sent to prophesy again to the nations and their kings (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed, the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mighty angel, shining with Christ’s reflected glory and with God’s promise over his head, claims the whole world for God and brings a message for it.

John does not rush his sevens. The seventh trumpet does not sound until 11:15. Twice now, just where a reader is braced for the end, the vision stops and turns to the church: before the last trumpet, God shows his people where they stand and what they are for.

Another mighty angel. Every detail of this figure is one the reader has met. The cloud is what God travels in and what Christ returns on (1:7). The rainbow was around the throne (4:3). His face like the sun is how the risen Christ was described (1:16), and his legs like pillars of fire recall 1:15 and the pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). Some serious readers have concluded that this is Christ himself (see below).

A herald in his master’s livery. When an ambassador arrives in the king’s colours, the point is not that he is the king but whose message he carries. Every ray on this angel’s face is reflected light, and the more glorious a servant of God appears, the more firmly he sends worship on to God (19:10; 22:9).

A little scroll open in his hand. It is little, and it is open, unlike the great sealed scroll of chapter 5, with which it is probably closely connected (see the box below). What the Lamb alone could open, the Lamb now gives away.

His right foot on the sea. The posture is a claim. Land and sea are the ancient way of saying everywhere, and planting a foot on territory is what a conqueror does: “Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you” (Joshua 1:3). And he has one foot on the sea, out of which the first beast will rise (13:1), and one on the land, out of which the second will rise (13:11). Hold that picture when the next chapters grow dark: before the dragon or either beast comes up, God has shown his church whose feet are on the ground they come from.

What is the rainbow doing in a chapter about judgment? It is God’s promise, worn over the head of his messenger. After the flood God set his bow in the cloud as the sign of his covenant with Noah that he would never again destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:13–16), and in Revelation the same bow encircles his throne (4:3). So even the heralds of judgment come with mercy over their heads. The judgments of Revelation are real and terrible, but they are not the outbursts of a God who has forgotten his covenant; they are a faithful God clearing the ground for a new creation, keeping every promise to his people as he does it.

Where Christians differ: is the mighty angel Christ? Some identify him with Christ himself, because of the cloud, the rainbow, the sun-like face and the fiery legs. Three things tell against it. The word is allos: another mighty angel, of the same kind as the mighty angel of 5:2. In verse 6 he swears by the one who lives for ever and ever, and swearing by a higher authority is not something Christ does or needs to do; when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13). And Revelation never calls Christ an angel, though it gives him many other names; he is the one the angels worship (5:11–12). This commentary’s view: he is most likely a powerful angel who reflects Christ’s glory and represents him. Angels who come from God’s presence share something of his glory, as Moses’ face shone after he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

Uncertain wording. How the “little scroll” relates to the scroll of chapter 5 is not certain. John uses a word meaning a small scroll (vv. 2, 9–10), yet in v. 8 he calls it simply “the scroll”, the word used for the sealed scroll the Lamb opened. Some take it as a separate, smaller message, perhaps the contents of 11:1–13; others as God’s purpose from chapter 5, now unsealed and handed to John to proclaim. The many links with chapter 5 make the second more likely.

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has spoken more than he has written down for us, and he has chosen to keep some things back. John hears the seven thunders and is forbidden to record them: the one sealed message in an unsealed book.

Like a lion roaring. A lion’s roar is not a warning shot. It announces possession of territory, and the prophets used it of God speaking: “The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?” (Amos 3:8; compare Hosea 11:10; Joel 3:16). In this book there is one Lion, of the tribe of Judah, who turned out to be a Lamb (5:5–6). The angel on sea and land roars with his master’s voice, and the roar says: this ground is claimed.

The seven thunders. “The” is odd and deliberate, as though John expects his readers to know which ones. The likeliest background is Psalm 29, where the voice of the LORD sounds seven times like thunder over the waters, and in his temple all cry, “Glory!” A full sequence of divine speech has just been uttered. And it was speech, in words: John understood it, since a man does not reach for a pen to write down noise.

Do not write it down. This reverses every other word John receives about writing. He has been told to write from the beginning (1:11, 19), and at the end he will be told, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true” (21:5). Once, with the pen already in his hand, he is told not to.

The one sealed sentence. Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9), and Paul, caught up into paradise, heard “things that cannot be told, which man may not utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). At the close of this book John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy, for the time is near (22:10). Revelation is the unsealed book. There is exactly one sealed message in it, and we do not have it.

Why were the thunders sealed? Perhaps they were further judgments that God has chosen to cancel or cut short, and the very next verse says there will be no more delay. Perhaps they are held back to show that the warnings already given are enough. Neither can be proved; nobody knows, because the point of the verse is that we were not told. What is certain is the lesson: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Note what the revealed things are for: not so that we may know, but so that we may do. The appetite for more than has been given, the date, the identity, the name behind the number, has a limit, and God set it.

His last and clearest word. The God of glory thunders, speaks in sevens and is never exhausted. He keeps back what he chooses, and owes no one an explanation. Yet about the one thing that matters he has not spoken in riddles: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The thunders were sealed; the Son was sent. In Christ God has given us his last and clearest word, and with it himself.

What it does not mean. The sealed thunders do not invite speculation: anyone who claims to reveal them claims what John was forbidden to give. The canon, the list of the books of Scripture, is closed (22:18–19). We have everything we need for life and godliness in what is written (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). So when a book, a video or a preacher offers you the hidden key to the end times, remember that an apostle with the pen in his hand was told to stop.

Does this mean the Bible is incomplete? No. It is complete for its purpose, which is not the same as exhaustive: God has told us not everything he knows, but everything we need to know him, be saved and live for him until Christ returns. A father does not tell a child everything about the family finances, and the child is not the poorer; he is told what he needs by someone who loves him and knows the rest. Scripture’s silences are as deliberate as its words, and a believer who keeps to what is written is missing nothing God meant him to have.

When God does not answer my question. Some believers have spent years asking God something unanswered: why that happened, why there was no child, why a good man’s prayer seemed to come to nothing. The thunders spoke and John understood: the answer exists, and the withholding is deliberate. And the God who withholds it is the God who did not withhold his own Son (Romans 8:32). He can be trusted with what he keeps. When the question returns in the night, put beside it what he has plainly said: that he works all things together for good for those who love him, and that nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:28, 38–39).

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has sworn that when his moment comes there will be no more delay, and his whole saving purpose, long announced through the prophets, will be complete. The waiting has an end, fixed by the Creator himself.

He swore. Raising the hand was the gesture of a solemn oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40), and the scene is drawn from Daniel 12:7, where a man clothed in linen raises his hands to heaven and swears by him who lives for ever. People swear by something greater than themselves, and in oaths the final confirmation ends every argument (Hebrews 6:16). This angel swears by the greatest there is: the Creator of the very sea and land he stands on. Because God made it all, he has both the right and the power to bring it to its end; a maker may finish what he began.

No more delay. This answers the souls under the altar, who asked how long (6:10) and were told to rest a little longer. Here, under oath, the little longer has run out. When the trumpet sounds, the door will be shut, like the door of the ark and the door to the wedding feast (Genesis 7:16; Matthew 25:10); so every day before it is a day on which a rebel may still come home.

The mystery of God would be fulfilled. In the New Testament a mystery is something once hidden and now disclosed: God’s plan of salvation in Christ, including the gathering of Gentiles with Jews into one people (Ephesians 3:3–6; Colossians 1:26–27), and its completion when all things are united in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:9–10). The seventh trumpet will announce it: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (11:15). The Greek verb for “fulfilled” is closely related to the cry from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30). What the seventh trumpet completes before the whole world is what Christ finished at the cross, brought at last to its full and visible end.

Just as he announced to the prophets. What the seventh trumpet completes is the programme God published through Isaiah and Daniel and Amos and the rest: “For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). And the word for “announced” is the verb behind our words “gospel” and “evangelise”. God’s final victory is good news he has been telling for centuries. What God began in a garden he will finish in a city, and not one word he preached to his prophets will fall to the ground.

In the flow. Between the martyrs’ cry (6:10) and the seventh trumpet (11:15–18), chapters 10 and 11 show what the church does with the time that is left: it takes the word and speaks it.

The hardest thing is the waiting. Often it is not the suffering but its open-endedness. This verse does not tell the church when, but that the when has been fixed and sworn to by the Creator. A prisoner who knows the date of his release can bear a great deal. Whatever you are waiting on God for, you may still have to wait, but not wondering whether he means it.

But if there is no more delay, why has it been two thousand years? Because the oath concerns what happens when the seventh trumpet sounds, not a stopwatch started in John’s day. Revelation shows the age between Christ’s comings in several cycles, each ending at the edge of the last judgment; the oath says that when God’s moment arrives there will be no last extension. Peter answers the same question: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:8–9). Each passing year is not God forgetting but God gathering the last of his elect, and the day he has fixed will not move.

How should this change the way I read the news? It should make you sober without making you frantic. The world will not drift on for ever, collapse by accident, or end when men decide; it will be brought to its goal by the God who made it, at a moment he has sworn to. You do not need to decode current events to know where history is going; you need to know who is finishing it. That frees you to grieve real evils without despair, to work for good without imagining that everything depends on you, and to pray, as the church always has, Come, Lord Jesus.

Textual note. The King James Version translates “that there should be time no longer”, which some have taken to mean the end of time itself. The Greek word chronos can mean delay, and the context, answering the martyrs’ How long?, shows that this is the meaning here.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word must be taken in before it is passed on, and those who take it in find it sweet as honey, then bitter to carry. John eats the scroll, as Ezekiel did, and both tastes are true.

Go, take the scroll. The voice that told him not to write now tells him to move. John does not snatch; he asks, and a mighty angel with his feet on the world hands a book to an old man who asked for it.

Take and eat it. The verb is strong: devour it, eat it up. Ezekiel was given this exact commission some seven hundred years earlier: he ate a scroll full of lamentation and woe, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 3:1–3); afterwards he went in bitterness, in the heat of his spirit, and sat among the exiles seven days, overwhelmed (Ezekiel 3:14–15). Jeremiah too ate God’s words with joy (Jeremiah 15:16), and his ministry brought him great suffering.

Why eating? A herald could be handed a script to read out; eating makes a thing part of you, slowly, inwardly and for good. To eat the scroll is to take God’s word in until it is part of oneself, and only then to speak it to others; a prophet cannot pass on what he has not first taken in. Our Lord lived this himself: hungry in the wilderness, he answered the tempter from Deuteronomy, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3).

Sweet as honey. Both tastes are true of the gospel at once. It is sweet because it is the word of God, “sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb” (Psalm 19:10), full of grace, telling of his victory and the salvation of his people.

Why bitter? Because of what is in it: judgment on the unrepentant, and suffering for those who proclaim it. John will be shown two witnesses killed in the street, a dragon hunting a woman, a beast conquering the saints, and a city drunk on the blood of the martyrs, and no one can take that in and feel nothing. The word that saves is also the word that judges, and nobody who loves people can carry the second half of that sentence lightly.

Sweet first, bitter after. The angel warned him in the reverse order, bitter then sweet, as though preparing him for the sting; John reports it in the order he experienced it. Every honest Christian recognises that order. We are won by being told we are loved and forgiven, and it is honey. The bitterness comes later, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is the taste of a truth taken in by a person who now has to live in a world that does not want it.

Where their Lord was crucified. What John swallows is the purpose the Lamb has unsealed (5:5–9), and its sweetness is the Lamb’s victory. The bitterness follows the Lamb’s own path: the very next chapter shows two witnesses lying dead in the street of the great city where their Lord was crucified (11:8). The scroll’s bearers follow the Lamb wherever he goes (14:4), and he went by a cross. The cost of carrying God’s word is not a sign that the message has failed. It is the mark of belonging to the one whose own witness ended at a cross, and then at an empty tomb.

He would not drink it. The word of the Lord is sweeter than honey, and he feeds his servants with it before he sends them. The bitterness, too, he knows from the inside. At Golgotha, before they crucified him, they offered him wine mixed with gall, and when he tasted it he would not drink (Matthew 27:34): he would not dull one moment of what he had come to bear. He took the full bitterness of judgment, so that the bitterness left for his people is only the cost of witness, never condemnation. He tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9), and he gives them honey from the rock.

The taste of ministry. Anyone who has had to say a true thing that might cost a friendship knows the sequence: the delight of knowing it, then the churning at two in the morning, much of it the fear of losing someone’s good opinion. But the one who carries God’s word is already approved where it matters most, by the God who sent it, and that frees him to risk a friend’s displeasure for the friend’s good (Galatians 1:10). A preacher who finds Scripture only bitter has forgotten why he started. The prophet gets both, in that order, from the same scroll.

What does eating the word look like for an ordinary Christian? It is the difference between reading the Bible and taking it in. Read a passage slowly, more than once. Ask what it shows you of God, what it says to you, and what it asks of you. Turn it into prayer before you put it down. Carry one verse through the day, and memorise some, because what is in you cannot be taken away. You will not do this perfectly, and your standing does not hang on it: Christ kept his Father’s word perfectly in your place. But a short passage chewed is worth more than a long one swallowed whole and forgotten by lunch.

Why is Revelation so hard to read? This verse is the honest answer: it was never meant to be comfortable. It is sweet, for the Lamb reigns, the martyrs are vindicated and God wipes away every tear; and bitter, because the road there runs through chapters 11 to 20. If parts of it trouble you, you are reading it as its first reader did. Keep reading to the end: the bitterness is real, but it is not the last taste.

What if the Bible has only felt bitter to me lately? You may be exactly where this verse describes, and God has not left you. The bitterness may be the cost of obeying, or grief at seeing sin and judgment clearly, the word doing its work. Or you may have been reading the commands without the promises, the law without the gospel. Go back to the honey: read a Gospel, a psalm of trust, Romans 8, Isaiah 53, and look at Christ for yourself, not only at your duty. The scroll is sweet first. Ask God to let you taste that again, and he will.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s work is not over: he is sent again with God’s word to the whole world and its rulers, and the church carries the same commission. An old exile is given the widest assignment of his life.

You must again prophesy. John is very probably an old man under Roman banishment, with no congregation and no way home, his work apparently behind him. “Must” is the word used in 1:1 of the things that must soon take place, and the word Jesus used of his own suffering. It is a commission renewed: he has already prophesied, and now he must go on, with the second half of the book.

Many peoples and kings. The fourfold phrase is the one John has used since 5:9 and 7:9 for the whole human race, with kings in place of tribes, because from chapter 11 onward the book turns to the powers of the earth. A prisoner with no legal standing is given a commission covering every nation and its rulers, and his only equipment is a small scroll he has eaten.

A verdict on the present. Prophecy in Scripture is rarely prediction for its own sake. It is God’s verdict on the present, delivered out loud, usually to people who did not ask for it. Emperors who thought themselves gods are about to hear what heaven thinks of them from a man they had exiled, and through his book and the church that takes up his commission (11:3–6), rulers still hear it. Those emperors are dust; his book is read across the world.

The Lamb’s nations. These are the very peoples the Lamb bought: by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (5:9). And the kings in the list will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14). So John is not sent to announce an open contest. He is sent to tell the nations who owns them, and to call them to the one who died for people among them.

When my useful years seem over. Age, illness or a church that no longer asks can persuade a Christian that his work for God is finished. John was exiled, elderly and isolated, and heaven’s word to him was “again”: the greatest assignment of his life came after everything that looked like his ministry had been taken away. The Lord of the nations is not finished with his servants when the world has finished with them. The work may look different now: prayer instead of travel, a letter instead of a sermon, faithfulness in a small room instead of influence in a large one. But no one who belongs to Christ is ever discharged from his service while he still has breath.

In everyday life. Pray for kings and all who are in high positions (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Then bring it closer: who in your small world needs to hear what God has said, and has no one else to tell them? You do not need John’s visions, only the scroll he ate, which is open on your table, and the Spirit who once made frightened disciples speak the word with boldness (Acts 4:31), and who lives in you.

Are there prophets like John today? Not in John’s sense. John received new revelation directly from God, and what he received is now the last book of the Bible, with a warning against adding to it or taking from it (22:18–19). That kind of prophecy has ceased, because the canon is complete. Many Christians in Pentecostal and charismatic churches believe God still gives prophetic words today, though most agree that no such word equals Scripture or adds to it; this commentary holds that the gifts of new revelation have ceased (the view called cessationism, from the word cease), and honours them as brothers and sisters who love the same Word. But the prophetic task of the church goes on. Every preacher who opens this book, and every believer who tells a neighbour what God has said, declares his word to peoples and nations and kings. We do not receive new thunders. We carry the scroll that has already been opened, and it is enough.

Uncertain wording. The small Greek word translated “about” can also mean “against”, and either fits here. “About” makes the nations the subject of John’s prophecy; “against” makes it a verdict on them, which suits the judgments that follow and the kings who will make war on the Lamb. Most likely both are in view: John speaks concerning the nations, and much of what he must say is against their rebellion.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire.<sup>2</sup>He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,<sup>3</sup>and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded.<sup>4</sup>And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”<sup>5</sup>And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven<sup>6</sup>and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay,<sup>7</sup>but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.<sup>8</sup>Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”<sup>9</sup>So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”<sup>10</sup>And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.<sup>11</sup>And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

keyVerse.quote: but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
keyVerse.note: The angel’s oath answers the martyrs’ cry of “how long?”: God’s saving purpose in Christ will be completed at his appointed moment, with no further delay. The word for “fulfilled” echoes “It is finished” from the cross, so the end of history is the full unveiling of what Christ has already done. The rest of the chapter, the sealed thunders and the eaten scroll, shows how the church lives until then.

10.reflection:
The mighty angel plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, the very places the two beasts will rise from (v. 2; 13:1, 11). What fears about the world or the future does that picture answer for you?

John is forbidden to write down what the seven thunders said (v. 4). How do you respond when God leaves your questions unanswered? What helps you trust him with what he keeps back, and do what he has plainly told you (Deuteronomy 29:29)?

The angel swears there will be no more delay (vv. 6–7), yet the church has waited for centuries. How should knowing that the end is fixed under oath shape the way you wait, pray and read the news?

The scroll was sweet in John’s mouth and bitter in his stomach (vv. 9–10). Where have you tasted both the sweetness of God’s word and the cost of living or speaking it? Who in your own world needs to hear it from you (v. 11)?

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 completes the pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets begun in 10:1, showing what the prophesying John has just been given (10:11) looks like in the life of the church; then the seventh trumpet brings the series to the end of history.

The message. God keeps his church safe, sends it to speak for him through this whole age, lets the world silence it for a little while, and then raises it; and the kingdom of the world becomes his and his Christ’s for ever. What the church is before God cannot be touched; what it has in the world can be trampled, but only for the time he has fixed.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia were small and under pressure, Antipas was dead (2:13), and some were tempted to buy safety with silence (see the introduction). Was faithful witness worth the cost? You are measured as his, comes the answer; you will not be cut off before your work is done; and you will be raised in full view of those who mocked you.

How the chapter makes its case. The measured temple is not a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, as dispensationalists expect, but the church (1 Corinthians 3:16), kept within while its outer court is trampled for forty-two months (vv. 1–2). Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy for the same 1,260 days with the powers of Moses and Elijah (vv. 3–6): most Reformed readers see in them the whole witnessing church (see the box at vv. 3–4). When their testimony is finished the beast kills them and the world celebrates (vv. 7–10); God raises them, and where plagues had hardened people (9:20–21), the survivors give glory to God (vv. 11–14). The seventh trumpet releases no plague: it announces the answer to the prayer “Your kingdom come”, declared as already done (vv. 15–19).

Where it leads. The witnesses walk the road their Lord walked first, to death in the city “where their Lord was crucified” (v. 8), resurrection and a cloud. The chapter ends by opening the true temple, where the ark’s mercy seat points to Christ, whom God “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25); and the God who was to come is praised as the one “who is and who was” (v. 17), because he has come.

For us. You are living in the 1,260 days. Do not mistake the trampling of the outer court for the fall of the sanctuary. Keep speaking, in sackcloth and not swagger, in the Spirit’s strength, and leave your vindication with God: the kingdom of the world has already changed hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church in this age is kept by God, sent to bear witness, silenced for a while by the world, and raised by him. John measures the temple, the altar and the worshippers but leaves the outer court to be trampled for forty-two months: God’s people are kept safe, their outward life exposed (vv. 1–2). Two witnesses, the olive trees and lampstands of Zechariah 4, prophesy in sackcloth for the same 1,260 days with the powers of Elijah and Moses (vv. 3–6). When their testimony is finished the beast kills them, and the world gazes at their unburied bodies and celebrates (vv. 7–10). Then God breathes life into them and calls them up in a cloud while their enemies watch, and after an earthquake the survivors give glory to the God of heaven (vv. 11–13). The second woe has passed (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God claims his people as his own and keeps their life with him safe, while their outward life in the world is left open to attack for a limited time.

A measuring rod. A reed used as a measuring stick (Ezekiel’s was about three metres long, Ezekiel 40:5). Measuring can mark out what God will protect, as with Ezekiel’s new temple (Ezekiel 40–48) and Zechariah’s Jerusalem, with the LORD as a wall of fire around her (Zechariah 2:1–5), or what he will judge (2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Here it is the first: an owner marking out what is his and what he means to protect. To be measured is to be claimed, and not one worshipper is left in the outer court by oversight.

Those who worship there. The temple is the sanctuary, the inner shrine (naos). The third item on the list is the surprise: you can measure a building and an altar with a reed, but not worshippers, unless the temple is made of them. In the New Testament the temple of God is the church, the people in whom he dwells: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; Ephesians 2:19–22). The rod says what the seal on the forehead said in chapter 7: God marks out his people as his own and guarantees their protection.

Leave that out. Literally “throw it outside”. In Herod’s temple the outer court was where Gentiles could come; here it stands for the church’s outward, visible life in the world, which is exposed to attack. Both the measuring and the leaving out are God’s decision: the trampling is permitted by him, for a set time.

Forty-two months. The holy city is God’s people, the church (21:2), and Jesus had said that Jerusalem would be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The book names this period in three interchangeable forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, and times, and half a time (12:14), all three and a half years. They come from Daniel, where the little horn wears out the saints for a time, times, and half a time (Daniel 7:25; 12:7), and they recall the three and a half years of drought in Elijah’s day (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).

Half of seven. Where seven is completeness, half of seven marks a period that is real, severe and broken off before it can run its course. On this commentary’s reading it is the whole time between Christ’s two comings, when the church witnesses and suffers, and it is bounded: God has already fixed the day it stops.

The temple of his body. The church is God’s temple only because of someone else. When Jesus said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, John explains that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). He is the true sanctuary, where God and man meet, and believers become living stones only by coming to him, the living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious in the sight of God (1 Peter 2:4–5). That is why the worshippers are measured with the temple: they are built into him, and to be in him is to be counted.

Protected and exposed. The church is not promised that nothing can be trampled, only that what the trampling can reach is not the temple. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed; none of that touches the sanctuary, the altar or the worshippers, and God has drawn the line himself. A Christian who expects only protection will be bewildered by the exposure.

If I am measured and protected, why do Christians still suffer and die? Because what is protected is not your circumstances but your belonging to God, your access to him and your final salvation. Jesus said both in one breath: some of you they will put to death, yet not a hair of your head will perish (Luke 21:16–18). The world can reach your body; it cannot reach the place where God has measured you as his own, and it cannot go on trampling beyond the time he has fixed.

In everyday life. When you are mocked for following Christ, or the church you love is shrinking, do not conclude that the sanctuary has fallen. Go to the altar: pray, and worship with God’s people on the Lord’s day. That is the measured ground, and nothing outside it can take it from you.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal temple in Jerusalem? Dispensationalists (who keep God’s plans for Israel and the church distinct and expect a future seven-year tribulation) hold that a third temple will be rebuilt in Jerusalem, with sacrifices restored, and that this passage describes it during a literal three and a half years. They want to take the words plainly, and they love the Scriptures. Preterists (who read much of Revelation as fulfilled in the first century) date the book before AD 70 and see here the Jerusalem temple about to fall to Rome, and Jesus’ words in Luke 21:24 give that view real weight. But on the usual dating John wrote around AD 95, a quarter of a century after the temple fell, so a literal reading needs a temple that does not yet exist. This commentary’s view: the temple is the church, the people of God. The New Testament never anticipates a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices; Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice has made the temple and its sacrifices obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:11–18). Revelation shows no temple in the new Jerusalem, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The worshippers are measured with the temple, so people are in view. And forty-two months is drawn from Daniel’s symbolic times, used in Revelation for the whole church age.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the whole of this age God gives his church authority to speak for him, a witness that mourns over the world and burns only with the oil of his Spirit.

My two witnesses. Witness is the church’s calling throughout Revelation (1:2, 9; 2:13; 6:9; 12:11, 17), and the Greek word gave us martyr, because so many who bore witness died for it. Two is the legal number for valid testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare Luke 10:1): this testimony will stand in God’s court. And their authority is granted by the one who calls them “my witnesses”.

For 1,260 days. Forty-two months again (v. 2): the trampling and the testimony run side by side for exactly the same time, so there is never a day when the church is being trampled and has nothing to say.

Clothed in sackcloth. Coarse black goat hair, the dress of mourning and repentance, worn by prophets (Isaiah 20:2) and by repenting Nineveh (Jonah 3:5–6). It sets the tone of the church’s testimony in this age: not swagger, but mourning. The witnesses do not gloat over the world they warn; they weep over it, as their Lord wept over Jerusalem.

The two olive trees and the two lampstands. In Zechariah 4 two olive trees beside a golden lampstand feed oil straight into its lamps. The trees are “the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:14): Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, who rebuilt the temple. In 1:20 the lampstands are the churches, so the witnesses are the church in its role of witness. Zechariah has one lampstand; here there are two, perhaps for the two witnesses the law requires, or for a church drawn from Jews and Gentiles.

Not by might, nor by power. The Zechariah vision turns on the word spoken to Zerubbabel in the middle of it: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). A lampstand cannot make light or oil; it holds up what is poured into it. That answers the sense that the church is too small, too tired and too compromised to be heard: the witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them, and they are joined to a supply that never runs dry, his Spirit, poured into frail lamps that could never light themselves.

The Anointed One behind the olive trees. In Jesus the two offices of Zechariah’s anointed ones, a governor of David’s line and a high priest, meet in one person. He is the Christ, the Anointed, the Son of David, and a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, who was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Psalm 110:1–4; Hebrews 7:1–3). He is also the faithful witness (1:5), who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate and was put to death (1 Timothy 6:13). Their authority is his, and so is their oil, for he has made his people a kingdom, priests to his God and Father (1:6). The church holds up, in mourning clothes, the light of the one who is both her King and her Priest.

Are the 1,260 days a literal three and a half years? Futurists take them as the second half of a future seven-year tribulation. But the three forms name one period (see the note on vv. 1–2), the whole age in which the church witnesses, is nourished in the wilderness and is persecuted by the beast (12:6, 14; 13:5). So you are living in the 1,260 days now: this chapter is about the church you belong to, this week.

Is this witness only for preachers? No. The witnesses are lampstands, and the lampstands are churches (1:20), so the calling belongs to every believer. A witness simply tells what he knows to be true: that Christ died for sinners, rose, and has forgiven you. You bear witness when you live honestly at work, speak of God without embarrassment, invite a friend to church, refuse to join in what dishonours Christ, and suffer patiently. Most witness is not a sermon but a life lived in the open with a reason for it, given gently and respectfully when someone asks (1 Peter 3:15). The Spirit supplies the oil. You hold up the lamp, and a lampstand is not meant to be impressive, only to hold the light where it can be seen.

Where Christians differ: who are the two witnesses? Many futurists (who expect most of Revelation to be fulfilled just before Christ returns) see two individual prophets in a future tribulation: often Moses and Elijah returned, because the powers in the next verses are precisely theirs and because those two stood with Christ on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:3); or Enoch and Elijah, the two men in Scripture who did not die (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11). Others suggest Peter and Paul, martyred in Rome. These readings take the Moses and Elijah details seriously and deserve a respectful hearing. This commentary’s view: the two witnesses symbolise the witnessing church throughout this age. The lampstands are churches (1:20). Their ministry lasts as long as the trampling, the whole age. The whole world sees their deaths (v. 9), which suits a worldwide church better than two individuals. And the beast makes war on them (v. 7) as it makes war on the saints (13:7). They are pictured with the powers of Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, because the church carries on the prophetic witness of the Old Testament in the power of the Spirit. On any reading the substance is unchanged: God has witnesses, they are given authority, they speak for a bounded time, they are killed, and they are raised.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The witnesses’ weapon is the word of God and their power is prayer; whoever sets himself against them sets himself against God, who will judge him.

Fire pours from their mouth. Not from heaven, as in Elijah’s day (2 Kings 1:10–12), but from the mouth, a settled image in this book: the sharp two-edged sword comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The weapon is the word, as God told Jeremiah: “I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them” (Jeremiah 5:14). The same word that consumes his enemies kindles faith in his elect.

This is how he is doomed to be killed. Stated twice, like a standing legal rule. Behind “doomed” is dei, “it must be”, the word for what God has decided. To oppose God’s witnesses is to oppose God, and such people will be judged by the word they rejected: “the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day” (John 12:48). The witnesses are not the executioners. They speak; the judgment comes from God.

Power to shut the sky. That is Elijah exactly (1 Kings 17:1). Luke and James both give his drought this chapter’s length of three and a half years (Luke 4:25; James 5:17; 1 Kings 18:1 says only that the rain returned in the third year). James draws the lesson for every believer’s prayers: “The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working”, for Elijah was “a man with a nature like ours” (James 5:16–18).

Power over the waters to turn them into blood. That is Moses in Egypt (Exodus 7:17–20). The trumpet plagues are tied to the church’s prayers (8:3–5): the prayers of the saints rise before God, and fire from the altar is thrown on the earth. The witnesses’ word announces God’s judgments, and their prayers call them down.

As often as they desire. God does not ration his witnesses’ authority; yet in verse 7 people with power to shut the sky are killed in the street. So it is in every century: the word in believers’ mouths has world-altering force, and those who carry it are often humiliated and killed.

Moses and Elijah, and Jesus only. Moses and Elijah are the law and the prophets, and the two who appeared with Christ on the mountain and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30–31). Then the cloud came, and the Father said, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!”, and when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone (Luke 9:35–36). The church speaks with the authority of Moses and Elijah only because it speaks the word of the Son they pointed to, standing before every Pharaoh and every Ahab to say the true thing about him.

What it does not mean. This gives Christians no licence to call down judgment on their enemies. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55).

So how should I pray about evil in the world? Boldly, for the prayers of the saints are taken up into God’s purposes (8:3–5), and first, as Jesus taught, for his name, kingdom and will. Ask him, as the psalms do, to stop the wicked, defend the oppressed and bring down unjust rulers. But pray also for the conversion of those who do evil, as Stephen did for the men stoning him, and as Christ did from the cross (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from some early manuscripts but widely judged genuine). Leave the manner and timing of judgment to God. The witnesses’ fire is a word spoken, not a grudge nursed: your part is to speak truly and pray; his is to judge rightly, and he will.

Where Christians differ: should the church expect such miracles today? Some read these verses as promising that end-time believers will perform the miracles of Moses and Elijah, and some charismatic groups expect such signs as normal. This commentary’s view: the images picture the power of the church’s witness, which comes through the word of God and prayer. The miraculous signs of Moses, Elijah and the apostles confirmed new revelation at key moments in redemptive history (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and this commentary holds that such sign gifts ceased once the apostles’ foundational work and the canon of Scripture were complete (Ephesians 2:20). Many faithful believers, continuationists who hold that all the gifts continue today, weigh the evidence differently, and they are brothers and sisters to be honoured, not dismissed. God still answers prayer and judges the world, but the church’s fire is the word it speaks, not miracles performed at will.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s witnesses have finished the testimony he gave them, and not before, he allows the persecuting power to kill them and leave them in disgrace, as the world once did to their Lord.

When they have finished their testimony. The first words change everything. The beast does not interrupt them: God’s witnesses are immortal until their work is done.

The beast that rises from the bottomless pit. The word means a wild animal. He appears here unannounced, as if already known from Daniel 7, where a horn of the fourth beast “made war with the saints and prevailed over them” (Daniel 7:21), and he is described in full only in chapter 13. He is the power of the state, or of any human system, set against God and persecuting his people. And the abyss could be unlocked only with a key that had to be given (9:1–2): even the beast comes out only by God’s permission.

Conquer them. The verb of the promise in every one of the seven letters, used of Christ himself in 5:5, is used here of the beast against the saints, successfully (again at 13:7). Revelation does not pretend the church always wins its battles: it loses, visibly, at the hands of a power permitted to defeat it.

Same verb, opposite direction. But the book gives that defeat a new meaning. The beast conquers by killing witnesses. The Lamb, standing as though it had been slain (5:6), conquered by being killed. The church conquers by being faithful unto death, as the Lamb was: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death” (12:11). What looks like defeat is victory.

The great city. Everywhere else in Revelation the great city is Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10), the world system opposed to God; the whole book is a tale of two cities, this one and the holy city (v. 2). The bodies lie in its street: public humiliation, in whatever form a century gives it.

Symbolically called Sodom and Egypt. “Symbolically” is literally “spiritually”: these names describe the city’s character, not its place on a map. It is Sodom in its wickedness (Genesis 19; Isaiah 1:10), Egypt in its oppression of God’s people.

Where their Lord was crucified. Jerusalem, which in rejecting him became what Isaiah had long before called her, addressing her leaders as “rulers of Sodom” (Isaiah 1:9–10). But the great city is more than Jerusalem: it is wherever the world rejects Christ and persecutes his witnesses, one city under many names in every generation. As their Lord was treated, so are they: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:18–20).

He went that way first. He who holds the keys of death and Hades decides when each witness has finished, and he knows what finishing costs. He completed the work his Father gave him (John 17:4), and on the cross he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). The street where the bodies lay is the street where he was led out to die, and he went that way first, so that no witness of his would ever walk it alone.

A promise you can put weight on. The verse does not say the witness will be protected, but that it will be finished. Nobody in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident; the man who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on the testimony of this verse, completed it. The missionary who dies in her first year on the field, the young pastor buried before his church was built, the mother who did not live to see her children grown: each was given a testimony to bear and allowed to finish it. By God’s measure no faithful life is cut short.

If the beast can conquer the church, how is Christ winning? The way he won at the cross: by what looks like defeat. The beast has power over bodies, not souls (Matthew 10:28), and can kill the witnesses only when their testimony is finished, only where and when God permits, and only to send them where their Lord has gone. And the story does not end in the street: read on to breath from God, a voice from heaven, a cloud. The beast’s victories are real, temporary and already reversed in the counsel of God. Christ’s victory is real, permanent and already won.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a short time the world makes a spectacle of the silenced witnesses and celebrates their death, because their message had troubled its conscience.

For three and a half days. Three and a half days against three and a half years of witness, and the proportion is the message: the humiliation is real, and it is brief.

Some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations. In 5:9 these four terms described the ransomed multitude (compare 7:9). Now they describe the spectators: the same world that the Lamb bought stands in the street looking at the bodies. They gaze, as at a spectacle; any generation that has watched someone’s humiliation passed around for days will recognise the appetite.

Refuse to let them be placed in a tomb. In the ancient world burial was owed even to an enemy; refusing it said that a person did not count as human. The psalmist lamented exactly this over Jerusalem: they have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, and there was no one to bury them (Psalm 79:2–3).

Make merry and exchange presents. Sending gifts is the language of a festival, as at Purim (Esther 9:19, 22): a grotesque holiday, held because two preachers are dead. The book has two parties, held for opposite reasons; the other is heaven’s joy when Babylon falls (18:20; 19:1–3). The world sent gifts to celebrate the death of God’s witnesses; God sent his only Son to die for the world. “Those who dwell on the earth”, twice in this verse, is John’s fixed name for unbelievers (8:13): people whose home and hope and heart are nowhere else. Every Christian lives on the earth; none is called an earth-dweller.

A torment. The word used of the locusts in 9:5. The witnesses had only a message, and the call to repent tormented the world’s conscience, for people hate the light that exposes their deeds (John 3:20). Ahab said it to Elijah’s face: “Is it you, you troubler of Israel?” (1 Kings 18:17).

The people stood by, watching. It happened first in the city where their Lord was crucified. The crowds came to look: the people stood by, watching, and the rulers scoffed (Luke 23:35), and the multitudes had assembled for the spectacle (Luke 23:48). But the likeness breaks at the tomb. His body was not left in the street: Joseph of Arimathea laid it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57–60), and on the third day it was empty. The witnesses’ disgrace is the disgrace he bore first, and it will end the way his ended.

A warning and a comfort. The warning: a witness that troubles nobody is probably not a witness. The comfort: when Christians are treated as a problem to be removed rather than an opinion to be debated, nothing has gone wrong; it is the treatment their Lord received in the same city.

Should I try to be offensive, then, so that I know I am faithful? No. The torment comes from the truth, not the manner. The witnesses wear sackcloth, not armour; they mourn over the world, they do not sneer at it. Peter tells Christians to make sure that if they suffer, it is for doing good and for the name of Christ, not for being meddlers or for doing wrong (1 Peter 4:15–16), and to give their reasons with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). A Christian resented for rudeness has not been persecuted; he has been rude. Be kind, honest and clear, and let any offence be the offence of the cross.

In everyday life. When a Christian is publicly humiliated, justly for a real fall or unjustly for faithfulness, refuse to join the crowd that gazes: your Lord was once its spectacle, and he did not leave you in your own disgrace. Do not pass the story on; pray, and if the person belongs to Christ, stand with them.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raises his slain witnesses and calls them up to himself in full view of their enemies: the church will share its Lord’s resurrection and ascension, and its vindication will be public.

A breath of life from God. The wording is Ezekiel’s valley of dry bones: breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet (Ezekiel 37:10). One word means both breath and spirit, in Ezekiel’s Hebrew as in the Greek here. The world had refused them burial and declared them finished, and now, raised by God as their Lord was, they stand up in the street.

Great fear fell. The party stops mid-sentence: the corpses stand up. The resurrection of God’s people is their vindication and their enemies’ dismay.

Come up here! The call John himself heard in 4:1, summoning them into God’s presence.

In a cloud, and their enemies watched them. So Christ ascended (Acts 1:9), and so he will return (1:7): the witnesses are given their Lord’s death, resurrection and ascension, in that order. And the last clause matters. When Jesus rose, the world did not see it; the guards saw an angel roll back the stone, became like dead men, and were afterwards paid to say something else (Matthew 28:2–4, 11–15), and the risen Christ appeared to chosen witnesses, not to all the people (Acts 10:40–41). Here the vindication is public, and those who arranged the deaths stand in the street with their gifts still in their hands. Every Christian written off, misrepresented or made ridiculous for saying something true is being shown the end of that story: not a private consolation, but a summons heard out loud and a departure the accusers have to watch.

The grave cannot keep what he has claimed. The breath that moved over the waters at creation, filled Adam’s nostrils and swept through the valley of dry bones is the breath that raised the Lord Jesus from the tomb, and it will raise every one of his people. The Lord who called “Come up here!” knows where every one of them lies.

What the witnesses do not do. They do not argue, retaliate or explain. They stand up, are called, and go. Vindication in Scripture is something God does, usually later than we would choose, as Peter told the churches of Asia Minor: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).

Will my body really be raised? Yes. The Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal body (Romans 8:11).
