The Christian hope is not that the soul escapes the body for ever, but that the body itself is raised and glorified like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests in the grave, still united to Christ, until the last trumpet. Then the dead in Christ will rise, those alive will be changed, and together they will meet the Lord, in full view of the world that buried them.

In everyday life. Whatever happens to you for Christ’s sake, God will have the last word, and it will be resurrection. So you need not win every argument or clear your name in every circle. Tell the truth, do what is right, and leave your reputation with God.

Where Christians differ: is this the rapture? Some read this as a rapture, a catching up to heaven in the middle of a future seven-year tribulation, whether of two prophets or of the church. Many who expect such a rapture learned it from teachers they rightly love, and they long for Christ as truly as anyone. This commentary’s view: if the two witnesses are the church, their resurrection and ascension picture the resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ rise and the church is caught up to meet the Lord in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). It is public, not secret; it follows the church’s whole period of witness and suffering; and it is followed at once by the seventh trumpet and the final judgment (vv. 15–18), as Paul links the resurrection with the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52). There is one visible return, with one resurrection of the righteous and the gathering of the church at that time. That return may be near, but it will not be secret, and Scripture names events that come before it (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s vindication of his witnesses shakes the city, and where plagues had only hardened people, many now turn and give glory to God. Then John marks the second woe as past and the third as near.

A great earthquake. Earthquakes accompany God’s coming in judgment (6:12; 8:5; 16:18), and “at that hour” the vindication of the witnesses and the shaking of the city are one event.

A tenth of the city fell. A fourth was struck in chapter 6, a third in chapters 8 and 9; here only a tenth, a tithe perhaps, given up in judgment while the rest is spared to repent.

Seven thousand. Literally, seven thousand names of men; seven speaks of completeness. In Elijah’s day seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were kept as a remnant (1 Kings 19:18); here it is reversed: seven thousand fall, and the great majority are spared.

Gave glory to the God of heaven. In the Old Testament giving glory to God sometimes means confessing the truth and turning to him in repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16), and in this book giving God glory is what repentance does (14:7; 16:9). Set it against 9:20, two chapters earlier: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent”. The same kind of survivors, and the opposite outcome (on whether this is true repentance, see the box at the end of this note).

The second woe has passed. Like 9:12, this keeps count of the eagle’s three woes (8:13), which are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. The third is announced as soon, and the very next verse sounds the seventh trumpet.

The grain that dies. If so, the chapter has shown how the world is reached. Plagues did not do it; two witnesses in mourning dress did, refusing to stop speaking, killed for it, and raised. It is their Lord’s pattern. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, Jesus said, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit, and his servants must follow him on the same road (John 12:24–26). His death and resurrection began the gathering of the nations; theirs, joined to his, carries it on. Tertullian put it in a line the church has never forgotten: the blood of Christians is seed.

Then why do disasters not bring people to God? Sometimes they do, for a while; churches fill after a catastrophe and empty within months. Fear alone hardens as often as it humbles (9:20–21; 16:9). What turns hearts is the word of God, carried by witnesses whose lives and deaths make it credible, and applied by the Spirit; so the church must not wait for a crisis to do its evangelism. Crises shake people; Christ, preached by people who love him more than their own lives, saves them.

In everyday life. Perhaps you have prayed for someone and spoken to them for years without visible result. This chapter does not promise you will see the harvest, but it shows how harvests come: through patient, costly witness that does not stop. Keep speaking and praying: the breath of God that raised the witnesses is the Spirit who gives your words life, and the seed is in the ground.

Where Christians differ: is this genuine repentance? Some careful interpreters take “gave glory” as a terrified, forced acknowledgement of God, not true conversion. This commentary’s view: in Revelation the phrase is used for true worship and repentance: in 14:7 the angel calls the nations to fear God and give him glory, and in 16:9 those who did not repent refused to give him glory. Here, unlike 9:20–21, the response is positive. It shows the fruit of faithful witness, many from the nations turning to God, and fits the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last trumpet brings no plague but the announcement heaven has waited for: the world now belongs to God and his Christ for ever. Loud voices proclaim that the kingdom of the world has changed hands, and the elders leave their thrones to thank the God who has taken his great power and begun to reign (vv. 15–17). Their song says what that reign means: the nations’ rage answered, the dead judged, God’s servants small and great rewarded, the destroyers destroyed (v. 18). Then the temple in heaven opens to show the ark of his covenant, the sign that God has kept every promise (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was, for the one to come has come, and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the last trumpet heaven announces that the whole world has become the kingdom of God and his Christ for ever, and the elders fall down to thank the God who has begun to reign. It is the answer to the prayer “Your kingdom come”, declared as already done.

The seventh angel blew his trumpet. The last trumpet and the third woe (v. 14), the moment when the mystery of God would be fulfilled (10:7), the trumpet at which, Paul says, the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). It brings no plague, only an announcement, the sentence the whole book has been climbing towards.

The kingdom of the world. Singular; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read the kingdoms, but the earliest have the singular. One worldly kingdom under many governments, the world system under Satan and the beast, has changed hands. “Christ” is the Anointed One of Psalm 2, the King whom God set on Zion while the nations raged.

Has become. Past tense: a herald reading out a result, not a forecast. Heaven announces a transfer so certain it is described as done.

The result announced at half-time. It comes with eleven chapters still to run, before the dragon appears, the beast is described or Babylon falls. That is a key to the whole book: it is the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

What it meant to the first hearers. Told that the empire would get worse and they would be conquered and killed, they were told in the same breath that the world had already changed owner: not to hope for a victory, but to live inside one not yet visible.

He shall reign forever and ever. “He” is singular: the Father and the Son reign as one, on one throne (22:1, 3), with no thousand-year limit and no end. Daniel foresaw a kingdom God would set up that would never be destroyed, given to the Son of Man and to the saints of the Most High (Daniel 2:44; 7:14, 27), and the song of Moses at the Red Sea ended with the same words (Exodus 15:18).

The twenty-four elders. Figures with thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor: not analysis, but adoration.

Who is and who was. The divine title in this book has been threefold from the first chapter: who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold. The third term is gone, because the one who is to come has come: at the seventh trumpet the future tense drops out of the name of God. Nothing in the chapter says more, and it is said by leaving a word out.

You have taken your great power. Taken, not given. God did not lack power before; now his reign is openly established over all opposition, and what was contested is settled.

Not seized by the sword. The last time the kingdom of the world stood face to face with the Christ, in a Roman governor’s hall, it held all the power in the room. “My kingdom is not of this world”, Jesus said; his servants did not fight, and the soldiers crowned him with thorns and crucified him under a notice that called him King (John 18:36; 19:2, 19). Now the kingdom of the world has become his, not seized by the sword but announced by the trumpet, and twenty-four thrones stand empty because their occupants are on their faces. Hallelujah, for the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (19:6).

If Christ reigns now, why does the world look the way it does? Because his reign is real now but not yet visible to all. He has all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), gathers his people through the gospel and restrains evil within limits he has set; but he is patient, and allows the outer court to be trampled for the appointed time. Hebrews says it exactly: we do not yet see everything in subjection to him, but we see him, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). We live by what we see in him, not in the headlines; at the last trumpet the two will match.

In everyday life. When the news makes it look as though the kingdom of the world belongs to whoever is loudest or cruellest, say to yourself the sentence heaven has already said: it has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Give thanks, as the elders did, before you see it: the thanksgiving of the faithful is always ahead of the evidence.

Where Christians differ: does Christ’s kingdom come gradually or suddenly? Postmillennialists expect the gospel gradually to transform the world until most of humanity is Christian, and then Christ to return. Premillennialists believe Christ will return to set up a thousand-year earthly kingdom (20:4–6), and dispensationalists add a distinct future for national Israel in it; both take the promise of a renewed earth with welcome seriousness. This commentary’s view: Christ already reigns now, at the Father’s right hand (1:5; Ephesians 1:20–22), and his kingdom grows through the gospel. But the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ in full only at his return, at the last trumpet, when he judges the living and the dead. There is no thousand-year interval between the last trumpet and the eternal reign; he will reign for ever and ever from the moment of his return. This amillennial view reads the thousand years of chapter 20 as Christ’s present reign, and it rests on passages like this one, where the last trumpet brings in the eternal kingdom at once. Many godly Christians read chapter 20 otherwise, and they love his appearing as much as anyone.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “and art to come” after “who is and who was”. The best manuscripts do not have it, and its absence is deliberate: at this point in the vision, God has come.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders’ song says what God’s reign brings: the nations’ rage answered by his wrath, the dead judged, every servant of his rewarded and the destroyers destroyed. Then heaven’s temple opens to show the ark, the sign that his covenant stands for ever.

The nations raged. From Psalm 2, which Revelation has quoted since 2:27, and past tense: the raging is over, and answered. In Greek “raged” and “wrath” share a root: the nations’ anger against God is met by his anger against them, theirs futile, his just and final.

The time for the dead to be judged. The appointed moment of the final judgment of all the dead (20:11–15): everyone, including everyone who died believing that death was the end of the matter.

Both small and great. The longest clause in the verse, and its generosity is the point: prophets, saints, and simply “those who fear your name, both small and great”. No one is too insignificant to be noticed; not even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones will lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). The two witnesses who shut the sky and the one who visits, prays, sets out the chairs and is never thanked are in the same sentence.

Reward and grace. God intends to reward people for what they did, and the New Testament is unembarrassed about it (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 11:6). But the reward Christ brings (22:12) is grace, not wages. The servants were bought before they served, their works were prepared by God beforehand (Ephesians 2:10), and when he rewards them he is crowning his own gifts. Grace does not abolish reward; it is what makes reward possible at all.

Destroying the destroyers. The same Greek verb twice, meaning both to ruin and to corrupt: those who ruin the earth, morally and physically, by violence, idolatry and corruption, will be ruined, as Babylon is, who corrupted the earth (19:2). God made the earth good, and he will judge its destroyers and renew it.

The ark of his covenant. The ark held the tablets of the law in the Most Holy Place, where the high priest sprinkled atoning blood on the Day of Atonement (Exodus 25:10–22; Leviticus 16). It is never heard of after Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC (Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid it, 2 Maccabees 2:4–8), and Jeremiah had said the day would come when people would no longer say the ark of the covenant of the LORD, nor miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). For a Jewish reader this may have been the most astonishing sentence in the chapter: the ark only the high priest ever saw, lost for centuries, in the temple in heaven, in plain view, with the doors open.

What the ark means. It says that the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side of it, and that the place where blood was applied for a nation’s sin is still there: the ark’s gold lid, the mercy seat. And the New Testament names what it always pointed to: the Greek word for the mercy seat (Hebrews 9:5) is the word Paul uses of Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25). A propitiation absorbs the judgment the sinner deserved, so that God’s anger is spent and turned aside: the wrath announced here against the nations was borne by Christ for everyone who comes to him. The law lay in the box, and the blood on the lid covered the sins of those who had broken it; Christ kept that law in full, and his blood covers for ever. The Most Holy Place stands open, and the chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part of it to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

Lightning, thunder and hail. John’s signal that God has acted, growing each time, from 4:5 to 8:5 to here, and again at the end of the bowls (16:18–21). The last sound in the chapter is thunder over an ark that nobody had seen for centuries, the sound of a God who has kept every promise he ever made.

What it does not mean. Not that history ends at chapter 11. Revelation is not a straight timeline: chapter 12 goes back to the birth of Christ and shows the same age again, from the angle of the spiritual war behind it.

Does the open temple mean I can come to God now, or only at the end? Now. The vision shows what is always true in heaven and will be visible to all at the end. When Christ died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), and Hebrews says we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us (Hebrews 10:19–22). You need no priest, pilgrimage or special state of feeling. You come through Christ, in prayer, at any hour, and you are welcome; the ark in heaven guarantees that the covenant under which you come will never be broken.

How can a God of love be angry? Love that is never angry at evil is not love but indifference: a father who shrugs at the man beating his child does not love the child. God’s anger does not flare and cool like ours; it is his holiness standing steadily against everything that wrecks what he made. And for those who trust Christ, that wrath fell on him, so that they are saved from it (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 5:9). The cross that shows how seriously God takes evil also shows how far he will go to save the people who did it.

Isn’t it mercenary to be good for a reward? Most of us feel that a kindness done for a prize is not quite kind. Jesus warned against good deeds done to be seen (Matthew 6:1), and yet in the same breath he promised, “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:4). C. S. Lewis, in The Weight of Glory, drew a distinction that clears the air. Some rewards have no natural connection with the thing done to win them: a man who marries for money is mercenary, because money is no part of love. Others are the activity itself brought to its fullness: marriage is the proper reward of a man who truly loves a woman, and nobody calls him mercenary for wanting it. God’s reward is of the second kind. It is not a bonus for putting up with him but God himself, the joy of being with the one you served, which only people who love him would want. And even that love was not earned: it was kindled by a Master who served them first, to the point of death (Mark 10:45).

Who will save the planet? Few causes now carry more moral weight, or more fear; many young people hesitate to have children because of it, and its language is strikingly religious: guilt, confession, sacrifice, an approaching end. In 1967 the historian Lynn White blamed Christianity for teaching that humans were set over nature to use it: a fair warning against a careless reading of Genesis, but the Bible gives the stronger answer itself. The earth in this verse is neither raw material nor a goddess. It is God’s, and he takes its ruin personally enough to name its destroyers at the last judgment. That frees us from both our culture’s moods: we cannot shrug, because the earth is not ours to waste, and we need not despair, because its future does not finally rest on us. The one through whom it was made has died to redeem it, and he means to make it new (21:5). So Christians can work hard for the world without needing to be its saviours. It already has one.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

keyVerse.quote: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.
keyVerse.note: Halfway through the book, before the dragon, the beast or Babylon has even appeared, heaven announces the outcome. The verb is past tense: the transfer is so certain it is described as done, and the reign it begins has no end. Everything the witnesses suffer in this chapter, and everything the church suffers in the chapters that follow, is endured inside a victory already won.

11.reflection:
The temple, the altar and the worshippers are measured, while the outer court is trampled (vv. 1–2). What is the difference between what God protects and what he allows to be trampled? When have you been tempted to think the sanctuary had fallen when only the outer court was under attack?

The two witnesses are lampstands burning with oil they do not supply, and they speak in sackcloth (vv. 3–4). What would it look like for your church, and for you, to bear witness in the Spirit’s strength and with grief rather than swagger, at work, at home or online?

The beast can kill the witnesses only “when they have finished their testimony” (v. 7), and God raises them in full view of their enemies (vv. 11–12). How does this change the way you think about faithful believers who die young or suffer unjustly, and about defending your own reputation?

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world “has become” Christ’s, and the elders give thanks before the end is visible (vv. 15–17). What would it mean for you this week to give thanks ahead of the evidence?

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 opens the central section of the book (chapters 12–14), drawing the curtain back to show the war underneath the church’s suffering. From here to chapter 20 we meet the dragon, his two beasts and their city, and then watch them fall in reverse order.

The message. The church suffers because it is caught up in a war that has already been decided. Satan tried to devour the Messiah and failed; thrown out of heaven, he has lost his case against God’s people, because the Lamb was slain. Now, furious and short of time, he turns on the church, but God carries and feeds her through the whole age, and her children conquer him by the Lamb’s blood and their testimony.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia were small and pressed by Rome and its loyal cities, with Antipas dead and Smyrna warned of prison (2:10, 13; see the introduction). They needed to know who their real enemy was, and whether he could win.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–6 tell the story of Christ in three moves: a woman in labour, the people of God (on whether she is Mary, see the note on vv. 1–2); a great red dragon, Satan, whose seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, waiting to devour her child; and the child caught up, untouched, to God’s throne. Verses 7–12 show the result in heaven: Michael throws the dragon down, and a voice explains that the accuser has no case left. Verses 13–17 show the result on earth: the woman is carried on eagles’ wings into a wilderness where God feeds her, the flood from the dragon’s mouth is swallowed, and he turns to make war on her children.

Where it leads. Michael wins in heaven, but the song that follows says where the victory was really won: the dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain. The serpent had been waiting for the woman’s offspring since Eden (Genesis 3:15); when the child came, he went past the dragon’s open mouth, through death, to the throne.

For us. When you suffer for Christ, or your conscience accuses you, you are not losing; you are facing the rage of a defeated enemy with little time left. Stand on the blood, keep speaking, and trust the God who feeds his people in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The dragon tried to destroy the Messiah at his birth and failed completely, and the people from whom he came are kept by God through this whole age. Two signs appear: a woman clothed with the sun and in labour, the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes, and a great red dragon wearing seven royal crowns, waiting to devour her child (vv. 1–4). She bears the King of Psalm 2, who is caught up to God’s throne untouched, and she flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared, where she is fed for 1,260 days, the whole time between his ascension and his return (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman, the covenant people, Israel and the church, bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people, glorious as heaven sees them and in agony on earth, are the mother from whom the promised Messiah comes. Before John shows us the enemy, he shows us the woman and the child the enemy cannot defeat.

A great sign. The first time Revelation uses the word, and John says so before he describes anything: this is a sign; read it as one.

A woman clothed with the sun. The imagery says who she is. In Joseph’s dream the sun, the moon and the stars were his father, mother and brothers (Genesis 37:9–10); add Joseph, and there are twelve. Sun, moon and twelve stars is Israel. The twelve stars are the twelve tribes, and also, as the book will show at the end, the twelve apostles (21:12–14). She is the people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah came, continuing as the church.

Glory and agony at once. She is clothed in glory and she is in agony, and that is the Bible’s whole teaching about the people of God in one picture. Seen from heaven, the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars; seen from the street, she is a woman in labour, crying out. Both are accurate. God did not abandon the woman in her agony; he made her agony the way the Saviour came.

Pain with an outcome. The prophets pictured Zion as a woman in labour, longing for deliverance (Isaiah 66:7–9; Micah 4:10; 5:3), and in Scripture birth pain is suffering with an outcome. Isaiah confessed that Israel’s labour had brought forth only wind, then heard God promise that the dead would rise (Isaiah 26:17–19). Jesus called the troubles before the end “the beginning of the birth pains” (Matthew 24:8), and Paul heard the whole creation groaning in the pains of childbirth (Romans 8:22). In God’s hands the pain of his people is real, severe, and going somewhere. And if you have known a labour that ended in loss, this picture does not mock your grief: the Lord who wept at a grave is near to the broken-hearted, and he has promised that the dead will rise.

The true story behind the myths. Genesis 3:15 had already set the woman, her offspring and the serpent against one another. John’s hearers also knew a pagan version: in Greek myth the dragon Python pursued the goddess Leto, pregnant with Apollo, and emperors such as Nero liked to be associated with Apollo. Revelation tells the true story behind the myths: the real child is Christ, and the real dragon is Satan.

Born of woman. The labour has one child in view. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman” (Galatians 4:4), and the promise made at the gate of Eden became a baby in Bethlehem. On the night before the cross Jesus used this very picture of his own death and rising: a woman in labour has sorrow, but when the child is born she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy; so the disciples’ sorrow would turn to joy when they saw him again (John 16:20–22). The pains of God’s people are the pains of a birth, because the one they wait for has already come out of the grave.

How should Protestants think of Mary, then? With great honour, and without worship. Mary was a real woman of faith, chosen by grace to bear the Son of God, who called herself the Lord’s servant and God her Saviour (Luke 1:38, 47); all generations rightly call her blessed. But she was a sinner saved by her Son, and Scripture never asks us to pray to her or through her: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5–6). The best way to honour Mary is to do what she said at Cana: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).

Where Christians differ: is the woman Mary? Roman Catholic tradition has long identified the woman with the Virgin Mary, and used this passage in support of Marian devotion and her bodily assumption into heaven. Its love for the mother of the Lord is not wrong in itself. This commentary’s view: the woman is the people of God, Israel and then the church. There is a secondary allusion to Mary, who literally gave birth to the Messiah and belongs to the people of God. But the woman’s experiences cannot be Mary’s: she is persecuted in the wilderness for 1,260 days after her child ascends (v. 6), and she has other offspring who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus (v. 17), who are believers. The twelve stars point to the twelve tribes. Nothing here supports praying to Mary, or giving her a special role in salvation.
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind every attempt to destroy God’s people and their Saviour stands a real and murderous enemy, Satan, wearing royal crowns that are not his. From the beginning he has waited to devour the promised child.

A great red dragon. A sign again: not what Satan looks like but what he is, and verse 9 names him. In the Old Testament the sea monster or dragon (Leviathan, Rahab) stands for chaos, for evil powers opposed to God, and for empires such as Egypt (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13–14; Ezekiel 29:3). “Red” is fiery red, the colour of bloodshed, like the second horseman (6:4): he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).

Seven heads and ten horns. Seven, the number of completeness, pictures complete cunning or power; ten horns, great strength, as on the fourth beast of Daniel 7, a world empire (Daniel 7:7, 24). The sharpest detail is the diadems: the woman wears a victor’s crown of stars; the dragon wears seven royal crowns. Satan claims royal authority over the world (Luke 4:5–6; John 12:31), but his crowns are claims, not rights. The beast of chapter 13 will look like him, because the beast is his agent.

That he might devour it. That sentence is the plot of the Old Testament. After the fall God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), and everything after is the serpent trying to get to the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1). Athaliah destroys the royal family of Judah and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree to destroy every Jew in the empire (Esther 3). When the child is finally born, Herod sends soldiers to Bethlehem to kill every boy under two (Matthew 2:16). And finally there is the cross. Matthew reports Herod’s massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it. Yet the Lord who brought Israel out of Pharaoh’s reach and hid the infant Joash from Athaliah’s sword guarded his promise through every century. And see how little the dragon achieves: in the next verse the child is taken to God’s throne, and he does not lay a finger on him.

The second layer. Few parts of Scripture show history’s second layer as directly as this chapter (compare Job 1–2; Daniel 10): the events are real, and behind them is someone also real, hostile and personal. Paul says it without the picture: “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (Ephesians 6:12).

Who the crowns belong to. The rider on the white horse will come with many diadems on his head (19:12), and the Gospels tell how he came by them. The first crown anyone put on Jesus was twisted out of thorns by soldiers who knelt before him in mockery (Matthew 27:29). The usurper grasps at royalty; the true King accepted shame, and so we see him crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). The dragon’s crowns were seized. Christ’s were given him by his Father, on the far side of a cross.

Is the devil a real person, or a symbol for evil? He is real: the dragon is a picture of someone, as the lion is a picture of Christ. Jesus spoke to him in the wilderness, named him a liar and a murderer, and spoke of his fall (Matthew 4:1–11; John 8:44; Luke 10:18). He is a created spirit, a fallen angel, not God’s equal and not everywhere at once, with a will and a strategy. So Scripture tells us to be sober and watchful (1 Peter 5:8), never fascinated or terrified. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

Does every bad thing happen because of Satan? No. Scripture names three enemies: the world, the flesh (our own sinful nature) and the devil (Ephesians 2:1–3). Much evil comes from our own desires (James 1:14), and much suffering simply from living in a fallen world; blaming the devil for every sin can become a way of avoiding repentance. But behind the great persecutions and lies of history, and sometimes behind attacks on one believer’s faith, stands a personal enemy. Take sin seriously as your own, take the devil seriously as real, and keep your eyes on the child who went past him to the throne.

In everyday life. When you read of persecution, of children harmed, of attempts to silence the church, recognise the old pattern. Pray and act against it, and remember that the dragon has stood with his mouth open many times before and gone away hungry.

Uncertain wording. What the sweep of the dragon’s tail refers to is not certain. Stars can stand for angels (1:20; 9:1), so it probably means the angels who fell with Satan, thrown down with him in verse 9. Or it may picture his attack on God’s people, like the horn in Daniel that threw some of the stars to the ground and trampled on them (Daniel 8:10). Either way his reach is real and limited: even at his most successful he takes a third. Two thirds stayed.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dragon’s attempt on Christ failed completely: the child went to God’s throne, and his people are kept and fed by God through the whole age until he comes again.

A male child. Literally “a son, a male”, echoing Isaiah 66:7, where Zion gives birth to a son. The words “rule all the nations with a rod of iron” settle who he is: they come from Psalm 2:9, the Messiah’s coronation psalm, which this book applies to Christ and to those who conquer (2:27; 19:15). The child is Christ, the Messiah-King.

From birth to throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no miracles, no cross, no empty tomb. More than thirty years pass in a comma, because this is the story of the dragon’s attempt on Jesus, and from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report except total defeat. He stood there with his mouth open, and the child went straight past him to the seat of God.

Caught up. Snatched, seized with force: the word Paul uses of the man caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2) and of believers caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Whatever the dragon intended, the child was snatched out of his reach.

The cross was not avoided. The Lamb standing as though slain is the central image of the book, and in this chapter the saints conquer by his blood (v. 11). The compression means that the cross, which seemed to be Satan’s victory, led to Christ’s enthronement: the route to the throne ran through a grave that could not hold him.

Into the wilderness. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert: the position of the church between the ascension and the end. In Scripture the wilderness is a place of testing but also of God’s provision, where a nation was fed for forty years by bread that arrived each morning, Elijah was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:2–6; 19:4–8), and the holy family fled from Herod (Matthew 2:13–15). It is a hard place to live, but she is not abandoned there.

A place prepared. “Prepared by God” uses the same verb as the place Christ has gone to prepare for his people (John 14:2). She is not in the desert by accident; God had her place ready. The church lives as exiles (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11), not yet home, but provided for.

Nourished for 1,260 days. Fed, sustained; the Greek says literally “they feed her”, without saying who “they” are. 1,260 days is the period of the witnesses’ prophesying (11:3), the whole age between Christ’s ascension and return. The church in this age is a woman in a desert, fed by an unseen hand, for a period that has already been measured.

She shall not want. He who was laid in a manger sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the nations are his inheritance. The God who seated him there prepared the mother’s place before she fled and numbered her days before they began. The Shepherd of Israel, who rained down manna and set a table in the wilderness, is the Shepherd of his church, and she shall not want.

How does God feed his church in the wilderness? By the ordinary means he has appointed: his word, read and preached; prayer; the Lord’s Supper and baptism; and the fellowship of believers. That is our manna, and like manna it must be gathered daily; yesterday’s portion will not do for today. If you feel starved, ask first whether you have been at the table. A church that neglects the word and gathered worship is not being left hungry by God; it has stopped coming to where he lays the food.

In everyday life. If you are in a dry stretch, with no prospects and no visible progress, this verse tells you what that place is: not where God loses track of his people, but where he feeds them himself, with the bread that comes down from heaven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Satan has been thrown out of heaven, and the voice that explains it says where the battle was really won: at the cross. Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is named four ways, the great dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, and hurled down to the earth (vv. 7–9). Then heaven explains it as a court case: the accuser of the brothers has lost his standing, because the saints conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony (vv. 10–11). Heaven rejoices; the earth is warned, because the devil is furious and his time is short (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The accuser who recited your sins before God has been thrown out of court, because Christ paid for them. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan has lost his place in heaven: he fought and was not strong enough, and he was thrown down to the earth. The verses that follow say where that victory was really won.

War in heaven. Michael’s name is Hebrew for “Who is like God?” Scripture names him only in Daniel, Jude and here: the great prince who has charge of God’s people (Daniel 12:1), and the archangel who, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment but said, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9). It is Michael, not God or Christ, who fights the dragon: Satan is not God’s rival, but a creature defeated by another creature. And the real victory has already been won by the Lamb (v. 11); Michael’s victory in heaven reflects Christ’s victory on earth. “He was defeated” is literally “he was not strong enough”: powerful, but not powerful enough, which sums up his whole career.

No longer any place. What was Satan doing in heaven at all? The Old Testament answer is the key to the chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man to God’s face: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (Job 1:9). In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, and the priest is wearing filthy garments, and the accusation is true (Zechariah 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench, and he has lost it (v. 10).

That ancient serpent. Four names, each a job description. The great dragon: raw destructive power. That ancient serpent: the serpent of Eden who deceived Eve (Genesis 3:1), whose head the woman’s offspring would crush (Genesis 3:15). The devil and Satan: “devil” is Greek for slanderer, “Satan” Hebrew for adversary, and both mean accuser, the point of the next verse.

The deceiver of the whole world. His method has not changed since the garden, where the first conversation opened not with a threat but with a question: “Did God actually say …?” (Genesis 3:1). He blinds the minds of unbelievers and disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 4:4; 11:14), and deceives the nations through the beast and the false prophet (13:14; 20:3, 8). In this book he is not mainly a torturer, or even a tempter, but a liar and an accuser: he deceives the world and brings charges against the church.

He was not strong enough. “Thrown down” comes three times in one verse: he did not withdraw; he was removed by force. Who is like God? Not the dragon, with all his heads and crowns. Not even Michael, whose very name is a confession. The Lord Jesus disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15). He saw Satan fall like lightning (Luke 10:18), and he has the final word over him.

If Satan was defeated at the cross, why is he still so active? Because a defeated enemy is not yet a removed enemy. In a war whose decisive battle has been won, fighting can go on in the provinces until the final surrender: the outcome is settled; the danger is real. Satan has lost his place as accuser and, on the reading of chapter 20 this commentary follows, his hold on the nations (20:2–3), so that the gospel goes freely to every people. But he can still tempt, deceive and persecute, within limits God sets. So Peter calls him a roaring lion and in the same breath tells you to resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). You fight a real enemy from the side that has already won.

In everyday life. When you face temptation or accusation, remember that the devil’s greatest lie is that he is winning. His voice usually sounds like a question about God’s goodness (did God really say? does God really care?) or a verdict on your worth (you will never change; you are not really his). Answer it with what God has actually said, as Jesus met every temptation with “It is written”.

Where Christians differ: when was Satan thrown down? Some place this at Satan’s original fall before creation, linking it with Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28; others, many futurists among them, in the last days, at the midpoint of a seven-year tribulation. Both readings take Satan’s defeat seriously. This commentary’s view: the context places it at Christ’s death, resurrection and ascension. The child has just been caught up to God’s throne (v. 5), and the voice in heaven says that salvation and the kingdom have now come, because the accuser has been thrown down, and that believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). The cross is where Satan was defeated (John 12:31–32; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). His original rebellion lies behind this, and his final destruction lies ahead (20:10), but his decisive defeat happened at Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan has lost his case against God’s people, because the Lamb’s blood has answered every charge; believers overcome him by trusting that blood and speaking for Christ, whatever it costs. So heaven rejoices, while the earth is warned of the devil’s fury, which is fierce but short.

Now the salvation. Salvation is not only future: it arrived at the cross and resurrection, and Christ now has all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18).

The accuser of our brothers. The explanation is a court case. The dragon is the prosecutor, accusing believers “day and night”, pointing to their sins before God and arguing that they deserve condemnation, and accusing them in their own consciences. Paul gives the verdict: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” Christ Jesus died, was raised, and intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

The file is accurate. This names something many Christians experience. There has been, in the presence of God, a voice reciting a list, and it was not inventing the charges: as in Zechariah 3 (see the note on vv. 7–9), the accusations against you are, on the whole, true. Yet the accuser has been thrown out, not because the charges were false, nor because God stopped listening, but because Christ has paid for every sin, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Justification is the Bible’s name for it: the Judge pronouncing guilty people righteous, not by pretending the charges are false, but because Christ bore them and his righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is hard news for anyone hoping to answer the accuser with a better record. The record is the problem; only the blood answers him.

He did not dispute a line. The accuser stood before the throne with a true list of our sins, and the Lamb did not dispute a line of it. He paid it. The prosecutor’s bench is empty because the Judge’s own Son took the sentence, and the blood that now speaks in that room speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

By the blood of the Lamb. Here the book’s central verb, conquer, promised in all seven letters, is defined in three clauses. First, the blood of the Lamb, the ground of the other two: the accuser was beaten not by an argument or the saints’ record, but because the charges were paid, and that blood goes on cleansing those who walk in the light from all sin (1 John 1:7).

The word of their testimony. Second, and it follows from the first: speaking the truth about Jesus to people who do not want to hear it, what they said, not what they achieved. The deceiver is defeated when the truth is told.

They loved not their lives. Third, the cost. Not that they hated living, but that when it came to a choice between life and testimony, the testimony won. Satan’s last weapon is the threat of death, and it has no power over those who do not cling to their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). Jesus said that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). They are following their Christ, who loved not his life unto death so that his people might conquer through him.

The shape of Christian courage. The three clauses do not begin with bravery. They begin with a verdict already won by Christ’s blood, go on to speech, and only then come to the cost. Nobody here is asked to be fearless first. You are asked to stand on the blood, to open your mouth, and to trust God with what it costs.

Rejoice, O heavens. “You who dwell” is literally “you who pitch your tent there”. Unlike the earth-dwellers of the rest of the book, God’s people, even while they walk the earth, are counted among those whose tent is pitched in heaven, and they share its joy.

Woe to you, O earth. His defeat makes him more furious, not less, and his time is short: literally a little time, the same period as the 1,260 days (see the note on vv. 5–6). The persecution of the church is the rage of an enemy thrown out of the courtroom who has read the timetable. It is short as heaven measures it: not always short to a suffering church, but short all the same.

What it does not mean. Conquering by the blood of the Lamb is not using the phrase as a magic formula, as in some deliverance practices, but trusting Christ’s finished work as the answer to every accusation.

What do I say when my conscience accuses me? First, be honest: if the accusation is true, do not argue with it. Confess the sin to God, and where needed put it right with the person you wronged. Then answer the accusation with Christ. Do not say, “It was not so bad.” Say, “It was worse than that, and Jesus died for it.” If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9), and Christ himself is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Learn the difference between the Spirit’s conviction, which is specific and leads you to Christ, and the accuser’s condemnation, which is vague, endless and drives you away from him. The first is a mercy; the second has been thrown out of court.

A world full of accusers, and no advocate. Our culture thinks it has left behind the old religious obsession with guilt. It has only moved the courtroom: a pile-on in the comments, an old post dug up, a reputation tried and sentenced in an afternoon, with no end date to the sentence. We have kept the prosecutor and lost the mercy seat. So people deny everything, or live in dread of being found out, or join the crowd so that the stones fly at someone else. The religious and the irreligious are alike here, both trying to keep a record clean enough to survive the hearing. The gospel is stranger: it agrees with the accuser about the facts, more thoroughly than any critic would, and then points to a verdict already given and paid for in blood. Only people who no longer need to be innocent can afford to be honest, and only they can put the stones down.

Does loving not my life mean I must be ready to die? In principle, yes: every Christian is called to love Christ more than life itself (Luke 14:26), and in some places that is a daily reality. But for most believers it is lived out in smaller deaths first: not loving comfort, reputation, career or safety more than their testimony. The man who will not risk a colleague’s scorn is not yet ready for a lion. Do not manufacture courage for a martyrdom that may never come; be faithful in today’s small cost, and trust God to give you dying grace if he ever asks you to die.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unable to reach the child, the dragon turns his fury on the church, and God protects her. She is given eagle’s wings, as Israel was carried out of Egypt (Exodus 19:4), and fed in the wilderness for a time, and times, and half a time (vv. 13–14). The flood he pours from his mouth is swallowed by the earth (vv. 15–16). So he makes war on the rest of her offspring, marked by obedience to God’s commandments and the testimony of Jesus, and the chapter ends with the dragon standing on the shore (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children, those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to reach Christ, Satan turns on his people; but God carries them through this age as he carried Israel out of Egypt, and feeds them every day of the time he has set.

He pursued the woman. He cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and he cannot go back to the courtroom, so he turns on the mother, the child’s people, the church. Persecution of the church is Satan’s revenge on Christ.

What persecution means. That does not make it less real, but it settles what it means: not that the dragon is gaining ground, but that he has lost the only ground that mattered and has nowhere else to go. Jesus said as much on the Damascus road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). To strike the church is to aim at Christ, and to miss.

The two wings of the great eagle. She does not grow the wings or buy them; they are given. The image is the exodus: “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4). As God carried Israel out of Egypt, he carries his church through the wilderness of this age, beyond the dragon’s reach.

For a time, and times, and half a time. From Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: one year, two years and half a year, three and a half years, the same period as the 1,260 days and the forty-two months (11:2; see the note on vv. 5–6), a time of persecution limited by God. He who numbered the days feeds his people every one of them, and the place he prepared waits at the end of the desert.

The exodus all over again. The chapter now holds a complete exodus: a tyrant killing children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unseen hand, eagles’ wings, and next a flood swallowed by the ground. John is telling seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in the book of Exodus, and already know how it ends. And the church walks the exodus road because her Lord walked it first. Matthew saw it in the child’s own life: carried into Egypt out of Herod’s reach and called out again, to fulfil the word, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and his people’s flight through the desert is a share in his.

If the church is protected, why do some churches die out? Because the promise is to the church of Christ as a whole, not to every congregation or denomination. The seven churches of chapters 2 and 3 have long since disappeared from most of their cities, as Jesus warned Ephesus he might remove its lampstand (2:5). Churches can lose the gospel and die. But the people of God has never died out, and never will: when the church declined in one land it grew in another, and today it is found in nearly every nation. Pray for your own church to be faithful, and rest in the promise that Christ’s church cannot fail.

In everyday life. When you have no strength left, remember who gives the wings. Waiting on the Lord is not passive: it is turning to him in prayer and his word when you would rather give up, and finding, again and again, that he carries you.

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan tries to sweep the church away with a flood of lies and fails, so he makes war on her children, the ordinary believers who obey God and confess Jesus. Then he takes his stand by the sea, to call up his allies.

Water like a river. Two mouths: the dragon’s pours out a river; the earth’s swallows it. The deceiver of the whole world (v. 9) works by speech, and the flood is lies, false teaching, slander and propaganda; as the witnesses’ fire was their word (11:5), so Satan’s flood is his. In the Psalms overwhelming waters picture hostile speech and danger: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck” (Psalm 69:1). A flood is how a reputation is destroyed or a truth buried: not one accusation, which can be answered, but so many, arriving so fast, that the truth is simply under water.

The earth came to the help of the woman. In this book the earth is usually where the trouble is; here it swallows a river, as the ground swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:32), and as Israel sang of Pharaoh’s army at the sea: “You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them” (Exodus 15:12). God is not restricted to the instruments a believer would expect. He has used a pagan king’s decree, a famine, a shipwreck and an earthquake in a prison to protect his people, and here he uses the ground.

The rest of her offspring. Frustrated at the mother, he turns on the children. Literally the rest of her seed, the phrase reaches back to Genesis 3:15 and the enmity between the serpent’s offspring and the woman’s. Christ is her first offspring, who crushed the serpent’s head at the cost of his own heel; believers are her other children, his brothers and sisters, whom he is not ashamed to call his own (Romans 8:29; Hebrews 2:11–13). That is why they are hunted, and why the hunt cannot succeed. Paul applies the old promise to an ordinary congregation: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

Commandments and testimony. John defines them by two marks. They keep the commandments of God: ordinary, unglamorous obedience in the things God has actually commanded. None keeps them perfectly; they are the people who conquered by the blood (v. 11), whose standing rests on the Son who kept his Father’s commandments in their place (John 15:10; Romans 5:19), and their obedience is the fruit of that blood, not its price. And they hold to the testimony of Jesus: they have not stopped saying openly who he is. Obedience to God and loyalty to Jesus are Revelation’s definition of a true believer (14:12), and Satan’s targets.

How short the list is. Not those who understand this book, or identified the beast correctly, or never suffered. Obedience and confession, held on to: that is all it takes to be on the dragon’s list.

And he stood on the sand of the sea. The dragon takes his stand at the shoreline, and the next sentence is: “And I saw a beast rising out of the sea”. Satan works through human agents and systems, and the end of chapter 12 and the start of chapter 13 are a single movement.

The Lamb stands on Mount Zion. The Lord sits enthroned over the flood; the Lord sits enthroned as king for ever. The dragon poured out a river of lies, and the God who split the Red Sea made the earth itself swallow it. The children he hunts belong to the Son, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). The dragon stands on the sand. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion, and the next time the curtain opens, his people are standing with him (14:1).

Watching without panic. The reader now has all he needs for what comes next: the child is on the throne, the accuser has no case, the woman is fed. The dragon on that beach, about to summon the worst thing in the book, is a defeated prosecutor short of time.

How do I keep from being swept away by the flood of lies? Know the truth well enough to recognise the counterfeit, as bank clerks learn to spot forged notes by handling real ones: read the whole Bible regularly, sit under faithful preaching, and learn the great truths of the faith, perhaps through a good confession or catechism. Be slow to believe what you hear about fellow Christians, and test every teaching by Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Notice which voices make God seem less good, sin less serious or Christ less necessary, and turn them off. And stay close to the church: a flood sweeps away one person standing alone far more easily than a people holding on together.

In everyday life. Where does the flood reach you most this week, through a screen, a conversation, a fear? Put God’s word in its place. Obey him in the plain things today, in the strength of his Spirit, and when you fail, go back to the blood that silenced the accuser: it answers today’s failures too.

Textual note. The last sentence is numbered 12:18 in some Bibles and 13:1 in others. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “I stood on the sand of the sea”, making John the subject. The best manuscripts read “he stood”, referring to the dragon.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.<sup>5</sup>She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,<sup>6</sup>and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.<sup>7</sup>Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back,<sup>8</sup>but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.<sup>9</sup>And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.<sup>10</sup>And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.<sup>11</sup>And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”<sup>13</sup>And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.<sup>14</sup>But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.<sup>15</sup>The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood.<sup>16</sup>But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.<sup>17</sup>Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

keyVerse.quote: And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s answer to how a small, pressed church can overcome a dragon. The ground of the victory is Christ’s blood, which leaves the accuser with no case; its weapon is plain speech about Jesus; and its cost is life itself, held loosely. The verse defines what Revelation means every time it promises a reward to “the one who conquers”.

12.reflection:
The woman is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars, and at the same time crying out in labour (vv. 1–2). How does holding both pictures together help you understand your church, and your own suffering?

The accuser is thrown down not because his charges were false but because of the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). When your conscience accuses you, how do you usually answer? What would it look like to answer with Christ instead of with your record?

The saints “loved not their lives even unto death” (v. 11). What smaller costs of faithfulness are you facing now, in comfort, reputation or career, and what makes them hard to pay?

The woman is fed in the wilderness by God’s own hand (vv. 6, 14). Where are you in a dry place at the moment, and how could you come more regularly to the places where God has promised to feed his people?

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 runs straight on from 12:17: the dragon, standing on the seashore, calls up the two allies through whom he makes war on the woman’s children, a beast from the sea and a beast from the earth.

The message. Satan works through human power that demands the worship belonging to God alone: political might wearing divine titles, and persuasive religion that makes bowing to it seem reasonable, a counterfeit of the Holy Trinity and the pattern of every power that claims what is God’s. They may conquer bodies and squeeze livelihoods, but all they have was given, for a limited time, and they cannot erase one name from the Lamb’s book. So the saints answer them not with the sword but with endurance and faith.

Why it was said. In Asia the emperor was hailed as lord and god, leading citizens ran his cult, and guild life turned on honouring the gods and Caesar (see the introduction). Christians faced death, and the quieter cost of being shut out of the market; some were tempted to treat a pinch of incense as a formality.

How the chapter makes its case. The first beast rises from the sea with the dragon’s features and Daniel’s four beasts in one body (vv. 1–2; who it is, is weighed in the box there). A healed mortal wound makes the world ask, “Who is like the beast?” (vv. 3–4). It is given a blaspheming mouth, forty-two months and war on the saints, yet those in the Lamb’s book do not worship it (vv. 5–8); the reader is called to endurance (vv. 9–10). The second beast looks like a lamb and speaks like the dragon, with signs, a speaking image and a mark without which no one can buy or sell (vv. 11–17). The number 666 calls for wisdom (v. 18; on Nero and the 616 variant, see the note there).

Where it leads. Every feature of the beast parodies Christ: a healed death wound, horns like a lamb, a name on the forehead. The counterfeit only makes sense because the original is real: the Lamb was truly slain and truly lives, refused the dragon’s offer of the kingdoms, and wears by right every title the beast forges. The beast’s number falls short; his name is above every name.

For us. Learn the beast’s marks, so that you recognise its many costumes, and refuse it worship, whatever it costs. You are kept not by your courage but by the Lamb’s grip on your name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Satan’s power reaches the world through a human empire that claims God’s place, but it rules only by permission, and God’s people meet it with endurance. A beast rises from the sea with the dragon’s features, Daniel’s four beasts in one and blasphemous names on its heads; a healed mortal wound makes the whole earth worship it (vv. 1–4). It is given a blaspheming mouth, forty-two months of authority and permission to conquer the saints, and all the earth-dwellers worship it, except those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life (vv. 5–8). Then John turns to the reader: the saints answer the beast not with the sword but with endurance and faith (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan exercises his power through human government that claims God’s titles and demands worship; the beast is the dragon’s own image, every godless empire gathered into one. Yet everything it has, it was given.

A beast rising out of the sea. The dragon stood on the shore (12:17); this is what he calls up. In Daniel 7 four beasts rise from the sea, a lion, a bear, a leopard and a terrifying fourth beast with ten horns, usually understood as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. The sea stands for chaos and evil: before God’s throne it lies still as glass (4:6), and in the new creation it is gone (21:1). Empires rise out of that restless chaos, and for John’s readers Rome came from across the sea.

Ten horns and seven heads. The features match the dragon of 12:3: the beast is the dragon’s image, what he looks like when he takes the form of a government. In 17:9–12 the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, and the ten horns ten kings.

Ten diadems and blasphemous names. The dragon wore seven diadems on his heads; the beast wears ten on its horns, the instruments of force. The blasphemous names are titles that belong only to God, and to a first-century reader that was no metaphor: coins, inscriptions and court flattery called the emperors divine, son of god, saviour of the world, even lord and god.

Leopard, bear and lion. John names three of Daniel’s beasts in reverse order and gives their features to one animal: what Daniel saw as a succession of empires, John sees gathered into a single creature. There has only ever been one beast, wearing different national costumes in every century, the spirit of every empire that sets itself against God. Anyone who has decided the beast is one particular regime should notice that John has just merged four.

The dragon gave. The beast’s power comes from Satan, a grim imitation of the Father giving authority to the Son (2:27). Power, throne and authority recall the devil’s offer to Christ in the desert, showing him all the kingdoms of the world: “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me” (Luke 4:6). Christ refused. The beast accepts. That is the whole difference between the two kingdoms in this book: one takes a throne from the dragon, the other takes a cross from his Father.

Every one of them already had an owner. The beast’s titles were stolen from heaven. A Samaritan town said of Jesus that he is indeed the Saviour of the world (John 4:42), and a doubting disciple, shown the wounds, answered him, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). The beast borrows its throne from a dragon who has none of his own; the Lamb is in the midst of the throne of God, and wears by right every name the beast can only forge.

How do I tell when a government has become beastly? By the marks this chapter gives. A beastly power claims what belongs to God: divine titles, final authority over conscience, the right to define good and evil without reference to him. It demands worship, not merely obedience: total loyalty, public affirmation, the bowing of the mind. And it punishes those who will not give it, by exclusion or by force. A government can be unjust, corrupt or foolish without being the beast; governing authorities are instituted by God (Romans 13:1–7), and Christians must still honour such a government and obey it in everything lawful (1 Peter 2:13–17). But when it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

In everyday life. Pay your taxes, keep the law, speak honourably of rulers and pray for them by name. And keep back what no government may have: your worship, your conscience and your confession that Jesus is Lord.

Where Christians differ: who is the beast? Preterists, who read the book as fulfilled mainly in the first century, identify the beast with the Roman Empire and the emperor Nero. Historicists, including many Reformers, who read it as a map of church history, identified it with the papacy. Futurists, who expect most of the book to be fulfilled just before Christ returns, see a single future world dictator, the Antichrist. This commentary’s view: the beast is the persecuting power of the state, or any human system, that claims divine authority and demands worship, empowered by Satan. In John’s day it was clearly the Roman Empire and its emperor cult; through history it has reappeared whenever a power demands the total loyalty that belongs to God alone; and Scripture expects a final, intensified manifestation before Christ returns, the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3–10). Many Reformers were right to see beastly features in the persecuting medieval church, but the beast is wider than any one institution. This combined view gathers what is true in each of the others: it honours the first readers, every generation, and the end.
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast imitates Christ’s death and resurrection, and the world, awed by a power that seems unbeatable, follows it and worships the dragon behind it.

A mortal wound. Literally “slain to death”, the word used of the Lamb standing as though it had been slain (5:6). Its healing parodies Christ’s resurrection: a figure bearing a death wound and alive anyway, demanding the worship that belongs to the one who really died and rose.
