Whatever the wound refers to (see the box below), its effect is clear: a power that seemed finished and came back looks unbeatable, and so the world believes in the beast.

Satan invents nothing. That is the key to this chapter and the two that follow. Everything the dragon produces is an imitation: a beast with a resurrection, a second beast with horns like a lamb, a mark on the forehead, an image that breathes. He copies closely enough to deceive the careless, so the best protection is close acquaintance with the real thing, and the real thing is a person. The beast’s wound heals and it goes on demanding to be worshipped. The Lamb kept his wounds and showed them to Thomas (John 20:27); he laid down his life and took it up again (John 10:18), and he rose to give life, not to take it.

The whole earth marveled. “Followed” is literally went after, as disciples follow a master: the world follows the beast as the church follows the Lamb (14:4), and everyone is following someone. The beast has a scar and a counterfeit life; the Lamb has the marks of the nails and an endless life, and heaven marvels at the original, the one who died and is alive for evermore and holds the keys of death and Hades (1:18).

They worshiped the dragon. Worshipping the beast is really worshipping Satan, for all idolatry has a demonic source: “what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20). People who would never knowingly kneel to the devil kneel to him anyway, through the thing he has dressed up for them.

Who is like the beast? The chant parodies the song of the exodus: when Israel came through the sea, Moses and the people sang, “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?” (Exodus 15:11), and the world’s worship uses the same sentence with a different object. And Michael, who threw the dragon out of heaven in the previous chapter, means “Who is like God?” The worshippers ask of the beast the question that belongs to God alone, and it has already been answered: Michael has defeated the dragon (12:7–9), and the Lamb will conquer the beast, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14).

The first act of worship is a calculation. The second half of the chant is the more revealing: “who can fight against it?” Nobody claims the beast is kind, or just, or true. Few people consciously decide to worship a tyrant; they conclude that resistance is pointless and a sensible person goes along. It happens in a nation, and in an office, a school, a family: the moment someone decides that the strongest voice in the room must be obeyed because it is the strongest.

When evil seems to have been beaten and then comes back, what should I think? That Revelation told you to expect it. Godless powers rise, fall and revive in new forms throughout this age. Do not put your final hope in any political victory, as though one election or revolution could finish evil off, and do not despair when the old evil returns in new clothes. Only one death and resurrection is final, and it is not the beast’s: the Lamb was really slain and really lives, and he alone will end evil, at his coming.

Uncertain wording. What the healed wound refers to is not known. Some point to Nero, whom many in the east expected to return from the dead with a Parthian army; some to the empire itself, which nearly fell apart in the civil wars of AD 68 to 69 and then recovered under Vespasian; some hold it is still future. The pattern fits each: a power that seemed finished, returning.

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast’s great weapon is its mouth, blaspheming God and slandering his people, but it speaks only by permission and only for the time God allows.

A mouth was given. “Was given” comes four times in verses 5 to 7: the beast does nothing except by permission. Verbs like these, which do not name the giver, point to God; the chain of permission runs past the dragon to God’s throne, and that is why a Christian can read this chapter without despair. “Haughty” is literally “great things”, the phrase of Daniel’s little horn (Daniel 7:8). Behind it stands Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Greek king who persecuted the Jews in 167–164 BC, called himself God manifest and desecrated the temple, a forerunner of the king who exalts himself above every god (Daniel 11:36).

Forty-two months. It did not seize its term of office; it was allowed one, on licence, with an expiry date printed on it. It is the same period as the trampling of the holy city and the woman’s protection in the wilderness (11:2; 12:6): the same clock governs the persecution and the preserving.

His name and his dwelling. It blasphemes God’s name, who he is, and his dwelling, which John explains in case anyone imagines a building: those who dwell in heaven. God’s dwelling is with his people (21:3), believers seated with Christ in the heavenly places (12:12; Ephesians 2:6). So the beast mocks and slanders the church.

To slander the church is to slander God. The voice on the Damascus road said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). What is done to the body is done to the head. No insult reaches his people that does not first strike him, and he has borne insult before: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

The beast’s chief weapon is its mouth. It has ten horns and the dragon’s authority, yet these verses are about its mouth. The great opposition to the church in this book is not chiefly a police force but a false account of the world, repeated everywhere with confidence, in which God is small, his people are contemptible and the beast is the only realistic option. Christians braced for a knock at the door are sometimes worn down instead by years of being told, pleasantly, that what they believe is ridiculous. Against a mouth, the church has been given a mouth of its own: the word of their testimony (12:11), and behind it the sharp sword that comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The beast’s words are loud; Christ’s word is true, and it will have the last say.

The one condemned for blasphemy. Daniel’s little horn speaks great things until the Ancient of Days takes away its dominion and gives an everlasting dominion to one like a son of man (Daniel 7:8–14). At his trial Jesus claimed that vision as his own: “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven”. The high priest tore his garments, and the council condemned him for blasphemy (Mark 14:62–64). The Son was condemned as a blasphemer for telling the truth about himself, while the beast, which really blasphemes, is worshipped. The verdicts will be reversed. The beast’s mouth runs for forty-two months; the Son of Man’s dominion is everlasting.

How do I stay steady when everything around me mocks my faith? Expect it; this chapter told you it would come. Keep your mind full of the truth, because constant mockery works by slow erosion more than argument: spend more time with God’s voice than with the voices that belittle him, in Scripture, worship and the company of believers. Remember that the mockery is aimed at God first, and he is not threatened by it. And refuse to answer contempt with contempt: a gentle, unashamed, cheerful faith is a reply the beast’s mouth cannot answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is allowed to overcome Christians in body and to rule the unbelieving world, but it cannot touch the names the Lamb’s book has held since before creation.

Allowed to conquer them. Daniel’s horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came (Daniel 7:21–22). One of the hardest sentences in Revelation: the beast is permitted to make war on Christians, and to win (11:7). Revelation will not tell the church that faithfulness guarantees survival.

Two kinds of victory. Hold that beside 12:11, where the same people conquered the dragon, with the same verb, because they loved not their lives even unto death: in Revelation those killed for their faith are the true conquerors (15:2). The beast wins the battle of bodies; the saints win the battle of faithfulness, and only one of those victories is visible from the street.

Every tribe and people. The fourfold phrase of 5:9, a parody of the Lamb’s redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation. The beast’s rule seems universal, but it is given, and from every one of those peoples the Lamb has already ransomed people for God.

All who dwell on earth. John’s fixed name (8:13) for the unbelieving world: people whose home, hope and treasure are all here. Everyone worships something, and those who do not worship God will worship the beast.

The book of life of the Lamb. Then the comfort of the chapter: there is a register. “Written” is in a tense meaning it was written and still stands written, from the foundation of the world, before anybody had done anything to deserve entry or exclusion. Those who resist the beast are those written in the Lamb’s book by God’s eternal choice, and their perseverance rests on his election, not their strength; yet no one’s idolatry is excused by it, and faithful endurance is its fruit. Election is not a locked door to worry at. It is the foundation under the feet of everyone who has already come in.

The title of a wound. Before the mountains were brought forth, the Father wrote his children’s names in a book that bears the title of a wound: the book of life of the Lamb who was slain, opened in eternity and paid for at Calvary. The beast may conquer bodies, but it cannot erase a single line, and the Son will lose nothing of all that he has been given, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39).

Is it fair for God to write some names and not others? No one in this verse is treated unjustly. Those outside the book are not dragged to the beast; they marvel at it, follow it and worship it gladly, and are judged for what they chose (14:9–11). Those inside did not earn their place; every name was written before its owner had done anything. No one receives less than justice, and some receive mercy instead. Paul met the same objection by bowing first before God’s right to have mercy (Romans 9:14–20). The wonder is not that some names are missing, but that any are there at all, and that whoever comes to the Lamb finds his name among them.

Could I be deceived into worshipping the beast without realising it? The verse says the opposite: those whose names are written are kept. That is not a promise that a believer will never be frightened, waver or fail: Peter denied Christ three times in a courtyard, and was restored. It is a promise about who does the holding. Jesus said it without symbols: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). The register is not a list of the people who held out.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is: whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and if you are trusting Christ alone, that is the evidence that you were chosen. So if you fear you would not stand firm under pressure, look away from your own strength to his grip. That makes you grateful, not careless, and gratitude is a far stronger defence against idolatry than fear.

Where Christians differ: what does “from the foundation of the world” go with? The Greek word order allows “the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (as in the King James Version) or “written from the foundation of the world in the book of life” (as in the ESV). This commentary’s view: the second is more likely, because 17:8 clearly uses the same phrase of names written in the book of life. Both truths are biblical: Christ was foreknown as the sacrifice before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), and God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). The verse teaches unconditional election: God wrote the names of his people in the Lamb’s book before they were born, not because of anything they would do, and he keeps them from worshipping the beast. Christians in the Arminian tradition (who hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe) read such verses differently, and they too rejoice in the Lamb’s book; this commentary holds that a choice made before anyone had done anything fits this verse and Ephesians 1:4–5 best.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saints meet the beast not with the sword but with endurance and faith, accepting what God has appointed rather than deny Christ.

If anyone has an ear, let him hear. The call of the seven letters (2:7), where it always ran on, “what the Spirit says to the churches”; here those words are gone. Having described a beast conquering the saints, John turns to whoever is listening: this is for you personally.

To captivity he goes. The saying comes from Jeremiah (15:2; 43:11), the language of a sentence already passed. Some believers will be imprisoned, and some executed, within God’s sovereign purpose. That is not fatalism (on fleeing, see the question below). It sounds bleak until set beside a Christianity that promises deliverance from every hard thing, and so leaves a believer, when the arrest comes, concluding that God has failed. Nothing that happens to a Christian at the hands of the beast is outside what was appointed, or a surprise to the one who holds the keys.

The endurance and faith of the saints. The point of the whole passage. “Endurance” is staying power, holding a position under weight; “faith” is faith and faithfulness, for the Greek covers both. This is how the saints conquer.

What is not on the list. Not violent resistance, clever manoeuvring, political leverage or withdrawal into a compound, but: stay where you are and keep trusting him. That is not passivity. It is trust in the one who holds the keys, and some of the hardest work a believer ever does.

The Lamb who would not draw the sword. The endurance asked here is the way the Lamb himself went. In the garden Peter drew his sword, and Jesus told him to put it back; he could have appealed to his Father for more than twelve legions of angels, but then how should the Scriptures be fulfilled (Matthew 26:52–54)? So he was taken captive and put to death under Roman authority, like a lamb led to the slaughter, silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). Peter, who had swung that sword, learned the lesson and passed it on: Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:21–23). His endurance is the pattern of ours and the power of ours: the saints conquer by staying where he has put them, because he stayed on the cross for them.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never defend themselves or others, or that believers should seek martyrdom. It means that the church does not advance its cause by force, and that when persecution comes because of faith, believers accept suffering rather than deny Christ or take up arms for the gospel.

May a Christian flee persecution, or must he stay? He may flee, if he can do so without denying Christ. Jesus said, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket. What this verse forbids is escape by compromise: buying safety with a denial, a pinch of incense, a lie. If the way out is clean, a believer may take it; if it runs only through unfaithfulness, captivity is the appointed road, and Christ walks it with him.

In everyday life. Endurance is learned in small things before it is needed in great ones: keeping your word when it costs you, staying kind to someone who mocks you, going on praying when prayer seems unanswered. The Spirit of the Lamb grows it in you. You will still flinch and fail; the Lamb never did, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so failure sends you back to him, not out of his company.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the second line. Some read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a warning against taking up the sword, as in Matthew 26:52 and the King James Version. Others read “if anyone is to be killed with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a call to accept martyrdom. Either way, the lesson is the same: believers must not resist the beast by violence, but endure in faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The beast’s power needs a persuader, and the second beast is religion in the service of the state, looking like the Lamb and speaking for the dragon. Later called the false prophet, it makes the world worship the first beast (vv. 11–12). It works signs, even fire from heaven, sets up an image that speaks, and has those who will not worship it killed, as in Daniel 3 (vv. 13–15). It marks everyone, small and great, on the hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the beast’s name (vv. 16–17). The number, 666, calls for wisdom: it is the number of a man (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark, the beast’s name, without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second power, religious and persuasive, looks like the Lamb but speaks for the dragon, and its whole work is to make people worship the first beast.

Another beast out of the earth. The first beast came out of the sea, from far away; this one comes from the land, local and familiar. Between them the dragon seems to have the world covered, but the mighty angel of 10:2 had already planted one foot on the sea and one on the land: both belong to God. This beast is later called the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10).

Two horns like a lamb. It looks harmless, even Christlike, a parody of the Lamb at the centre of the book. But the true Lamb has seven horns, the fullness of power (5:6), and holds it because he was slain; this one has two, and has never bled for anyone. Religious deception often looks gentle and attractive.

And it spoke like a dragon. It looks like a lamb but sounds like the serpent, deceiving as he did in Eden. Jesus warned of false prophets in sheep’s clothing who are inwardly ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15), and Paul said that since Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, it is no surprise if his servants disguise themselves as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). The test is not appearance but speech. Ask of a teacher, movement or message not whether it feels, looks or sounds Christian (the horns are convincing), but what it says when it speaks at length, and whether that is what the dragon says: that God is not to be taken at his word, that his commands are a cage, that sin is not so serious, that Christ is one way among many, that safety lies in accommodation.

All the authority of the first beast. The second beast is no rival; it works for the first, like a department of its government. Many readers call dragon, beast and false prophet an unholy trinity, a counterfeit of Father, Son and Spirit. The dragon gives his authority to the beast, as the Father to the Son; the beast bears a death wound and lives; and the false prophet draws no attention to himself at all: his entire function is to make the world worship the beast, which is precisely what the Holy Spirit does for Christ. “He will glorify me”, Jesus said (John 16:14).

Worship the first beast. The false prophet’s role is religious: to promote the worship of political power. In every age that means whatever religion, philosophy, media or education persuades people to give a human power the devotion that belongs to God. In Asia the priests of the imperial cult were not Romans sent from abroad but leading men of the cities, who organised the festivals, sacrifices and games: neighbours, patrons, people the church knew. The pressure to worship came not only from the sea but up out of the local ground.

There is only one Lamb. He never flattered, never deceived, and never asked anyone to worship any but God. The unholy trinity can only imitate what the holy Trinity is: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God, whose glory no counterfeit can steal and whose voice his sheep know.

Can the false prophet be inside the church? Yes, and that is the most sobering point here: the most effective deceivers have always spoken from within Christian circles. The letters to Pergamum and Thyatira warned of Balaam and Jezebel, teachers inside the congregations who taught believers to compromise with idolatry (2:14, 20). Whenever a church leader says that faithfulness to Christ can wait, that the culture’s demands must be accommodated, or that the gospel needs updating to suit the powers of the day, the lamb’s horns are showing. Test teachers by Scripture, however gentle their manner (1 John 4:1).
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophet makes the beast’s worship look reasonable with counterfeit signs and an image that speaks, and those who will not bow are put to death.

Great signs. “Signs” is the word John’s Gospel uses for the miracles of Jesus. These are counterfeits, and Scripture is consistent that supernatural power proves nothing by itself. Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ miracles (Exodus 7:11, 22). Moses warned that a prophet might give a sign that came to pass and still lead Israel to other gods, and that God was testing them by it (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul warned that the lawless one would come with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9). Deception is the false prophet’s weapon, as it is Satan’s (12:9), and even its miracles happen only because it is “allowed”.

Fire from heaven. That is Elijah’s sign on Carmel, when fire from the sky settled who the true God was (1 Kings 18:38). The false prophet reproduces Elijah’s credential, as the two witnesses of chapter 11 had Elijah’s powers: both sides in this book have fire; only one has the truth. The false fire deceives for a while; the fire of the LORD settles the question for ever.

An image for the beast. Idolatry of the state, of its leader or of its ideology. Behind it stands Daniel 3: an image set up on a plain, an order that everyone bow at a signal, and a furnace for anyone who would not. In the province of Asia statues of the emperor stood in temples and public squares, and Christians were sometimes required to offer incense before them to prove their loyalty, as Pliny reported from neighbouring Bithynia around AD 112.

Breath to the image. Breath, or spirit (the word means both): a parody of God giving breath to the witnesses (11:11). The Old Testament’s standing mockery of idols is that they cannot speak: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see” (Psalm 115:5), a psalm John used at 9:20. This idol talks back, and what it says is a death sentence. Ancient temple statues were sometimes made to seem to speak by hidden devices; whether the mechanism is a priest behind a wall or something uncanny, the demand is the same: bow, or be killed. The image speaks for a season and is silenced; the Word who was in the beginning speaks and worlds are made.

Signs that point to him. In John’s Gospel the signs of Jesus were written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name (John 20:30–31); the beast’s signs point to an image and end in a death sentence. And Jesus would not perform wonders on demand: to those who asked for a sign he promised only the sign of Jonah, his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:38–40). The deceiver performs in order to be worshipped. The Son of God went to the cross, and that is the sign by which his people know him.

Those who would not worship. Three young men said no on the plain of Dura, and said what ought to be carved over this chapter: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Daniel 3:17–18). But if not: the endurance of the saints in three words.

Force and plausibility. The first beast supplies the force. The second makes worshipping it seem reasonable: the signs, the wonders, the reasons, the respectable local men who explain that this is only a formality. Raw power alone has never commanded worship for long; it needs somebody with lamb’s horns to make the case.

What are the images that demand worship today? Few people today bow to statues, but the pattern recurs wherever a human power or idea is set up as ultimate and refusal is punished: a leader whose portrait must hang in every home, an ideology that requires public affirmation of what God calls sin, a national or tribal cause placed above Christ. Often the punishment is not death but loss: of job, standing, reputation or access. The question is simple: am I being required to say or do what amounts to confessing that something other than Christ is Lord? If so, answer with the three young men: we will not serve your gods.

In everyday life. When something spectacular is offered as proof that a teacher or movement is from God, ask what it is leading you to worship. And practise the three words now, in small matters, so they are ready in large ones: God is able to deliver me. But if not, I will still not bow.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone bears the name of the one they worship, and the beast presses its name on all, making a person’s livelihood depend on their allegiance.

Small and great, rich and poor. Three pairs covering every social division: the demand reaches the senator and the slave in one sentence.

Marked on the right hand or the forehead. “Mark” is a stamp or brand, the impression of a seal on a document or coin; slaves were sometimes branded with their owner’s mark, and soldiers with their general’s name. It is a counterfeit: in 7:3 the servants of God were sealed on their foreheads, and in 14:1 the 144,000 have the Lamb’s name and his Father’s name written there. Everyone in this book is marked, with God’s name or the beast’s, and the only question is whose name is on you. The Lamb marks his redeemed for ever: in the city to come they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (22:4).

Hand and forehead. In Deuteronomy 6:8 God’s commandments were bound on the hand and between the eyes: what you do and what you think. The beast demands what God demanded, in the same two places. And the text itself defines the mark (v. 17): not a device but a name, a declaration of who owns you.

No one can buy or sell. Here the chapter stops being theoretical. The threat is not only to life but to trade: keep your convictions and lose your livelihood, or make one small gesture and go on feeding your family. The trade guilds of Asia required members to honour patron gods and the emperor (2:14, 20), and Christians who refused could lose their living; that may lie behind Smyrna’s poverty (2:9). Later, under the emperor Decius in the third century, citizens had to obtain a certificate stating that they had sacrificed to the gods, and papyrus copies of such certificates survive.

The sign in the greengrocer’s window. Václav Havel, the Czech playwright whom the communist regime later imprisoned, asked in his essay “The Power of the Powerless” why a greengrocer puts the slogan “Workers of the world, unite!” in his shop window among the onions and carrots. He does not believe it, and nobody reads it. What it really says, Havel argued, is: I am obedient, so leave me in peace. A whole system of lies is held up by millions of such small gestures, and the day the greengrocer takes his sign down he begins to live in the truth, and pays for it. That is the mark in its everyday form: not a dramatic act of devil worship, but a small sign that lets you go on trading. Every age has its window, and the question is not only whether the sign is true, but whose name it puts on you. The freedom to take it down does not come from a braver heart. It comes from knowing that your name is already written in the Lamb’s book, and that the God who fed his people in the wilderness can feed a greengrocer.

The marks of Jesus. Paul, beaten and stoned for his Lord, wrote, “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (Galatians 6:17), using the word for the brand a master burned into a slave. But the deepest mark is not on the servant; it is on the Master. The Lamb carries in his hands and side the wounds by which he bought his people (John 20:27), and the name he writes on their foreheads (14:1) is the name of one who was marked for them first. The beast stamps its people to own them. Christ was pierced to redeem them, with his own precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

What if I take the mark by accident? Nobody in this chapter takes it by accident. It is the sign of a worship already given, by people who have marvelled, worshipped and decided that nobody can fight the beast. And those whose names are in the Lamb’s book are not the ones who take it (see the note on vv. 7–8). If you are afraid of having the mark, that fear is itself evidence that your heart belongs to Christ. Those who bear the beast’s mark are not worried about it; they are proud of it.

What does this look like at work? It is the moment when keeping your job, winning the contract or being promoted requires you to do what Christ forbids: to lie on a report, to affirm what God calls evil, to join a ritual of loyalty to something other than him, or to stay silent when silence would be a denial. Most working days involve no such choice, and a Christian should work hard and well for ordinary employers (Colossians 3:23). But when the choice comes, the issue is whose name is on your hand. Settle the answer before the day arrives, and trust the God who feeds the birds to provide for you if obedience costs you your income.

In everyday life. If you know a believer who has lost work for refusing to compromise, help them: a church that shares its bread blunts the beast’s economic threat.

Where Christians differ: what is the mark of the beast? Over the centuries the mark has been identified with barcodes, credit cards, identity cards, microchips implanted in the hand, even vaccines: every generation since printing with its own newest technology, and so far every generation has been wrong. Those who worried were usually sincere believers afraid of betraying Christ, and that fear deserves a gentle answer. This commentary’s view: the mark is not a physical device that someone might take by accident. It is a symbol of allegiance, the counterpart of God’s seal, which is also invisible (God’s name, 14:1, and his Spirit, Ephesians 1:13). To receive the mark is to give one’s worship and loyalty to the beast, to think and act as its servant, and no one receives it without choosing to worship the beast (14:9–11). Christians should not fear new technologies as though they might take the mark by accident, but watch their loyalty, and refuse to compromise their worship of Christ, whatever the economic cost.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast’s number marks it as merely human, a power that always falls short of God, and it pointed John’s first readers to Nero. What it calls for is not calculation of names in the news but the wisdom to recognise the beast.

This calls for wisdom. Not cleverness but spiritual discernment, to recognise the beast for what it is (17:9). Few verses have been used more irresponsibly.

Calculate the number. To count up: the verb comes from the word for a counting pebble. In Hebrew and Greek, letters also served as numbers, so every name had a value, and adding up a name’s letters (gematria) was a familiar game: a scribbled line on a wall at Pompeii reads, “I love her whose number is 545.” John is setting a puzzle for people who had the key, and many hearers probably recognised what he was asking. Nero Caesar, written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr), adds up to 666.

The number of a man. The beast, for all its claims to divinity, is merely human (on the wording, see the box below).

His number is 666. Six is one short of seven, the number of completeness and perfection. Three sixes: falling short again and again, a counterfeit trinity that never reaches the divine. Jesus’ name in Greek adds up to 888, as some early Christians noticed, and they linked eight, one beyond seven, with the eighth day, the day of resurrection and new creation.

A portrait, not only a cipher. In whatever century it appears, the beast is magnificent, terrifying and world-conquering, yet always one short of seven: a portrait of every human power that reaches for God’s place. Every empire that reached for heaven fell short and fell down; every ruler who wore the titles of God has gone to the dust, and the Lord sits enthroned for ever. Set beside it the one man who did not grasp at God’s place. Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross; therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6–9). The beast grasps at deity and stays a six. The Son, who is God, stooped to become a man, and God lifted him up.

What it does not mean. The number 666 is not unlucky or dangerous in itself. Christians need not fear house numbers, phone numbers or dates containing it; its meaning lies in what it symbolises.

So what am I meant to take from this chapter, if not a name? A recognition. The beast is whatever demands the allegiance that belongs to God, backed by force, made plausible by religion, and enforced through the ability to buy and sell. It has worn many costumes and will wear more, until its final form before Christ returns, and every one is a six. So learn to recognise its marks, refuse its worship, endure its pressure, and keep your eyes on the one whose name is above every name.

In everyday life. The next time a book, a sermon or a viral post claims to have identified the beast in today’s headlines, smile, close it, and open the Gospel instead. You do not need to know the beast’s name to resist him. You need to know the Lamb’s.

Where Christians differ: who is 666? The number has been applied to countless figures: popes, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, various modern politicians, and titles such as the papal title Vicarius Filii Dei. This commentary’s view: the number pointed first to Nero, the emperor who began Rome’s persecution of Christians in AD 64 and became the pattern of the persecuting beast; and its symbolism, six falling short of seven, describes every human power that claims to be divine. Attempts to fit it to later figures, often by earnest believers under real pressure, have repeatedly failed and brought discredit on the church. The right response is not number-crunching names in the news, but the wisdom to recognise and resist any power that demands worship.

Uncertain wording. “The number of a man” is literally “a number of a human being”: either the number of a particular man, a name to be counted, or a human number, belonging to humanity as such. The first fits the call to calculate and the Nero reading; the second, a claim to deity exposed as merely human. Both may be in view.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts read 616 instead of 666, as the early church father Irenaeus noted around AD 180. He defended 666 as the original, which the best manuscripts support. The variant may have arisen because 616 matches the Latin spelling of Nero Caesar, which shows that early readers connected the number with Nero. A variant that changes the number by exactly the value of one dropped letter is hard to explain as coincidence.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads.<sup>2</sup>And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation,<sup>8</sup>and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.<sup>9</sup>If anyone has an ear, let him hear:<sup>10</sup>If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

keyVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
keyVerse.note: After all the beast’s power, this is the chapter’s word to the church, and it returns at 14:12. The saints are not told to out-argue or out-fight the beast, but to hold their ground and keep trusting, as the Lamb did on his way to the cross. They can, because their names were written in his book before the beast ever rose (v. 8).

13.reflection:
Every feature of the beast copies something true of Christ: a wound that heals, horns like a lamb, a name on the forehead (vv. 3, 11, 16). Why does Satan imitate rather than invent? How does knowing the real Christ well protect you from the counterfeits?

The world’s worship begins with a calculation: “Who can fight against it?” (v. 4). Where are you tempted to go along with the strongest voice in the room, at work, in your family or online?

Verses 9–10 call for endurance and faith rather than force. What would that look like for Christians under pressure where you live, and how do the three young men of Daniel 3 help?

The mark is about whose name you bear, and it reaches into buying and selling (vv. 16–17). What small “signs in the window” are expected of you to keep your place, and how could your church stand with someone who loses work for refusing them?

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 closes the look behind the scenes begun in chapter 12. Chapter 13 left the beasts apparently in control and the world marked with the beast’s name; before the bowls (chapters 15–16) and Babylon’s fall (chapters 17–18), this chapter shows how it all ends.

The message. The beast’s triumph is not the last word. The Lamb stands on Zion with every one of his people, God is still calling the world to himself, Babylon is as good as fallen, and history ends in a harvest. There are only two destinies, set side by side so that people choose now whom they will worship, and the Lamb’s people hold on.

Why it was said. Refusing to honour the emperor could cost the churches of Asia a living, friends or life itself (see the introduction). Was it worth losing everything? Had the dead lost? The beast’s mark, comes the answer, leads to God’s wrath, and those who die in the Lord are blessed.

How the chapter makes its case. First comes the other marked crowd (vv. 1–5): the full 144,000 with the Lamb on Mount Zion, bearing his name, kept from the beast’s idolatry, following him wherever he goes. Three angels then bring an eternal gospel for every nation, the news that Babylon is fallen, and a warning that the beast’s worshippers will drink God’s wrath unmixed (vv. 6–11). A call to endure and heaven’s blessing on the dead in the Lord follow (vv. 12–13). Last come two harvests (vv. 14–20): one like a son of man reaps the earth from a white cloud, and the vine of the earth is thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath.

Where it leads. The Lamb secure on Zion is the one who drank the cup this chapter describes (Matthew 26:39). The winepress is trodden outside the city, where he “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The one who reaps the earth is the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died (John 12:24). Everyone gathered into his harvest is there because he was first trodden for them.

For us. Every life bears a name on the forehead. Refuse the beast’s mark and Babylon’s wine, endure, speak the gospel while it still flies overhead, and bury those who die in the Lord with hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whatever the beast does, the Lamb keeps every one of his people, and they are wholly his. Where chapter 13 ended with a crowd marked by the beast, John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the full 144,000, his name and his Father’s on their foreheads, while heaven sounds with a new song that only the redeemed can learn (vv. 1–3). Then he describes them: they have kept themselves from the beast’s idolatry, they follow the Lamb wherever he goes, they belong to God as firstfruits, and no lie is found in them, for the Lamb’s blood has made them blameless (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: The song of the cross is learned by coming to the Lamb, and no one who comes is turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb stands secure on God’s holy hill with every one of his people, who bear his name and sing a song only the redeemed can learn. Chapter 13 ended with a crowd marked on the forehead with the beast’s name; chapter 14 opens with another marked crowd, wearing in the same place the name of the Lamb and of his Father.

On Mount Zion stood the Lamb. Mount Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where David’s city and the temple stood, and it became a name for God’s dwelling and his people: in Mount Zion, said Joel, “there shall be those who escape” (Joel 2:32). The dragon stood on the sand of the sea (12:17), and the beasts rose from the sea and the earth; the Lamb stands firm on Zion, where God installs his King in defiance of the raging nations (Psalm 2:6). This is the heavenly Zion, where the church has already come (Hebrews 12:22). In 5:6 the Lamb was standing as though slain; here he simply stands, and the company with him is counted and complete.

Who are the 144,000? The company sealed in 7:4, with not one missing after all the beast’s war on the saints, and their seal is now revealed as the Lamb’s name and his Father’s. They are the complete people of God, redeemed and sealed; not a literal number from ethnic Israel, nor the special class of “anointed” taught by Jehovah’s Witnesses. Many dispensational readers, who rightly take God’s promises to Israel seriously, see them as Jewish believers of the last days; this commentary reads them as the whole church, because in chapter 7 John hears a counted number and then sees a multitude no one could number, from every nation (7:4, 9). The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand: the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, the whole people of God of both covenants, multiplied to fullness. If you belong to Christ, you are in this number, and not one of his people is left out of the count.

Many waters, thunder and harps. The roar of many waters is the voice of the risen Christ (1:15) and the sound of God’s glory returning to the temple (Ezekiel 43:2); thunder is the voice of God at Sinai. Then, in the same breath, harps, the gentlest of sounds. On earth a harp cannot be heard over a waterfall; the worship of heaven is both at once, overwhelming and tender.

A new song. Scripture sings a new song when God has done something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1; 98:1), and one was sung once before in this book, when the elders praised the Lamb who by his blood ransomed people for God (5:9). That is the subject of this song too.

No one could learn that song. Only the redeemed can sing the song of redemption, because only they have lived it; anyone can read the words. Angels praise God for salvation (7:11–12), and long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), but they cannot sing as those bought with the Lamb’s blood.

Slain, and yet standing. Worthy is the Lamb who stands on Zion. Neither the raging nations nor the war of the beast could move him or strike one name from his company. He bought them, every one, with his own blood, and wrote his Father’s name where the world could see it. The song they sing he taught them by redeeming them, and every line of it is about him: slain, and yet standing; the price paid, and the purchase complete.

What if I cannot sing, or worship feels dry? The new song is not a matter of musical ability or Sunday feelings, but the confession of a redeemed heart: I was bought by the blood of the Lamb, and I belong to him. You can sing it in a quavering voice, or say it silently in a hospital bed, and heaven hears it in the great chorus. Dry seasons come to every believer: keep gathering with God’s people, keep singing the true words when your feelings lag behind, and look again at the cross the song is about. The feelings usually follow the looking.

In everyday life. When you are tempted to compromise to keep your place, your income or your friends, say to yourself: I belong to the Lamb, and his Father’s name is on me.

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb’s people have kept themselves wholly for him, follow him wherever he leads, belong to God as the first of his harvest, and are truthful and blameless because he has redeemed them.

They are virgins. One of the hardest sentences in the book to read well. The word can be used of men as well as women, and it is a picture. The prophets called God’s people his virgin bride (Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4) and idolatry adultery or prostitution (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16), and Paul betrothed the Corinthians to Christ as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). In Revelation idolatry is sexual immorality (2:14, 20), Babylon is the great prostitute (17:1–5), and the church is the Lamb’s faithful bride (19:7–8). So “virgins” are those who did not go to bed with the beast: they kept themselves for one Lord in a world offering many.

Holy warriors. They are also soldiers of the Lamb, counted by tribes in chapter 7 as Israel counted an army. Soldiers under a holy-war vow kept from sexual relations for the campaign (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5), as Uriah would not go home to his wife while the ark and the army were in tents (2 Samuel 11:11). That was a rule for a campaign, not a judgment on marriage or on women, and the company includes every believing woman. Both pictures say one thing: this company has kept itself wholly for the Lamb.

They follow the Lamb wherever he goes. “Follow” is the word for discipleship, the book’s simplest definition of a Christian. “Follow me” was the first thing Jesus said to fishermen at their nets, and the last he said to Peter (John 21:19, 22); the world follows the beast (13:3). The weight is in “wherever”. This book has shown where the Lamb goes: to a cross, and through death. To follow him wherever is to give up in advance the right to refuse any road he takes; that is the difference between a disciple and an admirer. And every road he leads them on he has walked first: the road to Jerusalem, the road to the cross, the road out of the tomb.

Firstfruits. The first sheaf of the harvest, brought to God before the rest was gathered (Leviticus 23:10): it belonged wholly to God and promised more to come. James calls believers “a kind of firstfruits” of God’s creatures (James 1:18), and Paul calls Christ himself “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Here the whole church is the firstfruits offered from all humanity, the pledge of a renewed creation, and the word prepares for the harvest of verse 15, the gathering of the redeemed.

No lie was found. The phrase echoes the Servant, in whose mouth there was no deceit (Isaiah 53:9), and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13. In a book whose villain is “the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9), truthfulness is the mark of the other side. They did not say “Caesar is Lord”, and they did not deny Christ. There was no deceit in the Lamb’s mouth, and he has put a true song in theirs.

Blameless. Without blemish: the word for a sacrificial animal without defect, which Peter uses of Christ, “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Nobody here achieved it: they were redeemed (v. 3) and washed their robes white in his blood (7:14). God counts the Lamb’s perfect record as theirs, because on the cross he counted their sins as his (2 Corinthians 5:21). Scripture’s word for it is justification, a judge’s verdict that the guilty now stand in the right for Christ’s sake. It is not sinless perfection in this life, but over a lifetime he makes them in fact what he has declared them to be.

I have not kept myself pure. Is there a place for me here? Yes, if you come to the Lamb. Not one of the 144,000 was pure by nature; the Corinthians Paul wanted to present to Christ as a pure virgin included former idolaters, adulterers and thieves, and he told them: “such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Past sexual sin and spiritual unfaithfulness are real, and must be confessed and turned from, but they do not bar you from the Lamb’s company. His blood makes the defiled clean, and from now on you follow him.

Does following the Lamb wherever he goes mean I must give up everything? It means you give him the right to ask for anything. Most days he asks for ordinary faithfulness; some days for something costly: a relationship you must end, a career move you must refuse, a reputation you must lose for his sake. The disciple does not decide in advance which roads he will take with Christ and which he will not.

In everyday life. The Lamb bought you and counts you blameless, so speak the truth, even when a lie would be easier. Think of the small lies that smooth a day: the excuse, the exaggeration, the pretended agreement. The people of the Lamb are known by their mouths.

Where Christians differ: does this praise celibacy? Some, from the early church onwards, have read this verse as praising celibacy as a higher Christian life, and used it to support celibate monks, nuns and clergy. Many who choose celibacy do so from real devotion to Christ, which deserves honour. This commentary’s view: the virginity here is spiritual purity from idolatry, the faithfulness of the Lamb’s bride. Scripture honours marriage (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24), calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and does not count marriage defiling. Celibacy is a good gift for some (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), but not a higher state of holiness. The 144,000 are the whole church, married and single, who refused to commit spiritual adultery with the beast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the end comes, God calls the whole world to himself and tells his people why they must hold on. A first angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation: fear God, give him glory and worship the Creator, for the hour of his judgment has come (vv. 6–7). A second announces Babylon fallen, three chapters before she is described (v. 8). A third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed, for ever (vv. 9–11). So the saints are called to endure, and heaven has John write that the dead who die in the Lord are blessed: they rest from their labours, and their deeds follow them (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the end, God sends his gospel to every people on earth, calling them to fear and worship their Creator because the hour of his judgment has come. Three angels follow one another through verses 6–11, in the order the gospel usually arrives: an appeal to turn to God, the news that the proud world is doomed, and a warning of what awaits those who refuse.

Directly overhead. Literally “in mid-heaven”, the highest point of the sky, where the eagle cried woe (8:13). Now an angel brings good news there, where all can hear: when the world had bowed to the beast, God answered first not with fire but with a gospel.

An eternal gospel. The only time Revelation uses the noun gospel: eternal because it never changes and its effects last for ever. It does not mention the cross, but in this book the whole of chapter 5 is the gospel, and the slain Lamb has been at the centre of every scene since. And to people under a beast, the news that the true God is still calling them to himself is good news of the most concrete kind.

To those who dwell on earth. John’s standing term for the people who have settled for this world, the same people who worship the beast (13:8). To them God offers the gospel, “to every nation and tribe and language and people”, as Jesus promised: “this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

Fear God and give him glory. To give him glory is to repent and worship (11:13; 16:9). To fear God is neither cringing terror nor mild respect, but settled awe before one far greater than we are, to whom we must answer (Proverbs 1:7). To people terrified of a beast, this is the remedy for fearing the wrong thing: not fearlessness, but fearing the right thing. As Jesus said, “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28). The one who fears God need fear no one else.

The hour of his judgment has come. The good news includes the warning. Good news that ignored judgment would not be good; it would be a lie told to people walking towards a cliff.

Him who made heaven and earth. The Creator, who alone deserves worship (4:11), in words that echo the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:11). Heaven, earth, sea and springs of water are the four realms struck by the first four trumpets (8:7–12). This is where Paul began with pagans who had no Bible (Acts 14:15): people who do not share our Scriptures still live under the same sky, made by the same God.

By a man whom he has appointed. The hour of judgment has a face. When Paul made this appeal at Athens, he ended it with a person: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31). The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and the Judge is the one who died for sinners. So the call to fear God and give him glory is a call to come to the Judge while he still stands as Saviour.

Is the angel’s call to give God glory a kind of vanity? In anyone else it would be. But God is the one being of whom all praise is simply true, and he commands it because it is good for us. Everybody worships something. To be told to give glory to the God who made heaven and earth is to be told to stop handing your heart to things that cannot bear it: a career, a reputation, a nation, another person. Every lesser god takes from its worshippers; this God gave his own Son for his (Romans 8:32). And in worship a creature finds his joy: “in your presence there is fullness of joy” (Psalm 16:11).

How do I share the gospel with someone who does not believe the Bible? Start where the angel and Paul started: with the God who made them. Everyone lives in a world they did not make, with a conscience they did not invent. Speak of the Creator, the sin that has turned us from him, the judgment coming and the Saviour he has sent. Do not hide the cross, the heart of the message, but you need not begin with a debate about the Bible. Begin with the shared sky, and let God’s word do its own work as you open it.

In everyday life. Who, of everyone you know, seems furthest from God? The gospel is for that person too. Make them your daily prayer, and look for one natural opening to speak of the God who made us and the Christ who saves us.

Where Christians differ: is this a last chance after death, or a different gospel? Some have read the eternal gospel as a final chance of salvation after the church’s age, or as a gospel different from Christ’s, without the cross. This commentary’s view: the eternal gospel is the same gospel of Jesus Christ preached throughout this age, summed up here as the call to turn from idols to the living God, where the apostles began with pagans (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul says there is no other gospel (Galatians 1:6–9). It is proclaimed to the living, before the hour of judgment, not after death (Hebrews 9:27). The angel pictures the worldwide preaching of the gospel by the church before the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud world-city that seduces the nations is as good as fallen, because God has already pronounced her doom. Babylon appears here for the first time, announced as finished before she is described: the headline running ahead of chapters 17 and 18.

Fallen, fallen. Isaiah’s words over the first Babylon (Isaiah 21:9), doubled like a herald’s shout. The tense is past, twice, of an empire at the height of its power, because what God has decided is as good as done. It was exactly what a Christian in Ephesus needed: the empire in front of him was collecting his taxes and threatening his trade, and the message read out in his congregation used the past tense. He need not admire, envy or fear a city whose ruin God had already announced.

Who is Babylon? Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC and took God’s people into exile, but by John’s day it had long been a ruin, so the name is a picture, as Sodom and Egypt were at 11:8. Then it meant Rome, the city on seven hills (17:9, 18), which had destroyed the temple as Babylon had; Peter sends greetings from “she who is at Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13). But the name is older than Rome and outlives it. Babylon begins at a tower built so that a people could make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4), a project that has never closed. It stands for every proud human civilisation organised without God: its economics, culture, pleasures and power, however good its roads.

The wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Jeremiah had called the first Babylon “a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken” (Jeremiah 51:7). The word for passion can also mean wrath, and the double sense is deliberate. Babylon seduces the nations into idolatry and immorality, like a prostitute offering wine. It is seduction, not conquest: the nations were not forced; they were poured a drink. And it is intoxication: the loss of judgment, the cheerful certainty that everything is fine. The wine she pours becomes the wine of God’s wrath (16:19; see the note on vv. 9–11).

The sword and the glass. The beast comes with a sword and is obvious. Babylon comes with a glass; she is charming, pays well, and does not appear to be asking for anything at all. Probably more Christians have been lost to Babylon’s wine than to the beast’s sword. And she does not recruit only the irreligious: a churchgoer can refuse the beast’s mark on Sunday and still be drunk on Babylon’s wine all week, measuring his life by the same success, comfort and reputation as everyone else.

Why the past tense is safe. Babylon’s fall can be spoken of as finished because the decisive battle is already won. On the eve of the cross Jesus said, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31), and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). Babylon still glitters, but the power behind her was broken on a hill outside Jerusalem. Nineveh is dust, the old Babylon a mound in the desert, the Rome that killed the apostles in ruins, while the church of the Lamb gathers from every nation. Every proud city has its date already written; only one city has foundations, “whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10). The past tense of God is the future of the world.

How do I live in Babylon without drinking her wine? The way the exiles did in the first Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where God has sent you, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its gods. Daniel served the king faithfully, but would not eat his food or stop praying. So work hard, be a good neighbour, enjoy God’s good gifts with thanks. But watch what intoxicates you: the pull of money, status, comfort, entertainment and approval that slowly dulls your love for Christ. Ask what you could not give up without bitterness; whatever it is, hold it more loosely, and hold Christ more tightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever gives himself to the beast will drink God’s undiluted wrath for ever, in the presence of the Lamb he refused. This is one of the most terrible warnings in the New Testament, and it should be read exactly as it stands, without softening and without relish.

If anyone worships the beast. The warning is aimed at those who choose to worship the beast; no one takes the mark by accident. And the order of the angels is the mercy of the passage: nobody arrives at verse 11 without first being flown over by the eternal gospel of verse 6.

The wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength. The cup of God’s wrath is an Old Testament picture of judgment (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16). The image answers verse 8: Babylon poured a drink, and so does God, and those who drank hers will drink his. Wine was usually mixed with water; “full strength” means unmixed. The judgments of the seals and trumpets were mixed with mercy, partial and limited: a fourth, a third, forty-two months, a restraint on the winds. This is the cup with the water left out.

Fire and sulfur. What fell on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and what burns in the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8).

In the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb. Not that they watch with pleasure, but that the judgment is carried out under their authority, and is just: the one who refused the Lamb’s mercy faces the Lamb as judge. The holiness that is the joy of heaven is a consuming fire to anyone who stands before it with his sin uncovered (Isaiah 33:14; Hebrews 12:29). And the one present is the Lamb who was slaughtered, who wept at a tomb and prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34). Nobody finally lost will be able to say that the Judge did not offer himself first.

The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever. Isaiah said of Edom, “its smoke shall go up forever” (Isaiah 34:10). “Forever and ever” is literally “to the ages of the ages”, the phrase used for God’s eternal life (4:9) and for the saints’ reign (22:5).

No rest, day or night. Unlike the living creatures, who never rest from praise (4:8), and the dead in the Lord, who rest from their labours (v. 13). And the verse says twice who it falls on: the beast’s worshippers. Not people who were unlucky, or confused, or never called.

The cup in Gethsemane. On the night before he died, the Son of God fell on his face and prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). This was the cup. He drank it, full strength, on the cross, when he cried out that God had forsaken him. He went into the darkness that should have been ours, and stands between the cup and his people. The wrath that falls on the beast’s worshippers has no claim left on Christ’s people, because it fell on him.

What it does not mean. This warning is not meant to make Christians afraid that they might lose their salvation. It is meant to make them refuse the beast at any cost, and to warn the world.

How can the smoke of their torment rise for ever if God is love? Because his love is holy, and sin against him is infinitely serious. We measure a crime partly by the dignity of the one wronged, and to rebel against the infinitely good God who made us is no small matter. Hell is also God giving people what they have chosen: life without him, the source of all light, rest and joy. And those in hell do not repent there; this book shows the lost cursing God rather than turning to him (16:9, 11). Above all, remember that the Judge is the Lamb who drank this cup himself (see ‘The cup in Gethsemane’ above). No one is in hell who wanted the mercy offered.

What about someone I love who has died without Christ, as far as I know? Scripture never invites us to pronounce on the dead. You did not see their last days or the whole of their heart, and God is merciful beyond our knowledge. Leave them with the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and grieve honestly. For those still alive, the gospel is still flying overhead, and intercession is the very work you were made a priest to do (1:6): pray, and keep praying. Saul of Tarsus stood guarding the coats at Stephen’s death, and he became the apostle Paul.

In everyday life. Let this verse make you more urgent, not more harsh: more willing to speak of Christ to a friend, more earnest in prayer for the lost, and more grateful every time you take the cup of blessing at the Lord’s table, knowing whose cup made it possible.

Where Christians differ: is hell eternal conscious punishment? Annihilationists (or conditionalists) believe the wicked are punished and then cease to exist, and read the rising smoke as the lasting result of a complete destruction. Some who hold this love the Bible and are trying to be faithful to it. Universalists believe all will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: this passage teaches eternal, conscious punishment. The wicked are tormented, with no rest day or night, for ever and ever; and Revelation 20:10 uses the same language of the devil, the beast and the false prophet, which plainly cannot mean annihilation. Jesus spoke of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46). This is terrible, and it should be spoken of with tears, not glee. But it is what Scripture says, and it shows both the seriousness of sin against an infinitely holy God and the greatness of Christ’s love in bearing God’s wrath for all who trust in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because so much is at stake, the Lamb’s people must hold on; and those who die belonging to him are blessed, for they rest from their toil and their faithful works go with them.

The endurance of the saints. A like sentence came at 13:10, after the beast conquered the saints; here it follows the cup of undiluted wrath. The response sought is not panic, nor fighting back, but endurance. For people whose cup the Lamb has already drunk, the warning of verses 9–11 is a reason to stay faithful.

Commandments and faith. As in 12:17, obedience and faith together mark the true believer. No saint keeps the commandments perfectly (James 3:2), but Jesus was faithful to the end, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Their endurance rests on his.

Blessed are the dead. The second of the book’s seven beatitudes (1:3), and one of the few sentences John is specifically told to write down (compare 19:9; 21:5). To congregations that had buried people and expected to bury more, God stops the vision to dictate a sentence about the ones who did not survive. As Isaiah said, the righteous man perishes, but “he enters into peace” (Isaiah 57:1–2). The world calls them losers; heaven calls them blessed.

Who die in the Lord. Joined to Christ by faith, so that his death counts as theirs and his rising guarantees their own (Romans 6:5). Those three words carry everything. Death is not blessed in itself: Paul calls it the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and this book throws it into the lake of fire (20:14). What is blessed is dying in him, as Paul speaks of “the dead in Christ” who will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

Says the Spirit. Apart from the seven letters, the Spirit speaks in his own voice only here and at 22:17. “Labors” means toil, the exhaustion of service and suffering, and this is the rest promised the martyrs in 6:11: heaven described first as the end of being tired, in contrast with the restless torment of verse 11.

Their deeds follow them. Not going before them as a credential, nor staying behind as a legacy, but following, like servants behind their master into a house. Their faithful works go with them into God’s presence, as evidence of their faith and as the basis of their reward (22:12). This does not mean they are saved by their works. It means that in the Lord their “labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Why death in the Lord is blessed. Death can be blessed only because the Lord went into it first. He shared our flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). In the first chapter of this book he says, “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18). A believer’s death is a door whose key is in the hand of the one who loved him.

He crowns his own gifts. God gives his weary servants rest, and a stranger kindness still: he lets their works follow them in, though every good thing they did was his own work in them, prepared beforehand that they should walk in it (Ephesians 2:10). He crowns his own gifts and calls them theirs. And the Lord in whom they died receives them home and says to each, “Well done, good and faithful servant… Enter into the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21).

What it means to rest. Many people cannot rest even when they stop, because underneath, the heart believes everything still depends on us: our standing and worth are still being earned, so the work is never done. Timothy Keller often pointed out that keeping a Sabbath is a declaration of freedom from slavery to work, to others’ expectations and to our own insecurities. That rest stands on someone else’s finished work. Jesus does not say, Finish your labours and then you may rest, but “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28); and on the cross he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). The dead in the Lord have that rest in full; believers taste it now (Hebrews 4:10). So on the Lord’s Day, stop: not because the list is done, but because he has done what counted, and “he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2).

What will come of my whole life? People who expect nothing after death still badly want their lives to last, so we talk about legacy: the company, the children, the name on a building. Leo Tolstoy, with War and Peace and Anna Karenina behind him, found in middle age that he could not answer what he called the simplest question of all: what will come of what I am doing today, or of my whole life? He describes in A Confession how the question so emptied his success that he hid a rope from himself, afraid of what he might do with it. He was right: even the greatest legacy is a footprint on a beach with the tide coming in. Revelation offers something humbler and far greater. Your deeds are not left behind for people who will also die to remember for a while; they go with you to the God who forgets nothing. The ambitious cannot make their work last, and the anxious cannot make it count; but in the Lord neither has to, because it is kept by Someone else.

What should I say at the funeral of a believer? Say this verse, written down at heaven’s express command for exactly that moment. Grieve, because death is an enemy and the loss is real; Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb. But grieve as those who have hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The one you loved is not lost, not sleeping in the dark, not being purged somewhere, but with Christ, resting, conscious, at home, and one day the body laid in the ground will be raised in glory.

What if I feel my life has accomplished very little for Christ? The deeds that follow the dead in the Lord include every hidden kindness, every faithful year in a small place, every prayer for a child, every temptation resisted that nobody saw. God forgets nothing done in his name, not even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42). You are not asked to be impressive, but faithful, and the God who works in you “both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13) will see that what he has done through you follows you home.

Where Christians differ: do believers go to purgatory, or rest?
