Roman Catholic teaching holds that many who die in God’s grace must still be purified in purgatory before heaven; others, that the soul sleeps until the resurrection. Catholic friends hold purgatory from a real sense of God’s holiness, a right concern; the question is what Christ’s blood has already done. This commentary’s view: the dead in the Lord are blessed from the moment of death, and they rest. There is no purging of sin after death; Christ’s blood has cleansed them completely (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 10:14), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their rest is conscious enjoyment of Christ (6:9–11), not unconscious sleep. They wait for the resurrection of the body, but they are already with him.

Uncertain wording. “Their faith in Jesus” is literally “the faith of Jesus”: the saints’ faith in him, as the ESV takes it, which suits its pairing with keeping God’s commandments, or the faithfulness Jesus himself showed. “From now on” may mean from this point in history, as persecution intensifies, or from the moment of death, and it may belong with the Spirit’s reply that follows. On every reading those who die in the Lord are blessed at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: History ends in a harvest, and the Lord of the harvest decides when it is ripe. One like a son of man, crowned and seated on a white cloud, reaps the earth at the hour the Father has set (vv. 14–16). Then, at the word of the angel from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers rose, the grapes of the vine of the earth are gathered and trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city, a judgment covering the whole earth (vv. 17–20). Together the two harvests show the two outcomes of the last day.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the hour the Father has set, the crowned Christ comes on the clouds and reaps the harvest of the earth. The end of the age arrives, as Jesus taught it would, as a harvest.

One like a son of man. Daniel’s figure coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13), and the phrase this book used of the risen Christ in its first chapter (1:13). This is Christ, coming on the clouds (1:7).

A golden crown and a sharp sickle. The crown is the victor’s. And in his hand, instead of a sword or a sceptre, a farm tool, the curved blade for harvesting grain. Jesus had told parables of harvest at the end of the age, the wheat gathered into the barn and the weeds burned (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43); here is the harvester.

Put in your sickle. The words are Joel’s: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13). Some take the figure on the cloud to be an angel, since an angel tells him to start reaping, an odd thing for a creature to say to the Son of God. But the angel comes from the temple, God’s presence, with the Father’s timing. Of that day or hour, Jesus said, no one knows, “not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32). The angel does not command Christ; he conveys the moment the Son was waiting for.

Fully ripe. The timing is stated twice. The word means dried, over-ready: grain on the point of being lost. Anyone who has waited on a crop knows there is a right day. The point is not the violence of reaping but a decision about timing, made by someone who has been watching the field.

The answer to “How long?” The question has run through the book since 6:10. The delay was never indifference; it was a harvest not yet ready, and Peter says what was ripening: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

The earth was reaped. After chapters of seals, trumpets, beasts and dragons, the end arrives in a single sentence with no resistance recorded: a sickle swung once by a man on a cloud. Revelation tells the story of this age more than once: the bowls of chapters 15 and 16 cover the same ground again, and each telling arrives at the same single return of Christ (19:11–16).

The grain of wheat. The one who reaps the earth once sowed himself into it: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Now he reaps what his death has grown.

Is this the rapture? It is the one gathering of God’s people at Christ’s visible return, which is what the New Testament means by our being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), with no hint of a secret removal of the church years before the end. Many believers were taught a secret rapture by teachers they love, and share this longing for the Lord; this commentary differs because in the New Testament the church is gathered at his visible appearing, after events Scripture names (Matthew 24:29–31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–4). That is the hope of every believer: not escape from history halfway through, but the Lord himself coming at its end to gather his harvest home.

In everyday life. If you are tired of waiting for the Lord to come, remember why he waits: there is grain still ripening, perhaps in your own family. Use the time, and pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers. And if you are anxious about the end, look at who holds the sickle: the Son of Man who loved you and gave himself for you.

Where Christians differ: is the grain harvest salvation or judgment? Some see both harvests as judgment, following Joel 3:13; others see the grain harvest as the gathering of the redeemed and the grape harvest as the judgment of the wicked. This commentary’s view: the grain harvest is most likely the gathering of God’s people at Christ’s return. Christ himself reaps it, as he gathers his elect (Matthew 24:31); in the Gospels the grain harvest is regularly salvation (Matthew 9:37–38; 13:30; John 4:35–38); and the 144,000 have just been called firstfruits (v. 4), the beginning of this harvest. Nothing is said about destroying the grain. The grape harvest, by contrast, is explicitly thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath. Together they picture the two outcomes of the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rebellious world, ripe in its sin, is gathered into the winepress of God’s wrath: the answer to the martyrs’ prayers, and a judgment covering the whole earth.

From the altar. The order to this second reaper comes from the altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered with incense (8:3–4), from which fire was thrown on the earth (8:5), and beneath which the martyrs cried, How long? (6:9–10). The martyrs asked; the answer comes from the place where the asking was received.

The vine of the earth. In contrast with Christ, the true vine (John 15:1), and with Israel, God’s vine, which yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7). The earth’s vine is humanity in rebellion, ripe in its sin.

The great winepress of the wrath of God. In a winepress grapes were trodden in a stone vat, and the red juice ran down into a lower vat. John is drawing on Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1–6, where the LORD comes from Edom with garments stained crimson: “I have trodden the winepress alone… I trod them in my anger… their lifeblood spattered on my garments” (Isaiah 63:3). In 19:15 Christ himself treads the winepress.

Outside the city. Executions were carried out outside the city (Leviticus 24:14), and judgment falls outside, where God’s enemies are (on which city, see the box below). Outside the camp the sin offering was burned, and outside the gate Jesus died: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

As high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia. A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (184 miles), roughly the length of the land of Israel from north to south. The numbers are symbolic and the imagery deliberately horrific: 1,600 is four times four times a hundred (or forty times forty), four being the number of the earth with its four corners, so it pictures a judgment covering the whole earth. Jewish writings used similar language (1 Enoch 100:3 has the horse walking up to its chest in the blood of sinners). It is not a forecast of casualties but a statement of scale, and of horror.

Two harvests, one day. The chapter ends without comment or apology, holding one of the book’s gentlest sentences (v. 13) and one of its most terrible. The two harvests are two sides of the one final coming: “The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels” (Matthew 13:39).

Two treadings outside the city. Here is the mercy hidden inside one of the most violent verses in the book: there are two treadings outside that city. At the first, on the cross, Christ went in alone and bore God’s wrath himself, and the blood was his own. Everyone trodden at the second will have refused the first.

Pruned, never trodden. Holy is the Judge who forgets no drop of his people’s blood, and answers from the altar the prayers that rose from it. The vine of the earth will meet a just end. But there is another vine, whose vinedresser is the Father. Its branches are pruned, never trodden; they are cut only to bear more fruit, and their fruit remains (John 15:1–2, 16). Every one of them once belonged to the vine of the earth, was joined to the true Vine by grace, and lives by his life.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal river of blood to be measured. Nor does it portray God as cruel. It is the just answer to the blood of the martyrs (6:10; 16:6; 19:2), and it falls only on those who refused his eternal gospel (v. 6).

Should I be glad about the judgment of the wicked? Glad that God will put every wrong right, yes; the martyrs pray for it, and heaven rejoices at his justice (19:1–2). But never in a gloating way, nor as though you deserved to be on the other side of the city wall. God himself takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Hold together justice and tears, as Jesus did over Jerusalem, and pray and speak while the gospel is still flying overhead.

In everyday life. When you hear of great evil and wonder whether anyone will ever answer for it, remember this winepress: no injustice will be overlooked. And when you are tempted to think your own sin small, remember the first treading, where the blood was his.

Uncertain wording. John does not say which city. Most take it as God’s city, where his people are, “the beloved city” of 20:9; some suggest Jerusalem, recalling Joel’s judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3:12–14), others Babylon, the great city (16:19). The first fits Revelation best, and on any reading judgment falls outside, away from the people God has gathered.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles, roughly the length of the land of Israel; a stadion was about 607 feet.

keyVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.
keyVerse.note: Every vision in the chapter is given for this. The Lamb secure on Zion, the gospel still flying overhead, Babylon already fallen, the cup of wrath and the coming harvest all tell believers under pressure that faithfulness to Christ is worth what it costs. The next verse shows where that endurance ends: in rest, with their deeds following them.

14.reflection:
The chapter opens with a crowd bearing the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, straight after the crowd marked by the beast (13:16; 14:1). What names or loyalties compete for that place in your life, in what fills your thoughts and what you are known for?

The three angels bring an eternal gospel, the news of Babylon’s fall and a solemn warning (vv. 6–11). Why does the good news include the warning? How does knowing that the Judge is the Lamb, who drank the cup himself, change the way you speak to others about judgment?

Babylon wins people with a glass of wine rather than a sword (v. 8). Where do you feel her pull most: money, comfort, approval, entertainment? What would it look like to hold it more loosely this month?

Heaven commands John to write that the dead who die in the Lord are blessed, that they rest and their deeds follow them (v. 13). How does this speak to your fear of death, your grief for believers you have lost, or your sense that your life has accomplished little?

21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Where we are. Babylon has fallen, the Rider on the white horse has come, and the dead have been judged (17:1–20:15). Now John sees where the whole Bible has been heading, in a vision that runs on to 22:5.

The message. God will live with his people, in person and for ever, in a creation made new, and everything that has spoiled his world, death, tears, sin and night, will be gone. The holy city that comes down is a people before it is a place, the bride of the Lamb, and at its centre is not a building but a Person. And the water of life is offered now, free, to anyone who is thirsty.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia were small, some poor and some compromised, under cities proud of their temples and trade (see the introduction). Babylon looked permanent, and martyrs like Antipas (2:13) seemed to have died for nothing. This chapter shows which city lasts, and what faithfulness is worth.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–8 give the new creation in a few strokes: the city coming down as a bride (vv. 1–2), God dwelling with his people and wiping away every tear (vv. 3–4), God himself making all things new and giving the water of life without payment (vv. 5–6), and the two destinies, the conqueror’s heritage and the second death (vv. 7–8). Verses 9–27 show the bride close up as a city, the opposite of the prostitute Babylon: one people of Israel’s tribes and the Lamb’s apostles (vv. 9–14), a jewelled cube like the Most Holy Place (vv. 15–21), with no temple, sun or night because God and the Lamb are there, and open only to those in the Lamb’s book (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. This is not a consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed but the goal for which the whole story was told, and every thread comes home to the Lamb: the bride is his wife, the temple is God and the Lamb, the lamp is the Lamb, the register is his book. The one who said “I thirst” on the cross gives the water of life away.

For us. Our hope is not escape from the world God made but that world mended, so faithful work and patient grief are not wasted. Come to the spring while it is offered, and hold on to Christ when it costs you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will make his world new and live in it with his people for ever. John sees the first creation pass away and the holy city come down from God as a bride for her husband (vv. 1–2). A voice from the throne announces what that means: God’s dwelling is with man, and every tear, every death and every pain is gone (vv. 3–4). Then God himself speaks, guaranteeing his words, declaring the work done and offering the water of life free to the thirsty (vv. 5–6). Last come the two destinies: the one who conquers inherits God as Father, while those who persist in unbelief have their portion in the second death (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth, renewed rather than replaced, and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make this world new, and his people, the bride of the Lamb, will come down from him to live on it.

A new heaven and a new earth. The Bible opened with “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), and here it says it again with one word changed. Isaiah had promised “new heavens and a new earth”, where the sound of weeping would be heard no more (Isaiah 65:17–19; 66:22). The Greek word for “new” (kainon) usually means new in quality, made fresh, rather than newly made. What has passed away is the first form of things, fallen and under the curse (20:11), not God’s handiwork itself: he is not scrapping his creation but making it new.

The pattern of the resurrection body. The risen body of Jesus shows what this means: the same body that was laid in the tomb, transformed and glorified, with the wounds still in the hands. So the Christian hope is not escape into something vaporous, but this world, soil, water, bodies, work, cities, put right. What God did for Jesus’ body he will do for the whole creation. He does not abandon what he made.

The sea was no more. This troubles people who love the sea, but John is not talking oceanography. In this book the sea is the ancient image of chaos: lying like glass before God’s throne (4:6), the source of the beast (13:1), the swallower of the dead (20:13). And John is writing from an island, cut off by the sea from his churches. The next chapter has a river, so the promise is not that there will be no water, but that nothing will be left that separates, threatens or devours.

The holy city, new Jerusalem. The city is the fulfilment of all God’s promises to Zion. Ezekiel’s vision ended with its name, “The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35), and Abraham “was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

Coming down out of heaven from God. The city is God’s gift, not a human achievement, and most popular pictures of the Christian hope get the direction backwards. Babel tried to build up to heaven (Genesis 11:4); the new Jerusalem comes down from it. Believers will rise to meet the Lord at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17), but to welcome him on his way down, not to leave the earth behind. The Bible ends not with humanity evacuated to the sky but with heaven arriving on a renewed earth, as Christians have always prayed without noticing: “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. “Adorned” (kekosmēmenēn; our word cosmetics comes from it) means made beautiful. The city does not house the bride; it is the bride, a people, as verse 9 makes plain when an angel offers to show John the Bride and shows him a city.

The husband is the Lamb. Verse 9 names the one she is adorned for, and even her fine linen was granted to her (19:8). So Scripture’s last picture of God’s people is not of people who finally made themselves worthy, but of a bride whom a crucified and risen Husband has washed and dressed for himself.

In everyday life. The garden you tend, the work you do well, the city whose good you seek: these are not meaningless because this world is passing, for God intends to make it new. And if you are weary of a broken world, a broken body or a broken family, look up. What is coming is not an escape from all that God made, but all that God made, mended.

Is heaven now the same as the new earth? Not yet. A believer who dies goes to be with Christ in heaven, conscious and at rest, which is far better than this life (Philippians 1:23). But the end of the story is the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return and life with God on the new earth: with Christ in heaven at death, then with him in the new creation, bodily, for ever. Talk of going to heaven speaks truly of the first stage; this chapter is about the second, and it is better still.

Will we be ourselves, and will we know each other? Yes. Resurrection raises the same person, not a stranger. The disciples recognised the risen Jesus, Moses and Elijah were known on the mountain (Matthew 17:3), and Paul says, “then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Jesus does say that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), probably because the marriage every human marriage pointed to, Christ and his bride, has arrived. But nothing good in the love of husband and wife, parents and children, or friends in Christ will be lost; it will be taken up into something larger.

Where Christians differ: will this earth be destroyed and replaced, or renewed? Some, reading 2 Peter 3:10, where the KJV says the earth and its works will be burned up, believe the present creation will be annihilated and replaced (the earliest manuscripts there read that the earth will be exposed, or laid bare, and most modern Bibles follow them). Others think of eternity as a purely spiritual existence in heaven. Faithful Christians have held each view, and all expect the same Lord. This commentary’s view: this creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Paul says creation will be set free from its bondage (Romans 8:21); Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things (Matthew 19:28); Peter speaks of the restoration of all things (Acts 3:21). The fire of 2 Peter 3 purifies, as metal is refined, and lays the earth bare to judgment. As our bodies will be raised and transformed, not replaced, so will creation.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will live with his people for ever, and everything that made them weep will be gone.

The dwelling place of God. “Dwelling place” (hē skēnē) is the word for a tent, the tabernacle: God will pitch his tent with them (7:15). Follow that word and the whole Bible is on one thread. God walked with the man and the woman in a garden, and they were sent out. He told Moses, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8), and a tent was pitched in the middle of the camp. Solomon built a house and the glory filled it, and Ezekiel watched that glory leave. Then the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us, and John, who is writing this, is the man who wrote that sentence (John 1:14). Then the Spirit came and made a temple out of ordinary people (1 Corinthians 3:16). And here is the end of it: no tent in a camp, no house on a hill, no veil, no exclusions; God with man, permanently, in the open. What Eden had, and sin lost, is restored and surpassed. The Lord has been his people’s dwelling place in all generations (Psalm 90:1); now he makes his dwelling with them.

They will be his people. The heart of God’s covenant all through Scripture, I will be your God and you shall be my people, and I will dwell among you (Leviticus 26:11–12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27), is here reported not as a promise but as a fact.

God himself. Not an angel, not glory at a safe distance, not merely his gifts, but God himself: Immanuel, God with us, in full. What the Bible has been arranging all along is not better circumstances but his presence.

He will wipe away every tear. The promise is made twice in this book (7:17), and both times God does it himself, with his hand, on a face: not an angel with a cloth, not time healing it. Isaiah promised it first: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isaiah 25:8).

Death shall be no more. Four things are abolished. Death comes first, which has taken everyone we have ever lost, now thrown into the lake of fire (20:14; 1 Corinthians 15:26). Mourning is the heaviness that settles on a house after a death; crying (kraugē) is the outcry grief makes; pain includes the toil laid on us by the curse in Genesis 3, now undone. Isaiah heard it too: sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10; 65:19).

The former things have passed away. Every one is answered by removal, not by explanation; nobody here is told why it happened. The promise is not that the tears will finally make sense, but that God will wipe them away and the thing that caused them will be dead. This is the verse to hold when the reason for a grief has never arrived and probably never will.

In everyday life. These are verses for funerals and hospital corridors, worth having by heart before the phone rings. When you sit with someone who is mourning, you need not explain their loss; be present, and if the moment is right, read them these verses. And when your own pain comes, tell yourself: this is one of the former things, and the former things are passing away.

Is it wrong to grieve now, if this is coming? No. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus, shortly before he raised him (John 11:35), so tears and hope can stand side by side in the same heart. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve, but not to grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love that has lost its object for a while; this verse does not shame it but promises it an end. So weep honestly, at the graveside and in the car, and bring the tears to the God who has promised to wipe them away himself.

Will we remember those we loved who are lost? Scripture does not explain, and we should not claim to know more than it says. But we will be ourselves, known and knowing (1 Corinthians 13:12), and God himself will wipe away every tear. We will see as God sees and share his perfect justice and love, and nothing we remember will spoil the joy he gives. That is a reason now to pray for those we love, and to speak to them while there is time.

Textual note. Many of the earliest manuscripts read “peoples”, plural, in “they will be his people”. Either way the promise once made to Israel now embraces people from every nation (5:9; 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself guarantees the new creation: he is already making all things new, his purpose is complete, and he gives the water of life free to anyone who is thirsty. This is one of the very few places in Revelation where the One on the throne is plainly the speaker; the last was 1:8.

I am making all things new. “I am making” is present tense: it is happening, not merely scheduled. And it is all things new, not all new things: renewal, not replacement. Isaiah heard the same voice: “Behold, I am doing a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19).

Trustworthy and true. The third and last time John is told to write a sentence down (14:13; 19:9), each a promise a suffering church would find nearly impossible to believe, each with its guarantee.

It is done! The same cry as at the seventh bowl (16:17): the whole plan of God is complete. It echoes in thought, though not in the same Greek word, the cry from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30): the finished work there made this final victory certain.

The Alpha and the Omega. The title from 1:8, from the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. God was the first letter when there was nothing yet to write, and he is the last now that everything has been written; nothing in history has slipped out from between them. He is the Alpha, before the first star, and the Omega, after the last tear.

Without payment. At the summit of the book, after the great white throne and the lake of fire, comes an offer: not a wage but a drink given away. “Without payment” (dōrean) is the word Paul uses of being justified “by his grace as a gift” (Romans 3:24), and it answers Isaiah’s call: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). The only qualification is thirst, not desert or improvement, and the book makes the offer once more with the doors held open (22:17).

The spring has a face. John’s Gospel shows who carries out this offer. At a well in Samaria a tired man asked a Samaritan woman for a drink and then offered her living water, so that whoever drinks it “will never be thirsty again” (John 4:10–14). At the feast he stood and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). In this book the Lamb guides his people to springs of living water (7:17). The water of life is not a substance handed over a counter but life with God, and it comes through his Son.

It was not free to him. The God who owes no one anything ends history by giving a drink away. It is free to us because it was not free to him: the Son who offers it hung on a cross and said, “I thirst” (John 19:28), and went without, so that all who come to him might drink and live.

What he is making new now. This is not only a promise for the far end of history; the One who says it has already begun. On Easter morning a body that had been dead came out of the tomb, the first piece of the new creation set down in the middle of the old (1 Corinthians 15:20). Since then the risen Christ has been making people new by his Spirit, so that anyone in him “is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17; 3:18), and the renewal will spread until creation itself is set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). So nothing in your life is too old or broken for his reach: a hardened habit, a marriage gone cold, a grief that has set like concrete. Bring it to him by name, ask him to make it new, and take the small step of obedience in front of you, leaning on his work, not your resolve. Where he has not yet mended something, hold on. He is not finished.

Why the new never stays new. Our culture loves the new: the latest phone, the fresh start, the reinvented self. Advertising promises that this time the newness will last, and it never does; the new life after the move or the promotion soon feels like the old one, because we brought ourselves along. Reinventing yourself is exhausting for the same reason: if I must make myself new, I am also the worn material I have to work with. The Bible is more hopeful and less flattering. The longing for newness is right, because the world and we are both worn out, but real newness cannot be bought or performed. God does it, to old things, from the inside, and it does not wear off. The One on the throne does not say, Make yourself new. He says, I am making all things new, and anyone who is in Christ is already part of it.

What if I do not feel thirsty? Then ask God to make you thirsty, and notice that you are already asking. Thirst is not a religious feeling but need, there whether you feel it or not: the restless dissatisfaction no achievement fills, the guilt you cannot shake off, the fear of death, the longing for something you cannot name. Many come to Christ simply tired of drinking from wells that do not satisfy (Jeremiah 2:13). Come as you are. The offer is to the thirsty, and the Spirit who makes people thirsty is the same Spirit who brings them to the spring.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who holds on to Christ will inherit God himself as Father; those who finally refuse him will have their share in the second death.

The one who conquers. Each of the seven letters ended with a promise to the one who conquers (chapters 2–3): the tree of life, hidden manna, the morning star, white garments, a seat on the throne. Here is the sum of them all. Chapter 12 showed who conquers: those who hold on to Christ at cost. “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11).

This heritage. The last promise to the conqueror is not a thing at all but God himself, as Father. The meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), and believers are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17): everything else promised to the conqueror described what belongs to a son in his father’s house.

I will be his God and he will be my son. God said this to David about the son who would sit on his throne (2 Samuel 7:14), and it was fulfilled in Christ. Paul applies it to all believers: “I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me” (2 Corinthians 6:18). Here it is handed, without qualification, to anyone who conquers: through Christ, the Son, believers become sons and daughters by adoption, heirs with full rights (Galatians 4:4–7). God takes those who were by nature “children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3) and gives them his name, his love, his house and his inheritance, with no trial period and no second-class rank. Adoption is an act of God, not a feeling, given to all who receive Christ (John 1:12), and he does not undo it.

The cowardly. Eight kinds of people follow, and the first will stop any honest reader: the cowardly, ahead of the murderers, in a book written to people with every reason to be frightened. The word does not mean a Christian who is afraid. If fear disqualified, the list would include Elijah under a broom tree, Peter in a courtyard and every apostle on the night of the arrest; Christ said “Fear not” to John precisely because John was on his face and terrified (1:17). It names the person whose fear made the decision: who denied the name, took the mark, said “Caesar is Lord”, went home safe and never came back. Cowardice here is not an emotion but abandoning Christ for safety. A believer who reads verse 8, trembles and runs to Christ shows by that very reaction that it does not describe him. And Peter, who denied Christ three times with oaths, was given breakfast on a beach and a commission (John 21).

The faithless and the detestable. The faithless are those who refuse to trust Christ; the detestable share Babylon’s abominations (17:4).

All liars. Those who belong to the father of lies (John 8:44). The last item closes a loop: the dragon, the second beast and Babylon all deceive, and of the redeemed on Mount Zion John wrote, “in their mouth no lie was found” (14:5). One thing that finally separates the two companies is whether they belong to the truth.

Their portion. The conqueror’s heritage and the portion of the faithless stand side by side: an inheritance in the Father’s house, or a share in the lake. There is no third place.

The Heir who made us heirs. The heir of all things, who had every right to the inheritance, went to the cross so that rebels, cowards and liars could be washed, adopted and given his name. The final reward of this book is not property but sonship.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who has ever committed these sins is beyond salvation. Paul lists similar sins and then says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). It describes those who persist in these sins without repentance, refusing the free water of life (v. 6). Even a murderer or an idolater who comes thirsty to Christ will be given it.

In everyday life. Watch the two sins on this list that sound smallest: cowardice and lying. Where are you tempted this week to keep quiet about Christ to stay safe, or to shade the truth to look better? Say the true thing, kindly. You have not received a spirit of fear but “the Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15), and he makes timid children bold to own the Christ who first owned them.

Does “all liars” mean that a Christian who has lied is lost? No. It describes the settled character of those who belong to the lie (22:15), not believers who have sinned and repented. Every believer has lied, and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). The warning is for those who make falsehood their way of life, and a call to everyone to come to Christ.

How can the God who wipes away every tear also have a lake of fire? Because the God who wipes away tears takes seriously what caused them. A judge who shrugged at murder, cruelty and lies would not be kind but indifferent to their victims, and the tears of verse 4 would never truly be dried. Hell is not God losing his temper. It is a holy God giving sinners, at the last, the just reward of their sin and what they have insisted on all along: life without him (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And the offer of free water (v. 6) comes before the warning (v. 8). No one in the lake is there because the spring was closed to him.

Do I have to be a hero to be one who conquers? No. In Revelation conquering is holding on to Christ when it costs you, and the Lamb is the model: he conquered by being slain (5:5–6). The one who conquers is the ordinary believer who keeps trusting Christ through illness, mockery, temptation and loss, who falls and gets up, and does not give him up: a persevering faith that is God’s own work, kept alive by him to the end (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). If you are still clinging to him today, however weakly, you are among the conquerors, and the inheritance is yours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bride of the Lamb is a city where God lives among all his people with nothing between. John is shown it as the twin and opposite of the prostitute Babylon (17:1–3), radiant with God’s glory (vv. 9–11). Its gates carry the names of Israel’s tribes and its foundations the Lamb’s apostles: one people, built on their witness to him (vv. 12–14). Measured as a vast cube, it is the Most Holy Place enlarged to hold everyone (vv. 15–17), built of jewels, gold and pearl (vv. 18–21). It needs no temple, no sun and no locked gate, because God and the Lamb are there, and none enter but those written in the Lamb’s book of life (vv. 22–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube, the Most Holy Place enlarged, with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart into the Holy Place is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel who showed John the prostitute now shows him the Bride, and she is a city shining with the glory of God. From here to 22:5 John is shown the city in detail, in a section built as the twin and opposite of 17:1–19:10.

One of the seven angels. At 17:1 one of the bowl angels said, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute.” The same rank, the same opening word, and a different woman: the hands that poured out the bowls of wrath now draw back the curtain on the bride, and only one city is left standing.

The Bride, the wife of the Lamb. The marriage of 19:7 has happened: the church is now the Lamb’s wife. Every wedding in the Bible, from Adam waking to find Eve to the wedding at Cana where the wine ran out, has been a rehearsal for this.

A great, high mountain. For the fourth time John is “in the Spirit” (1:10; 4:2; 17:3). To see the prostitute he was carried into a wilderness; to see the Bride, to a great, high mountain, where Ezekiel too was shown a city (Ezekiel 40:2). Many readers also hear a contrast with another mountain, where the devil showed Jesus the kingdoms of the world and their glory (Matthew 4:8). Jesus refused that glory for the cross, and here is what the Father gives him.

The holy city Jerusalem. The angel promised a Bride and showed a city, and John sees no change of subject: the people are the place. For the second time the city comes down (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Having the glory of God. The first thing said about the city is not its size but the glory of God, the presence later Jewish teachers called the shekinah, which filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and the temple so that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:11; Ezekiel 43:2–5). What had to be curtained off is now the city’s ordinary lighting.

Like a jasper. Jasper is how 4:3 described the One seated on the throne, so the city looks like him. A bride wearing her husband’s likeness is not a bad definition of what the church is finally for (2 Corinthians 3:18). The bride of the Lamb, gathered from the slums and the palaces of every age, so often unfaithful and so often forgiven, wears at last the likeness of the One on the throne.

How can the church I know be this bride? The church you know is quarrelsome, slow, sometimes hypocritical, and you are part of the problem. Christ knows that better than you, and loves her anyway. He “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her”, and he will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). She is not beautiful because she made herself so; she shines with the glory of God. What you see now is the bride on the way to the wedding, dusty from the road. Do not despise what Christ is making beautiful. Stay in her, serve her, and pray for her.

Uncertain wording. “Jasper” translates iaspis, but ancient names for stones do not map neatly onto ours. Modern jasper is opaque, while John’s is “clear as crystal”, so some think a diamond or another clear, brilliant stone is meant. The point is not in doubt: the city shines like the One on the throne (4:3).

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city has a boundary that holds, and Israel’s tribes and the Lamb’s apostles are built into it as one people of God.

A great, high wall. A wall had one purpose, to keep an army out, but this city has no enemy left (20:10, 14), and its gates are never shut (v. 25). The wall says that this place has an inside: nothing unclean will ever enter it (v. 27). Every good thing you have known could be got at, the marriage, the friendship, the church, the health; something always found a way in, usually from the inside. Here at last is a good thing with a boundary that holds.

At the gates twelve angels. The first heavenly guards in the Bible are cherubim outside a garden with a flaming sword, posted to keep people out (Genesis 3:24). Here twelve angels stand at twelve gates that never close (v. 25). The sentries are still at their stations, with nothing left to do but watch the nations walk in.

The names of the twelve tribes. Three gates on each side follow the camp of Israel in the wilderness, three tribes on each side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2), and the plan of Ezekiel’s city, with twelve gates named for the tribes (Ezekiel 48:30–35). God’s promises to Israel are kept, and every believer enters through a gate with an Israelite name over it, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22).

On the east three gates. People “will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:29). This city has no back door, and nobody arrives at the wrong side.

Twelve foundations. Israel and the church are built into one structure, neither an extension bolted on to the other, one reason many readers take the twenty-four elders (4:4) as Israel and the church together. Paul said the same thing without the architecture: “members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:19–20).

The twelve names of the twelve apostles. Twelve men are named in the stonework of the eternal city, and every reader knows what they were like: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, a man who denied Christ with oaths, and a man who would not believe the resurrection without putting his hand in the wound. Babylon’s great ones were her merchants (18:23); this city’s are twelve provincial nobodies who suffered for saying that a crucified man had risen, many of whom, as the early church remembered, died for it. Grace builds with unlikely stones. God does not choose the impressive; he makes the chosen glorious.

Apostles of the Lamb. The words “of the Lamb” carry the weight. These men are in the foundations because they were with him, saw him die and rise, and told what they had seen (Acts 1:21–22; 1 John 1:1–3); the city stands on their witness. And the gates bear Israel’s names because all the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). He is the son of Abraham and the son of David, Israel’s Messiah, and every Gentile who walks in comes as a guest of Israel’s King. Tribes on the gates, apostles below, and the Lamb holding the whole city together.

What it does not mean. Not that there are two peoples of God, one Jewish and one Christian, with different destinies. There is one city, one bride, one people, built on Christ.

Then does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Christians differ on the details. Many Reformed readers, from the Puritans onward, have understood Romans 11:25–29 to promise a future turning of many Jews to Christ before the end, because “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”; others read “all Israel” there as the whole elect people of God, Jew and Gentile. Both agree with this chapter: whatever God does for Israel, he does through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and into the one city. So pray for Jewish people to know their Messiah, honour the people through whom the Scriptures and the Saviour came, and reject every form of contempt for them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God measures the city to claim it as his own, and its shape shows that the whole of it is the Most Holy Place, vast enough for all his people.

A measuring rod of gold. Ezekiel watched an angel measure the new temple and city (Ezekiel 40–48). Measuring in this book means claiming and protecting. At 11:1 it was partial; this one is total: the city is complete, secure, and God’s.

The city lies foursquare. “Foursquare” means square: nothing lopsided or left over. A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 12,000 stadia is about 2,220 kilometres (1,380 miles), roughly the distance from London to Athens, in every direction, including up. Nobody is meant to picture this; the figure answers a fear few Christians admit, whether there will be room. 12,000 is 12 × 1,000, the people of God (twelve) in fullness (a thousand): room for the great multitude no one can count (7:9).

Its length and width and height are equal. There is one cube in the Bible. In Solomon’s temple the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high (1 Kings 6:20), and one man, the high priest, entered it once a year with blood. The new Jerusalem is that room expanded to the size of a continent, with all God’s people living where once only the high priest could go. That is why John will see no temple (v. 22).

The forerunner behind the curtain. How can a whole people live in a room once closed to all but one? Hebrews answers. Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). And he did not go in to come out again alone. He went behind the curtain “as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:19–20), the first of a great company. Every believer in the city stands where Christ has gone first, welcomed because he is welcomed.

144 cubits. 144 is 12 × 12, the number of God’s people, as in the 144,000 (7:4). At about 45 centimetres to the cubit, that is some 65 metres (216 feet), around a city over two thousand kilometres high. The proportions are deliberately impossible: the wall is a boundary, not a defence (see the note on vv. 12–14).

In everyday life. When you pray, you are not shouting through a closed door; through Christ you already have access to the Father (Hebrews 10:19–22). Come in boldly, and come often. And if you have feared that there will be no room for you, because of your past, your weakness or your failures, look at the size of the city. God did not build it small.

If the numbers are symbols, is the new creation real? Yes, entirely. Symbols in Scripture say not less than the truth but more than plain words can carry. The cube tells you what no floor plan could: every one of God’s people will live as near to God as the high priest ever was, and nearer. The new creation is as real as the risen body of Jesus, which could be touched and ate fish (Luke 24:39–43). The symbols stop us shrinking it to the size of our imagination.

Uncertain wording. John does not say whether 12,000 stadia is each side or the distance all round (most take it as each side), nor whether 144 cubits is the wall’s height or its thickness. “By human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement” most likely means that the angel used ordinary human units. Either way, the symbolism is the same.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is built of the most precious things imaginable, because it is the dwelling of God with his priestly people. Even its foundations recall the high priest’s breastpiece.

The wall was built of jasper. Jasper is the appearance of the One on the throne (4:3; see the note on vv. 9–11). Isaiah promised Jerusalem foundations of sapphires, battlements of agate, gates of carbuncles and walls of precious stones (Isaiah 54:11–12). Babylon wore gold, jewels and pearls (17:4); here they belong to the bride.

Pure gold, like clear glass. “Pure gold” (chrysion katharon) recalls the gold-covered Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20), but this gold lets light through, a kind unknown on earth, and so does the street: purity and glory together, with nothing to cast a shadow or hide what is behind it.

Every kind of jewel. The high priest of Israel wore a breastpiece set with twelve stones, one for each tribe, and he bore “the names of the sons of Israel” on his heart when he went into the Holy Place, “to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD” (Exodus 28:29). About eight of John’s twelve names appear in the Greek translation of that list, and the others may be other names for similar stones. So the foundations are the breastpiece, laid out flat and built into the ground. What one man carried over his heart into the holy place is now the foundation everybody walks on.

The first was jasper. John names the stones one by one, like a man walking along a wall naming colours: overwhelming beauty and variety, like the many nations of the redeemed. Jasper and carnelian, the first and sixth stones here, are the two John used of the One seated on the throne, and emerald, the fourth, was the colour of the rainbow round it (4:3).

Each of the gates made of a single pearl. Pearls were among the costliest things in the ancient world; Jesus told of a merchant who sold all that he had to buy one “pearl of great value” (Matthew 13:45–46). A gate of a single pearl is beyond imagination, and these are never shut (v. 25). Revelation says who may walk through: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates” (22:14), and the robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). The gates are priceless; the way through them was paid for by him.

The street of the city was pure gold. Babylon’s cargo list began with gold and silver and jewels and pearls (18:12), and merchants wept when they could no longer sell it. Here gold is paving: everything the world killed for turns out, in the only city that lasts, to be what people walk on. The only treasure anyone in the city looks at is the face of God (22:4).

Does this mean God wants me rich now? No; this is the opposite of a prosperity gospel. The gold is under feet precisely so that no one will ever want it again. Jesus warned that “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15), and Paul that “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). God gives some of his people wealth to steward and many poverty to bear, and loves both the same. This verse promises that the poorest believer will one day walk on what the richest unbeliever spent his life chasing.

Uncertain wording. The ancient gem names are uncertain, and did not always mean the stone that bears the name today: ancient “sapphire” was probably lapis lazuli, and chrysolite and jacinth are hard to identify, so translations vary. The sense is not in doubt: twelve brilliant stones of many colours.
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city has no temple, because God and the Lamb fill all of it and nothing stands between them and their people. There is no holy place to go to, because the whole city is one.

I saw no temple in the city. For Israel the temple was the centre of life, where God dwelt and sacrifices were offered, and Ezekiel spent nine chapters on a new one (Ezekiel 40–48). A Jewish reader would expect a glorious temple here. There is none. A temple answers one problem: God is holy and people are not, so there must be a set-apart place, priests to go between, rules for approach, and a barrier between the god and the worshipper. Israel’s had a court for the nations, courts beyond it for Israel and for priests, and behind a curtain a room one man entered once a year with blood in his hands.

Its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Worship has not ended; the problem a temple exists for, how sinful people can be near a holy God, has been solved by Someone, and the verse names him. God and the Lamb together are the temple, for the Son shares the Father’s presence and glory. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on a particular mountain (John 4:21–24); here that hour has fully come.

There is no temple because there is a Lamb. The last two words, “the Lamb”, are the answer. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51): from the top, by Someone reaching down. This verse is that tearing carried to its conclusion. He is not merely the priest and not merely the sacrifice; he is the building. In the temple courts he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, and “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19–21). They destroyed it on a hill outside the city wall, and on the third day God raised it, alive for evermore. In the city to come the Temple has a face.

Nearness no one earns. There is no outer court, no restricted section; nobody is nearer to God than anybody else, and nobody waits outside for a priest to come back and tell him it went well. Plenty of people, churchgoers and sceptics both, assume that nearness to God is earned by ceremony, effort or decency. In this city nobody is nearer for having tried harder, because there was only ever one way in, and it was a Lamb. The redeemed do not go to a holy place; they live inside one, with its Maker in the middle. Praise to the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, the temple, the priest and the sacrifice, in whose presence we shall dwell for ever.

What it does not mean. No temple does not mean no worship: the whole city is a temple, and all of life is worship. Nor does God’s final plan hold a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices; Christ’s sacrifice has fulfilled them all. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists (who expect a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth with a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem), read the prophets differently, and they are brothers who love the same Christ. This commentary reads the thousand years of chapter 20 as Christ’s present reign (the view called amillennial) and expects no temple, because Hebrews says Christ’s one offering has made the old system obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:12–14).

Then do church buildings and Sunday worship matter now? Yes, but not as temples. A church building is a meeting place, not a holy house where God lives and elsewhere he does not; the temple of God now is his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22), and the Lord meets them wherever two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). Gathering matters greatly, for God tells us not to neglect it (Hebrews 10:24–25), and the Lord’s Day is a rehearsal for the city: his people together before his face. But no place, priest or ritual stands between you and God. Through Christ you may draw near anywhere, at any hour, and on that day there will be nowhere that is not his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s glory is the city’s light, shining through the Lamb, and by that light the redeemed nations live in perfect safety and welcome.

No need of sun or moon. The second thing missing, after the temple, is the sun. Isaiah 60 lies behind these verses: nations coming to Zion’s light, gates open continually, and the promise that “the sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19). The sun and moon have been doing a job on loan for the whole of history, and the owner has arrived.

Its lamp is the Lamb. “Lamp” (lychnos) is a household lamp. God’s glory is the light, and the Lamb is the lamp through which it shines. So he has been since the first chapter, where “his face was like the sun shining in full strength” (1:16), and what he said of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). We see “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). No one in the city will ever see God’s glory except through the Lamb, and no one will ever need to see it any other way.

By its light will the nations walk. The redeemed of every nation, their diversity preserved (Isaiah 60:3). Babel scattered the nations in confusion; the Lamb gathers them, not into one language and one culture, but into one light.

The kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. The phrase was used of those who committed immorality with Babylon (17:2) and made war on the Lamb (19:19), but John is not saying that rebels are let in unchanged; he means redeemed people from every nation, kings among them. The good things of human culture, cleansed of sin, are brought into the new creation. The text does not list this glory, and guessing is a poor substitute for reading, but what the peoples of the earth have made and been is not simply erased. That is a real word to anyone who wonders whether ordinary work has any future: whether music, building, and the raising of crops and children and languages and cities are all going into a fire. The gates are open, and something is being brought in.

No night there. In ancient cities the gates were shut at sundown for protection. This city’s never shut, because the hour for shutting them never comes: perfect safety and perfect welcome. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning knows what is being taken away. Night in Scripture is when the thief comes and the enemy moves, when a person is alone with what he has done, when the sick get worse and the frightened more frightened. There is none of it, ever again.

Like a flame through a lamp. The Light of the world hung on a cross while darkness covered the land, and on the third day he rose before the sun was up. Now the glory of God shines through him like a flame through a lamp, the nations he bought walk by his light, and kings who once made war on him walk in carrying gifts. Glory to the Lamb, the lamp of the city, in whose light we shall see light.

In everyday life. When night comes, literally or in your soul, the sleepless hour, the dark diagnosis, remember that night has an end, and the city is coming where the Lamb is the lamp and the gates are never shut.

Will there still be different nations and cultures? It seems so. John sees nations walking by the light, and earlier a multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (7:9). The new creation is not a grey sameness. As each believer will be himself, made perfect, so the peoples seem to be there as themselves, cleansed of pride and hostility, every tongue confessing “that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:11). So love believers whose culture is not yours. You will be living with them for ever, and their way of praising the Lamb will be part of the glory.

Will we be busy, or bored? Neither. Scripture pictures the age to come not as idleness but as reigning, serving and worshipping (22:3, 5), with bodies that do not wear out and hearts that do not drift. Boredom is the soul running out of interest, and with an infinite God there will always be more to know and enjoy. If worship for ever sounds dull, that is because our worship now is so thin. Ask God this week to give you a taste of it, and read Revelation 4–5 aloud.

Where Christians differ: does this mean the nations outside are finally saved? Some read the nations and kings coming in as unbelievers saved after the final judgment, so that all will eventually enter, a tender hope. This commentary’s view: the nations here are the redeemed nations, the great multitude from every nation (7:9), who come into the city because their names are written in the Lamb’s book (v. 27). The lake of fire is final (20:15; 21:8), and outside the city are those who practise wickedness (22:15). The passage shows the redeemed drawn from every nation, and the best of human culture brought in, purified; it does not teach a second chance after death.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it”, adding “of them which are saved”. The best manuscripts simply read “the nations”. The addition explains correctly who the nations are.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of every nation is brought into the city, but nothing unclean ever enters; only those written in the Lamb’s book of life come in. The two verses guard each other.

The glory and the honour of the nations. Verse 26 is the widest sentence in the chapter: the glory of the nations, not of one nation or of the church only, as Isaiah foresaw: “the wealth of the nations shall come to you” (Isaiah 60:5, 11). The multitude from every nation (7:9) does not arrive empty-handed (see the note on vv. 23–25).

Nothing unclean will ever enter it. The gates are always open, but not unguarded. This is not a city where everything is welcome, but one where everything welcome has been made clean. Isaiah had promised that “there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean” (Isaiah 52:1). “Unclean” (koinon, literally “common”) is the word Jews used for what was defiled and could not come near God’s holy things (Acts 10:14). This is not fussiness; it is what holiness is. “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5), and a city that is all his dwelling can no more hold uncleanness than noon can hold midnight.

Detestable or false. The sins of Babylon and the beast. Detestable is the Old Testament’s word for idolatry, written on the prostitute’s forehead (17:5); false comes last in a book where the dragon, the false prophet and Babylon all ruled by deceit. The city of the One who is true has no room for a lie.

The Lamb’s book of life. Entry is not decided by a moral record. The one qualification is belonging to the Lamb: not works, nationality or religious heritage, but the Lamb’s choice and the Lamb’s blood. These are those whose names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). At 13:8 the KJV joins from the foundation of the world to the Lamb slain instead; the Greek can be read either way, and 17:8 favours the reading given here. This is the last mention of the book of life in Revelation (the KJV has one more at 22:19, where the Greek manuscripts read tree of life), and it lands exactly where it did at the great white throne (20:12, 15): not on what a person achieved but on whether his name is in a register belonging to a Lamb who was slain.

How the unclean become clean. The two halves of these verses are not in tension. Nothing unclean enters, and the whole book has shown how the unclean become clean, in the most impossible image it could find: “They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). Nobody walks in on his own record. Everybody who walks in has had something done to him first.

In the flow. The chapter break is a later convenience; John goes straight on to the river and the tree (22:1–5). These verses gather up the chapter: verse 8 said who has no part in the new creation, verse 27 who has no way through its gates; verse 6 offered water without payment, and the Lamb’s book names those who drink it.

Because he is there. Before there was a world to fall, the Lamb had a book; he set his love on people who would one day be unclean, and went to the cross to wash them. Now every name in the book walks through the gates, and not one is missing. God himself is with them. There is no temple, because he is there. There is no sun, because he is there. There is no night, because he is there. And there are no tears, because he has come over and attended to their faces with his own hand. “To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood... be glory and dominion forever and ever” (1:5–6).

In everyday life. If your name is in the Lamb’s book, the gates of pearl are open to you, so live clean in the light of that day. Is there anything you do in secret that would not belong inside that city? Put it out of your life this week; confess it, and ask a trusted brother or sister for help. Not to earn your entry: the Lamb paid for it, his perfect obedience is counted as yours, and your faltering obedience is accepted for his sake. Do it because you are going to live in a city of light, and the Spirit who will make you perfect there is at work in you here.

Will I still sin there? No. The struggle every believer knows, wanting to do right and finding evil close at hand (Romans 7:21), will be over. Those who enter are not only forgiven but made perfect in holiness (Hebrews 12:23), and “when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Nothing unclean will ever enter, including the remnants of sin in you. For a tired Christian this is one of the sweetest promises here: no more sorrow, and no more sinning.

How can I be sure my name is written? Not by searching a secret register, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. The names written there are the names of those who trust him, and Jesus said, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). If you are resting on Christ alone, and not on your record, you may be sure. Assurance grows as you see the Spirit’s fruit in you, as you walk in obedience, and as “the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16). If you are not sure, do not try harder to feel sure. Come to him again.
