He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.<sup>4</sup>He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”<sup>5</sup>And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.”<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.<sup>7</sup>The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son.<sup>8</sup>But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”<sup>9</sup>Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.”<sup>10</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,<sup>11</sup>having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.<sup>12</sup>It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed—<sup>13</sup>on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.<sup>14</sup>And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls.<sup>16</sup>The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.<sup>17</sup>He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.<sup>18</sup>The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass.<sup>19</sup>The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald,<sup>20</sup>the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.<sup>21</sup>And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.<sup>22</sup>And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.<sup>23</sup>And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.<sup>24</sup>By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it,<sup>25</sup>and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.<sup>26</sup>They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations.<sup>27</sup>But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
keyVerse.note: This verse names the goal of the whole Bible: not improved circumstances but God himself living with his people, with no veil between. Everything else in the chapter follows from it: the end of tears, a city shaped like the Most Holy Place, no temple, no sun and no night. And it is the promise begun when the Word became flesh and “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and finished by the Lamb.

21.reflection:
Verses 1–2 picture this world renewed and heaven coming down to it, not souls escaping to the sky. How does that change the way you think about your body, your work and the created world now?

In verse 4 God answers grief not with an explanation but by removing its causes and wiping tears away with his own hand. How might that shape the way you grieve, and the way you sit with others who mourn?

The water of life is given “without payment” to the thirsty (v. 6), and the only way into the city is to be written in the Lamb’s book (v. 27). Why do we find it so hard to receive something free? What would it look like to come to Christ thirsty this week?

The city has no temple and no lamp but God and the Lamb (vv. 22–23). What does it tell you that the centre of the Christian hope is a Person rather than a place, and how should that change what you long for now?

22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 22 finishes the vision of the new Jerusalem begun at 21:9, and then closes the book, and the whole Bible, with an epilogue that answers its opening (1:1–8). It gathers up the threads of the whole story.

The message. The end of the story is better than its beginning. What was lost in Eden is given back, and more: the curse is gone, God lives among his people, and they will see his face. The Christ who promises this is coming soon, so keep his words, wash your robes, come and drink while the invitation stands, and pray for his coming.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia were small, some facing prison and death, others comfortable and compromising (see the introduction). Could these visions be trusted? Was faithfulness worth what it cost? What should they do while they waited? The answer: these words are trustworthy and true, Jesus himself signs them, and his reward comes with him.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–5 complete the city and return to Eden, but to something greater: the river now flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the tree once guarded by cherubim stands open on both banks, the curse is lifted, and God’s servants see his face and reign for ever. Verses 6–16 seal the book. The angel guarantees it and Christ promises for the first of three times, “I am coming soon” (vv. 6–7); John bows to the angel again and is told, “Worship God” (vv. 8–9); the book is left unsealed because the time is near (vv. 10–11); Christ brings his reward as the Alpha and the Omega (vv. 12–13); the last beatitude blesses those who wash their robes (vv. 14–15); and Jesus signs with his own name (v. 16). Verses 17–21 end with the widest invitation in Scripture, a warning against tampering with the book, Christ’s last promise, the church’s answering prayer, and grace.

Where it leads. Between the fenced-off tree of Genesis 3 and the open tree of this chapter stands another tree, on which Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The face that Moses could not see was struck and spat on so that sinners might look on it and live. The last words of Jesus in the Bible are a promise to come, and the last word of all is his grace.

For us. Drink now from the water he gives freely, hold to his words when they cost you, tell the thirsty where the water is, and learn to pray with the whole church, “Come, Lord Jesus!”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The end is better than the beginning: what was lost in Eden is given back, and more, because God himself is at the centre. The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life, guarded since Genesis 3, stands open on both banks, with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations (vv. 1–2). The curse is gone; God’s servants worship him, see his face, bear his name, live in his light and reign with him for ever (vv. 3–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face, seen at last and lived by.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives back what was lost in Eden, and more: life flowing from his own throne, and the tree of life open to all his people. The Bible that began in a garden ends in a garden-city, with river and tree in endless supply.

The river of the water of life, from the throne. Eternal life, abundant and flowing (7:17; 21:6): what was a cup offered in the last chapter is a river here. One throne, two names, and John does not pause to explain how: all life flows from God himself, through the Lamb, by the Spirit (John 7:39). And what flows from it is not judgment but water. Earlier in the book lightning and thunder came from the throne (4:5); at the end, a river does.

Down the street. The river runs down the middle of the main street: life is at the very centre of the city. Babylon’s streets were full of merchants and their cargoes; this street carries the water of life past every door.

The tree of life. What Adam and Eve lost is restored, as promised to the first of the seven churches: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God” (2:7). Twelve kinds of fruit, twelve being the number of God’s people, and fruit every month: no more seasons of want. Fruit trees rest; this one never stops (Ezekiel 47:12).

The healing of the nations. The previous chapter has just abolished pain, but the Greek word (therapeia) means care and tending as much as cure: the leaves keep the city’s people in health. And “nations” has been a hostile word for most of this book: they raged, and they drank Babylon’s wine. Here they are the ones being tended. The long wound of peoples divided at a tower and at each other’s throats ever since has leaves growing for it.

Eden, Ezekiel and Zechariah. Behind these verses stand Genesis 2–3; Ezekiel’s water trickling from under the temple threshold until it is a river no one can cross, with trees of healing on both banks (Ezekiel 47:1–12); and Zechariah’s living waters flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). Genesis 3 ends with cherubim and a flaming sword “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24), and from that verse to this one, more than eleven hundred chapters later, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens between a tree fenced off and a tree handed back.

Not simply Eden reopened. The differences are the point. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, with all the work and culture of humanity gathered around the tree, not exiled from it. Eden had one tree of life; here it lines both banks. Eden could be lost; this cannot. God does not take his people back to where they started but somewhere better, and the road ran through a cross.

By another tree. The word for tree (xylon, wood) is also used of the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24). The tree once guarded by a flaming sword is given back by the One who was hung on a tree in our place and bore the sword himself.

Could we ever lose the tree of life again? No. Adam stood on probation, able to fall, and fell. The redeemed stand in Christ, who has passed every test for them, and enter the city made perfect in holiness. The tree is now theirs by right (v. 14), and what Christ gives by right he never takes back. There will be no second fall, because there will be no second serpent and no unrenewed heart.

What about the wars and hatreds between peoples now? The divisions of race, nation and tribe are not permanent; they are among the things the leaves of the tree will heal. So the church is meant to be a foretaste of that healing now: Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, one in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16). If there is someone of another background in your church whom you avoid, or a people you were taught to despise, you will spend eternity with the redeemed of them. Begin now.

In everyday life. You are not waiting for the river to start: Jesus said that rivers of living water would flow from within whoever believes in him, by the Spirit (John 7:38–39). So drink today, in prayer and in his word, and let what flows to you flow on: forgive the person who wronged you, and bring some healing where you can.

Uncertain wording. The Greek has no punctuation, so “through the middle of the street of the city” may end the sentence about the river (as in the ESV) or begin the sentence about the tree (as in the King James Version: “In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life”). And “tree” is singular, though it stands on both banks: perhaps an avenue of trees of one kind, or one tree spanning the river. The picture is impossible to draw and easy to understand: life runs through the centre of the city, and the tree of life is within reach of everyone in it.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curse is gone for good, and God’s people will live in his presence, see his face and reign with him for ever. Everything sin spoiled is undone, and the best thing promised in Scripture is given at last.

No longer will there be anything accursed. “Accursed” (katathema) means under God’s curse. Zechariah promised that Jerusalem would never again be under a decree of utter destruction (Zechariah 14:11), and this clause reaches back further, to the ground cursed because of the man, thorns and thistles, and a return to the dust (Genesis 3:17–19). Every exhausting labour and failing body has stood under that sentence, and it is lifted. Not managed, not explained: removed.

The throne of God and of the Lamb. The throne has been the fixed point of the vision since chapter 4, always in heaven. Now it is in the city, on the renewed earth, with the river running out of it.

His servants will worship him. “Worship” (latreusousin) is the word for serving God as priests, and “him” is singular: God and the Lamb together as one. John has spent the book watching heaven worship; now the redeemed on the new earth join in for ever.

They will see his face. The summit of the promise, the beatific vision, as the church has called it, and what Jesus promised the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8). Moses asked for exactly this and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live”; he was shown God’s back from a cleft in the rock (Exodus 33:18–23). Even the high priest behind the veil needed a cloud of incense over the mercy seat so that he would not die (Leviticus 16:13). Isaiah saw the Lord and cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). Earlier in this book kings begged the mountains to hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne (6:16). And here, in a short clause: they will see his face. Ordinary people, a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who once denied Christ in a courtyard, looking directly at God; and they do not die of it, they live by it. To see his face is to know him fully, be fully known, and be fully accepted (1 Corinthians 13:12).

That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion or the end of trouble, though both are coming. It is a face. John made the same promise in a letter and admitted he could not describe it: “we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Everything else in these two chapters, the gold, the jewels, the river, is furniture in a room where that is happening.

His name on their foreheads. The last of the marked foreheads in this book (3:12; 7:3; 14:1); the beast’s counterfeit mark (13:16) is gone. They belong to him completely, publicly and for ever, and like the high priest who wore “Holy to the LORD” on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38), all are priests in his presence.

No night, and they will reign. God himself is their light (21:23), and they reign not for a thousand years only but for ever and ever, as Daniel promised the saints of the Most High (Daniel 7:18, 27). Redeemed humanity will finally fulfil Adam’s calling to rule under God (Genesis 1:26–28), and the promise to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, that the conqueror would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21), arrives in full.

Two trees. The curse was removed by Someone becoming a curse for us, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). There are two trees at the end of this book. On one, the cross, Christ bore the curse; from the other, the tree of life, the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

Close enough to touch. The face Moses was not allowed to see once came close enough to touch: the face of a baby in Bethlehem, a face set toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), a face that men spat on and covered and struck (Mark 14:65), so that the face of God might be turned toward sinners in blessing for ever. “The LORD make his face to shine upon you”, the priests prayed (Numbers 6:25), and at last the prayer is answered without limit.

How can we see the face of God, who is spirit? Scripture does not explain the mechanics, and we should not pretend to. But two things are clear. We will see God in Christ: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and God’s glory shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). And the seeing will be more than sight: knowing God directly, with nothing between. What Moses could not survive, we will be able to bear, because we will have been made like him.

Will there be work in the new creation? Yes, but not toil. Serving and reigning are active words. The curse made work painful and futile, but work itself came before the fall (Genesis 2:15). What is lifted is the curse, not the calling. Imagine work that never fails, never wearies, never goes to waste, done for the joy of God: not boredom, but what you were made for.

In everyday life. If seeing God’s face is the goal of everything, seek his face now (Psalm 27:8), in his word and in prayer, and ask what is competing with that longing: ambition, comfort, a relationship, a grievance. And when the curse bites, the aching back, the job that frustrates, the illness that does not lift, remember that it is one of the last things on its way out. You will one day work without thorns and rest without fear, and look up into his face.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book is true and its Lord is coming, so keep it, worship God alone, and wash your robes. The epilogue answers the opening of the book (1:1–8). The angel guarantees its words, and Christ breaks in with the first “I am coming soon” and a blessing on those who keep them (vv. 6–7). John, overwhelmed, bows to the angel and is told, “Worship God” (vv. 8–9). The book stays unsealed because the time is near and lives are setting into their final shape (vv. 10–11). Christ comes with his reward as the Alpha and the Omega (vv. 12–13); the last beatitude blesses those washed in his blood and names those left outside (vv. 14–15). Then Jesus signs the book with his own name (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again: Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this book is God’s own true word, and Christ himself promises that he is coming soon: blessed are those who keep it. The book ends as it began.

Trustworthy and true. As in 21:5, the whole book is guaranteed, and it closes by going back to its first sentence (1:1): the same chain of revelation, the same angel, the same servants, the same things that must soon take place. It is for all God’s servants, not a spiritual elite.

The God of the spirits of the prophets. The God who spoke through Isaiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, whose words echo on nearly every page of this book, has spoken here. Revelation stands in their line and with their authority (2 Peter 1:21), closing a Bible God had been giving for some fifteen centuries.

I am coming soon. Without warning the speaker is Christ himself. He says it three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), the drumbeat the book ends on. The great hope of the church is not an event, a date or a programme, but a Person arriving: the Jesus who said in the upper room, “I will come again and will take you to myself” (John 14:3). The one who is coming is the one who was pierced (1:7), and he is coming for his own.

The one who keeps. The sixth beatitude of the book, almost word for word the first (1:3). “Keeps” (tērōn) means obeys and holds fast. The blessing is not for the one who identifies the beast but for the one who keeps the book: it is to be obeyed, not merely studied.

Soon, after two thousand years? Three things answer it. First, “soon” stresses that his coming is the next great event in God’s plan, sure and sudden, not that it will come within a set number of years. It is always near, though Scripture names things that come before it, such as the rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so the church is to watch, not to set dates. Second, the New Testament dates the last days from the resurrection (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2): we have lived at the edge of the end ever since. Third, Peter answered this very objection while it was fresh: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and he is not slow but patient (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is mercy, and somebody is being brought in during it, perhaps someone you love.

How do I keep a book so full of symbols? Keep what it plainly asks. Worship God alone and refuse every rival, whether Caesar, money or comfort. Hold to Jesus when it costs you. Do not compromise with the sins the letters to the churches name. Endure suffering without giving up the faith. Tell the truth. Long for Christ’s coming, and invite others to come to him. Many believers who never solved a single symbol have kept this book faithfully.

In everyday life. If arguments about the end times have made you anxious or proud, lay them down for a while. Read the book again for its commands and its comfort, and let Christ’s promise, “I am coming soon”, shape your week.

Uncertain wording. “The spirits of the prophets” may mean the prophets’ own spirits, which God moves and directs (compare 1 Corinthians 14:32, “the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets”), or the one Holy Spirit at work in each of them, as “the seven spirits” before the throne (1:4) seem to picture the Spirit in his fullness. The first is the more natural reading of the plural. Either way the point stands: the God who inspired the prophets has inspired this book.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even an apostle, overwhelmed by the glory he has seen, can bow to the wrong one: worship belongs to God alone. The angel who showed John everything refuses a single bow and turns him to face the throne.

Heard and saw. John signs his testimony as an eyewitness: he did not invent these visions; he received them. In Israel’s law a matter was established by witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John’s Gospel and first letter stress the same (John 19:35; 21:24; 1 John 1:1–3). On whether this John was the apostle, see the introduction; either way he signs as a witness.

I fell down to worship. A second time: he did it at 19:10, was stopped in almost these words, and here he goes down again. It does him no credit, and he wrote it down to warn us. It happens not at the dragon or the lake of fire but straight after the river and the tree and the face. It is the beauty that undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong. A man overwhelmed by glory bows to the nearest one carrying it.

You must not do that! I am a fellow servant. No created being deserves worship. And the angel’s list is longer than at 19:10: a fellow servant with John, with the prophets, and, this is new, with those who keep the words of this book. That last group is the reader. An angel of God has put himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

Worship God. Two words, the summary of twenty-two chapters: the choice all through the book has been whom to worship, God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast. And all through the book the Lamb has received the same worship as God, from angels who would never accept it themselves (5:8–14). The angel refuses worship because he is a creature; the Lamb receives it because he is not.

Only ever a window. The mighty angel who showed John the city of gold stands beside an old man on an island as a fellow servant. Every glory John has seen was only ever a window, and the One beyond it is worthy of everything a creature can give. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, and to him and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory for ever.

A comfort in a repeated fault. One of the last things the apostle records about himself is a mistake he had made before. God did not withdraw the revelation; the angel corrected him and the book went on. Repeated failure is a reason to be humble and watchful, not a sign that God has given up on you.

In everyday life. The church’s permanent danger is giving God’s due to those through whom he speaks, preachers, writers, worship leaders, and most of all when what they bring is genuinely glorious. Ask whom you quote most, whose approval you most want, what spiritual experience you chase. Thank God for them, then look past them to him.

Is it wrong, then, to pray to angels or saints? Yes. If this angel would not accept even a bow, no angel or departed saint may be prayed to or venerated. There is one Mediator, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and through him we come straight to the Father (Hebrews 4:14–16). We may thank God for the saints and follow their faith (Hebrews 13:7), but we pray only to God, through Christ, by the Spirit. Anything else, however well meant, gives a servant what belongs to the Master.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This book is left open for everyone to read now, because the end is near and every life is already setting into the shape it will have for ever. The time to turn, and the time to persevere, is now.

Do not seal. The exact reverse of what Daniel was told: “shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4; compare 8:26). Daniel’s vision was for the far future; John’s is for now. It also reverses John’s own instruction at 10:4: “Seal up what the seven thunders have said.” There is exactly one sealed message in Revelation, and we do not have it. Everything else is open, on purpose: not a locked document awaiting a key (on keeping it rather than decoding it, see the note on vv. 6–7).

Let the evildoer still do evil. The hardest verse in the chapter, and not to be softened: not permission to keep sinning, but a warning that time is short and character is being fixed. Those who persistently refuse God’s call harden themselves, and when Christ comes there will be no more opportunity to change. Three things settle its meaning. Its position: between “the time is near” and “I am coming soon”, urgency on both sides, the opposite of saying nothing can change. Its form: a prophetic announcement, like Daniel’s word that the wicked shall act wickedly (Daniel 12:10) and Ezekiel’s, “He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse” (Ezekiel 3:27). There is a point beyond which a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination; we know it of habits, and the verse says it of lives. And what it does to the reader: it asks which of these four descriptions fits the direction you are already going. The door is open now, and the invitation is six verses away, but not for ever. If a reader trembles here, fearing he has already hardened, the fear itself shows he has not: the hardened do not worry about hardening, and the invitation of v. 17 is for him.

The righteous still do right. Do not give up because the end seems delayed or the world seems to win. Holiness, too, is a direction that becomes a destiny, and it is God’s work in his people before it is theirs (Philippians 2:13): what they practised in weakness here is what they will be in glory.

The Lamb has broken the seals. Why can John’s book stay open when Daniel’s was shut? In chapter 5 no one could open the sealed scroll, and John wept; then the Lamb who had been slain took it, because by his blood he had ransomed a people for God (5:4–9). What Daniel waited for has begun. A sealed book belongs to an age still waiting for its Lord; an open book belongs to the age in which the Lamb has conquered. God has opened this book and set it in every church, so that no one may say he was not warned or not invited.

Is it too late for someone I love? While a person is alive, the invitation stands; treat no one as beyond reach. The thief on the cross turned in his last hours; Manasseh, one of Judah’s worst kings, repented after decades of evil (2 Chronicles 33:12–13); Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, saved as an example of Christ’s patience (1 Timothy 1:15–16). This verse warns that the door will close at Christ’s coming or at death, not that it has already closed on your son or your friend. So keep praying, keep loving, and keep telling them the truth. The urgency of this verse is what makes your prayers matter.

In everyday life. Your daily choices are shaping who you will be for ever. The small kindness, the resisted temptation, the hour in prayer: by the Spirit at work in you, these are forming the person you are becoming. And if you know a direction in your life is wrong, turn today.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is coming with his reward in his hand, and as the beginning and the end of all things he will give each person what his life has shown. The one who judges is the one who began everything and will finish it.

My recompense with me. The second of the chapter’s three announcements, with the reward (misthos, wages) already in his hand: not sent for afterwards, not calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it of the coming of God, “his reward is with him” (Isaiah 40:10), and Jesus said it of himself (Matthew 16:27).

Each one. “What he has done” (to ergon, his work) is singular: the whole pattern of a life, as in 20:12–13. No one’s record has ever earned entry to the city, for no record is clean but Christ’s, and his perfect obedience is counted as his people’s (Romans 5:19). But works show whose a person is, and the flawed works of believers, accepted for Christ’s sake, are the measure of the reward he gives. No one is lost in the crowd: the visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water, each by name. Every good thing his people did, he did in them first, and then he rewards it as though it were theirs.

Alpha and Omega, first and last. All three titles together. God said “Alpha and Omega” in 1:8 and 21:6; Christ said “first and last” in 1:17 and 2:8, and in Isaiah that is a title God keeps for himself alone: “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6). Now Christ claims them all, the clearest statement in Revelation that Jesus shares the identity of the one God, equal with the Father in being, glory and worship, who became man without ceasing to be God (John 1:1, 14). Revelation never argues for the deity of Christ; the titles pass between Father and Son without a seam, as though the question could not arise. The one who began all things will end them.

But what if I have nothing to bring? This verse keeps some quiet Christians awake. A man converted at sixty, or a woman ill in a back bedroom for twenty years, reads “repay each one for what he has done” and thinks there is nothing of theirs to bring. Two things answer them. What is rewarded is not what they achieved but what Christ produced in them, and he does not fail to produce: the vine bears the fruit, and the branch only carries it (John 15:5). Patient suffering, quiet prayer and faithfulness in small things are works too. And Christ told a parable about this very complaint: those hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as those who bore the burden of the day, and the owner wronged nobody (Matthew 20:1–16). Nobody will stand in that scene feeling short-changed, and nobody will think he earned what he is holding.

Will some in heaven be happier than others? Scripture does teach rewards that differ: the servants whose mina made ten and five are given different charges (Luke 19:16–19), and some works survive the fire while others burn (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). But no one in the city will be unhappy, envious or lacking. A thimble and a bucket can both be full. Every vessel will be filled to the brim with God, everyone will rejoice in the honour given to the others, and every crown will be cast at the feet of the One who earned them all (4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those washed clean in the Lamb’s blood have free access to the tree of life and the city; those who love their sin remain outside. The last dividing line runs through the blood of the Lamb.

Blessed are those who wash their robes. The seventh and last beatitude of Revelation lands on the one act the whole book has been describing. Not blessed are those who understood it, or those who suffered, though many did, but those who wash their robes, and 7:14 has said in what: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” “Wash” (plynontes) is present tense: keep washing.

The right to the tree of life. “Right” (exousia) means authority, right of access. The tree guarded by a flaming sword since the fall is now reached by right rather than by trespass: not earned, but a standing Christ won and gives, as John wrote, “he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

By the gates. Through the gates, always open (21:25). Not carried in or admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home.

Outside. As in 21:8. Dogs were unclean scavengers, and the law used the word of what was excluded from the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 23:18); Paul used it of men who added requirements to the gospel (Philippians 3:2). “Loves and practices falsehood”: not merely tells lies, but loves them. The dragon has deceived the whole world since 12:9, while in the mouths of the redeemed no lie was found (14:5); at the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth. Those outside are not just beyond the walls in the new creation; they are shut out of God’s presence, in the lake of fire (21:8). Yet none of these sins is beyond forgiveness. Anyone who washes his robes in the Lamb’s blood, whatever his past, may enter, and two verses later the invitation says how (v. 17).

Back to the tree he lost. Adam went out of the garden with nothing in his hands, and his children come back through open gates in robes washed white. Sinners from every list in this book, sorcerers, the immoral, liars, idolaters, have walked through those gates, because they washed in the fountain opened to cleanse from sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1), and the fountain is the Lamb’s own blood. Blessed be the Lamb, who makes the filthy clean and gives the outcast the right to come home.

What does it mean to keep washing my robes? Living by daily repentance and faith. You were washed once for all when you first trusted Christ: justified, forgiven, declared clean (1 Corinthians 6:11). But you still sin, and Jesus told Peter that one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet (John 13:10). So each day bring your fresh sins to him, name them honestly, and trust his blood again, not to be saved again but to walk in the joy of being saved (1 John 1:9).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Blessed are they that do his commandments” (poiountes tas entolas autou) instead of “Blessed are those who wash their robes” (plynontes tas stolas autōn). The two phrases look similar in Greek capital letters, and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other. The best and earliest manuscripts read “wash their robes”, which fits 7:14 exactly. The difference matters: one reading makes entrance depend on obedience, the other on being washed. The manuscripts favour the second, and so does the book’s steady teaching that the Lamb’s blood is what makes people clean (1:5; 5:9; 7:14).
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note), which is the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus signs the book in his own name: he is David’s promised son and David’s Lord, and the morning star that tells the church the dawn is coming. The whole vision comes with his personal guarantee.

I, Jesus. The only place in Revelation where Jesus names himself this way, after twenty-one chapters of titles: the Lamb, the faithful witness, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, given to a carpenter’s son in a village. “To you” is plural: this enormous vision, thrones and dragons and a city two thousand kilometres high, was given to be read aloud in rooms, to small assemblies like the seven on a road in Asia (1:11).

The root and the descendant of David. As in 5:5, both at once, fulfilling Isaiah’s shoot from the stump of Jesse and root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1, 10). To be David’s descendant is to come after him, the promised son of the royal line. To be David’s root is to be what David grew out of: a root is not produced by the tree; it produces the tree. Jesus once set that riddle in the temple, and nobody could answer it: “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matthew 22:41–45). This verse is the answer, given by the man who asked the question. He is David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature: the Lord before whom David bowed, born in David’s town, laid in a manger, nailed to a cross under a sign that called him King.

The bright morning star. Venus, the brightest light in the sky before dawn, heralding the new day. The conquerors at Thyatira were promised the morning star (2:28), unexplained; here it is explained: it is Christ himself (compare 2 Peter 1:19). Behind it very likely stands the prophecy of Balaam, of all people: “a star shall come out of Jacob” (Numbers 24:17). The morning star rises when the sky is darkest and the night has gone on longest. It means the sun is on its way, which this book has been telling frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises that the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it. The title does not link Christ with Lucifer, the “Day Star” of Isaiah 14:12: the King James Version’s Lucifer is simply the Latin word for the morning star, used there of a proud king’s fall. Christ is the true light; the fallen king of Babylon was a false one.

Why does it matter that he is both David’s root and son? Because only such a Saviour could save us. If Jesus were only David’s son, a good man of the royal line, he could not bear the infinite weight of our sin or give eternal life. If he were only David’s Lord, God but not man, he could not stand in our place, die our death or sympathise with our weakness. He is both, one person, true God and true man, as the Westminster Confession (8.2) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (8.2) confess. That is why he can be the Lamb who was slain and the Alpha and the Omega in the same chapter, and why you can trust him with everything.

In everyday life. When your night feels long, a grief that will not lift, a prayer still unanswered, a church in decline, look for the morning star. Say his name this week in the hard moment: Jesus. It is the name he signed this book with, and it means the LORD saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Bible ends with a free invitation, a solemn warning and a promise answered by prayer, all wrapped in grace. The Spirit and the Bride call the thirsty to take the water of life without price (v. 17). Because these are Christ’s own words, no one may add to them or take from them (vv. 18–19; compare Deuteronomy 4:2). Then Christ promises a third time that he is coming soon, the church answers, “Come, Lord Jesus!”, and the last word is grace (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha: Our Lord, come.

Now: A book full of judgment ends with grace, and the invitation is open to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bible’s last invitation is open to anyone who is thirsty: come to Christ and take the water of life as a free gift. After all the judgments of this book, God ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it.

The last invitation. After the dragon and the beast and the lake of fire, in what many find the most frightening book in Scripture, one of the last things God says to the human race is, come and have a drink.

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” The Holy Spirit and the church speak with one verb between them (erchou). They pray to Christ, “Come” (as in v. 20), and they invite the world to come to Christ. That is the mission of the church in a few words: the church does not invite on its own authority, and the Spirit does not work around the church. They say it together.

The one who hears. Everyone who hears this book read in church (1:3) is to join the invitation, with no interval and no qualification: not the one who has matured or been trained. The person who has just heard is immediately in the chorus.

The one who is thirsty. Now the direction reverses: the church was calling out; this is somebody walking in. Thirst is the only qualification: not worthiness, not understanding, not improvement. Then even thirst, which might sound like a condition, gives way to “the one who desires”.

Without price. The same word as at 21:6: as a free gift. The last offer in the Bible is free grace. Isaiah cried it: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1). Jesus cried it on the great day of the Feast of Booths: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And he said it quietly to one woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

Where the verse is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and sorcerers and murderers were outside the gate; one verse later comes a solemn warning. In between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture, the last word on the character of the God whose judgments have filled most of the book. So the answer to the question raised at 20:15, whether a name is written in the book of life, is not, have I done enough? Nobody has. It is whether a person is thirsty, and whether he will take what is being handed to him for nothing.

The water comes from the Lamb. The invitation is to a Person, not a principle. The river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (v. 1), and Jesus says, “whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). To come is to come to him; to take is to trust him. It is free to us because it cost the Lamb his life: the Son was thirsty on the cross so that we would never thirst again.

What if I am not sure I am chosen? Then come anyway, for the invitation is addressed not to the chosen but to the thirsty, and to whoever desires. You do not need to read the Lamb’s book before you drink; you learn your name is written there by coming. No one has ever come to Christ and been told he was not on the list. Jesus promised the opposite: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Election is a comfort to those who have come, not a barrier for those still thinking about it. If you want the water, take it.

How do I actually invite someone? Simply, honestly and personally, as one thirsty person telling another where the water is. Pray for them, ask God for an opening, and live in a way that raises questions. When the moment comes, speak of Christ himself, not only of church: who he is, what he did on the cross, and that the water of life is free. Ask, would you like to read one of the Gospels with me? or, can I tell you why I trust Jesus? Invite them to hear the word preached, and leave the results with the Spirit, who says “Come” alongside you.

Where Christians differ: if salvation depends on God’s choice, is this invitation sincere? Some argue that if God has chosen who will be saved, a universal invitation is meaningless; others that the invitation proves people have free will to come in their own power. Both sides want to protect something true: God’s sovereignty, and the sincerity of his offer. This commentary’s view: the gospel invitation is sincere and is to be offered freely to everyone without exception. Whoever wants to may come, and no one who comes will be turned away (John 6:37). At the same time, no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and those who come are those whose names were written in the Lamb’s book (13:8). God’s sovereign grace does not make the invitation less real; it makes it effective. The Spirit who says “Come” is the Spirit who gives the thirst and the will to come.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because this book is Christ’s own testimony, no one may add to it or take away from it, and those who do so face God’s judgment. The warning guards the voice of Jesus speaking to his churches.

I warn everyone. To testify, to declare solemnly. It is probably Jesus speaking (v. 20, “He who testifies to these things”), and the warning reaches every congregation and reader. It is severe but not new: Moses warned Israel, “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2; compare Proverbs 30:6), and ancient treaties and books sometimes carried curses against tampering. John is sealing the finished text.

If anyone adds, if anyone takes away. Adding means supplying what God did not say: new teaching claiming divine authority, a date for Christ’s return, a name for the beast, an extra requirement, a private revelation that completes what Scripture left open. Taking away means quietly setting aside parts of God’s word, the judgment, Christ as the only way, his return, because they are unpopular. The penalty is the loss of eternal life itself, and it fits the offence exactly: add to the words, and the plagues are added to you; take away from them, and the tree and the city are taken from you.

The testimony of Jesus. The book guarded here is not a loose collection of predictions but “The revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:1), backed by the faithful and true witness (3:14). To add to it is to put words in his mouth; to take away is to silence him. And the share that can be lost, in the tree of life and the holy city, is a share in him. Nothing needs to be added to Christ, and nothing in him can be taken away.

A God who can never contradict you. We would not tear pages out of a Bible. We do it more politely: we keep the parts that suit our moment, the love, the welcome, the concern for the poor, and quietly set aside the parts that offend it, as if our century’s feelings were the fixed point for measuring every other. But every age is offended by a different page. The ancient world admired the moral teaching and found the cross absurd; ours admires the welcome and stumbles at the judgment. Timothy Keller often pointed out that if your God never disagrees with you, you may simply be worshipping an idealised version of yourself. A friend who can never say no to you is not really a person to you at all. The God of this book loves us too much to be edited by us. Being contradicted by him is the first sign that we are dealing with Someone real, and the voice we cannot edit is the voice of the One who loved us and gave himself for us.

What it does not mean. The warning does not condemn faithful copying, translation or teaching of the Bible, but deliberately adding false teaching or cutting out what we dislike. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John wrote is the opposite of tampering: it makes sure nothing has been added or lost.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? No. The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that they never truly belonged to Christ: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). Christ’s sheep will never perish (John 10:28). For believers it is a reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful. A Christian who misunderstands a verse, or struggles to believe a hard one, is not in view; it describes the person who sets himself above the word and edits God.

What about Christians who hear words from God today? This commentary holds, charitably, that the gifts of new revelation ceased with the apostles, because the foundation has been laid and Scripture is complete. Many dear brothers and sisters believe God still gives prophetic words, and most of them agree that no such word can add to Scripture, bind the conscience or carry its authority. That agreement is what matters most here. Test every impression, dream or prophecy by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If anything claims to add a new doctrine, requirement or date, do not receive it. The Bible is enough.

What about the extra books in some Bibles? The Apocrypha, found in Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, were not part of the Hebrew Scriptures that Jesus and the apostles received, and the New Testament never quotes them as Scripture. The Reformed confessions say they are not inspired and no part of the canon, though they may be read as human writings (the Westminster Confession 1.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.3). The sixty-six books are the whole of God’s written word: not the church deciding what God said, but the church recognising the books God gave.

In everyday life. We are tempted to do privately what the verse forbids: to add a chart the text does not authorise, or to skip the parts that are hard to hear. Which passages do you avoid? Read one of them this week, slowly, and ask God to make you willing to receive it.

Where Christians differ: does this verse close the whole canon of Scripture? Strictly, the warning applies to Revelation, and some therefore argue it says nothing about the rest of the Bible. Others give a later voice authority beside Scripture: Roman Catholic teaching sets sacred Tradition, as interpreted by the church, alongside the Bible, and groups such as the Latter-day Saints add new scriptures like the Book of Mormon. Most Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words make no such claim, and agree that nothing may be added to Scripture. This commentary’s view: the direct reference is to Revelation, but it applies the principle of Deuteronomy 4:2 to the final book of the New Testament, written, as the early church believed, by the last surviving apostle, and it fittingly closes the whole canon. With the apostles the foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20), and the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God has spoken his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and Scripture is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). No later revelation, vision, tradition or book may be added to it with equal authority, and no part of it may be removed. The canon is closed, and Scripture alone is our final authority.

Textual note. Where modern Bibles read “his share in the tree of life”, the King James Version reads “his part out of the book of life”. Almost all Greek manuscripts have tree, and book seems to have entered the printed Greek text from the Latin, so modern Bibles follow the manuscripts; the meaning is much the same.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s last words in the Bible are a promise to come soon; the church answers with a prayer for his coming, and the Bible ends with grace. His promise, our longing, and his undeserved favour: so the story closes.

Surely I am coming soon. He who testifies is Jesus, the faithful witness (1:5), and “surely” means yes, truly. The third and final “I am coming soon” is the last recorded word of Jesus Christ in the Bible: not a command, a warning or a doctrine, but a promise about arriving. John answers for the church with Amen, so be it: barely a word, an agreement.

Come, Lord Jesus! The Greek form of an Aramaic prayer, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”, from the first believers in Jerusalem. Paul dropped it untranslated into a letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22), and it appears in the early church manual called the Didache (10:6), a prayer people said without needing it explained. It is the Bible’s final prayer: of a bride for her bridegroom, a persecuted church for its deliverer, a groaning creation for its renewal (Romans 8:22–23). Not fear but longing; not a strategy or timetable but a prayer that Someone would come, said by people who cannot make him come and are certain he will.

Grace. Revelation ends as a letter, as it began (1:4), and like Paul’s letters it closes with grace. After four horsemen, a third of mankind dead, a dragon waiting to devour a child, bowls of wrath, a city drunk on the blood of the saints and burned in an hour, a great white throne with the books opened, in one of the most terrifying documents ever written, the last word is grace, unearned favour for people who have nothing to bring. Everything in the Bible, from the first word to the last, rests on the grace of the Lord Jesus. “With all” does not mean grace will save everyone regardless of faith: the blessing is for the church the book addresses, those who hear and keep its words (1:3). And the last word of all is Amen: it is firm; it is so.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and a woman walking with God in the cool of the day; it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude from every nation looking directly at his face. Between the two a curse fell on the ground and was carried away on a cross; and at the centre stands a Lamb, looking as though it had been slain, who took the scroll nobody else was worthy to open, and opened it.

After everything, grace. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. He was dead, and behold, he is alive for evermore, and he has the keys of Death and Hades. He walks among his churches, holds the stars in his right hand, and is coming soon. The last thing he says to his people is a promise, and the last thing he leaves with them, after everything, is grace. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

A gentle test. A person who says “Come, Lord Jesus” and means it holds nothing in this life so tightly that he would rather Christ delayed. Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what a person might want to keep. If the test finds you wanting, you are not lost (see below on finding this prayer hard).

How should I live while I wait? Watchfully, not anxiously; busily, not idly. Jesus told of servants found working when the master came (Matthew 24:45–46), and Paul rebuked those who stopped working to wait for the end (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). So do your work well, love your family, serve your church, tell others about Christ, and keep your hope fixed on his coming (Titus 2:13), neither setting dates nor growing careless. Live each day as a servant who may be called to give account tonight, and would be glad of it.

In everyday life. Make this your daily prayer: Come, Lord Jesus. Say it in the morning before you look at your phone, at night when you lie down, at the graveside and when the news is bad. You do not have to hold yourself together until he comes; his grace is with you, and it will be enough for every day between now and then.

What if I find it hard to pray “Come, Lord Jesus”? Nothing need be wrong with you; you are being honest, and honesty is where prayer starts. Many believers love this world’s good gifts, a marriage, children, a calling, and fear losing them, or fear the judgment itself. Bring both to God. His coming takes away no good thing; it gives every good thing back, perfected, with him at the centre. The Judge is your Saviour, so you need not fear condemnation. Ask him to make you long for him more than for his gifts, and pray the prayer even when it is small: desire grows by being exercised, and he is pleased with the smallest true longing.

Is longing for Christ’s return just a way of escaping the world? The reverse. Escapism wants to get away from the world and leave it as it is. This prayer asks the Lord to come to the world and put it right: to lift the curse, judge the oppressor, dry the tears and make all things new (21:4–5; 22:3). So the hope makes believers more useful here, not less. Those who know their labour in the Lord is not in vain can give themselves to it fully (1 Corinthians 15:58), and those who know the Judge is coming can leave vengeance to him and love their enemies now (Romans 12:19–21). The prayer is not a retreat but the church asking for the one thing that will make every good work complete.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the last line. Some read “with all”; others, “with all the saints” (followed, for example, by the RSV); others, followed by the King James Version, “with you all”. The meaning is essentially the same: grace for all God’s people. Some manuscripts omit the final Amen.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.<sup>3</sup>No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him.<sup>4</sup>They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, “These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place.”<sup>7</sup>“And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”<sup>8</sup>I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me,<sup>9</sup>but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”<sup>10</sup>And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.<sup>11</sup>Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.”<sup>12</sup>“Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.<sup>13</sup>I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”<sup>14</sup>Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates.<sup>15</sup>Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.<sup>16</sup>“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”<sup>17</sup>The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.<sup>18</sup>I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book,<sup>19</sup>and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.<sup>20</sup>He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!<sup>21</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

keyVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!
keyVerse.note: The Bible ends on this exchange: Christ’s promise and his people’s answer. Everything in vv. 1–5 is what his coming will bring, and everything in vv. 6–19 is how to live until then: keep his words, wash your robes, come and drink. The book that opened by announcing that every eye will see him (1:7) closes with his church asking him to come.

22.reflection:
Verses 1–5 describe the end of the story as better than Eden, and their summit is a single clause: “They will see his face” (v. 4). How does it change your picture of heaven to see that its centre is a Person, not a place? What in your life now competes with that longing?

John falls down before the angel a second time, overwhelmed by what he has seen, and is told, “Worship God” (vv. 8–9). Who or what, even good things or gifted people, are you most tempted to give what belongs to God alone?

The last beatitude blesses “those who wash their robes” (v. 14), and the last invitation is to “the one who is thirsty” (v. 17), free of charge. Why do you think the Bible ends with these two pictures rather than a list of achievements? Who could you invite to come and drink?

Jesus’ last words in Scripture are “Surely I am coming soon”, and the church answers, “Come, Lord Jesus!” (v. 20). Do you find that prayer easy or hard to pray? What would help you long for his coming more, and how should that hope shape the way you live this week?

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15, the shortest in the book, opens the third and last series of seven judgments, the bowls, which are poured out in chapter 16. After the look behind the scenes in chapters 12–14, John returns to the judgments at their final intensity.

The message. Before a single bowl is poured, heaven sings. God’s last judgments come from his holy presence, carried out by his servants in priestly dress, and those who have come through the beast’s persecution declare that all his ways are just and true. His wrath has an end, and his people stand safe on the far shore.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia faced a beast that seemed to win: believers lost their trade, their freedom and their lives for refusing its image and mark (see the introduction). They needed to know that the faithful dead had conquered, and that the judgments to come were not chaos but the holy justice of their God. Heaven sings before it acts, so that the bowls are not misread.

How the chapter makes its case. Verse 1 announces the sign: seven angels with the last plagues, in which God’s wrath is finished. Verses 2–4 show the conquerors standing beside a sea of glass mingled with fire, like Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea, singing the song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God. Verses 5–8 open the heavenly tent of witness, where the covenant law is kept; seven angels dressed as priests receive golden bowls full of wrath, and smoke from God’s glory fills the sanctuary until the plagues are finished.

Where it leads. The song joins God’s two great saving acts, the exodus and the cross: the God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb, and Moses the servant pointed to the Lamb whose song this finally is. The word “finished” (v. 1) echoes what Jesus cried from the cross: for everyone in Christ, God’s wrath was finished there, borne by him in their place. And the sanctuary that closes at the end has stood open through this whole age, held open by the crucified High Priest who tore the curtain.

For us. Refuse the beast’s demands when they cost you, trust God’s justice when you cannot see it, sing of his holiness as well as his comfort, and come into the open sanctuary while there is time, bringing others with you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the last judgments fall, the people who suffered under the beast stand safe and sing that God is just. Verse 1 announces seven angels with the last plagues, in which God’s wrath is finished. Then John sees the conquerors beside a sea of glass mingled with fire, like Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea (v. 2). They sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God: his deeds, his ways, his name and his righteous acts, until all nations come to worship him (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished: it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s last judgments on a rebellious world are about to fall, and with them his wrath in history reaches its end. Even the plagues are counted, seven, and they are the last.

Another sign in heaven. The third and last sign in heaven, after the woman and the dragon of chapter 12 (12:1, 3): the mother, the enemy, and now the end.

Great and amazing. An odd pair of words for a plague, and the song uses the same pair for God’s deeds (v. 3). The plagues are not the collapse of God’s plan but one of his works, seen in heaven with wonder.

The last plagues. Plagues are blows, strokes: that is what the word means. These are the last series. The seals struck a quarter of the earth (6:8), the trumpets a third (8:7–12); the bowls strike everything.

The wrath of God is finished. This clause governs the whole of chapter 16. The verb means to complete, to carry to its goal, the same root as the word Jesus spoke from the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30). God’s anger is not a reservoir with no bottom: his wrath in history has a goal, and a last plague after which there are no more.

His mercy has no last plague. Scripture says again and again that his steadfast love endures for ever, and never once says that of his anger. His anger is for a moment and his favour for a lifetime (Psalm 30:5); he does not keep his anger for ever, because he delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18). His judgments have a stopping point written into them; his steadfast love is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him (Psalm 103:17).

The plagues of Egypt. The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt even more closely than the trumpets did: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs, hail. And the scene by the sea recalls Israel singing beside the Red Sea after God destroyed Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 15). John’s first readers would have heard their own deliverance in that shape: a tyrant, plagues that broke his power, a sea, a far shore, and a song.

Two places where wrath is finished. If the wrath of God can be completed, where was it completed for a Christian? At the cross, where John’s Gospel uses the same verb and where the same wrath fell (Romans 3:25; Galatians 3:13; 1 John 4:10). There God’s wrath against his people’s sin was finished, borne in full by Christ in their place; here his wrath against the unrepentant world is completed. For everyone who trusts in Christ, the first happened before any of this began, on a cross outside the city, where a single word declared that nothing was left to pay.

What it does not mean. “Last” does not necessarily mean that the bowls come after the seals and trumpets in strict time. They are last in John’s sequence of visions and in intensity, describing the final outpouring of judgment, which the earlier series also reached in their own way (6:12–17; 11:15–19).

In everyday life. When the news is full of disaster, remember that even God’s judgments are counted, seven, and the last. And when you think of friends who do not know Christ, let the word “last” move you: the blows will not go on for ever, and the time to turn is now.

Does “finished” mean the wicked stop being punished? No. God’s judgments on this present age reach their goal: the plagues stop, history is wound up, and Christ returns. But Revelation is plain that the punishment of those who refuse him is conscious and without end (14:10–11; 20:10, 15). What is finished is the series of warning blows in history; after that comes not a fresh start but the final judgment. That is why “finished” is such good news for a Christian and so solemn a word for anyone else.

How can a God of love have wrath at all? Because a love that could watch the beloved destroyed and feel nothing would not be love. God’s wrath is not petulant; it is the same holiness that makes him faithful and kind, turned against evil. The conquerors by the sea do not apologise for his judgments; they sing that his ways are just and true (v. 3). And the gospel does not say that God set his wrath aside to love us, but that he loved us so much that he bore his own wrath in his Son (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The cross is where love and wrath meet, and neither is diminished.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whom the beast seemed to defeat are the real conquerors, standing safe beyond the sea of judgment with harps in their hands. They won by refusing to bow, even at the cost of their lives.

A sea of glass mingled with fire. The sea is the place of chaos the beast came up from (13:1). In chapter 4 it lay before the throne, still as crystal (4:6). Now there is fire in it, most likely the fire of judgment, the fire taken from the altar and thrown on the earth (8:5), or else the reflection of God’s blazing holiness.

Those who had conquered. At 13:7 the beast was allowed to conquer the saints; here the same people are the conquerors. John uses the same verb for both, telling one encounter from two sides. From the street, the beast won: the believers were arrested, tried and killed. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing, instruments in hand, and the beast is not in the room. Winning did not mean surviving (12:11). It meant refusing to let go, and losing their lives was part of the victory, not a failure of it.

A victory made of refusals. Note what they conquered: the beast and its image and the number of its name. Not an army, but a demand. They were asked to bow, to worship an image, and to take a number that would have let them keep buying and selling (13:16–17). Their whole victory consists of things they did not do: no to a mere formality, again and again, at rising cost, and heaven calls that conquering.

Beside the sea of glass. The picture is Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea, with Pharaoh’s army under the water behind them (Exodus 14:26–31). They have come through the great tribulation (7:14), and the first thing they do is sing.

Harps of God. Harps given by God for his worship (5:8; 14:2). On the far shore, with the sea of fire behind them, he puts a harp into hands that were once in chains.

So it was with their Lord. He too was arrested, tried and killed, and from the street it looked as if Rome had won. Three days later the grave was empty, and the defeat turned out to be the victory of the ages. His people conquer the way he did, and because he did: they stand on the far shore only because the Lamb went through the deepest waters first.

What is the beast today, and what is its mark? The beast is the power of state or culture setting itself up as God and demanding the loyalty that belongs to Christ; Rome was its form in John’s day, and it takes new forms in every age. Its mark is not a microchip or a tattoo that someone could receive by accident. It is the stamp of belonging, seen in what a person thinks (the forehead) and does (the hand), the opposite of the seal of God on his servants (7:3; 14:1). So the question is not whether you have been scanned but whom you worship, and whether you will keep your loyalty to Christ when it costs you.

I have never been persecuted. Am I really among the conquerors? If you belong to Christ and are holding fast to him, yes. Conquering is measured not by how dramatic the pressure was but by whether faith held. For most believers the beast’s demands come quietly: the colleague who expects you to laugh along, the promotion that requires a lie, the cultural script that says your faith must stay private, the slow pull of comfort and money. Every time you choose Christ over those, you are refusing the image and the number. And the strength to do it is his gift, not your achievement. He keeps his people, and every one of them will stand on that shore (John 10:28–29).

Uncertain wording. Two details are unclear. What the fire “mingled” in the sea stands for is not explained: judgment (as in 8:5) is the likeliest meaning, but it may picture the sea lit by the glory of the throne. And the preposition translated “beside” (epi) can also mean “on”: the conquerors may stand on the glassy sea or on its shore. The Red Sea background favours the shore; either way, the beast cannot reach them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The redeemed sing one song for one great deliverance, praising God alone as just, true and holy, and looking to the day when all nations worship him. Before the last judgments fall, the people who suffered most declare that every one of God’s ways is right.

The song of Moses and of the Lamb. Probably not two songs but one, called by two names, because there is only one deliverance and it has two chapters. Moses’ song celebrated God’s victory over Pharaoh: “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness” (Exodus 15:11). Israel came out of Egypt through water, these out of the beast’s empire through fire and death, and the God who did the first did the second.

The redeemed sing in quotations. The words that follow hardly quote Exodus 15 at all. They are pieced together from the Psalms and the prophets: great and amazing deeds (Psalm 111:2; 139:14), just and true ways (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 145:17), “Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?” (Jeremiah 10:7), and the nations coming to worship (Psalm 86:9). The worship of heaven is made of the Scriptures God’s people were given on earth: the Bible you read this morning is the hymnbook of eternity.

Every line is about God. There is not one word about the beast, about what they suffered, or about their own endurance. Every clause is about God: his deeds, his ways, his name, his righteous acts. Heaven makes people so taken up with God that their own story becomes a footnote to his. Much of our singing and praying is about ourselves; heaven reverses that, and those who stop being the subject are not made smaller but freer and happier than ever.
