O Lord God the Almighty. Almighty, as in 1:8, means the one who holds all things in his hand. The beast seemed to rule the world for forty-two months; the singers know who was holding it the whole time.

Just and true. True here means faithful, genuine, real. Anybody can affirm the justice of God from a comfortable chair. These people were killed for refusing a number, they have come out the other side, and the first thing they say about the way God ran history is that it was just. Not because nobody ever asked: the martyrs under the altar asked loudly how long God would wait (6:10). But the question has been answered.

Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? The question expects the answer nobody: everyone ought to fear him and give him glory. To fear God is not to cower but to stand in awe.

You alone are holy. The reason to fear him is not his power but his holiness, a word used of God in Revelation only here and in 16:5. The beast that demanded worship for forty-two months does not belong in that class at all, and every rival claim to ultimate loyalty, ancient or modern, is answered by those four words.

All nations will come. The widest sentence in the chapter, startling in a book so full of judgment. The nations who raged (11:18) and drank Babylon’s wine (14:8) will come and worship. It is Psalm 86:9 almost word for word, and the promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). What brings them in is not that God overwhelmed them but that his righteous acts were seen clearly, and the result is the great multitude from every nation (7:9), no remnant but a crowd no one could number.

Moses the servant, Christ the Lamb. Servant of God is Moses’ great title in the Old Testament (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2). Hebrews draws the line exactly: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). The servant led the people through the sea; the Lamb led them through death by going into it first. Moses was always pointing to the one whose song this finally is.

In everyday life. When you cannot understand what God is doing, in your own life or in the world, say this song before you say anything else: your ways are just and true. You may still bring the question; the martyrs did. But bring it as someone who already knows how the song ends.

How can people in heaven praise God for judging people they loved? Because in heaven they will see what we only believe now: that God has been perfectly fair to every person, that no one is condemned who did not freely refuse him, and that his patience was longer than anyone deserved. Our hesitation comes partly from love, which is good, and partly from limited sight and a sense that sin is not so bad, which is not. The redeemed will not love less; they will love as God loves and see as God sees. Until then, the right response to the thought of the lost is not to doubt God’s justice but to plead with people while there is time, and to trust the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25).

Should we still sing of God’s justice in church? Yes. The songs of heaven are full of it, and a church that sings only of God’s comfort and never of his holiness and justice is singing of a smaller God than the one who is there. For persecuted and wronged believers especially, God’s justice is not a threat but a hope: no evil will go unanswered. And it should always be sung with the cross in view, because the justice that will judge the world is the justice that was satisfied for us in Christ.

Where Christians differ: will all nations, and so all people, be saved? Universalists sometimes cite “All nations will come and worship you” as proof that everyone will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: “all nations” means people from every nation, not every individual in every nation. The great multitude comes from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9), but Revelation is clear that those who worship the beast and refuse to repent are judged for ever (14:9–11; 21:8; 22:15). The song celebrates the worldwide reach of God’s salvation, fulfilling his promise to Abraham, and the universal acknowledgement of his justice. Every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), but not every knee bows in love.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on God’s title in v. 3. Many manuscripts read “King of the nations”, which the ESV follows; others, including some of the earliest, read “King of the ages”; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “King of saints”. All three are true of God; “nations” fits the song’s theme of all nations coming to worship.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s final judgments come from his holy presence, as acts of his covenant justice, not blind destruction. The tent of witness, where the covenant law is kept, opens, and seven angels in priestly linen and golden sashes come out of it (vv. 5–6). One of the living creatures who worship before the throne hands them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and smoke from his glory fills the sanctuary, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by one of the worshipping living creatures. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgment rests on God’s covenant law, kept in the ark since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it: pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last judgments come out of the very place where God’s covenant law is kept, carried by his holy servants: they are acts of his justice, not blind destruction. Even his wrath comes dressed in white.

The tent of witness. The tabernacle in the wilderness was called the tent of witness or testimony (Numbers 17:7; 18:2), because it held the ark containing the tablets of the law, the testimony of God’s covenant (Exodus 25:16; 31:18). The sanctuary is the inner shrine, and the tent in heaven is the reality of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy (Hebrews 8:5). The tablets are God’s witness to the covenant, and his witness against a people who agreed to keep it and did not.

Wrath from the place where the covenant is kept. The bowls come not out of an armoury but out of the tent that holds God’s law. What is coming is not mere destruction but has a legal basis, and the document it rests on has been in the same box since Sinai.

Out of the sanctuary. At 11:19 the sanctuary opened to show the ark; now it opens again to release seven angels from God’s very presence. The judgments are holy acts, carried out by those who stand before God.

Pure, bright linen. They are dressed as priests (Leviticus 16:4), with the golden sash of the risen Christ (1:13), and “bright” is the word used of the Bride’s dress at 19:8. Nothing that comes out of that door is dirty. Whatever a reader says about the severity of chapter 16, the hands carrying it out are not unclean.

Judgment as liturgy. These are not demons let loose, nor soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, carrying out a service of worship, which is what liturgy means. The judgment of God is not a loss of control: the holiness praised in the song is carried out in the plagues.

The lid on the box. In the tabernacle the tablets of the testimony lay inside the ark, and over them was the mercy seat, where once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest sprinkled the blood of the sin offering (Leviticus 16:14–15). Paul uses the word for that lid of Christ: God put him forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25). Propitiation, the Greek Old Testament’s word for the mercy seat, means a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath by bearing it. Not a bribe that changes God’s mind, but God himself providing the blood that covers the sin (1 John 4:10). So the tent that sends out the bowls also holds the answer for anyone in Christ: the law’s witness against them is covered by his blood. The bowls fall on those who refused the covering, and they face the testimony bare.

In everyday life. Take God’s law seriously, not as a price to pay for his favour but as the shape of the life he is making in you. Read the Ten Commandments this week and ask honestly where your heart is out of step with them. Then take each failure to the one who kept them all for you.

Why does God’s law still matter if Christians are not saved by keeping it? Because the law expresses God’s own holy character, and it is the standard by which the world is judged (Romans 2:12–16; 3:19–20). It cannot save us; it shows us our need of Christ, who kept it perfectly and bore its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). For the believer it remains the good and holy rule of life, now written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). The tent of witness in heaven tells us that God has not lowered his standard. What he has done is meet it himself, in his Son.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “stone” instead of “linen”: in Greek the two words differ by a single letter. “Linen” suits the priestly dress and is followed by most translations; if “stone” were original, the angels would be pictured shining like precious stones.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bowls of God’s final wrath are handed out from his holy presence, and the sanctuary is closed to all until the judgment is finished. The door of intercession, open through this whole age, shuts only at the very end.

Seven golden bowls. The handover is made by one of the four living creatures, who say “holy, holy, holy” day and night (4:8): nothing in this chapter lets judgment be handled by anyone outside the worship of God. Golden bowls were used in the temple for incense and the blood of sacrifices (1 Kings 7:50). A bowl is a shallow, wide dish that empties in a moment. A trumpet is a warning, giving time to respond; a bowl is tipped once, and it is gone. The time of warnings is running out.

The same bowls. At 5:8 the elders held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. God’s judgment is the answer to his people’s prayers. The martyrs asked how long God would wait (6:10), and these are the vessels in which the answer is delivered. Not one of their prayers is lost.

Full of the wrath of God. Filled to the brim. This wrath is not a passing mood but holiness set against evil, and it belongs to the one who lives for ever and ever: no tyrant can outlive it, and no evil can wait it out.

Smoke from the glory of God. When the tabernacle was finished, the glory of the LORD filled it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34–35). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:4–5).

No one could enter. At the tabernacle and the temple the exclusion was brief and joyful, for God had come to dwell. Here it is colder. The sanctuary is where a priest goes in to intercede, and for the duration of the seven bowls nobody goes in: the door of intercession closes, not because God has become unwilling to hear, but because the warnings have been given, the case is closed, and the answering has begun.

Until. The mercy in the verse is one word: until. The closure has a limit, set in v. 1, when the wrath of God is finished. Beyond it lies the new creation, where the dwelling place of God is with man (21:3) and no one is ever shut out of his presence again.

The curtain that was torn. This verse marks the end of an age that began on the afternoon Jesus died, when “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38). Hebrews explains what that meant: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). The whole age in which the church prays and the gospel is preached is the age of the open sanctuary, held open by a crucified High Priest. The smoke marks the day that age is over. Until then, the way in is his body, and it has never once been closed to anyone who came.

Not a shut door. Yet the story does not end with a shut door. In the city to come John saw no temple, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22), and his servants will see his face (22:4). The glory that drove even priests out of the sanctuary will be the light his people live by, and the answer to every prayer they prayed: to be with him, unveiled, for ever.

What it does not mean. Not that it is too late today to pray or to turn to God. The scene describes the final judgment at the end of history. Today is still the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and Christ still intercedes for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

In everyday life. While the sanctuary stands open, pray: for yourself, and for the people whose names you would not want read out on the day the smoke fills the room.

Should I pray for God to judge my enemies? Pray first, as Jesus commanded, for their good and their salvation (Matthew 5:44), as Stephen did for the men stoning him (Acts 7:60). Yet it is also right to pray for God’s kingdom to come and evil to be ended, and the martyrs’ cry for justice is not rebuked (6:9–11). Leave vengeance with God (Romans 12:19). He will judge rightly, and he may answer your prayer for justice by turning your enemy into a brother, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. Either way, you do not have to carry the score.

Could it already be too late for me? If you are worried that you have gone too far, that worry is itself a sign that the door is still open. The people shut out in this verse are not anxious seekers but those who refused every warning to the end. As long as you are alive and Christ is offered to you, the sanctuary is open and the High Priest is inside it, praying for those who come to God through him. No one who comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37). Do not wait to feel ready. Come now.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

keyVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!”
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter: before the last plagues fall, the people who suffered most under the beast declare that God’s deeds are great and his ways just. The song of Moses and of the Lamb ties the exodus to the cross, one deliverance in two chapters, and teaches the church to read every judgment that follows through the worship of the redeemed.

15.reflection:
The conquerors in v. 2 won by refusing: they would not bow to the beast, its image or its number, even when it cost them their lives. What quiet demands to compromise your loyalty to Christ do you face at work, online or among friends, and what helps you say no?

The song of vv. 3–4 has no word about the singers’ own suffering; every line is about God. How does that compare with the way we usually pray and sing? What would change if God were more often the subject of your worship?

The redeemed call God’s ways “just and true” before the bowls are poured out. When you cannot understand what God is doing, in your life or in the world, how can this song help you bring your questions without losing your trust?

The sanctuary is closed only at the very end (v. 8); until then Christ keeps the way in open. Whom do you know who needs to come in while the door is open, and how could you pray for them and speak to them this week?

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 showed seven angels holding the seven last plagues; chapter 16 pours them out. It is the last and fullest series of seven judgments: the seals struck a quarter, the trumpets a third, the bowls everything. The seventh bowl names Babylon, whose fall chapters 17–18 describe.

The message. God’s patience with a world that has chosen the beast has an end, and his judgment is complete, just and final. Heaven, even the altar where the martyrs cried “how long”, says it is right. Those struck curse God and do not repent: punishment by itself changes no one. The voice from the throne says, “It is done!”

Why it was said. The churches of Asia watched the beast’s worshippers prosper while believers lost livelihoods and lives (see the introduction), and the martyrs’ “how long” (6:10) was theirs. The answer is: not for ever. Two quieter fears are answered too: that God’s wrath might be excessive, for his murdered people pronounce it just; and that a little compromise with the beast costs nothing, for its mark ends in a wound.

How the chapter makes its case. Five bowls fall on the beast’s worshippers, the sea, the rivers, the sun and the beast’s own throne (vv. 1–11), echoing Egypt’s plagues and the trumpets, but no longer in part. The angel of the waters and the altar declare God just (vv. 5–7), and the refrain sounds: they cursed God and did not repent (vv. 9, 11). Froglike spirits gather the kings to Armageddon, while Christ breaks in: stay awake (vv. 12–16). The seventh brings “It is done!”, the greatest earthquake in history, Babylon’s cup, and a last curse under the hail (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. These are the plagues of a final exodus, and the first exodus turned on a lamb: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). “It is done!” from the throne answers “It is finished” from the cross (John 19:30). The cup Babylon must drain, the Son of God drained first for everyone who trusts him; and where the beast’s people curse God under his hand, Jesus under the full weight of judgment committed his spirit into his Father’s hands.

For us. Do not envy the beast’s kingdom; it ends in the dark. Leave vengeance to God and pray for your enemies while the gospel still runs. Do not expect suffering on its own to soften hearts, including your own; ask God to do it. And stay awake, clothed in Christ, for he is coming like a thief.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s wrath finally falls, it is complete and it is just, but it does not change the hearts it strikes. The first three bowls fall on the beast’s worshippers, the sea and the fresh waters, as the plagues once fell on Egypt (vv. 1–4). Then the sequence pauses while the angel of the waters and the altar of the martyrs declare God’s judgments true and just (vv. 5–7). The sun scorches and the beast’s throne goes dark, and those who are struck curse God and do not repent (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne: the same targets as the trumpets, but no longer limited to a third. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgments true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and those who took the beast’s mark now bear sores.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s own command the last judgments begin, and the first falls on exactly those who took the beast’s mark. Unlike the seals and the trumpets, the bowls are not partial: they are the full and final answer to a world that has chosen the beast.

A loud voice from the temple. No one could enter the sanctuary (15:8), yet a voice comes out of it, almost certainly God’s own.

Pour out. The verb (ekcheete) is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for blood poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Psalm 79:6 prayed for exactly this: “Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you.” That prayer, and the saints’ prayers in 5:8, are being answered.

Harmful and painful sores. A festering wound (helkos), the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the boils of the sixth plague on Egypt (Exodus 9:8–11). Then the magicians could not even stand before Moses, because the boils were on them too. Whatever else Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it could not imitate health.

The mark becomes the wound. The mark was the ticket to a working life (13:17); now those who took it bear another mark on their bodies, and the passport turns out to be the wound. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence; he hands people over to what they insisted on having. Paul says “God gave them up” three times in one paragraph (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

Egypt and the trumpets once more. The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores (the sixth plague), water turned to blood (the first, Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (the ninth, Exodus 10:21–23), frogs (the second, Exodus 8:1–15) and hail (the seventh, Exodus 9:22–26). The God who broke Egypt has not changed, and as Pharaoh hardened his heart, so do the beast’s worshippers. The targets also match the trumpets almost item for item and in the same order (8:7–12; 9:13–14), a strong argument that the seals, trumpets and bowls describe the same period three times over, each time more intensely (other careful readers take them as successive stages). And the chapter has a refrain: three times those who are struck curse God, and twice we are told they did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

Plagues of an exodus. The Egyptian shape of the bowls tells the reader what story he is in. The plagues on Egypt set God’s people free, and they ended on the night when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts turned the destroyer away (Exodus 12:13). Paul says who that lamb was: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). When these last plagues fall, the redeemed have already been seen on the far shore, singing (15:2–3). On those who belong to the Lamb this judgment will not fall at all, because the wound it should have made was made already, in the hands and side of the Son of God. The bowls are the last chapter of an exodus the Lamb has already won.

In everyday life. Most of the marks on offer are small: the habit everyone in the office has, the shaded truth that keeps a sale, the loyalty that slowly crowds out Christ. Each promises to open doors and ends by festering. You already bear another name, and the Lamb can show you any mark you have been carrying that is not his.

Are the bowls still future, or happening now? Both, in a sense. Revelation shows the age between Christ’s comings several times over, and the bowls are the fullest view, pressing hard toward the end. The judgments they picture, sickness, disaster, the collapse of proud powers, recur through history as warnings and reach their climax before Christ returns. So we should neither label each disaster a particular bowl nor imagine that the God of these bowls is idle now.

If disaster strikes everyone, how are believers protected? Christians suffer the same illnesses, floods and wars as their neighbours, and sometimes the beast’s hatred besides. The promise is not that nothing will touch us, but that nothing that touches us is God’s wrath. For the believer the same events are a Father’s discipline, a trial of faith or a share in Christ’s sufferings, all working for good (Romans 8:28). The sealed belong to God (7:3), and no plague can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39).
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea and the fresh waters turn to blood: the world loses what it lives on, and this time nothing is spared. Where the trumpets warned, the bowls give the verdict.

Like the blood of a corpse. The comparison is deliberately revolting: not bright blood from a wound but blood as of a dead man (haima hōs nekrou), dark, thickened, going bad.

Every living thing died. The second trumpet killed a third of the sea’s creatures (8:8–9); here there is no fraction.

The rivers and the springs. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood so that the Egyptians could not drink from it (Exodus 7:20–21), and the Nile was the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown (Exodus 1:22). The river was given back to Egypt in the condition Egypt had put it in. So the world that rejected the living water (7:17; 21:6) loses even ordinary water.

What the world lives on. The sea carried the world’s trade; the springs are where a settlement drinks. At the third trumpet Wormwood made a third of them bitter (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man; blood cannot. The distance between the two is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

Everything belongs to somebody. The sea and the spring are not neutral machinery that happens to be reliable; they are upheld moment by moment by the Son, in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3). He gives rain on the just and the unjust and fills the hearts of his enemies with food and gladness (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). And the one who keeps every spring running hung on a cross and said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). The Maker of the rivers went without water while he bore the judgment of God, so that those who trust him would not be left to thirst under it. He still cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

In everyday life. Every glass of clean water is God’s gift, and turning on a tap can be a small act of worship. Somewhere today a Christian family is walking a long way for dirty water; remembering them, and helping where you can, is part of receiving the gift rightly.

Is every natural disaster a judgment on the people it strikes? No, and Jesus forbids that conclusion. When a tower fell and killed eighteen people, he said they were not worse sinners than anyone else, and then turned the question round: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:1–5). Disasters are signs that the whole world lies under the curse of sin and that God’s final judgment is coming, and they call every one of us, not just the victims, to repent. They are never a licence to say God is punishing a particular town or person. The right response to a flood on the news is compassion, help and self-examination.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven declares God’s judgments just, and the witnesses who say so are the angel whose waters were struck and the altar of the martyrs. In the middle of the plagues, heaven pauses to say whether this is fair.

Just are you, O Holy One. Just (dikaios, righteous); Holy One (hosios, as in 15:4). Jewish writings spoke of angels with charge over parts of creation, and Revelation has angels over fire (14:18) and the winds (7:1). The angel in charge of the waters has just watched every river in his care turn to blood; if anybody had grounds to object, it is he.

Who is and who was. As in 11:17, the usual third part of the name, who is to come (1:4, 8), is missing: he has come in judgment. And the angel names him holy, not powerful. This is not might making right, but judgment consistent with what God is.

Blood to drink. The oldest principle of justice, “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed” (Genesis 9:6): the punishment is the crime, served back. These people made the earth run with the blood of God’s people, and now there is nothing else to drink. This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry (6:10).

It is what they deserve! Literally “they are worthy” (axioi eisin), a grim echo of the praise of the Lamb, “Worthy are you” (5:9, 12). The Lamb is worthy of glory; the persecutors are worthy of judgment. But notice who does not say these words: no human being in this book pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs under the altar asked how long God would wait and left the verdict to him (6:10). Vengeance is God’s, and it is his alone because only he can be trusted to get it exactly right (Romans 12:19).

The altar answers. Under that altar the martyrs cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood?” (6:9–10), and from it the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5). Now the altar answers its own question in the same words, “holy and true” there, “true and just” here (alēthinai kai dikaiai, as the redeemed sang in 15:3). The verdict of the people who actually paid for the injustice is not “at last”, just “Yes”. Nobody in heaven thinks God has overdone it: to a Christian who finds these plagues hard to look at, the murdered, who waited longest, are the ones who declare it just.

Blood for blood, and one exception. By the principle of this verse, the men who shed the blood of the Son of God had earned the worst cup of all. Yet he prayed for them as the nails went in, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), and seven weeks later Peter told a Jerusalem crowd that they had crucified the one God made Lord and Christ, and about three thousand of them were baptised (Acts 2:36–41). The blood they shed became the blood that washed them. That is why the Lamb’s blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). The bowl of blood falls only where that blood has been refused.

What it does not mean. Praising God’s judgment is not rejoicing in suffering for its own sake. It is the recognition that God has put things right, that evil has not had the last word, and that the blood of the innocent has not been forgotten. Without God’s justice the world’s victims would have no hope.

In everyday life. When you see injustice that is never put right in this life, the abuser who is never charged, the regime that is never toppled, the lie that is never exposed, bring it to God in prayer and trust that his judgments will be true and just. Then put it down, and do good to the people in front of you. You are not the judge, and you do not need to be.

How does this fit with loving my enemies? Perfectly, once we see who does what. Our task is to love, bless and pray for those who wrong us (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:14) and to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21), and we can do that because God will judge. If there were no judge, every wrong would have to be avenged by us or swallowed as if it did not matter; because there is, we can forgive without pretending evil is nothing. Meanwhile we pray that our enemies will be saved, as many persecutors have been. The praise of this verse belongs to the day when God himself has acted.

Textual note. In v. 5 the King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”, following a late reading; the best manuscripts read “who is and who was, the Holy One”. In v. 7 the King James Version reads “I heard another out of the altar say”, but the best manuscripts read simply “I heard the altar saying”.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sun becomes a furnace, and those it scorches curse God instead of turning to him. Pain shows where a heart is facing; by itself it does not turn it round.

Allowed to scorch. It was allowed (edothē, it was given). Even at full strength, with the limits off, the sun acts only because God permits it. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, not even the sun.

Two companies, one sun. The fourth trumpet darkened the sun; the fourth bowl turns it up. The multitude of 7:15–16 were promised that the sun would not strike them, nor any scorching heat; for these it is a furnace. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whom you belong to. When the full heat of God’s anger against sin fell on a human being, it fell on the Son: he bore the burning so that his people could stand in the shade.

They cursed the name of God. The chapter’s refrain begins. They cursed (eblasphēmēsan, blasphemed): the verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have started to sound like the thing they worshipped. There is no ignorance here and no atheism: they know who is doing this and curse him for it. Suffering has not hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him.

They did not repent and give him glory. As in 9:20–21. Repentance is not merely feeling sorry; it is joined to giving God glory, the response the eternal gospel calls for (14:7) and some gave in 11:13. To repent is to hand back to God the glory that was given to something else, and these people gave it to a beast and are not taking it back.

Pain does not produce repentance. Many quietly hope that if things got bad enough, people would turn. But pain reveals what was already there, and it hardens as reliably as it softens. Two men lose the same thing in the same week; one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference is not the weight but the direction a person was already facing when it landed. (A believer whose prayers have gone quiet in grief or depression is not the man in this verse: numbness is not cursing, and the people here have no wish for God at all. The Lord who does not break a bruised reed waits for the quiet one, Isaiah 42:3.)

The one who did not curse. One man under the heavy hand of God did not curse. On the day Jesus died he bore not a judgment he had earned but the one his people had earned. When he was reviled he did not revile in return, and when he suffered he did not threaten, but kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He died praying, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Every curse in this chapter is answered by that prayer. He gave God glory under the full weight of wrath, so that people who had cursed God could be forgiven and taught to bless.

Is it fair for God to harden hearts? Scripture holds two things together, as Exodus does with Pharaoh. People harden themselves, seeing God’s hand and refusing him, and are fully responsible; and God as judge confirms them in the path they chose (Romans 1:24; 9:17–18). He never hardens a soft heart that is seeking him; he hands a rebellious heart over to its own rebellion. So no one in this chapter is a seeker who wanted to repent and was not allowed. If you want to turn to God, that desire is the sign he is softening you, not hardening you. Follow it now.

Why do some turn to God in suffering and others away? Suffering exposes what is there; only the Spirit makes a heart new (John 3:5–8; Ezekiel 36:26). So pray for people who are suffering rather than waiting for trouble to bring them round, and when you are hurting, run to God with the hurt, as the Psalms do (on bringing anger to God, see the note on vv. 10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast’s own throne goes dark, and still its people curse God rather than repent. The power that looked permanent is shown to be under judgment, and its subjects will change neither their worship nor their ways.

The throne of the beast … plunged into darkness. The first four bowls fell on creation; the fifth falls on a government, at the seat of the power the dragon gave it (13:2). The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt, three days in which nobody rose from his place, while all the people of Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). It was probably a blow at the sun god Ra (compare Exodus 12:12): to darken the empire is to show that its god cannot keep a lamp lit. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence: the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark.

Gnawed their tongues. A small, physical, entirely credible detail: what a person does with pain he cannot escape and cannot usefully cry out about. Jesus spoke of the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12; 22:13).

For their pain and sores. The sores are the ones from the first bowl, still there: the plagues accumulate, and nothing has healed. Their whole complaint is their own discomfort: this is where a life spent measuring God by how one feels comes out.

They did not repent of their deeds. The third mention of this refusal (9:20–21; 16:9), with a different ending. In v. 9 they did not repent and give him glory; here they did not repent of their deeds. Together the two cover everything: they will change neither whom they worship nor what they do.

Darkness at noon. The Gospels record one other darkness over a kingdom. When the King of the Jews hung on a cross with his title above his head, there was darkness over the whole land from the sixth hour until the ninth (Mark 15:33), as Amos had said of the day of the LORD: “I will make the sun go down at noon” (Amos 8:9). The beast’s throne goes dark because it is under judgment; Christ’s throne was a cross because he was bearing judgment for others, and on the third day he rose, the light of the world (John 8:12). As Goshen had light in Egypt’s darkness, so God has called his people out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9), and in the city to come there will be no night, for the Lamb is its lamp (21:23; 22:5). The beast’s kingdom ends in the dark; his ends in a morning that never fades.

In everyday life. God has already transferred you into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13), so you need not live as a citizen of one that ends in the dark. When you last had a grievance against God, was it only that he had not arranged your comfort? That is their complaint in a smaller form, and there is still time to tell him so and turn; he will not throw you out of his Son’s kingdom for being honest.

Is it wrong to be angry with God? It depends what you do with it. Scripture is full of believers who brought anger, confusion and grief to God: Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists (Psalm 13; 88). They argued, but they argued with him, to his face, in prayer, and they did not let go of him. That is faith in pain. This verse describes something different: cursing God and refusing to turn, with no desire to know him, only resentment that life is uncomfortable. If you are angry with God, tell him so, ask him to help you understand, open the Psalms, and talk to a mature Christian. Do not let anger become a wall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world gathers itself against God on the strength of a lie, and God ends the gathering with a word. The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates, the river by which old Babylon once fell, and froglike spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world for battle (vv. 12–14). Christ breaks in with his own warning to stay awake (v. 15), and the place is named Armageddon (v. 16). The seventh bowl brings the cry from the throne, “It is done!”, the great city split, Babylon given the cup of wrath, and a last curse under the hail (vv. 17–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth bowl opens the way for the world’s final gathering against God, and what gathers it is the lies of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. Yet it is God who dries the river, and the kings march only where he has appointed.

On the great river Euphrates. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction from which Assyria and Babylon had come; at the sixth trumpet four angels bound there were released (9:14). Now the barrier itself is gone.

A road cleared by God. A dried-up river is one of Scripture’s standard pictures of God clearing a road. He dried the Red Sea for Israel to walk through (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan for them to enter the land (Joshua 3:16). And when Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC, his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked into the city up the lowered riverbed, as the Greek historian Herodotus tells it (compare Jeremiah 50:38). A first-century reader would very likely think of how the old Babylon fell. Babylon is about to fall again.

The kings from the east. In John’s day the Parthians beyond the Euphrates were the empire’s nightmare. God is not defending the beast’s kingdom; he is opening the gate for what will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it, as in 17:16–17, where the beast and the ten kings turn on the prostitute because God has put it into their hearts.

Out of three mouths. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet (the second beast of 13:11), a counterfeit trinity, appear together here for the first time, and all three do the same thing: they speak. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9); the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs (13:13–14). The chief weapon of evil in this book is talk: the decisive struggle is not chiefly about power but about what the world is told and whether it believes it.

Like frogs. Frogs recall the second plague on Egypt (Exodus 8:6) and, to a Jewish reader, an unclean creature (Leviticus 11:9–12). They are also, deliberately, ridiculous. This book’s villains have been magnificent so far; shown at last, their propaganda hops and croaks. Evil is never as grand as it looks.

Demonic spirits, performing signs. As in 13:13–14. Lies rarely travel alone; they come with something impressive enough to make them believed.

To assemble them for battle. The Greek says “the battle”, the final one the prophets foretold: a last gathering of the nations against God and his people, which God would defeat (Joel 3:2; Zechariah 14:2; Ezekiel 38–39). The same battle appears in 19:19 and 20:8. The rulers of the world think they are gathering to fight; in fact God is gathering them to be judged. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet can gather the whole world, and they cannot gather it one step beyond where God has appointed. The sixth bowl fights no battle; it only gathers the armies, and shows why the world marches against God at all: it has believed a lie.

Three temptations, three answers. The dragon’s one method, from a conversation in a garden to the last coalition on earth, is to say something untrue convincingly, and the church’s one weapon is the word of truth (12:11; Ephesians 6:17). The pattern was set in a wilderness. The deceiver came to Jesus three times with offers that sounded reasonable, bread, a sign, the kingdoms of the world, and three times Jesus answered with Scripture: “It is written” (Matthew 4:1–11). Where Adam listened to the lie, the last Adam answered it. Before Pilate, the representative of the empire the beast stands for, he said he had come into the world to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). Against three mouths full of lies the church has one Lord, the faithful and true witness (3:14), the Word of God and the Truth in person. Their mouths produce frogs; from his mouth comes a sharp sword (19:15), and he has only to speak for every lie to be silenced.

In everyday life. Before you share, repeat or believe a message about God, his people or right and wrong, ask where it came from and whether it agrees with Scripture. Let the word of God have the first word in the morning, so that it has the loudest voice in your head.

How do I recognise the frogs’ voice today? Look for the marks this passage gives. It is talk, loud, repeated and everywhere. It is backed by signs: success, spectacle, numbers, things that look like proof. And it always gathers people against God, persuading them that Christ is the enemy of their freedom and his people the problem. Whether it comes from a government, a movement, a media culture or a false teacher in the church, the test is the same: does it confess Jesus Christ as Lord, and does it agree with Scripture (1 John 4:1–3; Isaiah 8:20)? Fill your mind with God’s word, and the croaking becomes easier to hear for what it is.

Where Christians differ: who are the kings from the east? John’s readers feared the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates. Futurist readers (those who expect most of Revelation to be fulfilled in the last years before Christ returns) look for a literal army from the east, often identified with a modern nation; they want to take John’s geography at face value, and that reverence for the text is right. But the bowls are full of Egypt and Babylon used as pictures, and the river belongs to the same world of images. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that John uses that ancient fear as a picture of the nations gathered by the dragon for the final battle (v. 14), not a prediction of a particular invasion.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the armies gather, Christ himself tells his people to stay awake and stay clothed, because he will come without warning. The kings are assembled at Armageddon, but the outcome is already settled.

Christ interrupts his own book. In the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs a different voice cuts in (the ESV’s brackets). Christ has scarcely spoken in his own voice since chapter 3; here, at the darkest point of the story, the armies are gathering and his concern is a Christian in Sardis or Laodicea staying awake. The cosmic scale of this chapter never displaces the person reading it.

Behold, I am coming like a thief! He said it to Sardis in the same words (3:3) and on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and Peter repeat it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point is unpredictability: there is no getting ready later.

Blessed is the one who stays awake. The third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Stays awake (grēgorōn) means keeps watch; keeping his garments on (tērōn ta himatia autou) is literally guarding his clothes. In the temple, the Mishnah records, a Levite found asleep at his post could have his clothes burned: to be caught asleep meant public shame.

Seen exposed. The word (aschēmosynē) means shame, disgrace. Garments in this book have a settled meaning: robes washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), the fine linen of the Bride (19:8). Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that the shame of its nakedness might not be seen (3:18), the same phrase. The garments are the righteousness of Christ received by faith, and the faithful life that flows from it. A Christian is covered before God not by his own record but by Christ’s, like a robe given to someone with nothing fit to wear (Isaiah 61:10). To keep one’s garments on is to keep trusting Christ and to keep living like it.

Not complicated and not heroic. While the kings assemble, a Christian is asked not to do anything about the coalition but to be found alert and dressed. Nor is he left to his own willpower: the robe was never his work. No Christian keeps watch perfectly, but Christ watched and prayed in Gethsemane while his friends slept, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); and the Spirit he has given is the one who keeps waking us.

Armageddon. The only occurrence of the word in the Bible, and John says it is called this “in Hebrew”, a signal to look for its meaning (on the derivation, see the box below). It most likely points to Megiddo, a fortress town guarding the plain of Jezreel and one of the most fought-over places in the land. There Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 5:19), and there King Josiah was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco, and all Judah mourned (2 Kings 23:29–30; Zechariah 12:11). To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield, and a symbolic name fits a book in which Sodom and Egypt are names for the great city (11:8).

The shortest battle in the book. What is certain is who wins. When the battle comes, in 19:19–21, it lasts a few lines, and the only weapon is a sword out of a mouth: the most famous battle in the world’s imagination is the shortest in the Bible.

A culture that cannot stop imagining the end. The modern world was supposed to have outgrown the apocalypse; instead it has more than John did: the asteroid film, the zombie series, the climate deadline, the bomb, the machine that turns on its makers. The literary critic Frank Kermode argued in The Sense of an Ending that we make sense of our lives the way readers make sense of a novel, from the end: only the ending tells us what the middle meant. Our secular endings come in two kinds. In one the world simply stops, and nothing we did meant anything: that leads to despair. In the other we save it ourselves, which lays the whole weight of history on our shoulders: that leads to exhaustion, and to fury at whoever is not helping. Armageddon is neither. The end is not a malfunction and not a project. It is a Person arriving, and the battle everyone dreads is over in a sentence. The world’s last day will be decided not by our fear or our cleverness but by the King whose hands still bear the nails.

What it does not mean. In Revelation “Armageddon” does not mean nuclear war or a global catastrophe caused by human beings, as the word is often used today. It means the day when God judges the world’s rebellion.

In everyday life. Staying awake means keeping short accounts with God, confessing sin the day you see it; keeping your hope fixed on Christ’s righteousness and not your own; and living each ordinary day, at the desk, the sink or the hospital bed, as if he might come before evening.

Does coming like a thief mean a secret rapture? No. The thief image is about timing, not visibility: his coming will be unexpected for those who are not watching, not invisible. Revelation says every eye will see him (1:7), and Jesus said his coming will be like lightning flashing across the sky (Matthew 24:27). Paul uses the thief picture in the same passage in which the Lord descends with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 5:2). There is one public and glorious return of Christ, when he raises the dead, gathers his people and judges the world, and here, in chapter 16, the church is still on earth being told to stay awake. Christians who expect a rapture before the tribulation answer that these are people converted after the church has been taken; they hold that view from a real desire to honour God’s distinct promises to Israel and the church, and they are our brothers and sisters. But nothing in the text marks out a second group, and the warning is the one Christ gave the churches (3:3).

If he comes like a thief, can anyone know when? No. No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and every attempt to set dates has failed and done harm. But believers are not in darkness, for that day to surprise them like a thief (1 Thessalonians 5:4): not because they know the date, but because they are ready whatever it is. A watchman does not know when the attack will come; he simply does not fall asleep.

Where Christians differ: is Armageddon a literal battle in northern Israel? Many futurists, including premillennial Christians (who expect Christ to return before an earthly reign of a thousand years) and dispensational Christians (a form of premillennialism that keeps God’s plans for Israel and for the church distinct), expect the armies of the world to gather literally in the valley of Megiddo for a final war in the Middle East before Christ returns. They take the place name as a real address and read Zechariah 12–14 as a real siege in the land; they are faithful brothers and sisters, reading with reverence. This commentary’s view: Armageddon is a symbolic name for the final conflict between the powers of the world and God, drawn from Israel’s history of decisive battles at Megiddo. The battle is described three times in Revelation (16:14–16; 19:17–21; 20:7–10), and each time no battle is actually fought: the enemies are gathered and then destroyed at once by Christ at his coming. It is the same final event, seen from different angles. It may involve a literal gathering of hostile powers, but its location and form are not the point; its outcome is. Christ wins without a fight.

Uncertain wording. The likeliest derivation is har Megiddo, “mountain of Megiddo”, but there is no mountain of Megiddo, only the mound of the town above the plain. Some therefore connect it with Mount Carmel nearby, where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal; others read it as “mountain of assembly”, the phrase Isaiah puts in the mouth of the fallen day star, who says he will sit on the mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13). The Megiddo reading remains the most likely, and on any reading the name points to the place where God’s enemies gather and are overthrown.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the seventh bowl God declares his judgment complete, and the whole created order shakes. The wrath announced in chapter 15 has run its full course.

Into the air. The last bowl is poured into the air, the one element the first six left alone, and the one nobody can stand outside of. Paul calls the devil the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2), the realm where demonic powers operate.

It is done! The voice comes from the temple and from the throne, which in this book means God himself. One word in Greek, gegonen: it has happened, it stands accomplished. The tense is perfect, a completed act whose result is permanent.

What exactly is done? Chapter 15 said it in advance: “with them the wrath of God is finished” (15:1). There is no eighth bowl; God’s judgment on this age has a stopping point, and it has been reached.

Lightning, rumblings, thunder. John’s standing signal that God has acted, growing through the book (4:5; 8:5; 11:19) to its fullest form here.

A great earthquake. God said through Haggai that he would shake the heavens and the earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews explains that this means the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain; therefore we are to be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:26–28). So the greatest earthquake in history is not demolition for its own sake but a sorting: everything that can be shaken is shaken, so that only what was never going to fall is left standing.

Three announcements of completion. The cry echoes two others, and they frame everything. On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), a different verb with the same force. At 21:6, from the throne, God says of the new creation, “It is done!”, almost the same word as here. The cross accomplished salvation, this word completes judgment, and the same word opens the new creation; because salvation was finished at the cross, believers can face the judgment unafraid.

What counts as shakeable in my life? Anything that belongs only to this age: money, reputation, health, career, national power, the approval of others, even the outward shapes of church life. Many are God’s good gifts, but none can bear the full weight of a soul. What cannot be shaken is God himself, his word, Christ’s finished work, the kingdom he gives and the people he has made his own. So a believer’s honest question on reading this verse is not “Will I survive this?” but “How much of what I am leaning on can be shaken?” Hold what can be shaken loosely, and what cannot with both hands.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings Babylon, and every city built on her pattern, to judgment; the old creation gives way, and humanity under the final blow still curses God. These verses open the way to chapters 17 and 18, which describe Babylon’s fall in full.

Split into three. The great city is Babylon (v. 19; 17:18), the phrase used at 11:8 of the city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. It is completely shattered; Ezekiel divided his hair into three parts as a sign of Jerusalem’s ruin (Ezekiel 5:1–2).

The cities of the nations. Every civilisation built without God was built on Babylon’s plan, and all of them fall with her.

God remembered Babylon. God’s remembering never means that something had slipped his mind; it means he is about to act on what he has long known. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Exodus 2:24). The thief on the cross asked to be remembered, and was told that today he would be with Christ in paradise (Luke 23:42–43). God had not forgotten Babylon’s sins (18:5): delayed judgment is not cancelled judgment.

Drain the cup. Drain it to the bottom: the cup of 14:10, poured full strength, which Babylon herself had passed round (14:8). She poured; now she drinks.

Islands and mountains. Two things that do not move. The sixth seal had already removed every mountain and island (6:14), more evidence that the seals and the bowls cover the same ground. Islands and mountains are what people steer by and shelter behind, and there are none left. The old creation is passing away.

Great hailstones. The seventh plague on Egypt was the worst hailstorm the country had ever seen (Exodus 9:18–26), and God threw great stones from heaven on the Amorite kings fleeing from Joshua (Joshua 10:11). There may also be an echo of the law: stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), and the chapter has recorded three times that these people blasphemed. If so, the sky itself carries out the sentence.

They cursed God. With the sky falling on it, humanity’s last act in this chapter is to curse: the true horror of sin is that it hardens until it cannot turn. Revelation has now said four times that judgment by itself changes nobody. What changes people is the witness and the gospel (11:13; 14:6), and the slain Lamb in the middle of the throne; until the day these bowls picture arrives, he is still saving.

The Son of God drained it first. God remembers: nothing evil escapes his memory, and nothing done for his name is forgotten. Yet for those who are in Christ he has made a promise that turns the whole chapter on its head: “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more” (Hebrews 10:17). The cup Babylon must drain to the bottom, the Son of God drained first, in Gethsemane and at Golgotha, for everyone who trusts him. There is no wrath left in it for us; there is only a cup of blessing, and a feast waiting at the wedding of the Lamb.

Could a Christian end up like this? A true believer will not, because God keeps his own and finishes what he began in them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29). But Scripture warns Christians about hardness precisely as one of the means by which he keeps us: exhort one another every day, so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Hardening is gradual: one sin excused, one warning ignored, one prayer neglected. If your heart feels cold, do not despair and do not drift. Confess it, go back to God’s word and God’s people, and ask him to soften you. A heart worried about being hard is not yet the heart in this verse.

Uncertain wording. “About one hundred pounds” translates a single word, “talent-weight” (talantiaia). A talent varied from place to place, so the exact weight cannot be known; the ESV’s figure (some 45 kilograms) is a fair estimate. The point is plain either way: stones no one could survive.

It is what they deserve!”<sup>7</sup>And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!”<sup>8</sup>The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.<sup>9</sup>They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.<sup>10</sup>The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish<sup>11</sup>and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.<sup>12</sup>The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east.<sup>13</sup>And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs.<sup>14</sup>For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.<sup>15</sup>(“Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”)<sup>16</sup>And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.<sup>17</sup>The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”<sup>18</sup>And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.<sup>19</sup>The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.<sup>20</sup>And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found.<sup>21</sup>And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!
keyVerse.note: In the one chapter given wholly to God’s final wrath, Christ breaks into the vision in his own voice, and what he says is addressed to his church. The bowls are shown to believers not to feed curiosity about the end but to keep them ready for it. The robe that covers them is his own righteousness, and the blessing belongs to everyone who keeps trusting him and living like it.

16.reflection:
The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt, and the mark of the beast turns into a festering wound (vv. 1–2). Where have you seen something that promised to open doors turn out to harm the person who took it? What “marks” are on offer in your workplace or community?

The angel of the waters and the altar of the martyrs declare God’s judgments “true and just” (vv. 5–7). How does it help to know that the people who suffered most are the ones who call God just? How does trusting God as judge free us to forgive and pray for our enemies?

Three times the people struck curse God, and twice they do not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21). Why does suffering drive some people to God and harden others? How should this shape the way we pray for friends who are going through hard times, and the way we handle our own pain?

In the middle of the gathering for Armageddon, Christ says, “Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on” (v. 15). What does staying awake look like in an ordinary week? What tends to lull you to sleep?

17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Where we are. The seventh bowl ended with God remembering Babylon (16:19). Now a bowl angel shows John who she is and how she falls; chapter 18 mourns her ruin, and chapters 19 and 21 set the Bride beside her.

The message. Beside the beast’s brute power stands a seductive one: a beautiful woman who offers the world everything without God, and is drunk on the blood of Jesus’ witnesses. Do not be dazzled by her. The beast she rides will turn and devour her, the kings who make war on the Lamb will lose, and even their wickedness carries out God’s purpose until his words are fulfilled.

Why it was said. For the first readers she was plainly Rome, the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of the earth (vv. 9, 18), whose wealth and trade pulled the churches of Asia towards compromise (see the introduction). Some, like Laodicea, were in more danger of admiring her than of dying at her hands, and even John marvelled (v. 6). How far she reaches beyond Rome is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: who is the prostitute?” at the end of the note on vv. 5–6.

How the chapter makes its case. First the vision (vv. 1–6): the prostitute riding the scarlet beast, dressed in purple and gold, holding a cup of abominations, drunk with the saints’ blood. Then the angel explains (vv. 7–18). The beast that “was and is not” mocks God’s eternal name and goes to destruction, while those in the book of life are kept (vv. 7–8). Its heads are Rome’s hills and a line of kings whose time is short (vv. 9–11), a much-debated passage set out here without forcing an identification. Ten kings make war on the Lamb and lose (vv. 12–14), and the beast and kings turn on the woman, because God put it into their hearts (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. The same invitation, “Come, I will show you”, will lead John to the Bride (21:9). The prostitute sells herself and is devoured by her lovers; the Bride was bought with her Bridegroom’s blood and is clothed in what he gives. And the conqueror is still the Lamb, Lord of lords and King of kings with the marks of his death on him, sharing his victory with those he called and chose.

For us. Babylon seldom persecutes the comfortable; she advertises. Receive God’s gifts as gifts, not gods. Do not climb on the beast for safety. Pray for the church she still persecutes, and take heart: the Lamb will not lose one of his called and chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world’s most dangerous enemy of the church is not only the beast that threatens but the woman who seduces, and her beauty hides a cup of filth and a thirst for the saints’ blood. One of the bowl angels invites John to see her judgment: the great prostitute, seated on many waters, who has drawn the kings into her bed and made the world drunk (vv. 1–2). In the wilderness he sees her riding the scarlet beast, dressed like an empress, holding a golden cup of abominations (vv. 3–4). Her forehead names her Babylon, mother of prostitutes, she is drunk with the blood of Jesus’ witnesses, and John marvels at her (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents, and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel shows John the judgment of the great prostitute, the seductive city that has drawn kings into her bed and made the whole world drunk. Babylon, whose fall was announced in 14:8 and 16:19, is now shown for what she is.

One of the seven angels. The guide is one of the bowl angels, which ties this chapter to the last: in 16:19 God remembered Babylon the great, and chapters 17 and 18 give the detail.

Come, I will show you. Judgment (krima) is the verdict, the sentence. Four chapters later another bowl angel will say almost the same words: “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb” (21:9). Two women, two cities, two invitations: the rest of the book is built on that contrast.

Why a prostitute? Not a word chosen for shock. Harlot (pornē) is the prophets’ regular word for unfaithfulness to God, who had bound his people to himself as a husband to a wife, and it is used most often of the people of God themselves: Israel is the wife who played the whore (Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16; Hosea 1–3), and Isaiah laments over the faithful city that has become a whore (Isaiah 1:21). Nineveh and Tyre are called prostitutes too, for selling themselves to whoever would trade (Nahum 3:4; Isaiah 23:15–17). The point is that she sells. A prostitute offers for a price, with no promise attached, what belongs inside the lifelong promise of marriage, and that is what Babylon does with every good thing there is: beauty, security, belonging, significance. It is why she is a more dangerous enemy than the beast. The beast demands; she offers.

Seated on many waters. Verse 15 interprets it: the waters are peoples, multitudes, nations and languages. But the image comes from Jeremiah’s oracle against the original Babylon, which literally sat on the Euphrates and its canals: “O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come” (Jeremiah 51:13). A fact of one city’s geography becomes a picture of influence over the nations.

The kings of the earth. The kings have joined her in idolatry and in the pursuit of wealth and power: the bargain between rulers and money on which every empire runs.

Drunk with her wine. Two groups, and the distinction matters. The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk, the ordinary people who never signed anything and simply drank what was poured. Few are in the room where the arrangements are made; what reaches the rest is a mood: what everyone assumes, what is obviously worth having, what only a strange person would refuse. And drunkenness is not chiefly wickedness but the loss of judgment: the inability to think clearly about God, while being quite certain you are walking in a straight line.

The setting. In John’s day Rome was the centre of a vast trading empire, rich, luxurious and the seat of the emperor cult; Roman writers themselves called it a city of vice. The goddess Roma was worshipped in Asia, and a coin of Vespasian showed her seated on Rome’s seven hills.

Without money and without price. Babylon sells beauty, security and belonging for a price, and promises nothing. The Lamb gives them freely and binds himself to his people for ever. Through Isaiah God called, “Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1), and the last invitation of this book is that whoever desires may take the water of life without price (22:17). John the Baptist called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29), and a bridegroom does not sell himself; he gives himself, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The Bridegroom gives everything and asks for the heart. He loved an unfaithful bride, as Hosea loved Gomer, and bought her back at the price of his own blood (Hosea 3:1–2; 1 Peter 1:18–19). The prostitute sells herself and is destroyed; the Bride was bought, and will be loved for ever.

What does Babylon look like where I live? Wherever a culture offers you everything good, comfort, pleasure, status, security, belonging, without God, and then asks for your heart in return, you are looking at her. In a modern Western city she rarely persecutes with swords. She advertises. She tells you that you are what you own, that sex is a right without a covenant, that a sensible person keeps religion private, and that the good life is one purchase away: in the shopping centre, the screen in your pocket, the career ladder and the endless feed. None of these is evil in itself; the question is whether they are being offered to you as substitutes for God.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees the woman riding the beast, magnificently dressed and holding a golden cup full of filth: the world’s seductive glory, carried on the back of brute power. Her beauty is real, and that is exactly her danger.

Carried away in the Spirit. The third of John’s four times “in the Spirit” (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10), each marking a new section. The location is deliberate. To see the Bride he will be carried to a great, high mountain (21:10); to see the prostitute he is taken into a desert. The wilderness sheltered the woman of chapter 12 (12:6); now it exposes the false one.

A woman on a scarlet beast. It is the beast of chapter 13, with the same seven heads and ten horns (13:1), political power empowered by Satan. Babylon, the world’s culture and economy, rides on the back of that power. She does not own the beast; she is carried by it. Her whole position depends on a creature she does not control, and v. 16 will show what that arrangement is worth. The beast’s scarlet matches hers, and the dragon’s (12:3): they are dressed for each other.

Purple and scarlet. Purple dye, from a Mediterranean shellfish, was fabulously costly, the mark of an emperor; scarlet was costly too, and Jeremiah pictured unfaithful Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and adorning herself with gold to attract lovers (Jeremiah 4:30). Gold, jewels and pearls are exactly the cargo the merchants of the earth will weep over in chapter 18 (18:12, 16). This is not a squalid figure in a doorway. She is the best-dressed woman in the world.

Nobody is seduced by something repulsive. That is the point of the whole picture. A child can recognise the beast; Babylon is beautiful, cultured and hospitable, and it takes a prophet in the Spirit to see what she is. The church has often found it easier to resist persecution than prosperity.

A golden cup. Jeremiah called Babylon a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunk (Jeremiah 51:7). Abominations (bdelygmata) are detestable things, especially idols; impurities (akatharta) are unclean things. It is the charge Jesus laid against the Pharisees: they cleaned the outside of the cup while inside it was full of greed and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:25).
