A counterfeit Bride. Her finery is a parody of the Bride, who wears fine linen, bright and pure (19:8), and of the new Jerusalem, adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (21:18–21). John stops to say what the Bride’s linen is: the righteous deeds of the saints, and it was given her to wear (19:8). One woman is covered in what she bought; the other is dressed in what she was given. The giver is her Bridegroom: the robes of his people were washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Her beauty is the fruit of his sacrifice, and that is why it lasts.

How can I enjoy good things without being seduced by them? By receiving them as gifts and not as gods. Everything God made is good and to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and the rich are told to set their hopes not on riches but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Danger signs: a good thing begins to define you, you cannot imagine contentment without it, getting or keeping it bends your conscience, or it crowds out God and his people. A simple safeguard is generosity: give freely of what you most enjoy. A thing you can give away has not yet captured you.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her name reveals what she is, the mother of every city that makes a name for itself against God, and her deepest guilt is the blood of Jesus’ witnesses. Even John is dazzled by the sight of her.

A name of mystery. A name on a forehead is never incidental in this book. God’s servants are sealed on the forehead (7:3), the 144,000 carry the Lamb’s name and his Father’s there (14:1), and the beast’s worshippers take its mark in the same place (13:16). One Roman writer suggests that prostitutes in Rome might wear a band on the forehead bearing their name, and Jeremiah told unfaithful Israel that she had the forehead of a prostitute and refused to be ashamed (Jeremiah 3:3). Mystery (mystērion) means a name to be understood spiritually: not the ancient city on the Euphrates, largely in ruins in John’s day.

BABYLON THE GREAT. The city of pride and rebellion, the destroyer of Jerusalem, whose story goes back to Babel, where people said, “let us make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). Here at last is that name, written on her forehead for everyone to read. John uses it as he used Sodom and Egypt at 11:8, as a symbolic name: in every age she is the human city organised against God.

MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS. Mother means source. She is not one city but the source of a family of them, reproducing in every generation. The old city on the Euphrates was a daughter; so was Rome; there will be others.

Who is she? For John’s first readers she is unmistakably Rome. The seven mountains (v. 9) are the city on seven hills, and the great city with dominion over the kings of the earth (v. 18) could in the AD 90s mean only one place. Peter, writing from that city, sends greetings from “She who is at Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13).

Drunk with the blood of the saints. She has served a cup; now we learn what she drinks. Martyrs (martyres) is the word for witnesses. Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many killed horribly, and early Christian tradition says that Peter and Paul died there.

I marveled greatly. Literally, I wondered with a great wonder (ethaumasa … thauma mega): the verb used twice of the world’s reaction to the beast (13:3; 17:8). An apostle, in the Spirit, has reacted as the earth-dwellers do, whether from horror or, uncomfortably, fascination. The angel’s next words, “Why do you marvel?”, suggest he should not have.

Persecuted in his people. The blood is the blood of the martyrs of Jesus, and the Lord takes it personally. When Saul of Tarsus was on the road to Damascus with warrants against Christians, the risen Christ did not ask why he was persecuting the church, but “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Every drop Babylon drinks is drawn from his body. And before any of them, she killed him: Jesus Christ is the faithful witness (1:5), condemned by a Roman governor and crucified by Roman soldiers. Her name is written on her forehead for shame; the Lamb writes on his people his own name and his Father’s, and his new name besides (14:1; 3:12). She is drunk on their blood; he counts their death precious (Psalm 116:15). The martyrs of Jesus died as he died, and they will rise as he rose.

What it does not mean. Seeing Babylon in the world does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, hate their cities, or treat individuals as enemies. They are called to seek the welfare of the city where they live (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its idols.

In everyday life. Christ counts the wounds of the persecuted church as his own, so pray for it by name: a particular country where Christians are suffering, and one believer there if you know of one.

Can a Christian be fascinated by Babylon? Yes, and John shows it. You can be appalled by a culture and still be more interested in it than in God: reading every outrage, knowing every detail of the world’s sin and little of God’s word. The line between prophetic concern and fascination is thin, and an apostle needed it pointed out. If your mind is full of Babylon, turn it deliberately to the Lamb. You become like what you gaze at.

Will ancient Babylon in Iraq be rebuilt? Some popular teachers expect it, as a world capital. But the name is a mystery, to be understood spiritually, and the angel identifies her as Rome (see “Who is she?” above). The issue is the spirit of Babel, alive in every capital and every heart that says, let us make a name for ourselves.

Where Christians differ: who is the prostitute? Many Reformers and later Protestants, Luther, Calvin, Knox and the Westminster divines among them, identified her with the Roman Catholic Church and the papacy, seeing in her purple and scarlet the robes of cardinals and in her drunkenness the blood of the persecuted Reformers. They lived under a church seated in Rome, rich, allied with kings and burning Bible-believing Christians, and they rightly saw that a church can become a harlot, as Israel did. Others see her as apostate Christianity in general, or a future one-world religion. Some preterists (readers who see most of Revelation fulfilled in the first century) take her as apostate Jerusalem, pointing to v. 6 and to Jesus’ words that Jerusalem kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37); the reading has real evidence behind it, but it does not explain the seven mountains or v. 18 as naturally. This commentary’s view: the prostitute is Rome, the great city of John’s day (v. 18), seen as the centre of a seductive world system of wealth, idolatry and persecution; and she stands for the godless world system in every age, the culture, commerce and false religion that seduce people from God and persecute his people. Wherever a church becomes rich, worldly and persecuting, as the Reformers saw in their day, it takes on Babylon’s features. The Reformers’ reading is not foolish but too narrow: Babylon was there before the papacy and remains wherever Christ’s people are seduced or persecuted. Nor does it license suspicion of Roman Catholic neighbours, many of whom love Christ; the warning is aimed at every church, Protestant ones included, that grows rich and worldly. She is the whole seductive world, which Christians are called to come out of (18:4).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once Babylon and her beast are explained, they lose their glamour: their time is short, their alliances are faithless, and God rules them all. The angel rebukes John’s wonder and explains the beast that was and is not, which goes to destruction (vv. 7–8). Its heads are seven hills and seven kings, and the beast is an eighth (vv. 9–11). Ten kings rule for one hour, make war on the Lamb and lose, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (vv. 12–14). Then the beast and the kings turn on the woman and destroy her, because God put it into their hearts, and she is named as the great city (vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not: a mocking copy of God’s name. It goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty; their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful, in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel explains the beast: it mimics God’s eternal name but has no lasting being and goes to destruction, while those written in the Lamb’s book of life are kept from its deception. The cure for marvelling at Babylon and her beast is to be told what they are.

Why do you marvel? … the mystery. A gentle rebuke: the world’s power and glamour should not impress the people of God. Mystery means what it always means in the New Testament, not a riddle but a secret now disclosed, and the angel explains each part in turn.

Was, and is not, and is about to rise. Set the clause against God’s name in this book: him who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast’s title is a mocking copy, and a poor one, because the middle has collapsed: God “is”, but the beast “is not”. It is also a counterfeit of Christ’s death and resurrection (13:3). The beast appears in one empire, falls, reappears in another and finally rises for a last time, and all of it ends in destruction (apōleia, perdition). The phrase probably plays on the Nero legend, the belief, widespread in the eastern empire, that the dead emperor would return; John takes the rumour and turns it into mockery.

Evil has no being of its own. Whatever the beast is, it does not have being as God has being. God was before the mountains were brought forth (Psalm 90:2), he is now, and he is coming; there is no gap in his being, no weakening, no “is not”. The beast flickers into history and goes to destruction; God endures for ever.

Written in the book of life. As in 13:8, the counterweight to everything alarming in the chapter: a register belonging to the Lamb, its entries made from the foundation of the world, before anyone had done anything to earn or forfeit a place. Election is God’s choice, made before the world began, of a people to belong to Christ, rooted in his free love rather than in any merit he saw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). That choice, not their own cleverness, is why they are not finally deceived, and no beast can rub their names out.

Slain, and standing. A parody shows what the original looks like. The beast seemed to come back (13:3), only to go to destruction; the Lamb was slain in truth, and John first saw him standing, still bearing the marks of slaughter, in the midst of the throne (5:6). His death was real, his rising was real, and where he went after it was not destruction but the right hand of God. The world marvels at a revival that ends in the pit; heaven sings to the one whose death was the defeat of death, and who will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Am I in danger of being taken in? The verse does not say the enrolled are cleverer or more discerning than others. It says they are written, who wrote them, and when. John himself marvelled and had to be corrected; the security is not in his reaction but in the register. Jesus said false christs would lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24), and “if possible” is the point: it is not possible. The Lamb keeps those the Father gave him.

How can I know my name is written in the Lamb’s book? Not by looking into the book, which no one can do, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. Scripture gives election not as a puzzle to solve but as a comfort to those who believe. If you have come to Christ, trusting him alone for forgiveness, and you love him and want to follow him, however weakly, that is the evidence that God chose you (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; John 6:37). The Father draws, the Son receives, and none of them is lost. Make your calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10), not by anxious introspection but by continuing to trust and follow him.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast’s heads point to Rome and its line of emperors, but the point is not a list of names: the beast’s time is nearly over, and it goes to destruction. What the first readers needed, and what every reader can grasp, is how short its rule is.

This calls for a mind with wisdom. As in 13:18, where the number of the beast was set as a puzzle, spiritual discernment is needed. Both times readers have been more confident than the evidence allows.

Seven mountains. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills, and Roman writers such as Virgil and Cicero refer to it so: the first readers could not have missed it.

They are also seven kings. The symbols have more than one meaning: the heads are both hills and kings. Seven is the number of completeness, so the seven kings stand for the full line of the rulers of the beast’s empire.

Five have fallen, one is. This is where certainty has to stop (see the box below). Most likely John’s point is that most of the beast’s rule is already past, the present ruler is in power now, and only a short time remains: history is nearer its end than its beginning. The Lord counts emperors’ reigns as a man counts his fingers: five fallen, one now, one brief.

An eighth. One beyond the seven, a final ruler, yet of the same line and spirit. Early Christians saw eight as the number of new beginning, because Christ rose on the day after the Sabbath, the eighth day; if John has that in mind, the beast’s eighth is a counterfeit resurrection, heading only for destruction. The beast is not a new thing but the seven again, wearing a new number. Empires are not a series of separate problems; they are one problem with a changing letterhead.

It goes to destruction. For the second time in three verses. A reader who cannot reconstruct the emperor list has still been given what matters: not who the kings are, but how long they last.

A kingdom that shall not pass away. The heads and horns come from Daniel 7, and that chapter does not end with beasts. After they have had their season, Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, and to him is given an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus took that title for himself, and at his trial told the high priest that he would be seen coming with the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:62). A reader who cannot work out the seventh king can still know the last King. Theirs is a little while; his is for ever.

In everyday life. When an election or a regime fills you with fear or excitement, put the leader’s name alongside this verse: one is, another is to come, a little while. Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), obey what is lawful, and keep your hope where it cannot be voted out.

Should I try to work out who the kings are? Studying the history is not wrong. But be very wary of anyone who claims certainty, and still more of anyone who matches the kings to present-day leaders. Every such scheme has failed, and many damaged faith when the dates passed. The wisdom John calls for is not cleverness with lists but the insight to recognise the beast’s character in any age, refuse its claims, and remember that its time is short.

Uncertain wording. Who the seven kings are cannot be settled. The emperors from Augustus to Domitian were Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero, then Galba, Otho and Vitellius (in AD 68–69), then Vespasian, Titus and Domitian. Matching the five, the one and the brief seventh to this list depends on where one starts counting and whether the three short-lived emperors are included; the sixth can come out as Nero, Vespasian or Domitian, each only by choices the text does not make for us. The eighth may echo the expectation that Nero would return in a new form, or Domitian, often seen as a second Nero. Since seven is the number of completeness, the likeliest meaning is the one given above: the whole line of the beast’s rulers, most of it past, and the end near.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers who give their power to the beast will reign only briefly; they will make war on the Lamb and lose, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and his people are with him. The outcome is stated before the battle is even described.

Ten kings. The ten horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast had ten horns, interpreted as ten kings (Daniel 7:24). Ten in this book stands for a complete but limited number (as in the ten days of 2:10), so these are most likely all the lesser rulers who serve the beast, still future from John’s point of view, rather than a list to be filled in with names.

For one hour. One hour (mian hōran): a very short time. The phrase returns three times in the next chapter, each time of Babylon’s ruin “in a single hour” (18:10, 17, 19). Their reign and her ruin are measured in the same tiny unit.

Of one mind. One purpose (mian gnōmēn): the nations united against God (Psalm 2:2). Nobody takes their power; they give it away (v. 13), the one thing a king exists to hold. Totalitarian arrangements have often looked like that from the inside: not a conquest of the powerful, but a queue of them handing something over in exchange for a share.

They will make war on the Lamb. The final battle of 16:14 and 19:19: ten kings, a beast with seven heads and the dragon’s throne behind it, against a Lamb. John does not switch to the title Lion (5:5) for the battle; the word is the one he uses of Christ throughout (arnion), the Lamb standing as though it had been slain.

The Lamb will conquer them. The Lamb who conquered by his death (5:5–6) conquers his enemies at his return. There is no description of fighting, and the reason given is not a strategy or a number of troops but a title. The outcome follows from who he is, which is why it can be stated before the event. “Lord of lords” is an Old Testament name for God: “the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2–3). It is given to the Lamb without a word of explanation, and will be written on his robe and his thigh at 19:16, in reverse order. The Babylonian and Persian kings who styled themselves king of kings were borrowing his title.

Called and chosen and faithful. Three words for believers, and the order shows how salvation works. Called (klētoi): summoned by God’s effective call (Romans 8:30), the call that does not merely invite but actually brings a person to come. Chosen (eklektoi, elect): chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Faithful (pistoi): trusting and loyal to the end. This is the one they do, but it comes third. Their faithfulness is the visible end of a chain God began before they existed, and he keeps them faithful by his power.

And still the Lamb. Lord of lords and King of kings, and still the Lamb: the wounds were not laid aside when he took the throne. The kings of the earth hold power for one hour, and even the hour is his to give; he holds his kingdom for ever, and he shares it, for he has made his called and chosen ones a kingdom, priests to his God and Father (1:6).

Outnumbered, and on the winning side. A Christian who feels outnumbered has counted correctly and concluded wrongly: ten kings and a whole world drunk, against a handful of congregations meeting in houses. The verse does not dispute the numbers. It tells them who leads them, and that he called and chose them.

What is the difference between being called here and in Matthew 22? In Matthew 22:14 the call is the gospel invitation, which goes out to everyone who hears it and which many refuse. Here, as in Romans 8:30, the called are those whom God has effectually drawn, whose hearts he has opened so that they come (John 6:44; Acts 16:14). The first is the preacher’s voice; the second is God’s voice through the preacher, raising the dead. So we offer Christ freely to all, confident that his sheep will hear.

I do not feel faithful. Am I really with the Lamb? Faithfulness is not a feeling or a flawless record but a heart that keeps returning to Christ. Peter denied him three times and was restored; Thomas doubted and was met. If you are still holding to Christ, still confessing your sins to him and wanting to follow him, you are with the Lamb. And remember the order: you are faithful because you were called and chosen, not the other way round. The one who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

Where Christians differ: what comes first, God’s choice or our faith? Many Christians, often called Arminian, understand God’s choice as resting on his foreknowledge of who would believe, and they love the same Lamb. This commentary’s view: it follows the order of this verse and of Romans 8:29–30, where God’s choosing and calling come before anything we do.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman’s throne rests on the shifting support of the peoples, and the very powers that carried her turn and destroy her. Babylon is not brought down by the armies of heaven but by her own allies: evil is not loyal.

The waters are peoples. The angel interprets his own image with the fourfold phrase used since 5:9 of the whole human race (5:9; 7:9), the same nations from which the Lamb ransomed his people. Her seat is popular support: she rules by being wanted. And water in this book is not solid ground. The sea is chaos; a river poured from the dragon’s mouth to sweep the woman away (12:15); the Euphrates dried up at a single bowl (16:12). A throne set on water rests on popular feeling, and feeling can ebb as fast as it rose.

They will hate the prostitute. The turn of the chapter, and the last thing a reader expects: she is destroyed by the beast she was riding and the kings who were her clients, as the prophets said the lovers of unfaithful Jerusalem would turn on her, strip her naked and leave her bare (Ezekiel 23:25–29).

Desolate, naked, devoured, burned. Desolate (ērēmōmenēn) is laid waste; naked is the woman in purple, scarlet and gold, stripped. Her flesh is devoured like Jezebel’s, eaten by the dogs by the wall of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:36), and burning was the law’s penalty for a priest’s daughter who became a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9). The four verbs escalate, and each answers something she did. She sold beauty and is left desolate; she traded on being clothed and is stripped; she drank the blood of the saints and is eaten; she lit Nero’s gardens with burning Christians, as the Roman historian Tacitus records, and is burned. Rome had a foretaste in AD 68–69, when it was torn apart in civil war and rival Roman armies burned the Capitol.

The one who was stripped. One other figure in the New Testament was stripped and shamed outside a city, and he had nothing to be ashamed of. The soldiers divided Jesus’ garments and cast lots for his tunic (John 19:23–24), and he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). She is stripped for her own unfaithfulness; he was stripped for the unfaithfulness of others, so that people who had gone after other lovers could be clothed in white and their shameful nakedness never be seen (3:18).

Evil is not loyal. The alliance between the seductive system and the brute power that carries it lasts only while it pays both; then the beast eats the woman. Christ has never once betrayed one who trusted him. He laid down his life for his friends while they were still his enemies (John 15:13; Romans 5:10). His love is not a contract that ends when it stops paying; it is a covenant sealed in his blood, and he carries his own all the way home.

Every idol eventually eats its worshipper. So with the quieter idols of an ordinary life. Make your career your salvation, and it will ask for your evenings, then your marriage, then your health, and when someone younger can do the job more cheaply it will let you go without a backward glance. Make your looks your worth, and your ageing body becomes the enemy. Make another person your god, and you will crush them with expectations no human being can carry, then resent them for failing. Whatever we ride to get what only God can give turns on us, because it could never love us back. Augustine, writing The City of God after Rome was sacked, observed that the earthly city which sets out to master the nations is itself mastered by its own lust to rule. The beast we ride becomes the beast that rides us. Only one Lord does not consume the people who serve him: he let himself be consumed instead, and those who live for him find, to their surprise, that they are being given back to themselves.

In everyday life. Christ already holds you, and no one will snatch you out of his hand (John 10:28), so you need buy no safety elsewhere. If you are tempted to a small accommodation for safety’s sake, a silence to keep your place, a compromise with someone powerful, remember that the thing you are riding has an appetite, and it is not sentimental about passengers.

Should Christians ever seek political power or allies? Christians may serve in government and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7; Romans 13:1–7); Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings faithfully. The warning is against climbing on the beast: making an alliance that requires us to compromise Christ’s truth, or trusting a political power to secure the church’s future. Whenever the church has bought favour by silence or sold its witness for protection, it has in the end been devoured. Serve honestly, speak truthfully, and never make any party, ruler or nation your saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind it all stands God, who steers even the kings’ wicked plans to carry out his purpose until his words are fulfilled; and the woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth. No plot against his people can go one hour beyond his word.

God has put it into their hearts. A daring sentence. The reason the kings agreed, the reason they handed everything to the beast, and the reason the beast turned on the woman, is that God put it into their hearts. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1). This does not mean that God tempted anybody, or that anybody here is innocent. They act freely and wickedly and are responsible for what they do; yet the deepest cause of Babylon’s collapse is a decision taken in heaven, carried out through the choices of men who thought they were serving themselves. Scripture says this without embarrassment: God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Pharaoh hardened his own; Joseph’s brothers meant evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20); Assyria was the rod of his anger and did not know it (Isaiah 10:5–7).

Handing over their royal power. Even their alliance with the beast serves God’s plan: the very unity they formed against him is the instrument he uses.

Until the words of God are fulfilled. God’s word sets the limit. The permission runs exactly as far as the promise and not one hour further.

The great city. In John’s day that was Rome (see “Who is she?” in the note on vv. 5–6). But the description is about what she does rather than where she is, and that role has never been empty for long. Babylon is whatever, in a given century, sits on the peoples, trades with the kings, dresses beautifully, offers everything without God, and will shed blood to keep its place.

The worst act, and the best. Peter said of the worst act in human history that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23). Out of that crime came the salvation of the world. If God could make the murder of his Son the means of our redemption, there is no scheme of the beast he cannot overrule.

Two women, side by side. Another woman and another invitation are coming (21:9), and the reader is asked which he has been dressing for. One is arrayed in purple and scarlet and gold, rides a beast she does not control, and is stripped and burned by the thing she was sitting on. The other is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, and comes down out of heaven from God, and her husband is the Lamb who was slain and is Lord of lords and King of kings.

In everyday life. When world events seem out of control, pray specifically: for rulers to be restrained, for the persecuted to be kept, for enemies of the gospel to be converted, and for God’s words to be fulfilled. Then go about your ordinary duties in peace. The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand, and so is yours.

How does this help a persecuted church? A believer watching a hostile power arrange itself has two possible accounts. Either history is a contest whose outcome depends on whether the good side can hold out, or the arrangements made against the church are themselves the means by which God dismantles what is arrayed against her. The second is harder to look at, and it is the only one that gives solid ground to stand on. No plot against you is outside his plan.

Where Christians differ: is God the author of evil? Some worry that saying God put it into their hearts makes God responsible for their sin, and so they soften the verse to mean only that God permits it; they are right to guard God’s goodness, and Scripture guards it too. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God ordains all that comes to pass, including the evil acts of creatures, without himself being the author of sin, and without taking away their responsibility (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). He does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13), nor infuse wickedness into their hearts; but he directs their evil desires to fulfil his good purpose. This mystery is not a reason for fear but for comfort: even the beast’s schemes serve God’s plan.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters,<sup>2</sup>with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”<sup>3</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns.<sup>4</sup>The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.<sup>5</sup>And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.”<sup>6</sup>And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

keyVerse.quote: They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of glittering seduction and tangled kings, this verse states the outcome before the story is told. The victory rests not on numbers or strategy but on who the Lamb is, and the slain Lamb bears the highest title there is. His people share his victory because he called and chose them, and they are faithful because he keeps them.

17.reflection:
Babylon is pictured not as a monster but as a beautiful, richly dressed woman offering a golden cup (vv. 3–4). Why is seduction often more dangerous to Christians than persecution? Where do you feel her offer most in your own life: money, comfort, status, pleasure or approval?

Even John “marveled greatly” at her and had to be asked, “Why do you marvel?” (vv. 6–7). What draws your fascination in the culture around you, even when you disapprove of it? What would it look like to turn your gaze more deliberately to the Lamb?

The beast and the kings end by hating and destroying the woman they carried (v. 16). Where have you seen something people relied on for security turn on them? How is Christ’s faithfulness to his people different?

Those with the Lamb are “called and chosen and faithful” (v. 14), and God directs even the kings’ wicked plans “until the words of God are fulfilled” (v. 17). How do these truths steady you when the world seems out of control or your own faith feels weak?

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a prostitute riding the beast, a religious and political power; chapter 18 shows her as an economy, and sings her funeral. It tells in full the fall announced in 14:8 and 16:19.

The message. The world city that seems permanent will fall in a single hour, and God’s people must not be found sharing her sins when she does. Babylon holds people less by fear than by comfort; but all she trades can be gone in an hour, and her deepest crime stands at the bottom of her cargo list: she dealt in human souls, and the blood of the saints was found in her.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia lived inside Rome’s prosperity. Some were tempted to share it through trade guilds and idol feasts, Laodicea had grown rich (3:17), and others were paying for their refusal (see the introduction). All needed to see what the glittering city really was, and how it would end.

How the chapter makes its case. The chapter is shaped like the prophets’ dirges over Babylon and Tyre (Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Ezekiel 26–28). A glorious angel announces her fall, and a voice from heaven calls, “Come out of her, my people”, for her boast, “I sit as a queen”, will be answered in a single day (vv. 1–8). Kings, merchants and sailors lament from a safe distance, mourning their share of her; at the centre stands the cargo list, running down from gold to “slaves, that is, human souls” (vv. 9–19). One verse breaks in: heaven and the saints are told to rejoice, for God has given judgment for them (v. 20). Last, a millstone is thrown into the sea, and every ordinary joy falls silent in her (vv. 21–24).

Where it leads. The city that bought bodies to use them up stands against the Lamb who by his blood ransomed people for God (5:9); the woman who dressed herself at others’ expense against the Bride whose linen is given her (19:8); and the cup Babylon mixed for others is the cup Christ drank to the bottom for his people. Her lamps go out, and the Lamb becomes the lamp of the new Jerusalem (21:23); her streets fall silent, and heaven breaks into the song of the marriage supper.

For us. Come out of her by belonging to another city while you live in this one. Refuse her sins, loosen her grip on your heart, treat no one as cargo, and lay up treasure where no fire reaches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon’s fall is certain, so God’s people must not be found sharing her sins. A glorious angel announces it as already done and names those who drank her wine: the nations, the kings and the merchants (vv. 1–3). A voice from heaven calls God’s people out of her, for her sins are heaped high as heaven (vv. 4–5). Her judgment will match her deeds, the cup she mixed for others handed back to her, and her boast that she will never see mourning is answered by death, mourning and famine in a single day (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her, not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city of wealth, pleasure and false worship is as good as fallen, and her ruin will show what she always was. Heaven announces it before it happens, and names everyone who drank her wine.

The earth was made bright with his glory. When the glory of God returned to the temple in Ezekiel’s vision, “the earth shone with his glory” (Ezekiel 43:2). The most magnificent city in the world looks like a candle at noon beside it, and the contrast runs to the end of the chapter, where Babylon’s lamps go out (v. 23).

Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! The announcement of 14:8 now fills a whole chapter, in the words of Isaiah’s watchman (Isaiah 21:9). It is in the past tense because her fall is so certain that it is as good as done.

A dwelling place for demons. The prophets said of the first Babylon that hyenas would cry in its towers and jackals in its pleasant palaces (Isaiah 13:21–22; Jeremiah 50:39). Worship given to anything other than God is never neutral (1 Corinthians 10:20), and the ruin simply shows who had been living there. The word haunt (phylakē) can also mean a prison: the city that offered the world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

The wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. As in 14:8 and 17:2, the nations drank what she poured and lost their judgment. A new group appears: the merchants (emporoi, wholesale traders), who dominate the chapter from verse 11. Chapter 17 showed a prostitute riding a beast; chapter 18 shows a market. They are the same city: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade.

The power of her luxurious living. Arrogant luxury (strēnous): the strength that comes from having far more than is needed. Babylon holds people not chiefly by fear but by comfort, the quiet promise that a little more will make life secure, which is why her grip is so seldom felt.

The setting. The chapter draws heavily on the prophets’ oracles against Babylon (Isaiah 13; 21; 47; Jeremiah 50–51) and their laments over Tyre, the great trading city of the ancient world (Ezekiel 26–28). In John’s day the wealth of the provinces flowed by sea to Rome through its port at Ostia, and Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder complained of its extravagance.

Fallen because the Lamb has conquered. The past tense is possible because the decisive battle has already been fought. On the eve of the cross Jesus said, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). Babylon’s fall is the victory of the cross working itself out in history, and the angel can announce it as done because, at Calvary, it was. Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and standing for ever is the throne of the one who was rich and became poor for the sake of his people (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Has Babylon already fallen? In John’s day Babylon was Rome, which fell slowly, over centuries, not in a single hour (v. 10). Some expect a literally rebuilt city of Babylon. More likely Babylon is the world system of wealth, power and false worship that Rome embodied, which has risen and fallen in many forms and whose final fall comes at Christ’s return. Every proud empire’s collapse rehearses this chapter.

Is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? No. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Paul does not tell the rich to give everything away but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, setting their hope on God rather than on uncertain riches (1 Timothy 6:17–19). But Jesus said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25), because wealth so easily becomes what we trust. Ask how you got it, what you trust in, whether you are generous, and whether you could lose it and still praise God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls his people to refuse Babylon’s sins while they still live in her, because her sins have reached heaven and her judgment is coming. Coming out of her is not moving away but belonging somewhere else.

Come out of her, my people. The prophets called the exiles to leave Babylon before its fall: “Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD!” (Jeremiah 51:45; compare Isaiah 52:11), as Lot was hurried out of Sodom (Genesis 19:12–22). Paul applied Isaiah’s words to the church (2 Corinthians 6:17). The word “my” matters. God’s people are still in Babylon, living among its temptations, and he claims them there.

Lest you take part in her sins. Take part (synkoinōnēsēte): have fellowship with. The danger is not living in Babylon but sharing her sins. And when a system falls, those profiting from it share in her plagues; it will be no defence that they were only doing what everyone did.

Heaped high as heaven. Heaped high (ekollēthēsan): glued together. A tower of sins stacked up to the sky takes the reader back to where Babylon began, at a tower whose builders wanted its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). She has reached heaven at last, but what arrived there is the record of her sins.

Not emigration but non-participation. It cannot mean physical withdrawal. Christians stayed in Rome; Paul greeted a congregation there and told them to pay their taxes (Romans 13:6–7). A Christian lives in the city, works in it and prays for it, but does not join in what it does or want what it wants, and that is far harder than moving house. It is decided a little at a time, over the compromises everyone makes: the invoice adjusted, the thing not mentioned, the standard that quietly relaxes because it is costing too much. Coming out of Babylon happens on ordinary Tuesday afternoons, and nobody sees it.

In the flow. The book has warned its churches about Babylon’s ways from the start, in Pergamum’s compromise, Thyatira’s Jezebel and Laodicea’s riches (2:14, 20; 3:17); here the warning reaches its climax.

Outside the gate. The New Testament tells us where coming out leads. Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood, and Hebrews draws the conclusion: let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, for here we have no lasting city (Hebrews 13:12–14). Coming out of Babylon is not first a moving away from something but a moving towards someone. Christians can refuse her sins because they have a better treasure, and bear her contempt because he bore it first.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s people can lose their salvation if they are found in the city when it falls. It is a call to be what they are: God’s holy people, not Babylon’s.

What does coming out look like on an ordinary day? Honesty in your accounts when everyone else rounds up; refusing to laugh at what degrades people; keeping sex within marriage; turning off what feeds greed or lust; paying fairly, giving generously, and speaking of Christ when silence would be safer. It also means rhythms that keep your heart in the other city: the Lord’s Day, the church gathered, the word of God and prayer. Name one arrangement you have quietly made with Babylon, and end it this week in the strength of the Spirit, not your own resolve. No one comes out cleanly; but the one who went outside the gate obeyed perfectly in our place, and his record, not ours, is what stands before God.

When should a Christian actually leave something? When staying would require you to sin, or when you cannot remain without being drawn into sin you have repeatedly failed to resist. A job that requires dishonesty, a relationship that pulls you from Christ, a deal that depends on exploitation, a church that has abandoned the gospel itself and not merely one with faults: there coming out may mean walking out. Seek counsel, pray, and act with humility. But do not stay in sin because leaving is costly.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christians should withdraw from society? Some Anabaptist and monastic movements have taken such passages to call for physical separation from the world; their seriousness about holiness is a rebuke to comfortable Christians. Others have used it to call believers out of churches they regard as Babylon. This commentary’s view: coming out of Babylon is mainly spiritual and moral: refusing to share the world’s idolatry, greed and sin, while still living in the world as salt and light. Jesus prayed not that his disciples would be taken out of the world, but that they would be kept from the evil one (John 17:15), and Paul told the Corinthians not to leave the world, but not to share the sins of professing believers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Faithfulness may sometimes require leaving a job, relationship or church that demands compromise, but the call is to holiness, not withdrawal.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s judgment will match her deeds: the cup she mixed for others is handed back to her, and her proud boast is answered in a single day. Her root sin is the self-glory that believes it can never fall.

Pay her back. The commands are plural, and the one addressed is not named, but it is not the church: 17:16 has already said who destroys Babylon, the beast and the ten kings. No Christian in this book ever repays anybody. As Jeremiah said of the first Babylon, “repay her according to her deeds” (Jeremiah 50:29): what she did to God’s people will be done to her.

Repay her double. Literally “double the double” (diplōsate ta dipla), in the cup she mixed: her own cup, her own recipe, folded back on her. Her judgment fits her sin precisely (on the word double, see the box below).

As she glorified herself. The root sin is pride, taking the glory that belongs to God, and self-indulgence goes with it. Babylon glorified herself and is brought low. Christ humbled himself, and God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name above every name (Philippians 2:8–9).

I sit as a queen. Babylon in her own words, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isaiah 47:7–8). Each claim denies what is true of every human power. “I sit as a queen”: her authority is permanent. “I am no widow”: nothing she depends on can die. “Mourning I shall never see”: she is exempt from grief. It is the boast of the city that called itself eternal. And it is less arrogance than the unexamined assumption of every prosperous society, that this will go on, which is why a comfortable church finds this chapter hard to feel. Laodicea said the same: “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing” (3:17).

In a single day. The three-part list echoes the horsemen (6:8), and her boast is answered item by item. No widow? Death comes. Never mourning? Mourning comes. Luxury? Famine comes. Something built over centuries goes in an afternoon (vv. 10, 17, 19): slowly, then all at once.

Mighty is the Lord God. Babylon was called the mighty city (v. 10); her strength was borrowed, his is his own, and never raw force: it is his holiness (15:4), not power alone, that makes his judgment of her right.

A cup he never mixed. The reader of the Gospels knows that cup. In Gethsemane Jesus asked that a cup might pass from him (Mark 14:36), and it was not his own: he had mixed nothing in it. It was the cup of God’s wrath that this book pours out on Babylon (14:10; 16:19), filled by his people’s sins, and he drank it to the bottom so that it would never be handed to them. Every sinner either receives the measure of his own deeds, or is one of those for whom Christ has already drained it. There is no third cup.

She will never be a widow. Babylon said, “I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.” The true King became a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, and stooped to the death she thought she would never meet. Because he did, a Bride who looked forsaken in Babylon’s streets will never be a widow: her husband died once and lives for ever, and every tear she shed in that city God himself will wipe away.

What it does not mean. The call for repayment is not a call for Christians to take revenge. It is God’s own sentence. Believers are forbidden to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19); they leave vengeance to God, who will repay.

How do I know if I am saying, “I sit as a queen”? Watch for the signs of quiet self-sufficiency: you rarely pray except in crisis; you assume your income, health and comfort will continue; you plan your future without reference to God (James 4:13–16); you feel little need of the church; other people’s suffering seems far away. The cure is not anxiety but humility: thank God daily for gifts that could be withdrawn, hold your plans with an “if the Lord wills”, and let others’ needs interrupt your comfort.

Uncertain wording. “Repay her double” is literally “double the double”. Double repayment was a principle of restitution in the law (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9), yet a penalty twice the crime would sit oddly beside “as she herself has paid back others” and “a like measure” (v. 7). Many scholars think the word can mean the full corresponding measure, a matching copy, rather than twice as much, as Isaiah 40:2 is often read (compare Isaiah 61:7). Either way her judgment is full, and in kind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who grew rich from Babylon mourn not her but what they have lost, while heaven is told to rejoice. Three sets of mourners, in descending rank as in Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre, stand far off and weep: kings (vv. 9–10), merchants (vv. 11–17a) and sailors (vv. 17b–19). At the centre stands the cargo list, ending with human souls (vv. 12–13), and not one mourner repents or mentions the blood of the saints. Then one verse opens a window in the funeral: God has given judgment for his people (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Threefold Lament

Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and weep, for their trade, not for her. The cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls. Heaven and the saints are called to rejoice because God has given judgment for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole Roman world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: Ask whose hands made what you hold, and whether your deepest grief would be for a person or for a market.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who profited from Babylon weep at her fall, but only for what they have lost. They keep their distance, and not one of them repents.

The kings of the earth will weep and wail. The first mourners shared her idolatry and luxury, and their grief is for themselves.

Far off. The phrase recurs in all three laments (vv. 15, 17). Her lovers, business partners and carriers all watch from a safe distance, the exact measure of what Babylon’s relationships were worth: every loyalty in Babylon lasts only while it pays.

Alas! Alas! Alas (ouai) is the word for woe. “In a single hour” (mia hōra) comes three times (vv. 10, 17, 19): centuries of power undone in an hour. And something is missing from all three laments: not one word of repentance, not one word about the blood of the saints, which verse 24 says was found in her. They weep because they are afraid, and because their trade is finished.

No one buys their cargo anymore. The second group, the traders, mourn the end of the market, not the city. Their reason for weeping shows what they loved.

The setting. Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre, the great trading city, has the same cast: princes of the sea, merchants and sailors standing on the shore, crying bitterly and throwing dust on their heads (Ezekiel 26:16–18; 27:29–36).

He did not stand far off. Jesus did not watch our ruin from a safe distance, afraid of sharing it. He walked into the middle of it, took the judgment on himself, and was forsaken so that his people never would be. Babylon’s friends stayed only while it paid; his love held all the way to death.

In everyday life. If the thing you would find hardest to lose were taken away, would the grief be for a person or for a market? The mourners are shown up not by their loss but by its reason. Treasure laid up in heaven is the one kind no fire reaches (Matthew 6:19–21).

Is it wrong to work in business or finance? No. Trade, banking and enterprise can be honourable callings that serve neighbours and glorify God: the woman of Proverbs 31 considers a field and buys it, and Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth (Acts 16:14). These merchants are condemned because they grew rich from Babylon’s sin and loved the market more than God or people. A Christian in business serves God by dealing honestly, paying fairly, refusing exploitation, and treating profit as a means of serving others, not the measure of a life.

Is this chapter just the resentment of the poor against the rich? No. A sceptic might call it a persecuted minority dreaming of its oppressors in flames, but the church is never told to seize Babylon’s wealth or burn anything. It tells them to come out of her sins (v. 4) and leaves the judgment to God (vv. 8, 20). Envy wants what the rich have; this chapter calls Christians not to want it, and warns wealthy Laodicea as squarely as Rome (3:17). The charge against Babylon is not that she was rich but that she was proud and cruel, trading even in human lives (v. 13). And the door is not yet shut: the eternal gospel goes out to every nation, tribe, language and people (14:6), including those who now trade in Babylon’s markets.
verseByVerse.note: The laments echo Ezekiel’s dirge over the trading city of Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s cargo list is the list of charges against her: it runs down from luxuries nobody needs to human beings bought and sold. It must be read, not skimmed, because its last item is the point.

Read it as a list. Some twenty-eight items come in groups: precious metals and stones, fabrics, materials for fine furniture, spices and perfumes, foodstuffs, livestock, and finally people. It matches the luxury imports of first-century Rome: gold from Spain, pearls from the Indian Ocean, silk from China, ivory from Africa and India, spices from India and Arabia, wheat from Egypt. Ezekiel’s list of Tyre’s trade, on which John draws, also ended in human beings (Ezekiel 27:12–24).

Gold, silver, jewels, pearls. The list opens with exactly what the prostitute was wearing (17:4). What Babylon traded at a fortune, the new Jerusalem is built of (21:18–21).

Fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth. Silk came overland from China and was enormously expensive; under Tiberius the Roman Senate, Tacitus records, forbade men to wear it as effeminate extravagance.

Scented wood, ivory, marble. Scented wood (xylon thyinon) is citron wood from North Africa, whose grained table tops could sell, Pliny says, for the price of an estate.

Cinnamon, spice, incense. Frankincense and myrrh were among the gifts brought to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11): what was laid at the feet of the true King was burned in Babylon for her own pleasure.

Wine, oil, flour, wheat. Food, from luxury (fine flour) to staples (wheat): Rome could not feed itself without Egypt’s grain. Then livestock, and horses and chariots (rhedōn, four-wheeled carriages).

Slaves, that is, human souls. The climax. The word translated slaves (sōmatōn) is literally bodies, the trade term for slaves, and a merchant’s list could set bodies beside livestock without a second thought. Rome held an enormous slave population, by some estimates a quarter or more of the city, bought and sold in markets across the empire. Then come words no merchant’s manifest carried: that is, human souls (psychas anthrōpōn), taken from the Greek of Ezekiel 27:13 and set at the end of the list like a correction written into somebody else’s paperwork. The market says bodies, in the same column as the cattle. The apostle stops the list to say what they are: people, made in God’s image.

Another purchase. Revelation has already described a second market: the Lamb is worthy because by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (5:9), and the verb is a market word (agorazō, to buy in the marketplace). Babylon’s merchants buy bodies to use them up; the Lamb buys people to set them free, and pays with his own blood. In his kingdom no one is cargo.

Thirty pieces of silver. The King of kings let himself be priced. Judas sold him for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the sum the law set on a slave (Exodus 21:32), so that bodies and souls could be carried out of the market. The Father’s house is full of sons and daughters where there were slaves, and every soul is held in a hand no merchant can open.

Every generation has its own version. The sin named here is not wealth but an arrangement in which people are entered as goods. The list asks a reader not whether he owns anyone, but whether he knows whose hands made what he is holding, and has ever wanted to.

What can an ordinary Christian do about modern slavery and exploitation? More than nothing. Slavery still exists, in forced labour, trafficking and debt bondage, and it touches ordinary supply chains. Pray for the enslaved and those who rescue them. Learn where common goods come from and, where you reasonably can, buy from companies that treat workers justly, even at a cost. Support agencies that fight trafficking. Treat the people who serve you, cleaners, delivery drivers, shop workers, as souls rather than services. And remember that the gospel itself is the great liberator: Christians like William Wilberforce opposed the slave trade because they believed every human being bears God’s image. To the church’s shame, other professing Christians defended slavery with the Bible in their hands; this verse, which calls the cargo human souls, stands against them.
verseByVerse.note: The cargo list ends with human beings — the slave trade on which Rome’s economy depended.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s whole economy was built to feed a craving of the soul, and everything it fed on is lost for ever. When her mourners try to praise her, all they can describe is her clothes.

The fruit for which your soul longed. A verse addressed to the city breaks into the lament. Longed (epithymias) is craving, desire, lust: the fruit of the desire of your soul. The silk, the citron wood, the frankincense, the bodies were never really about commerce but about wanting. That is not an attack on prosperity but a diagnosis of what prosperity is usually asked to do. People accumulate because something in them is hungry and things are what lies nearest. Augustine opened his Confessions by telling God that he had made us for himself, and that our hearts are restless until they rest in him. Babylon is that hunger for God fed with things instead, and organised on the scale of an empire.

Never to be found again. The Greek piles negatives on one another (ouketi ou mē): not merely lost, but unfindable. Her delicacies and splendours did not last, and could never have satisfied the longing even while she had them.

Alas, alas, for the great city. The merchants’ lament describes her in almost the words used of the woman in 17:4. Their tribute to a civilisation is a description of her clothes, every item from the lost cargo, without a word about anything she did, made, believed or was.

Two women in fine linen. In the next chapter another woman appears in fine linen, the Bride of the Lamb (19:8). The difference is how each got her clothes. Babylon bought hers, and they are lost in an hour. The Bride’s were granted to her, bright and pure, because her robes have been washed white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Her King was dressed in purple by soldiers as a joke (Mark 15:17) and then stripped at the cross. Babylon dressed herself at the expense of others; Christ was stripped at his own expense, so that his people would be clothed. Babylon’s splendours are never to be found again, but those who have found him have found what can never be lost.

In everyday life. The pull to buy, scroll or snack in an empty moment is usually a hunger in disguise. There is freedom in naming it, and bringing it in a short prayer to Christ, who is never lost, before reaching for anything else.

Why do the things I want never satisfy for long? Because you were made for God, and every created good, however lovely, is too small to fill a space shaped for him. C. S. Lewis observed that if we find in ourselves a desire no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that we were made for another world. The answer is to desire rightly: to receive good things with thanks, as signposts, and bring the deepest longing to Christ, who said that whoever comes to him will never hunger (John 6:35). Contentment is learned, Paul says (Philippians 4:11–13), and it is learned in him.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sailors’ grief shows what the city had become to them: a god, and she was gone in an hour. Like every mourner in the chapter, they weep for what they gained from her, not for her.

All this wealth has been laid waste. After the merchants come the humblest mourners: shipmasters, crews, everyone whose living came off the water, as on the shore of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:29–32).

What city was like the great city? The question is a parody, and the reader of Scripture has heard its form before. Israel sang at the Red Sea, “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?” (Exodus 15:11). The worshippers of the beast cried, “Who is like the beast” (13:4). Tyre’s sailors asked it of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:32), and these sailors ask it of a burning city. It is the question of worship, and it keeps being asked of the wrong subject: they had made the city their god.

They threw dust on their heads. A sign of grief (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; see mourning customs), as the sailors did over Tyre (Ezekiel 27:30).

Grew rich by her wealth. Three social classes, three laments, and one reason between them. Nobody mourns Babylon; they mourn their share of her. And all three say “in a single hour”, because what frightens them is not that Babylon was wicked but that she fell so quickly. Trade is not wrong; but everything on the cargo list can end between breakfast and lunch.

The question with one true answer. Revelation has asked one other question of this kind and answered it. In chapter 5 an angel asks who is worthy to open the scroll, and no one in heaven or on earth is found, until the Lamb who was slain takes it and heaven and earth sing his worth (5:2–13). Many cities have been like Babylon, and all of them burn. Nothing in history is like the Lamb, because nothing else has conquered by dying and stayed on the throne. Babylon’s wealth went up in an hour of smoke; the riches of Christ are unsearchable, and those who belong to him have an anchor no storm can drag, fixed behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of them (Hebrews 6:19–20).

In everyday life. Christ is the one foundation already laid (1 Corinthians 3:11), and nothing built on him burns. So finish this sentence honestly: “I would not know who I was if I lost my ...” Whatever completes it is the thing to hand to God this week, thanking him for it and telling him that he, not it, is your life.

Should a Christian save, invest or plan for the future? Yes, wisely. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the one who provides for his family (1 Timothy 5:8). The problem is not prudence but trust: saving is wise; making savings your security is idolatry. Jesus called the rich man a fool not because he had barns but because he laid up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So plan, save and work hard, but give generously, hold it all loosely, and remember that it could all be gone in an hour, while what you have given to Christ is kept for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven and God’s people are told to rejoice, not over suffering, but because God has ruled in their favour against the city that killed them. One verse stands in the middle of the funeral like a window opened in a closed room.

Rejoice over her, O heaven. The prophets foresaw heaven and earth singing for joy over Babylon (Jeremiah 51:48) because God avenges the blood of his children (Deuteronomy 32:43). The verse leads straight into the hallelujahs of 19:1–5.

Saints and apostles and prophets. All God’s people, especially those who led and suffered: apostles such as Peter and Paul, who by early tradition were killed in Rome. Their blood was found in her (v. 24). Those invited to rejoice are the wronged, and a victim relieved that justice is done is very different from a bystander enjoying somebody’s ruin.

God has given judgment for you against her. A legal phrase (ekrinen ho theos to krima hymōn ex autēs): God has judged your case against her. The saints brought their case to God’s court (6:10), and he has ruled in their favour. What is celebrated is not suffering but a verdict: not one martyr’s case lost in his files, not one apostle’s blood forgotten.

Their case is his case. The saints do not stand in this court alone. Babylon’s courts condemned Jesus first: a Roman governor sentenced him, and God overturned the verdict by raising him from the dead, which is why Paul says he was vindicated by the Spirit (1 Timothy 3:16). The martyrs go down the same road to the same reversal. When God gives judgment for his people against Babylon, he is finishing what he began on Easter morning, ruling in favour of his Son and of everyone joined to him.

The alternative is worse than it looks. A universe in which the murder of the innocent is finally shrugged at is not a kinder universe; it is one in which nothing matters. To be unable to rejoice that wrong has been put right is not compassion but a failure to believe the wrong was real. And the rejoicing follows the judgment; it never produces it (on who repays Babylon, see the note on vv. 6–8).

What about the wrong done to me that was never put right? This verse speaks to anyone carrying something unresolved: a crime nobody was charged with, a reputation destroyed, an abuse covered up, a death never accounted for. A day is coming when heaven will name your case out loud and tell you to be glad: not because you were owed revenge, but because you were owed a verdict, and it will be delivered. Meanwhile you may seek justice through proper means, the courts, the church’s discipline, the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:4), and you may bring your grief to him. You are not required to pretend it did not matter. It matters to God.

Where Christians differ: is it right to rejoice over judgment? Many Christians feel that rejoicing over anyone’s destruction contradicts Christ’s command to love our enemies, and Scripture does say, do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17). This commentary’s view: the joy here is not delight in suffering, nor personal revenge. It is joy that God has kept his promise, justice is done and the persecuted are vindicated. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and neither should we. But when the judgment is final, his people will see clearly that it was right, and rejoice in God’s justice. Now, before that day, we love our enemies, pray for them and seek their salvation, leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sixfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon will sink without trace, and with her goes every ordinary joy she spent on her trade. A mighty angel repeats the sign Jeremiah gave against the first Babylon and throws a great millstone into the sea (v. 21). Music, craft, the mill, the lamp and the voices of bridegroom and bride will be found in her no more (vv. 22–23). Three reasons close the chapter: her merchants’ pride, her sorcery, and the blood of prophets, saints and all the slain, found in her (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Millstone and the Silence

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon sinks. Music, craft, the mill, the lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom are heard in her no more, and in her is found the blood of the prophets and saints.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jeremiah had sunk Babylon’s doom in the Euphrates; John’s angel repeats the sign.

Now: The ordinary goods of life, bread, lamplight and weddings, were always worth more than the cargo. What is hidden will one day be looked for and found.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon will sink without trace, and every ordinary joy she traded away will fall silent in her, because of her pride, her deceit and the blood she shed. The chapter that spent so long on gold and silk ends by mourning the mill and the lamp.

A stone like a great millstone. An acted prophecy borrowed from Jeremiah, who had his prophecy against Babylon read aloud in the city, tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates, with the words that so Babylon would sink, to rise no more (Jeremiah 51:59–64). A millstone, the heaviest ordinary thing in an ancient town: one splash, and then nothing at all.

The sixfold silence. The phrase no more (ou mē … eti) tolls six times in three verses: once over the city itself, and then over five things that will be heard or found in her no more. Music goes first, then the workshops and skilled hands making something new, then the grinding of the handmills before dawn that told you there would be bread. Then the light of a lamp: not a public illumination, but the small light in one room where a family sits after dark. Every window in the city is black; in the new Jerusalem God is the light (21:23; 22:5).

The voice of bridegroom and bride. The last and the heaviest, taken from Jeremiah’s warning to Judah (Jeremiah 25:10): nobody is being married, so nobody is being born, so there will be no next generation.

Where Babylon’s true wealth was. Not palaces or treasuries, but music, craft, bread, lamplight and weddings; and she spent it on cargo.

Your merchants were the great ones of the earth. The first reason: wealth was worshipped. Isaiah said Tyre’s merchants were princes (Isaiah 23:8); the traders had become the aristocracy, as happens when a society decides that money is the only real rank.

Deceived by your sorcery. Sorcery (pharmakeia): magic, drugs, enchantment (9:21). The second reason: she bewitched the nations so that they could not see the truth.

The blood of prophets and of saints. The third and deepest reason is murder, and the indictment is enormous: the blood of all who have been slain on earth. Jesus said something with the same reach over Jerusalem, that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of Abel onward (Matthew 23:35). One city did not commit every murder. Babylon is the name for the human project of building without God, in every century and place, and every drop of innocent blood ever spilled was spilled somewhere inside it. And it was found: Babylon did not report it. Somebody looked, and the blood was in the foundations.

In the flow. The millstone clears the stage. Chapter 18 ends in silence, and chapter 19 opens with the roar of heaven’s hallelujah: the city where no bridegroom’s voice is heard gives way to the marriage of the Lamb.

The millstone Jesus spoke of. Jesus said it would be better for anyone who causes one of his little ones to stumble to have a great millstone fastened round his neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea (Matthew 18:6). Babylon did far worse than make them stumble: she killed them, and their blood was found in her. The one who warned with a millstone was not exaggerating, and he has not forgotten one of the little ones he spoke for.

Nothing good will be lost. Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).
