The song and the craft, the bread and the lamp, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride were his before Babylon touched them, and he will gather them into a new creation where the Lamb is the lamp and the Bridegroom calls his Bride home to the marriage supper.

In everyday life. The things these verses mourn are within reach of almost everyone: a shared meal, music, a job well done, a lamp lit at home, a wedding. Receive them as God’s gifts with thanks, guard time for them against the pull of earning and buying, and let each one remind you of the feast and the light still to come.

Will there be music, work and marriage in the new creation? Music, certainly: heaven in this book is full of harps and new songs (5:8–9; 14:2–3). Meaningful work too, it seems (21:24–26; 22:3). Marriage is different. Jesus said that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), because the marriage every human marriage pointed to will have arrived: Christ and his Bride, the church (Ephesians 5:31–32; Revelation 19:7). Every true joy is either kept or fulfilled in something greater.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah had a scroll against Babylon tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.<sup>2</sup>And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”<sup>11</sup>And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,<sup>12</sup>cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble,<sup>13</sup>cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.<sup>14</sup>“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”<sup>15</sup>The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud,<sup>16</sup>“Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!<sup>17</sup>For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off<sup>18</sup>and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”<sup>19</sup>And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

keyVerse.quote: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s one command to the church, set at the heart of a funeral song. Everything else in the chapter, the boast, the laments and the cargo list, shows why it matters: Babylon is about to fall, and God, who calls his people “my people” while they still live in her, does not want them sharing her sins or her ruin.

18.reflection:
Babylon holds people “from the power of her luxurious living” (v. 3), by comfort more than fear. Where do you feel the quiet promise that a little more will make life secure, and how does it shape your choices?

“Come out of her, my people” (v. 4) cannot mean moving out of the world. What arrangements with Babylon are Christians around you most tempted to make at work, at home or online, and what would coming out look like there?

The cargo list ends with “slaves, that is, human souls” (v. 13). How might ordinary buying, working and managing treat people as goods today, and what could we do differently?

The mourners stand far off and weep for what they have lost, while heaven is told to rejoice (vv. 9–20). What does it show you about Christ that he did not stand far off from our ruin, and what treasure of yours could not be lost in a single hour?

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Where we are. Babylon has fallen and her streets are silent (chapter 18). Chapter 19 is heaven’s answer, and the hinge to the end: the beast and the false prophet leave the stage here, the dragon in chapter 20, before the new creation.

The message. God reigns, and the Lamb’s wedding has come. Heaven praises him because the martyrs’ prayer has been answered; then Christ himself rides out of an opened heaven, Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords, and his enemies are taken without a fight. Every human being will be at one of two suppers: the marriage supper of the Lamb, or the great supper of God.

Why it was said. The seven churches confessed Jesus as Lord in cities that called Caesar lord, and some had suffered for it (see the introduction). They needed to know that their prayers had been heard, that the beast was no match for their Lord, and that their small, unseen faithfulness was being woven into a wedding dress.

How the chapter makes its case. Four hallelujahs rise over the judgment of the prostitute and over God’s reign and the marriage of the Lamb, whose Bride is granted fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints (vv. 1–8). The invited are blessed, and an angel refuses John’s worship (vv. 9–10). Then heaven opens, and the rider on the white horse comes out with the armies of heaven behind him, crowned, named and robed in blood (vv. 11–16). An angel calls the birds to the great supper of God (vv. 17–18), and the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. The praise comes before the battle is described, because the outcome was settled at the cross. The rider’s robe is dipped in blood before any battle begins, he fights with nothing but his word, and the one who judges is the one who was slain. The Bridegroom who gave himself for his Bride now comes to take her home.

For us. Keep praying for justice, sure that heaven will one day say Amen. Get ready for the wedding by faith and ordinary faithfulness, in the dress he gives. Worship no one but God. And urge those who have not yet answered the invitation to come to the Lamb’s table while it is open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Heaven praises God because his judgments are just and the marriage of the Lamb has come. The great multitude sings hallelujah over the judged prostitute, for God has avenged his servants, answering the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (vv. 1–3). The elders and living creatures add their Amen, and a voice from the throne calls all his servants, small and great, to praise him (vv. 4–5). The last hallelujah announces that God reigns and the Bride is ready, clothed in fine linen given to her (vv. 6–8). The invited are blessed, and an angel refuses John’s worship: worship God (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited, and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven praises God because he has judged Babylon justly and answered his martyrs’ cry for justice. Earth’s last word over the city was “Alas!” (18:10, 16, 19); heaven’s is “Hallelujah!”

A great multitude in heaven. As in 7:9: the redeemed, from every nation, more than anyone could count.

Hallelujah! A Hebrew word meaning praise the LORD (hallelu, praise; Yah, the short form of God’s name). It occurs in the New Testament only here, four times, at the funeral of an empire, and John leaves it untranslated, so a Jewish Christian would hear the praise of his own synagogue. The reasons follow at once, and they are not gloating.

Salvation and glory and power. As in 7:10 and 12:10. The praise is for the character of God, not for anybody’s suffering. Babylon had claimed all three, offering security, glamour and influence, and every one turns out to be God’s. Salvation is his: he planned it, purchased it and applies it. Glory is his: no city, empire or beast will ever share it. Power is his: he raised Christ from the dead and will raise all who are his.

True and just. As the redeemed (15:3) and the altar (16:7) declared: three times heaven has said the same two words, and never once had to take them back.

He has judged the great prostitute. She “corrupted the earth”, and corrupted (ephtheiren) means ruined, destroyed. She was among the destroyers of the earth (11:18), and now she herself is destroyed.

Avenged on her the blood of his servants. That answers a question asked thirteen chapters earlier. Under the altar the souls of the martyrs cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (6:10). Here are the same two verbs, judged and avenged, in the past tense. That is what a persecuted church most needs and most doubts: the prayer under the altar was not lost, but answered at the time appointed.

The smoke from her goes up forever. As with Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and Edom (Isaiah 34:10): a verdict that will not be reversed. The city that said, “I sit as a queen” (18:7), expected to last for ever. What lasts for ever is the smoke of her ruin.

The setting. In the Psalms hallelujah often begins or ends a psalm. Psalms 113–118, the Hallel, were sung at Passover, and Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn, probably from these psalms, after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). The first Hallelujah in the Psalter closes a prayer that sinners be consumed from the earth (Psalm 104:35): praise at the end of evil is as old as the Psalms.

Salvation by the blood of the Lamb. The first word heaven sings is salvation, and this book has already said what it cost. When the same cry was heard at 12:10, it went on: the brothers have conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (12:11). So the hallelujah over Babylon is not the cheer of the winning side in a war between equals. The decisive battle was fought on a cross outside Jerusalem, and the fall of Babylon is that victory made visible.

In everyday life. When you pray about an injustice unanswered for years, remember that the martyrs waited from chapter 6 to chapter 19. Keep praying, and add a hallelujah before the answer comes.

Does smoke for ever mean that the punishment of the lost is eternal? Yes. The same phrase, for ever and ever, is used of the worship of God (4:9–10; 5:13), of the torment of those who worship the beast (14:11) and of the devil (20:10). The fall of Babylon as a system is final, and the punishment of those who belonged to her and refused to repent is conscious and without end (Matthew 25:46). It is a terrible truth that should make us tremble and plead with people. Some careful Christians, called annihilationists, read it otherwise (their view is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ” in the note on vv. 19–21). And this permanence is also why the hallelujah is right: evil is never coming back, and nothing will ever again corrupt God’s world.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those nearest the throne say Amen to heaven’s praise, and every servant of God, small and great, is called to join it. No one in heaven’s choir is there on his own record.

The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures. Their last appearance in Revelation. They have been there since the first throne vision (4:4–11), and they close the worship of this age still on their faces.

Amen. Hallelujah! Two Hebrew words, and together one of the oldest congregational responses in Scripture: “And let all the people say, ‘Amen!’ Praise the LORD!” (Psalm 106:48; compare 1 Chronicles 16:36). Those closest to the throne add nothing original; they agree.

Praise our God. The voice from the throne says “our God”, not “your God”: the one who calls for praise counts himself among the worshippers. If the voice is Christ’s, as many have thought, the pronoun is deeply moving. The risen Jesus sent word to his brothers, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17), and Hebrews hears him say, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). Whoever the speaker is, the church sings under a leader who is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

Small and great. That means everyone, and wherever the phrase comes it puts everyone on one level (11:18; 13:16; 20:12), as the psalm promised: the LORD “will bless those who fear the LORD, both the small and the great” (Psalm 115:13).

No back row. Much Christian discouragement comes from suspecting that God ranks his people in tiers, rating us higher because we have done more, or lower because others have: an old craving for approval dressed up as religion. The people summoned here are described in two ways only: they serve him and they fear him. Our God is worthy of the worship of the highest creatures in heaven, who fall on their faces and add nothing but their agreement, and he is gracious enough to want the voice of the smallest of his servants in the same choir.

What am I saying when I say Amen? “This is true, and I put my weight on it.” It is a confession of faith, which the early church said aloud together (1 Corinthians 14:16), and Christ himself is called the Amen, the faithful and true witness (3:14), because all the promises of God find their Yes in him, and through him we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). So say it on purpose.

Will there be degrees of reward in heaven? Scripture does speak of rewards for faithfulness (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15; 2 Corinthians 5:10), and many Reformed teachers have held that capacities for joy may differ, as vessels of different sizes may all be full. But there are no degrees of acceptance. Every believer is welcomed on exactly the same ground, the righteousness of Christ, and every one is equally a child, a servant and a member of the Bride. Rewards themselves are gifts of grace, God crowning his own work in us. No one in heaven will feel second-class, and no one will want anything but to praise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has taken up his reign openly, and the marriage of Christ and his people has come: the Bride is ready, dressed in linen that is both his gift and her faithful life. This is the goal of all history.

Like the roar of many waters. The fourth and last hallelujah: a multitude, a waterfall and thunder at once, like Christ’s own voice (1:15) and the song of the 144,000 (14:2).

The Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Has begun to reign, has taken up his reign: that is the sense of the verb (ebasileusen). It is the great announcement of the Psalms, “The LORD reigns” (Psalm 93:1; 97:1), and of the seventh trumpet (11:15–17), now sung by the whole company. These are the words of Handel’s Hallelujah Chorus.

The marriage of the Lamb. The image is not an ornament. God is the husband of his people all through the Old Testament: “your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19), and Paul said that marriage itself had been a picture of Christ and the church all along (Ephesians 5:25–32). A Jewish wedding had two stages: betrothal, a binding commitment, and later the wedding itself, when the groom came to take his bride home, followed by a feast. Betrothed now by faith (2 Corinthians 11:2), the church will be united with Christ at his return. The book that opened with seven struggling congregations on a postal road in Asia ends with those congregations getting married.

His Bride has made herself ready. The church prepares for Christ by faithful living, holiness and perseverance, worked in her by his Spirit. The prostitute was dressed by her lovers and then stripped by them (17:4, 16); the Bride has been waiting for one husband.

It was granted her. Verse 7 says she made herself ready; verse 8 says the dress was given her (edothē). She did not buy it or earn it. Laodicea was counselled to buy white garments from Christ (3:18), and the multitude washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14): nobody in this book is wearing anything he produced. As Isaiah sang, “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10). Fine linen, in contrast with the prostitute’s purple and scarlet, gold and jewels (17:4): the Bride’s beauty is purity.

The righteous deeds of the saints. And yet the dress is made of something. Righteous deeds (dikaiōmata): the plural is concrete, the faithful lives of believers, their works of obedience and love. Their deeds follow them (14:13).

Both clauses are true. Paul held the two together: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). Justification is God’s once-for-all verdict that a sinner is right with him because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5); sanctification is the lifelong work by which the Spirit makes him holy (2 Corinthians 3:18). The first never changes; the second grows, and is never finished here. Even the saints’ best deeds are mixed with sin (James 3:2), yet the Father accepts them for his Son’s sake, because Christ’s perfect obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19; Westminster Confession 16.6). So the linen is a gift twice over: the righteousness that covers her is his, and the deeds woven into it are his Spirit’s work, received with delight though they were never spotless.

Kings marry to gain kingdoms. The first thing his open reign brings is a wedding. Before the foundation of the world the Father chose a bride for his Son; in the fullness of time the Son came to win her, not with gifts but with his blood; and through the ages the Spirit has been calling her, washing her and making her ready. Kings marry to gain kingdoms; this King already had all things, and married to share them. On the wedding day he will rejoice over her “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride” (Isaiah 62:5), and she will never stop singing hallelujah.

Why do we ask so much of romance? Songs, films and dating apps run on one story: two people find each other, and at last life makes sense. It is a beautiful hope, and it is crushing. Ask a husband or wife to give you the worth and security only God can give, and you lay on them a weight no one can carry; when they buckle, you conclude that you chose the wrong person. The Bible neither shrugs the longing off nor worships it; it treats it as a signpost. Every human wedding is a rehearsal for this one. That lifts an impossible load off marriage, which may now be a gift rather than a god, and it means that no single person is left out of the only wedding that finally matters. The Bridegroom we were really longing for has already given himself for us.

How does the Bride make herself ready? Not by trying to become lovely enough to be wanted; she is already chosen, washed and loved. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Christ did not love the church because she was lovely; he loved her in order to make her lovely, giving himself up for her “that he might sanctify her” and “present the church to himself in splendor” (Ephesians 5:25–27). Getting ready is the response of someone who knows she is loved. Keep the dress clean: when you sin, do not hide it; confess it the same day and bring it to the blood that washed you (1 John 1:9). Keep your heart for him: name the rival quietly courting you, whether comfort, approval or money, and turn it away, as a betrothed woman turns away other suitors (2 Corinthians 11:2–3). Do the deeds he has prepared: the linen is woven of ordinary faithfulness, kindness at home, honesty at work, care for the weak (Ephesians 2:10). Get ready together: the Bride is the church, so belong to it and help others get ready. And keep looking for him, for “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3).

What it does not mean. Not that individual believers are each married to Christ in a romantic sense. The Bride is the church together, the whole people of God.

If God already reigns, why does it say he has begun to reign? God has always been King over all (Psalm 103:19), but in this fallen world his reign has been resisted and hidden. What begins here is its open, undisputed exercise, like a rightful king who has ruled from exile and now enters his capital and is crowned in public. He was always King; now everyone sees it.

My life seems to have produced so little. What will I have to wear? The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the years of patience with a difficult person, the prayers for a wayward child, the refusal to tell a lie that would have paid: none of it is evaporating. It is being woven. Nothing done for Christ is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58; Matthew 10:42). And remember the first half: the dress is granted. Your place at the wedding depends not on the size of your contribution but on the Bridegroom who washed you, and when the Bride finally appears, what you did in his name will be part of what she has on.

Where Christians differ: is the Bride’s righteousness her own deeds or Christ’s? Some read “righteous deeds of the saints” as meaning that believers are made acceptable by their own good works; others, emphasising imputed righteousness (Christ’s righteousness counted to the believer), are uneasy with the phrase. This commentary’s view: both grace and works are in the verse. The linen was granted to her, and her robes were washed white in the Lamb’s blood (7:14): her standing before God rests wholly on Christ’s righteousness credited to her by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). And the linen is her righteous deeds, the fruit of that grace, the good works God prepared beforehand for her to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). Justification by faith alone is the root; sanctification is the fruit, and both are gifts. The Bride is dressed by her Bridegroom.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “the Lord God omnipotent reigneth”, following later manuscripts. The best manuscripts read “the Lord our God the Almighty reigns”. The meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who accept God’s invitation to the Lamb’s wedding feast are blessed, and God alone, not even his most glorious messenger, is to be worshipped. The one who stands above the angel is the Lamb whose wedding it is.

Blessed are those who are invited. The fourth of the book’s seven beatitudes (1:3; 14:13; 16:15), and like 14:13 and 21:5 it comes with a command to write, over something a suffering church would find hard to believe. Invited (keklēmenoi) is from the same root as “called” in 17:14. The feast is the one Isaiah promised, of rich food and well-aged wine on the mountain where God swallows up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8): the joy of the new creation and fellowship with Christ.

The least deserved document in the world. A wedding invitation is earned by no one; it says only that somebody wanted you there. In Jesus’ parable, when the invited guests would not come, the servants went into the streets and gathered all they found, both bad and good (Matthew 22:9–10).

These are the true words of God. A guarantee meant for the reader: a suffering church finds the wedding harder to believe than the beast.

I fell down at his feet to worship him. Overwhelmed, John makes a mistake, records it honestly, and makes it again in 22:8: a comfort as well as a warning. The instinct to worship is right; only the direction is wrong. The angel’s reply is urgent: “You must not do that!” (hora mē, see that you do not). He is a fellow servant (syndoulos): angels, however glorious, are servants like us (Hebrews 1:14), not senior but alongside.

Worship God. The New Testament warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18), and this is crucial evidence for Christ’s deity: the angel refuses worship, but the Lamb receives it (5:8–14). The book that forbids worshipping the highest angel shows the whole of heaven falling down before the Lamb, and no one tells them to stop.

The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. Witness to Jesus is the heart of all true prophecy (on the wording, see the box below). That is why the angel refused: the apostle on the floor and the angel standing over him are colleagues in one task, witnessing to Christ, and only God ranks above them both.

And then he serves the guests. The guests had no claim to be there; they are washed in the blood of the Lamb whose wedding it is. And at that table the roles are reversed beyond imagining: Jesus said the master “will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them” (Luke 12:37). The angel would not take John’s worship. The Lamb receives it, and then serves the guests. He is the Bridegroom, the host and the price of the feast, and the only one in the room worthy of worship.

A permanent hazard for the church. Those through whom God speaks are always in danger of being given what belongs to God: the preacher a congregation leans on instead of Christ, the writer quoted more readily than Scripture, the movement that becomes the thing believed in. Every faithful minister must say what the angel said: I am a fellow servant with you; worship God.

Am I invited to the marriage supper? If you will come, yes. The gospel invitation goes out to everyone who hears it: “The Spirit and the Bride say, ‘Come.’ … let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (22:17). You need not qualify first or prove you are chosen; you come by trusting Christ, who paid for the feast, and no one who comes to him will be cast out (John 6:37). The only people missing will be those who refused.

How is the Lord’s Supper connected to this? It is a foretaste and a promise of the marriage supper. Every time the church eats the bread and drinks the cup, it proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), looking back to the cross and forward to the feast. Jesus said he would not drink the cup again until he drank it new with us in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). So come to the Lord’s Table as a guest rehearsing for a wedding: humbled by what it cost him, and glad about where it is leading.

Where Christians differ: does this mean prophecy continues in the church? Some read “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” as meaning that every witnessing believer has a gift of prophecy, so that new revelations continue today. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, out of love for Christ and a longing to hear him, believe God still gives prophetic words, to be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). This commentary’s view: the verse teaches that the heart of all prophecy is witness to Jesus, and that every believer who bears that witness shares in the prophetic calling of the church (11:3). It does not promise new revelation. The prophetic word John received is now written and closed (22:18–19), and the church bears the testimony of Jesus by proclaiming the completed Scriptures. That, this commentary holds with charity towards those who differ, is how the prophetic gift functions now.

Uncertain wording. “The testimony of Jesus” can mean the testimony Jesus gave or the testimony about him; the Greek allows both, here and where the phrase recurs (1:2, 9; 12:17), and John may well intend both. Spirit may mean the Holy Spirit who inspires prophecy, or the essence and heart of prophecy. Either way the sense is close: true prophecy is moved by witness to Jesus and leads to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ returns as the conquering King, and his enemies are taken without a fight. Heaven opens and the rider on the white horse comes out, Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords, with the armies of heaven in white behind him (vv. 11–16). An angel calls the birds to the great supper of God, the dark counterpart of the Lamb’s wedding feast (vv. 17–18). The beast and the kings gather for war, but the beast and the false prophet are simply captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest fall by the sword from his mouth (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ comes out of an opened heaven to judge and make war as the faithful, all-seeing and rightful King, and his robe already bears the blood by which he conquered. This is his return in glory.

Heaven opened. At 4:1 a door stood open and John was called up. This time heaven itself is opened, and someone comes out.

A white horse! The horse of victory. Roman generals celebrated victory with a triumph, riding into Rome, often said to be behind white horses, with their army and captives. A reader will remember a white horse from 6:2, and the two must not be confused; that rider was a counterfeit conqueror. He had a bow; this one has a sword from his mouth. He was given a crown, a single stephanos, a victor’s wreath; this one wears many diadems, royal crowns, and nobody hands them to him. That rider was unnamed; this one has four names in six verses.

Faithful and True. As in 3:14, where Christ introduced himself to Laodicea as “the faithful and true witness”, and 1:5. The rider with a sword is the same person who wrote the seven letters, and he keeps every promise.

In righteousness he judges and makes war. Almost every war has been declared righteous by those fighting it; this is the one case in which the claim is true, because of who makes it: the king of Psalm 45 riding out for the cause of truth and righteousness (Psalm 45:3–6), the shoot from the stump of Jesse who judges the poor with righteousness and strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:3–4).

Eyes like a flame of fire. As in 1:14: the eyes that searched the hearts of Thyatira (2:18, 23) and saw what Sardis and Laodicea could not see about themselves (3:1, 17). No disguise survives his gaze, and no faithful act goes unseen by it.

Many diadems. The dragon wore seven (12:3) and the beast ten (13:1). This rider wears an uncounted number, and every crown either of them claimed is on his head.

A name written that no one knows but himself. A striking restraint at the moment of his greatest self-disclosure. “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matthew 11:27). After every doctrine has been correctly stated, there is something in Christ that no creature can fully know. He is more than all his titles.

A robe dipped in blood. Soaked, before the battle has been fought. Whose blood? The source is Isaiah 63, where a figure comes from Edom in crimson garments: “I have trodden the winepress alone”, and their lifeblood has spattered his garments (Isaiah 63:1–3). John quotes the winepress two verses later, so on that reading the blood is his enemies’, a sign of certain victory. But Revelation regularly reads the Old Testament’s pictures of war in the light of the cross, and the robe is mentioned before any battle, so it is most likely his own blood, shed on the cross, by which he conquered (5:9; 12:11), with a hint of judgment as well. Either way, the outcome was settled before the battle began, and the one who judges is the one who was slain.

The Word of God. Elsewhere only the Gospel and first letter that bear John’s name use this title of Christ: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1, 14; compare 1 John 1:1). A family signature. Everything God wants to say to us about himself he has said in a person (Hebrews 1:1–2). To look at Jesus is to hear God, and there is no further word behind him to wait for. It also explains the weapon: the conqueror whose name is the Word fights with his mouth (v. 15).

The pattern of going back. A reader taking the chapters in order may assume that the thousand years of chapter 20 begin after this return. This commentary reads chapter 20 as going back to show the whole age between Christ’s comings (see the box below), as Revelation has done before: chapter 12 goes back to the birth of Christ after chapter 11 has reached the end (11:15–18), and the seals, trumpets and bowls each reach the end in turn. On this reading the return of Christ in chapter 19 is the end of the thousand years, not the start of them.

What it means that he is faithful. We learn to trust promises only so far, having broken a few ourselves, and so we lean on our own record and resolve. But the rider’s first name is about his faithfulness, not ours. To be faithful is to be tomorrow what you said you would be today, whatever it costs, and he proved it on the night his friends ran and Peter swore he did not know him: he went on to the cross and kept every word he had spoken about them. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). That is why the Judge is named Faithful before anything else: for those who belong to him, his coming is a promise kept, not a threat carried out. So the next time you have failed him, do not begin with a fresh vow. Begin with his: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Then keep the small promise you made to someone this week, because you belong to one who keeps his. See Faithfulness in the Theological Dictionary.

How can the Prince of Peace make war? Because there can be no lasting peace while evil is free to destroy. The Christ who came first as a Lamb, offering peace, comes the second time as Judge, to end the rebellion of those who refused it (Acts 17:31). His war is not against the weak but against those who make war on him and his people, and it is fought with perfect justice, by one who himself bore the judgment for every enemy who repents. The hands that hold the reins bear the marks of the nails.

Where Christians differ: is this Christ’s return before a millennium, or his final coming? Premillennialists read 19:11–21 as Christ’s return to defeat the antichrist, followed in chapter 20 by a thousand-year reign on earth before the final judgment. They do so because John’s “and I saw” seems to carry the story forward, and because they want to take the thousand years and the two resurrections of chapter 20 at face value; a number of the earliest church fathers read it this way, and many faithful Christians do today. Dispensational premillennialists add a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation. Postmillennialists often read this rider as a picture of the gospel’s conquering advance through history. This commentary takes the amillennial view (the thousand years picture the present age, with no separate earthly reign after Christ’s return). This commentary’s view: this is Christ’s one, final, visible return, which brings the last battle, the final judgment and the new creation. Revelation is a series of parallel visions, and chapter 20 goes back to describe the whole church age again from another angle. The same final battle appears in 16:14–16, 19:19–21 and 20:7–10, described in almost the same words and drawn from Ezekiel 38–39 (the birds’ feast here, the fire there). There is one return, one battle, one final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s people ride with him in their wedding clothes, but he alone wins the victory, by his word, as King over every king. The army carries no weapons; the King needs none but his mouth.

The armies of heaven. Zechariah promised that the LORD would come “and all the holy ones with him” (Zechariah 14:5; compare 1 Thessalonians 3:13). Look at what this army is wearing: fine linen, which John has just explained as the righteous deeds of the saints (v. 8). Those with the Lamb are the called, chosen and faithful (17:14), saints and angels, dressed as the Bride. The church rides out to the last battle in its wedding clothes.

They carry no weapons. The army never strikes a blow: this book’s last word on whether Christians should fight for the faith by force. The saints have been told to endure, hold fast and conquer by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, never once to fight; when the fighting finally happens they are spectators in white. It also answers the charge that faith in a coming Judge breeds violence. The book that ends with the most terrible battle in Scripture forbids its readers to fight it: vengeance stays in the hands of the one person who can be trusted with it.

From his mouth comes a sharp sword. As in 1:16 and 2:16: his word. Isaiah said the Messiah’s mouth would be like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2), and the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one “with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). He conquers by speaking, as God created by speaking, and carries nothing in his hands. The saints’ own weapon all along, the word of their testimony, is a small version of the word with which he will end the war.

A rod of iron. As in Psalm 2:9, quoted at 2:27 and 12:5. The Son against whom the kings of the earth set themselves is the one who breaks them.

He will tread the winepress. As in 14:19–20 and Isaiah 63:3 (see winepress). Christ himself carries out God’s final judgment, for the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The one who drank the cup of wrath for his people now treads the winepress for his enemies.

King of kings and Lord of lords. The supreme title, as in 17:14, where the order is reversed: either way round, the two halves say one thing. It is God’s own title: Moses said, “the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17). Every emperor, king and lord is under him.

What it meant to the first hearers. The seven congregations lived where the emperor was called lord, and some knew the cost of refusing to say so. Into the room where they met to hear this book read came a sentence written on a rider coming out of an open heaven: King of kings and Lord of lords. Not a hope, not a slogan, not a consolation. A name, already written, on someone already riding.

The same mouth. He needs no army to win, yet he will not ride out without his Bride. The mouth that strikes the nations is the mouth that said to a dead man, “Lazarus, come out”, and to a dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise”. He rules the nations with a rod of iron, and he leads his own people gently, like a shepherd.

In everyday life. When an employer, a government or the culture demands something Christ forbids, remember the name on his robe. Be respectful and obedient wherever you can; where you cannot, say graciously and firmly that you belong to a higher Lord, and leave the outcome to him.

Will I be in that army? If you belong to Christ, yes. The armies wear the Bride’s linen, and the Bride is the whole church. When Christ appears, we will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4), and God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Believers who have died will come with him, and those still living will be caught up to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:17): one coming, and the whole people of God, living and dead, will share in it, not as soldiers who win the victory but as the Bride who shares it.

Uncertain wording. “On his robe and on his thigh” may mean two places, or one: the name written on the robe where it falls over his thigh, where it would be seen as he rode. Names were sometimes inscribed on a statue’s thigh. The exact picture is uncertain; the point is not: the name is displayed where no one can miss it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone will be at one of two suppers: at the Lamb’s wedding feast as guests, or at the great supper of God as the meal. The picture is meant to shock us towards the right table.

An angel standing in the sun. Blazing, visible to all. Directly overhead (en mesouranēmati) is the phrase used of the eagle in 8:13 and the gospel angel in 14:6. Warning, gospel and now this summons are each announced where nobody can miss them.

The great supper of God. The scene is Ezekiel 39:17–20 almost word for word, where God summons the birds to a sacrificial feast on Gog’s defeated armies. What makes it horrifying is where John places it. Eight verses earlier: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (v. 9). Here is the other supper, and the invitation goes out to carrion birds. It should not be softened: the birds are a picture, but the ruin they picture is real.

The flesh of kings. The word flesh five times, and a list that starts at the top: kings, commanders, strong men, cavalry, the whole apparatus of power, as at the sixth seal (6:15). Then: both small and great. As the redeemed include small and great (v. 5), so do the lost.

The last word on human greatness. To be left unburied and eaten by birds was the most complete disgrace in the ancient world, the fate David promised Goliath (1 Samuel 17:46). That is the last thing this book says about human greatness built against God: the rider has four names, but the great ones who opposed him are listed only as flesh.

The disgrace he carried. The gospel meets this picture exactly where it is most horrible. The law said that a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Jesus died under that curse: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Stripped, hung up in public outside the city and mocked, he took that disgrace on himself (though loving hands then buried him), so that everyone who comes to him can be moved from the one table to the other. No one at the marriage supper got there by escaping the curse; they got there because he bore it. Rank gives no protection at the great supper of God, and none is needed at the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the small and the great sit down together, saved by grace alone.

In everyday life. Who in your life has not yet answered the invitation to the Lamb’s supper (Luke 14:16–24)? Pray for that friend every day this week, and when an opening comes, tell them about the wedding.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal description of birds eating corpses at the end of the world, to be imagined in detail. It is a shocking symbol, drawn from Ezekiel, of total and shameful defeat for those who fight against God.

Why would Scripture use such a shocking image? Because we need to be shocked. We easily think of God’s judgment as a polite disappointment, and rebellion against Christ as a difference of opinion. The image strips the illusion away: to set oneself against the King of kings is to choose utter ruin and disgrace. It is set beside the marriage supper so that no reader can miss the choice. God shows us this not to frighten us into despair, but to drive us to the other table while the invitation is still open (Ezekiel 33:11).

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last battle is no contest: Christ’s greatest enemies are simply taken and thrown into final judgment, and the rest fall by his word. Every reader who has feared the beast is shown how little it amounts to when the rider arrives.

The beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered. The kings of Psalm 2 who “set themselves” against the LORD and his Anointed (Psalm 2:2), assembled as announced at 16:14–16 (Armageddon) and 17:14 (compare 20:8). The most famous battle in the world’s imagination is joined: watch how long it lasts.

The beast was captured. That is the battle. There is no account of any fighting at all. The verb is passive, and the beast that the whole earth worshipped (13:4), that made war on the saints for forty-two months, is simply taken. John has built up dread of the beast for chapters, and gives the battle not one sentence of drama. That is the point. An enemy who can be taken without a fight was never Christ’s equal.

And with it the false prophet. The second beast of 13:11–17, described by his crime: deception is what he is arrested for. In a book whose enemy is the deceiver of the whole world, that is the charge that matters.

Thrown alive into the lake of fire. The place of final, eternal punishment, first mentioned here. Later the devil is thrown there (20:10), then death and Hades, and all whose names are not in the book of life (20:14–15). It was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Alive is deliberate, perhaps recalling Korah and his company, who went down alive into Sheol (Numbers 16:33): they are not simply wiped out on a battlefield, but go on existing under judgment.

The rest were slain by the sword. By his word alone, and the great supper of God (v. 17) is served.

In the flow. The enemies of God entered the book in an order, the dragon (12), the beasts (13), Babylon (17), and they leave it in reverse: Babylon (18), the beasts (19), and last the dragon (20). Chapter 20 will step back to show the dragon bound during the age of the gospel, and then bring him to the same final battle and the same lake (20:7–10). The last enemy of all, death itself, follows him there (20:14).

What the seven churches were being told. The seven churches had no army, no legal standing and no leverage, and nothing in Revelation tells them to acquire any; it tells them to endure and bear witness (see the note on vv. 14–16). Then it shows them the end, in which they ride out in wedding clothes behind someone who does not need them, and wants them anyway. And the King who ends it all is the Lamb who was slain, who “loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood” (1:5).

Is the lake of fire literal fire? The language is picture language: fire and outer darkness cannot both be literal. But the pictures point to something worse than any image: conscious separation from God’s goodness under his just wrath.

Where Christians differ: are the beast and false prophet persons, and is the lake of fire eternal? Some say that since the beast and false prophet are symbols of systems, not individuals, the lake of fire may mean only their abolition, not eternal punishment. Others, sometimes called annihilationists or conditionalists, hold more generally that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished for ever; they are often careful students of Scripture, moved by its words destroy and perish, and they are not denying the gospel. This commentary’s view: the beast and false prophet represent systems of persecuting power and deception, and also, finally, the persons who lead them. Their being thrown into the lake of fire shows the total end of those systems and the eternal punishment of the persons who embody them, with all who follow them. Revelation 20:10 says the devil, the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night for ever and ever: the punishment is conscious and endless. Christ’s victory over every evil power is complete and permanent.

19.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,<sup>2</sup>for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.”<sup>3</sup>Once more they cried out, “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever.”<sup>4</sup>And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!”<sup>5</sup>And from the throne came a voice saying, “Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.”<sup>6</sup>Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.<sup>7</sup>Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready;<sup>8</sup>it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure”—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”<sup>10</sup>Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.” For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war.<sup>12</sup>His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself.<sup>13</sup>He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.<sup>14</sup>And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses.<sup>15</sup>From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.<sup>16</sup>On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.<sup>17</sup>Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God,<sup>18</sup>to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great.”<sup>19</sup>And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army.<sup>20</sup>And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.<sup>21</sup>And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

keyVerse.quote: Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready
keyVerse.note: Here is the goal of all history in one breath: God’s open reign and the wedding of Christ and his people. Everything in the chapter serves it: Babylon is judged so that the Bride can be presented, and the rider comes out of heaven to bring her home. It also tells a struggling church that its story ends not in defeat but in a marriage.

19.reflection:
The martyrs prayed “how long?” in 6:10 and are answered only here (vv. 1–2). What injustice have you been praying about for a long time, and how does this chapter help you keep praying, and even to praise God before the answer comes?

The Bride’s linen was “granted” to her, yet it is “the righteous deeds of the saints” (vv. 7–8). How do grace and our own faithfulness fit together, and what ordinary faithfulness might be part of the dress in your life this week?

John fell down before the angel and was told, “Worship God” (v. 10). Whom or what are Christians today tempted to honour in ways that belong to God alone: leaders, writers, movements, or something else?

The rider is called Faithful and True, and his army carries no weapons (vv. 11–16). What does this show you about Christ, and how should it shape the way Christians respond to hostility, and the way we speak to those who have not yet answered the invitation to the Lamb’s supper?

20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Where we are. The rider on the white horse has defeated the beast and the false prophet (19:11–21). Chapter 20 finishes the defeat of God’s enemies, the dragon behind them and then death itself, clearing the way for the new creation (chapters 21–22).

The message. Satan is a defeated enemy on God’s chain, unable to stop the gospel reaching the nations. Christ’s faithful people, even those the world killed, are alive and reigning with him. And everyone will stand before God’s throne, where one thing alone decides their destiny: a name written in the Lamb’s book of life.

Why it was said. The churches of Asia lived under a power that seemed to rule everything; believers had been killed (2:13), and others were tempted to compromise (see the introduction). Was the dragon winning? Had their martyrs died for nothing? Would the wrongs done to them ever be answered?

How the chapter makes its case. An angel binds the dragon so that he can no longer deceive the nations (vv. 1–3), as Jesus bound the strong man (Matthew 12:29). The souls of those killed or shut out for refusing the beast reign with Christ, beyond the reach of the second death (vv. 4–6). Released briefly at the end, Satan gathers the world against the saints, but fire from heaven ends it at once and the devil goes into the lake of fire (vv. 7–10). Then all the dead are judged by their deeds before a great white throne, the book of life decides, and Death and Hades are thrown into the lake (vv. 11–15).

Where Christians differ. This is the Bible’s only passage on a thousand-year reign, and Scripture-loving Christians read it in three main ways: premillennial, postmillennial and amillennial. This commentary follows the amillennial reading and sets out the others with respect in the note on vv. 1–3. All of them confess that Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked judged and the righteous glorified, and God will be all in all.

Where it leads. Read rightly, the chapter is a hymn to the Lamb. The serpent of Eden lies under the heel of the child he waited to devour (12:4; Genesis 3:15). The faithful reign because their King was condemned and vindicated first. And at the last throne nothing keeps a sinner out of the lake but a name in the book of the Lamb who was slain, who holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18) and throws death away.

For us. Do not fear the dragon: he is on a chain, and no one you pray for is beyond the gospel’s reach. Do not fear death: those who die in Christ go to reign with him. And do not try to make your record good enough for the last day; make sure, today, that you belong to the Lamb whose book decides.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Satan is a defeated enemy, and those who die faithful to Christ already reign with him. An angel binds the dragon so that he can no longer keep the nations from the gospel (vv. 1–3). Meanwhile John sees the souls of the faithful dead on thrones, alive and reigning with Christ, beyond the reach of the second death (vv. 4–6). At the end Satan is released for a little while and gathers the whole world against the camp of the saints, but fire from heaven ends it at once, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire for ever (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power; on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has bound Satan so that he can no longer keep the nations from hearing the gospel, until he releases him for a short time at the end. On the reading this commentary follows, the binding happened at Christ’s first coming, and the thousand years are the age we live in now.

An angel coming down from heaven. “Then I saw” marks the order of the visions, not necessarily the order of events. John has done this before: chapter 12 went back to Christ’s birth after the seventh trumpet had announced the end of the world.

The key and a great chain. The arrest is effortless: one angel, one key, one chain, and five verbs done to the dragon: seized, bound, threw, shut, sealed. The creature who deceived the whole world is handled by a single unnamed angel. A spirit cannot literally be chained; the key and chain picture authority and restraint, and say that Satan’s power is limited by God, whenever and however God pleases.

That ancient serpent. The four names are those of 12:9, in the same order: the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan. John reaches back to the serpent who spoke to Eve, and closes the file opened in Genesis 3. The Bible’s first villain is about to receive the Bible’s last sentence.

Bound him for a thousand years. “Bound” (edēsen) is the word Jesus used when he said that no one can plunder a strong man’s house “unless he first binds the strong man” (Matthew 12:29), explaining his casting out of demons as the sign that the kingdom of God had come. On the eve of the cross he said, “now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31; Hebrews 2:14). John shows from heaven’s side what Jesus did on earth. Millennium is simply Latin for a thousand years. In Revelation numbers are symbolic, and a thousand, ten times ten times ten, stands for a long and complete period whose length God alone sets.

Shut and sealed. “Sealed” (esphragisen) is the word used of the tomb of Jesus, when the authorities sealed the stone to keep a dead man in (Matthew 27:66). That seal failed, because the man inside was the Lord of life. This one holds, because the one who placed it is the same Lord.

So that he might not deceive the nations. This clause decides the whole chapter, because it gives the binding a stated purpose. Satan is not idle; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), tempts and persecutes. But he cannot stop the gospel going to the nations, or gather them for the final assault on the church until God permits. Since Christ, people from every nation have turned “from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God” (Acts 26:18): that is what a dragon prevented from deceiving the nations looks like.

A dog on a chain. A chained dog is still dangerous to anyone within reach, and Christians are told to resist Satan, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:9). But the dog cannot stop the house being plundered, or follow the plunderers down the road. Satan cannot keep the nations locked in his house while Christ carries his captives out of it, one by one, from every people on earth.

Released for a little while. “Must” (dei) is the word this book has used since 1:1 for what God has decided will happen: even the release comes only by his permission and for a limited time, a final outburst of deception and persecution at the end of history, before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

Three ways of reading the thousand years. The phrase occurs six times in six verses, and godly readers take it in three main ways, each with real support (the views are summed up in the box at the end of this note). The premillennial reading takes the chapter in the order it is written: Christ returns at the end of chapter 19 and reigns on the earth for a thousand years. In one form (George Eldon Ladd) the church goes through the tribulation; the dispensational form adds a rapture (a catching up of believers to meet the Lord) before a seven-year tribulation, and sees the millennium as the fulfilment of God’s promises to national Israel. Some of the earliest church fathers held a form of it. What favours it is considerable: the narrative flows on from chapter 19 with “Then I saw”; the Old Testament promises of a messianic kingdom on the earth, where the wolf dwells with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:20–25), are given a time and place; and, strongest of all, there is the verb in v. 5 (see the box at the end of the note on v. 4).

The postmillennial reading. Christ returns after a long era in which the gospel succeeds so widely that civilisation is Christianised. Jonathan Edwards held it. It is favoured by the steady growth in Jesus’ parables of the mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31–33), Psalm 72, the scope of the Great Commission, and the promise that Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), and its hope has fuelled great missionary labour. Its difficulty is the New Testament’s equally consistent expectation of apostasy and tribulation before the end (Matthew 24:9–13; 2 Timothy 3:1–5), and the final deception in this very chapter.

The amillennial reading. Amillennial means no separate earthly reign after Christ’s return: the thousand years are the present age, in which Satan is bound in exactly the sense verse 3 specifies and the saints reign with Christ in heaven, which is why verse 4 says John saw souls. This was the position of Augustine and the Reformers broadly, and this commentary follows it. Numbers in this book are symbolic throughout, and the chapter never mentions Christ’s physical presence on the earth. Its hardest point is the verb “came to life” in verses 4 and 5, and it should face that honestly (see the note on v. 4).

What all three agree on. Everything the historic creeds require: Christ has defeated Satan; he will return bodily and visibly; the dead will be raised and judged; the redeemed will live in a new creation; and the church’s duty now is faithfulness under pressure. The disagreement is about timing and sequence, and the right response to a brother who reads it differently is not suspicion but an open Bible and a warm handshake.

The stronger man. Behind the unnamed angel stands the one who did the binding, not by a show of force but by a death. Satan’s grip on the nations was our guilt and the accusation it gave him, and when Christ bore that guilt on the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). Every believer is plunder carried out of the strong man’s house.

In everyday life. The colleague who seems hardest, the neighbour who mocks, the relative who has refused for thirty years: none of them is beyond the reach of a gospel the dragon cannot block. So pray for them this week, and for the missionaries your church knows; the binding of the strong man is the reason those prayers are not in vain.

If Satan is bound, why does the world look so dark? Because the binding is specific, not total: the same book that binds the dragon has the beast making war on the saints. What has changed is that the gospel cannot be stopped. In John’s day the church was a few scattered congregations in one corner of the Roman Empire; today there are believers in nearly every nation, worshipping in thousands of languages. That did not happen with Satan free to keep the nations blind. So when the news is grim, read it inside this verse: darkness is real, but it is no longer in charge of who hears about Christ.

But does the rapture not come before all this? This commentary holds that there is no secret rapture. The New Testament knows one coming of Christ, and it is anything but secret: the Lord descends “with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and living believers are caught up to meet the King in public. Christians who hold a pre-tribulation rapture are brothers in Christ, and many of them love the Lord’s appearing more than we do. They rest on precious promises: God will keep his church from the hour of trial (3:10) and has not destined us for wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). But being kept from wrath is not being kept from trouble: the church is kept in it, not taken out of it (John 17:15). We watch for Christ’s coming every day; yet the New Testament also names things that come first: the gospel preached to all nations, a great falling away and the man of lawlessness (Matthew 24:14; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–4), and here the dragon’s brief release.

Does it matter which view I hold? It matters, but less than some arguments suggest. It shapes how you read all of Revelation, and whether you expect the world to get better, worse or both. But it need not divide Christians: you can sit under a pastor who reads it differently and sing the same hymns about the coming King. What you must not do is let a prophecy chart take the place of Christ himself. All three views wait for the same person.

Where Christians differ: what is the thousand years? Premillennialists, including dispensationalists, hold that Christ returns before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth, ruling from Jerusalem while Satan is bound, after which Satan is released and defeated and the final judgment follows. Postmillennialists hold that the gospel will gradually triumph, bringing a long golden age of Christian influence, after (post-) which Christ returns. Amillennialists hold that the thousand years symbolise the present age between Christ’s two comings, with Satan bound, the faithful dead reigning with Christ in heaven, and no separate earthly millennium after his return. This commentary’s view: the amillennial view fits Revelation best. The book repeatedly goes back over the same period in parallel visions, and chapter 20 does so again. The binding of Satan is what Jesus and the apostles say happened at the cross, and the reign is with Christ, who already reigns from heaven. The final battle of 20:7–10 is the same as 16:14–16 and 19:19–21, all drawn from Ezekiel 38–39 and told in almost the same words. And the rest of the New Testament teaches one return of Christ, bringing the resurrection of righteous and wicked together (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), the final judgment and the new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13), with no thousand-year interval. Premillennial and postmillennial believers are brothers and sisters in Christ, and Christians may charitably differ here; but the amillennial reading is the most faithful to the text.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers whom the world condemned and killed are alive with Christ and reigning with him now. John sees the faithful dead not in the grave but on thrones.

Thrones. Plural, and John does not at once say who is on them. Daniel saw that “thrones were placed” and “judgment was given for the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:9, 22); Jesus promised the one who conquers a seat on his throne (3:21); Paul says “the saints will judge the world” (1 Corinthians 6:2). Here those promises are kept. Earthly courts condemned these people; now God has ruled in their favour and seated them with the Judge (on “authority to judge”, see the box at the end of this note).

The souls of those who had been beheaded. “Souls” (psychas) is the word of 6:9, the souls under the altar: believers who have died, now alive in God’s presence. Beheading with the sword was how Rome executed its citizens, and tradition says Paul died this way. John names how they died because he wants us to see the cost.

Those who had not worshiped the beast. Probably the same company seen from another side (see the box below), all who conquered the beast (15:2), so that the reign belongs not only to the martyrs but to everyone who would not take the mark. Chapter 13 said that no one could buy or sell without the mark. These people could not buy or sell, and here they are on thrones.

They came to life and reigned. They lived, or came to life (ezēsan): everything turns on that verb. On the reading this commentary follows, it is not their bodily resurrection, which comes at the end (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52), but their entry into life with Christ when they died. Their bodies were killed, yet they live and reign with him, for “he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him” (Luke 20:38; John 11:25–26). They share his rule from heaven, where he reigns now (Ephesians 1:20–22), and the martyrs who cried “how long” under the altar (6:9–11) are seen on thrones.

The verdict reversed. Whatever a reader concludes about the verb, the purpose of the verse is not in dispute. Not one of those reigning held any office. They were beheaded, shut out of the market and tried in courts that found against them, and John sees them on thrones, beside the King who was himself condemned by a Roman court and hung outside the city. He was the first to have the world’s verdict reversed, on the third day, and every one of his people shares his vindication. Death did not defeat them; it delivered them to him.

What happens to a Christian the moment he dies? He goes at once to be with Christ, conscious, at rest and full of joy. Paul calls it “far better” (Philippians 1:23): to be “away from the body” is to be “at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). The thief on the cross was told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). There is no purgatory to pay off what Christ left unpaid, and no sleep of the soul until the last day: John sees souls alive and reigning. The body rests in the grave until the resurrection; the person is with the Lord (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). So Christians grieve at a graveside, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Do my loved ones in heaven see me, and should I talk to them? Scripture does not say what the departed see of earth, and it is wise not to build on guesses. It does say that they are with Christ and reigning with him, and that is enough. We should not pray to them or seek to speak with them; the Bible forbids consulting the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the one mediator between God and men is Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Speak to the Lord about them, thank him for them, and look forward to the morning when you will see them again in a body that cannot die.

Where Christians differ: is this a bodily resurrection to rule on earth? Premillennialists read “came to life” as a bodily resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, followed by a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Their argument from verse 5 is the strongest single argument in the debate: the identical verb is used one sentence later of the rest of the dead, whose coming to life is undisputedly bodily. Some amillennial readers take it of the new birth, for God “made us alive together with Christ” and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:5–6), and Jesus said the hour “is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25). This commentary’s view: John sees souls, not bodies, on thrones, which in Revelation, apart from Satan’s and the beast’s, are in heaven: this is the heavenly reign of believers who have died, during the present age. The verb simply means lived or came to life; it is used of the beast who was wounded by the sword and yet lived (13:14), and of Christ who was dead and is alive (1:18; 2:8), so the word alone does not settle whether a bodily resurrection is meant, and “souls” points to life after death. The parallel with v. 5 remains the strongest point on the premillennial side. The bodily resurrection of all believers comes at Christ’s single return at the end (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Either way, the comfort for persecuted believers stands: those who die for Christ are not defeated; they reign with him.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are compressed in the Greek. “Those to whom the authority to judge was committed” is literally “judgment was given to them” (krima edothē autois): either they were given authority to judge, or judgment was given in their favour, as in Daniel 7:22; John may mean both. And the grammar allows “those who had not worshiped the beast” to be a second group beside the beheaded, or the same company described again.
