The likely meaning is one company, all who refused the beast, with the martyrs as its sharpest example.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who share in the first resurrection are blessed: the second death can never touch them, and they will serve and reign with Christ. The rest of the dead come to life only at the end, to be judged.

The rest of the dead. Unbelievers, who come to life only to be judged, at the end (vv. 12–13). On the premillennial reading the parallel with v. 4 is decisive (see the box at the end of the note on v. 4). On the amillennial reading John distinguishes the two by calling only one the first resurrection, and by saying plainly that the other comes only when the thousand years are ended.

The first resurrection. The phrase occurs only here. Whoever believes “has passed from death to life” (John 5:24) and has been raised with Christ and seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1). On the reading this commentary follows, as there is a first death (physical) and a second (eternal), so there is a first resurrection (spiritual: life with Christ, begun at new birth and carried into his presence at death) and a second (bodily, at his return), when “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29). Believers share both resurrections and only the first death; unbelievers share both deaths and only the second resurrection, to judgment.

First and second of different kinds. John’s own language helps. The second death (vv. 6, 14) is plainly not a death of the same kind as the first: the first is a body in a grave, the second a lake of fire. If “second death” can name something of a different kind from the first death, then “first resurrection” may name something of a different kind from the second. That is the amillennial answer, and it is a real one.

Blessed and holy. The fifth of the book’s seven beatitudes, and the only one with a second adjective: holy (hagios), set apart, belonging to God. Three great promises follow.

The second death has no power. Not that they will probably escape it: it has no authority (exousia) over them, no right to bring a case against them. The second death is the lake of fire (v. 14), and Smyrna was promised the same: “The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death” (2:11). A Christian may be unsure about the timing of the millennium, but not about this. The reason is not their record but their names, written in the book of a Lamb who was slain. He went under the judgment in their place: he died the death that was theirs, rose with the life that is his, and shares that life with every one of them from the day he calls them out of the grave of sin.

Priests of God and of Christ. The kingdom of priests promised in 1:6 and 5:10 is here in place: people with access, who offer worship and carry others’ names into the presence of God. And they are priests “of God and of Christ”: Christ receives the same priestly service as God.

They will reign with him. With him, which keeps the reign from being a fantasy of revenge: its substance is being where he is and doing what he does. Priest and king together is what Israel was promised at Sinai, “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6), and never managed. Only one person holds both offices fully, the King of kings who is the Lamb who was slain, and his people share both because they are with him.

How do I know I share in the first resurrection? If you have been born again, you have. The first resurrection begins when the Spirit makes a dead heart alive and joins it to the risen Christ, and it shows in its fruit: you trust Christ for your salvation and not your record, you love him and want to obey him, you hate the sin you once enjoyed, and you love his people (1 John 3:14). None of that is perfect in anyone, and the fight against a sin you still fall into is itself the Spirit’s work (Romans 7:22–25; Galatians 5:17). None of it grows in a dead soul. If those things are in you, however weakly, the second death has no claim on you, and Christ will not lose you (John 10:28).

Does reigning with Christ start only after I die? In its full form, yes; but it has already begun. God “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6). A believer on earth already shares Christ’s victory: sin no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:14), he may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), and his prayers are part of how Christ rules the world (8:3–5). So reign now, by saying no to sin and yes to God, and by praying as one who has the King’s ear.

Where Christians differ: are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart? Premillennialists read the first resurrection as a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, and the second as a bodily resurrection of unbelievers after it. This commentary’s view: the rest of the New Testament teaches one bodily resurrection of righteous and unrighteous together, on the last day (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Daniel 12:2). Jesus says he will raise up believers “on the last day” (John 6:39–40, 44, 54), which leaves no room for a thousand years after their resurrection. The first resurrection is the believer’s sharing in Christ’s resurrection life, beginning at new birth and carried into heaven at death, while the body awaits the last day.

Textual note. One important early manuscript (Codex Sinaiticus) and some others omit the first sentence, “The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended”. Most manuscripts include it, and it is probably original.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of the age God will let Satan loose for a short time, and he will gather the whole world against God’s people. Even this last rebellion happens only by God’s permission.

Satan will be released. He does not break out; he is let out, and the verb is passive again. This is the final, brief time of deception and persecution that Jesus and Paul also foretold (Matthew 24:21–24; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

To deceive the nations. Released, he goes straight back to the work the chain had stopped, as the deceiver of the whole world (12:9). After a thousand years in a sealed pit, the first thing he does is start talking. Evil in this book never learns or changes; it only repeats itself with a larger audience. “Four corners”: the whole world.

Gog and Magog. In Ezekiel 38–39, Gog of the land of Magog, a ruler and his land, leads a vast coalition from the far north against God’s restored people, and God destroys them with fire and sulphur (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6). In Jewish tradition the names came to stand for the final enemies of God’s people, and here both name the nations. As with Babylon, and Sodom and Egypt in chapter 11, the name stands for a kind of enemy, not a place on a map: not a country but the last coalition of everything opposed to God.

To gather them for battle. “The battle”, with the definite article: the battle already described in 16:14 and 19:19, in nearly identical words, seen one last time from another angle.

Like the sand of the sea. Countless, and the phrase echoes God’s promise to Abraham: “I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore” (Genesis 22:17). The dragon’s last act is what he has done at every stage: he copies God’s work. He had a mark to match God’s seal, a prostitute to match the Bride, and now a countless host to match the countless family promised to a childless old man outside his tent at night.

The true offspring of Abraham. The promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, singular, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16); and “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). The multitude no one could number in chapter 7 is that promise kept. Two uncountable crowds end the book, and what divides them is not size but a person: one gathered by the deceiver for war, the other by the Son, through faith, for a city.

Why would God let Satan out at all? Scripture does not give every reason, but it gives enough. The release shows that the human heart, left to itself, does not become good with time or better surroundings: after a whole age of the gospel, the nations still gather against God the moment the deceiver speaks. It brings hidden rebellion into the open, so that all see the judgment is just. And it shows the church, one last time, that her safety never rested on Satan being chained but on God himself. A God who can chain the dragon with one angel loses nothing by letting him go for a little while.

How should I read prophecy headlines? With a calm mind and an open Bible. Every generation has had preachers who named the nation of Gog, the beast and the year of the end; all have been wrong, making the church look foolish and leaving believers frightened or cynical. No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). What we know is enough: opposition to God will gather worldwide, and Christ will destroy it at his coming. So watch the news without fear, pray for persecuted believers, and be found faithful whenever he comes.

Where Christians differ: is Gog and Magog a specific nation, such as Russia? Some popular prophecy teachers identified Gog and Magog with Russia, linking Rosh (Ezekiel 38:2, in some translations) with Russia and Meshech with Moscow. This commentary’s view: those connections rest on sound-alike words, not on language or history; Rosh is a Hebrew word meaning chief, and Meshech and Tubal were peoples in what is now Turkey. In Revelation, Gog and Magog are explicitly the nations at the four corners of the earth: not one nation but the whole world in rebellion. The point is not geography but the final, worldwide assault on God’s people, and its sure defeat.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final attack on God’s people ends the moment it begins: fire from heaven destroys the attackers, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire for ever. The saints do not lift a hand; God fights for them.

Over the broad plain of the earth. Literally the breadth of the earth: not a march on one valley but a tide covering every land.

The camp of the saints and the beloved city. Two images for the people of God. “The camp” is Israel in the wilderness, tribe by tribe around the tabernacle (Numbers 2): tents, no walls, defended by nothing but the presence of God in the middle. “The beloved city” is Zion, for “the LORD loves the gates of Zion” (Psalm 87:2), here the church: a camp still on the journey, and a city already at home with God. And it is encircled on every side, a hopeless military position.

Fire came down from heaven. That is the whole battle: one clause, as in chapter 19. Fire fell on Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and at Elijah’s word (2 Kings 1:10–12), and Ezekiel foresaw it on Gog (Ezekiel 38:22). This is Christ’s return, “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire” (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). It is the very thing James and John once wanted to call down on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is real, and it is not the church’s to call.

No fire fell. Once before, the beloved of God was surrounded. The Son of God hung outside Jerusalem with enemies on every side, the bulls and dogs of his own psalm closing in (Psalm 22:12–16), and no fire fell, though twelve legions of angels were his for the asking (Matthew 26:53). He let the enemy close over him so that the camp of his people would never fall. That is why the saints at the end stand empty-handed and unafraid: their Saviour has already borne their judgment. The God who loves the gates of Zion has never yet lost a single tent in the camp.

The devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake. The beast and false prophet were thrown there in 19:20, at the same final event; now their master joins them. His epitaph is what he did: not the great red dragon with seven diadems, but simply the one who told lies, and he “was thrown” into the lake by someone the verse does not even name.

Tormented day and night forever and ever. The torment is conscious and endless: the lake is not pictured as a furnace that burns things up in a moment. The serpent that spoke in a garden has said his last word. Cast out at the cross, bound, released for a little while, he is now finished, and the head that was promised to be crushed (Genesis 3:15) is under the heel of the child the dragon once stood waiting to devour (12:4). And the bruise on Christ’s own heel, his death on the cross, is the wound that saved us.

In everyday life. When you feel surrounded, by illness, by opposition, by a family that mocks your faith, you are standing where the saints stand in this verse. You are not asked to break out by your own strength, but to stay in the camp, near the presence, and trust.

Is this the same battle as 19:19–21? Most likely, yes. Both draw on Ezekiel 38–39, both gather the nations for the battle with the definite article, and both end at once with God’s judgment, without any fighting. Premillennial Christians see two battles a thousand years apart. But John has already shown the end of history several times, at the sixth seal, the seventh trumpet and the seventh bowl, and this is one more view of the same day: not a literal siege of Jerusalem but the world’s final assault on God’s people wherever they are.

How can the lake of fire last for ever if God is loving? A real question deserves a real answer. First, sin is not a small thing made large; it is rebellion against an infinitely holy and good God, and its seriousness is measured by the one sinned against. Second, Scripture never pictures anyone in the lake becoming sorry there; the impenitent in this book go on refusing God even under judgment (16:9, 11). Third, the punishment is just, according to what each has done, and no one suffers beyond what he deserves. Fourth, the clearest proof that God is loving is not that hell is empty but that his own Son went to the cross to bear it for sinners; the Jesus who spoke most about hell wept over Jerusalem and prayed for his executioners. And what decides who goes there is the book of life (20:15): the only way to be outside that lake is to belong to the Lamb, who still welcomes everyone who comes (22:17).

Where Christians differ: is the punishment of the lost, as well as the devil’s, conscious and unending? Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, the torment being only for the devil and his agents. They point to Scripture’s words destroy and perish (Matthew 10:28; 2 Thessalonians 1:9) and to pictures of chaff burned up, and are often moved by real compassion; they remain brothers and sisters who trust the same Saviour, and the question between us is how to read those words, not whether Christ saves. This commentary’s view: the punishment of the lost, like the devil’s, is conscious and without end. “Forever and ever” is the New Testament’s strongest phrase for duration, used of God’s own life (4:9–10) and of the saints’ reign (22:5). The lost share the same lake (v. 15; 14:10–11), “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41), and Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in one sentence (Matthew 25:46): if one is endless, so is the other. This commentary holds it with grief, not with satisfaction.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fire came down from God out of heaven”. The meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every person will stand before God, and only a name in the Lamb’s book will save. Earth and sky flee from the great white throne, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what the books record of their deeds (vv. 11–12). No one is missing: the sea, Death and Hades give up every one of them. Then Death and Hades are themselves thrown into the lake of fire, and so is anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book, and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every person who has ever lived will stand before God’s throne and be judged by what they have done, but it is the book of life that decides who is saved.

A great white throne. The last of the book’s thrones. Great: its size settles who is in charge. White: in this book the colour of purity, holiness and verdicts. The one seated on it is God, who judges the world through Christ (Acts 17:31; Romans 2:16), for the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22); Father and Son share one throne (22:1, 3). John does not describe him; he says what happens in his presence.

Earth and sky fled away. Nothing is said to be destroyed; the universe simply cannot remain in the room. The ground and the sky, the very picture of permanence, get up and leave (2 Peter 3:10), and the last judgment has no scenery: only a throne, the one seated on it, and the people standing. Their flight also clears the ground for a new heaven and a new earth, “for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away” (21:1). Judgment is the doorway into the new creation.

The dead, great and small. All humanity, raised for judgment. “Great and small” flattens the last hierarchy: emperors and slaves, the men whose statues filled the forum and the women whose names were never written down, on the same floor. No one is too important to be judged or too insignificant to be overlooked.

Books were opened. As in Daniel’s vision, “the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:10). Books, plural, and then a book, singular, and the distinction is the gospel. The books record every person’s deeds. God knows all that people have done, said and thought (Ecclesiastes 12:14), and “on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak” (Matthew 12:36).

The book of life. The Lamb’s book (13:8; 21:27), holding the names of those chosen before the foundation of the world (17:8). The books show what each person deserves; the book of life shows who belongs to the Lamb. It is not a second, better record of the same kind but a register of names, and verse 15 says it decides. Earth and sky cannot stay in the presence of the One on the throne, yet a sinner washed in the blood of the Lamb can stand there unafraid, because the Judge of all the earth has already judged his sins, in the body of his Son, on a hill outside Jerusalem. His throne is white with holiness, and his book is written with mercy.

According to what they had done. The judgment is perfectly just, based on the evidence. How then can judgment be by works if salvation is by grace? The New Testament holds both: nobody is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). They answer different questions. The books of deeds establish the case, and everyone standing there is guilty on the record. The book of life asks not what did you do, but whose are you. That cuts both ways. The moralist who hopes his file is good enough will find that it is not, and the sceptic who assumes there is no file will find that there is. Both are offered the same thing, and neither earns it: a name written by grace in the Lamb’s book.

When the universe leaves the room. Carl Sagan opened his television series Cosmos with a sentence that became a creed for many: “The Cosmos is all that is or ever was or ever will be.” If matter is what lasts and persons are passing arrangements of it, there is nobody to answer to, and in the end nothing is answered at all. John’s vision turns that round. The universe, the thing we took for bedrock, is what cannot stay; the persons, great and small, are left standing. That is sobering, because our lives will be weighed. It is also the ground of real hope: if the cosmos were all there is, every injustice would simply be lost as the stars cool. Because a Person sits on the throne, nothing is lost, and that same Person has made a way for the guilty to stand before him unafraid.

What it does not mean. The books of deeds do not mean that believers will be shamed by a public display of their forgiven sins. Their sins are removed “as far as the east is from the west” (Psalm 103:12) and blotted out (Isaiah 43:25), and they stand clothed in Christ’s righteousness.

In everyday life. Nothing done for Christ in secret is wasted; it is all in the books, and the Lord who reads them is generous. Nothing done against your neighbour in secret is hidden either. No Christian’s file is clean, not even its best pages; but for those in Christ the worst of it has been answered at the cross, and his perfect obedience is counted in its place. So put right this week, without dread, whatever you would not want read aloud.

Do believers stand before this throne? All the dead stand there, great and small. For believers the book of life decides: their names are written, they are acquitted in Christ, and their works are reviewed for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10). Premillennial Christians often distinguish a judgment of believers from this one, a thousand years earlier; the more likely reading is one final judgment, where the book of life separates the saved from the lost, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats in a single scene (Matthew 25:31–46).

Should a Christian be afraid of this day? Serious, yes; terrified, no. A believer should feel its weight: every word and deed is known to the Lord who will review it. But fear of condemnation is not for those in Christ. The Judge on that throne is the Saviour who died for you, and he will not condemn the people he bought. We may “have confidence for the day of judgment”, because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:17–18). If you dread the throne, do not try to make your file look better. Go to Christ again, today, and rest in what he has done.

Can my name be removed from the book of life? No, if it is truly there. And if you fear that yours is not, that fear is itself a reason to come to Christ now, for “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The names were written before the foundation of the world (17:8), by God who does not change his mind, and the Lord Jesus promised the one who conquers, “I will never blot his name out of the book of life” (3:5). It is the Lamb’s book because it lists the people he bought with his own blood, and he does not lose what he has paid for (John 6:39). The warnings of Scripture are real, and God uses them to keep his people trusting; but a believer’s name is not written in pencil.

Where Christians differ: if judgment is by works, how is salvation by grace? Some take judgment according to works to mean that final salvation depends on our works. Others think that believers are not judged at all. This commentary’s view: everyone is judged according to works, because works reveal what is in the heart. Unbelievers’ works condemn them, because all have sinned (Romans 3:23). Believers’ names are in the book of life; they are saved by grace through faith alone, because Christ has borne their condemnation (Romans 8:1; John 5:24), and their works are the evidence of their faith and the basis of their rewards (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). No one is saved by works; but no one is saved without the works that true faith produces (James 2:14–26). The book of life is what finally decides (v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one will be missing from the judgment, and death itself will be destroyed; only those whose names are written in the book of life escape the lake of fire.

The sea gave up the dead. Three keepers of the dead each hand over what they held. The sea is named separately because to be lost at sea was to have no grave, no body, no name on a stone, the most complete disappearance there was. No one is lost.

Death and Hades gave up the dead. Personified, as in 6:8. This is the general resurrection, and it reaches every forgotten person: the woman in an unmarked grave, the child in a plague pit, the soldier whose body was never found. And “each one of them” is judged: not a mass, but one at a time, by name.

Death and Hades were thrown into the lake. These are the two riders of the fourth seal (6:8): Death, and Hades (the realm of the dead) following him. The risen Christ said, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18), and this is what he does with them. God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8); “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Death is not going to be managed, or explained, or made bearable. It is going to be killed (21:4). To throw death into a lake means that dying itself will never happen again: no illness will end in a funeral, and no one will be parted from someone he loves. Everything a reader has lost to it, the diagnosis that came back, the phone call at four in the morning, was inflicted by something that is not coming back.

This is the second death. John defines his own term, here and at 21:8, after using it without definition at 2:11 and 20:6. The first death separates soul from body; the second is the final, eternal punishment of the whole person, body and soul, cut off from all God’s goodness and under his wrath.

Not found written in the book of life. The chapter’s last sentence is put negatively: the book is searched, and a name is not found. This is the decisive question. Not whether good deeds outweigh bad, not sincerity, not how a person compares with his neighbour: a name, in a book, belonging to the Lamb.

The last enemy dies. Death and Hades hand over every name they ever took, and then are thrown away like broken tools. The Lord Jesus once lay in a borrowed grave, in the grip of the very enemy he now destroys, and came out of it as the firstborn of the dead (1:5); every grave that opens on the last day opens because his did. And when the other books are closed, one book remains, written before the world was made, a list of people bought with his blood, and nothing in all the other books can get a name off it. The last enemy dies, and the Lamb lives for ever.

The question it leaves. This is either a most frightening sentence or a most reassuring one, depending on a single question. It is not, have I done enough? Nobody standing at that throne has. It is whether a person has come to the one who says, two chapters later, “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (22:17).

In everyday life. At the next funeral of a believer you attend, remember the end of this chapter: the grave you are standing beside is going to give back what it holds, and the thing that dug it is going into the lake.

Is the lake of fire literal fire? The fire is a picture, but what it pictures is worse, not milder. Scripture describes hell as fire and also as outer darkness (Matthew 25:30), which cannot both be literal in the ordinary sense; both point to something real: conscious, unending suffering under God’s just anger, cut off from every good thing he gives, light, love, rest, friendship, hope. No one should take comfort from the language being symbolic. The symbols of heaven in the next chapters are not less than gold and pearls; they are more. The same is true here.

What about babies, and people who never heard? Infants who die in infancy are in the hands of a merciful God; the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3), and many Reformed pastors, Spurgeon among them, have believed that every child who dies in infancy is among the elect. Many parents have rested on David’s words about his dead child: “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23). If you have lost a child, you may grieve with hope, and leave that little one with a God who is kinder than all our fears. Adults who never heard will be judged justly by the light they had, condemned not for rejecting a gospel they never heard but for the sins they knowingly committed (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That does not make them safe; it makes the missionary task urgent. The answer to the question is not speculation but sending.

What about someone I love who died without Christ? This is one of the heaviest griefs a Christian carries, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend. Three things are true. You do not know everything that passed between that soul and God in the last hours; the thief was saved on a cross, so do not pronounce what you cannot see. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25); on the last day no one, including you, will think him unjust. And your grief is not a lack of faith; Paul had “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his own people (Romans 9:2). Bring it to the Lord, who wept at a grave, and let it drive you to pray for the living.

Where Christians differ: is anyone saved apart from faith in Christ? Inclusivists hold that some may be saved through Christ’s work without consciously knowing or believing in him, by responding to the light they have; they are usually moved by concern for those who never heard, and they too confess Christ as the only Saviour. Pluralists hold that many religions lead to God. This commentary’s view: the book of life is the Lamb’s book (21:27), and “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). The saved are those who hold the testimony of Jesus and are washed in his blood (7:14; 12:11), which is why the church must take the gospel to every nation, tribe and language (14:6; Romans 10:13–15). God will judge every person justly, according to the light they had (Romans 2:12–16), and no one will be condemned unfairly; but salvation is through Christ alone, received by faith.

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain.<sup>2</sup>And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,<sup>3</sup>and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.<sup>4</sup>Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.<sup>5</sup>The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection.<sup>6</sup>Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.<sup>7</sup>And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison<sup>8</sup>and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.<sup>9</sup>And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them,<sup>10</sup>and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.<sup>12</sup>And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.<sup>13</sup>And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done.<sup>14</sup>Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.<sup>15</sup>And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
keyVerse.note: Whatever a reader concludes about the timing of the thousand years, this verse is beyond dispute, and it joins the chapter’s two halves: the reign of the saints and the lake of fire. It tells everyone who belongs to Christ that the second death has no claim on them, because the Lamb has died it in their place, and that their future is to serve and reign with him.

20.reflection:
Verses 1–3 picture Satan bound so that he can no longer deceive the nations, yet he still prowls and tempts (1 Peter 5:8). How does this change the way you read the news, and the way you pray for people who seem far from God?

Verse 4 shows people the world beheaded and shut out of the market seated on thrones. Where are you tempted to measure faithfulness by success or safety, and what does this vision say to believers who are losing out for Christ today?

Christians read the thousand years in different ways (vv. 1–6). What do all the views share, and how can we hold our convictions on this chapter firmly and still keep warm fellowship with those who read it differently?

At the great white throne the books record what everyone has done, but the book of life decides (vv. 12–15). Why is it such good news that the final question is “whose are you?” and not “have you done enough?”, and who in your life needs to hear it?
